text: ------------------------- Part 1: The science of scale ------------------------- Railroads, radio, electricity, telephones, internet, cloud-based services - all technologies that were found fit for scale. All had 4 layers: 1. Compute 2. Storage 2. Network 3. Application These layers form a stack that is imposed on every technology that requires scale. It will be the same with AI. The compute and storage layers are responsible for creating the signal that is transmitted through the network layer to applications. You can call these layers the "heart" of the AI stack. The Network layer then transmits the result of the work performed in the "heart" to the applications that use it. Notice that abstraction, segregation, and communication play a critical part here in the interface between layers: 1. The network does not care what it transfers as long as applications need it. 2. Applications do not care how the network layer is implemented as long as it brings them what they need. This way, stack components can be isolated and upgraded without forcing the entire system to stop. That said, while applications can be developed by independent entities that conform to the interface the network exposes to them, the layers above do not have this luxury, as they are responsible for creating a shared interface that is expected to be backward-compatible. For this reason, the layers above the application layer need to be constructed (and maintained) by large, often interdependent entities to create a coherent standard of work across layers, enabling the system to offer a robust, scalable, and predictable service to the application layer. Thus: 1. To scale a system, one must implement the 4 layers mentioned above. 2. The most important part in each implementation is the separation and communication between its components and components that implement other layers. A system must be coupled enough to provide a robust service but decoupled enough to maintain and upgrade it. Now, as we continue to examine how the layers above take shape in the AI stack, a note about nomenclature: 1. The layers above are theoretical concepts. 2. When these layers are concretized into specific structures that exist in practice, I call these concretizations implementations. I use "layers" and "layer implementations" interchangeably, but the distinction above applies. ------------------------- Part 2: Scaling AI ------------------------- The current phase we are in in the scale of AI is the construction of AI data centers - these form a very clunky implementation for the compute and storage layer of the AI stack because it is there where "AI" is created - the AI "Heart" - and it creates AI Tokens. The implementation has been insanely expensive and clunky, but if we can build (or implement) a suitable network layer and an application layer downstream to it, these upstream implementations can be upgraded later without interfering with the entire system. So we need an application layer and a network layer. To better understand where the network needs to be, we need to understand where the target applications are, and to better understand where the target applications are, we need to examine what AI offers. AI technology offers inference. For this reason, target applications will be those that require inference most. In other words, the products that form (implement) the application layer in the AI stack are inference-based applications. Inference can help in places where certainty is not easily predictable, and such a place is, in all honesty, the physical world, and pretty much everywhere in it. So the primary applications of AI technology are physical applications or devices interacting with the real world. In other words, inference-based physical applications operating across all environments will be the largest component of the commercial layer of the AI stack. This means that whatever network layer we build (or implement) needs to service AI tokens to these physical applications. How can you build a network that can service physical applications pretty much everywhere? The same way you did with railroads, radio, electricity, telephones, and the internet - you build bridges pretty much everywhere. Which leads me to the following conclusion: The biggest capex of the AI stack is still ahead - networks. ------------------------- Part 3: AI Network ------------------------- AI network buildouts will be carried out by network hyperscalers. Who can be hyperscalers in networking? Well - let's examine the "OG" Hyperscalers that are currently building AI data centers: 1. They had large cash reserves. 2. Most of the compute in the world happened in their facilities, and most of the storage of the world was used and offered by them. So, we can refer to these "OG" Hyperscalers as Compute Hyperscalers. Candidates for Network hyperscalers thus need to fit the following criteria: 1. They need to have large cash reserves. 2. They need to be able to build and manage a lot of networks. In the West, you only have 3 candidates, the telecom operators: 1. AT&T ($T) 2. Verizon ($VZ) 3. T-Mobile ($TMUS) Like the "OG" Compute Hyperscalers, once one starts upgrading its networks, all will join, creating the Network Hyperscalers. Why will these companies choose to spend so much on network capex? Well, lots of money, and they have no choice: 1. The Compute Hyperscalers can squeeze these telecom giants by directing AI token traffic through existing networks, thereby congesting them and rendering them unusable, forcing the telecom giants to upgrade. 2. If they don't offer the most relevant networks, they will become irrelevant. ------------------------- Part 4: Investment Opportunities ------------------------- Network Hyperscalers will need to build networks capable of handling large volumes of AI tokens. Who is currently building such systems? Whichever company it might be, it needs to act as if it anticipates very high demand for its products, and it also needs the capabilities to build a networking product capable of transmitting AI tokens. What does a company that anticipates a very high demand for its products do? 1. It tries to control as much of the production stack as possible to ensure continued, sustained production. There is a trade-off here between owning and maintaining more business components and achieving more control over product output, but if they know an insane demand is coming, they might be ready to move towards such supply chain and production consolidation. 2. Insiders in the company will probably buy the company stock like crazy. How can you transmit a lot of AI tokens? What do you need? 1. Experience with networks. 2. Experience with contemporary themes in network technology, especially optics and photonics. 3. Connection to a company that knows a thing or two about AI. A company that checks the above is $NOK , which has a deep connection with $NVDA . It is noteworthy that Nvidia invested in Nokia at the same time it invested in other interesting names in photonics, optics, and connectivity, which are all crucial for networking: 1. $LITE 2. $COHR 3. $MRVL Nokia is not the only potential beneficiary of a large AI Network capex. Besides the Network Hyperscalers, you also have more companies throughout the network supply chain: 1. $ERIC 2. $CSCO 3. $SPCX - The infrastructure AI network will require is determined by applications. Applications will not exist only on the ground or on earth. 4. Photonics, optics, and connectivity companies. This also includes upstream companies that deal with raw elements (refiners), substrates, and processing. I am sure I am missing many more companies. I suggest following @PhotonCap and @crux_capital_ for more. Funny story: $INTC saw the opportunity in photonics and optics for networking back in the dot-com era. In 1999, Intel spent $3.4B buying Level One Communications and Giga A/S. In 2006, these companies were sold for $115M to Cortina Systems. In 2014, Inphi Corp spent $131M to acquire Cortina's High-Speed Assets (including the optical divisions purchased from Intel). In April 2021, Marvell spent $8.2B to acquire Inphi. Small world, but the themes repeat - not just in connectivity, but also in railroads, radio, electricity, telephones, the internet - and now AI. By the way, I also believe the bubble will pop at the end, and it will be devastating, but we are not there yet.

Unlike past infrastructure cycles, where telecom investments were monetized over decades, AI's CapEx cycle is far more compressed. Capital deployment and revenue growth must stay closely aligned. Investors will not fund hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure indefinitely unless software revenue scales fast enough to justify it. 4. Situational Awareness: Absolutely Right on Trend, Absolutely Wrong on Portfolio Construction Being directionally right about AI does not protect you from poor portfolio construction. In the Long Term, Average Intelligence Will Be Free—and It Will Keep Getting Smarter As baseline models rapidly improve and commoditize, average intelligence will become abundant and nearly free. text: 1 in 7 homes up for sale across U.S. are in FL Liz Piedra, broker/owner of Horizon Palm Realty Group in Hernando County near Tampa says the housing market in her area, which includes Pasco and Citrus counties, has slowed from the 2021-22 COVID boom. State expert: Accurate, but not reason to panic Clayton Park USA TODAY NETWORK Florida now accounts for one in seven of all homes for sale in America even though the Sunshine State only has 8% of the nation’s housing stock, a new national report has found. “The Florida for-sale market is flashing warning signs,” wrote Jason Lewris in a post on the social media platform X about the findings of his company’s “Motivated Seller Index” report. Lewris is chief data officer and co-founder of Parcl Labs, a New Yorkbased housing data analytics firm. Lewris While Florida does in fact account for 14% of all homes on the market nationally, Lewris’s analysis lacks crucial context, said Brad O’Connor, chief economist for the statewide Florida Realtors association. Florida’s share is actually down from nearly 16% the two previous years. “The problem is the conclusion being drawn,” O’Connor told USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA of the Parcl Labs report. “Stripped of historical context, they can be read as a (Florida housing) market in decline — but the year-overyear trend tells the opposite story: inventory share and price cuts are both down from a year ago, which points to a market that’s stabilizing, not deteriorating.” Florida leading the nation in homes for sale is nothing new A look at Florida Realtors data dating back to 2013 shows the state’s share of all active and pending inventory of homes for sale nationally (in- cluding townhouses and condominium units) has consistently been 10% or higher even during the red-hot COVID housing boom in 2020, 2021 and 2022 when Florida experienced an unusually large surge of newcomers. That surge fueled dramatic increases in both home sales and median sale prices. Since 2023, home sales have slowed as has the rate of price increases. A home for sale in Hernando County's Spring Hill community on July 7. The asking price is $499,000. CLAYTON PARK/USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA Florida perennially accounts for a large percentage of the nation’s inventory of available homes because it has long been seen as a major retirement and vacation destination, according to Professor Ken Johnson, chair of real estate at the University of Mississippi. Of Florida’s approximately 10.8 million housing units, “1.1 million to 1.3 million are actually second homes,” said Johnson, who studies housing markets across the country and previously taught at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton. Given that context, “The supply of homes on the market in Florida compared to demand seems to be relatively balanced,” he said of the state’s current 14% share of the nation’s available housing inventory. The fact that Florida has an unusually large number of second homes also means it is quite likely some of the properties on the market are listed by owners who may be interested in selling, but are not motivated to do so if they can’t get the price they want, Johnson added. Said O’Connor: “The key thing here is that this share (of the nation’s homes for sale) is receding because inventory has largely leveled off in Florida, despite all these (social media) posts trying to make it look like Florida inventory is still expanding like it was two years ago.” What is median price for a single-family home in Florida? Lewris in his post on X wrote that his company’s Motivated Seller Index report found “45% of listings (in Florida) have taken a price cut,” noting that the percentage was 6.6 points above the national rate. He added that “1 in 10 homes are selling for less than the original owner paid.” On the first claim, O’Connor said Florida Realtors data confirms nearly half of all homes currently on the market in Florida have had a reduction in asking price at some point. But that percentage is down from 53% this time last year and not much above what the rate is historically. “In the ‘normal’ market of 2014-2019, the percentage of homes that took a price cut was around 40%,” he said. “It is common for sellers to aim higher than true market value when they first list their home.” An asking price, also referred to as list price, is not to be confused with property values or how much homes actually sell for. Sellers can set an asking price for whatever amount they hope to get, regardless of what comparable homes in their neighborhood are fetching. According to Florida Realtor data, the median price for what singlefamily homes in Florida actually sold for in May rose 2.4% year-over-year to $425,000. It was the third-highest statewide median sale price ever recorded, just a shade under the $430,000 record high set in April 2024. The median means half sold for more and half for less. Johnson said only two of the nine metro areas in Florida he regularly tracks are still seeing declining home prices: North Port and Cape Coral. “Both are on the southwest side of the state where they are still dealing with hurricane damage. The other seven — Miami, Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, Lakeland, Deltona (Daytona Beach) and Palm Bay are actually flat or trending up in the last six months,” he said. “The idea that Florida accounting for 14% of all homes on the market nationally means the state is headed for a housing crash just isn’t warranted,” said Johnson. “Florida is going to still be one of the more dynamic states to live in for generations to come. It’s going to continue to grow, just not at the rate that its been.” As far as Parcl Labs’ claim that one in 10 homes in Florida are selling for less than what the sellers paid, O’Connor said, “I don’t have a way of quickly verifying this with our own data, but it seems believable in some parts of the state. If you bought at the peak in 2021 or 2022, and you’re selling now, you may well be in that position.” Florida residents share recent buying, selling experiences In Hernando County’s Spring Hill community, which is part of the greater Tampa metro area, Erica Allen and her husband recently put their three-bedroom, twobath house with a pool on the market that they bought in 2022 for $345,000. It was put under contract within a matter of weeks at close to their asking price of $389,000. Allen doesn’t believe the national reports depicting a Florida housing market in deep trouble. “They lie,” she said, adding, “I don’t think we’re going to have a crash, but I don’t see prices rising as fast as they had.” Liz Piedra, the broker/ owner of Horizon Palm Realty Group in Spring Hill, offered a similar assessment. “I’ve been doing this for 24 years,” she said. “Yes, the market is sluggish, but I don’t see Florida’s housing market in trouble like we were in 2006-2007. Back then, you had people who had no business getting a mortgage. That’s not the case today. “Are homes selling? Yes! Is it slower than it was a few years ago (during the COVID housing boom)? Yes, but the homes are selling if priced right.” Piedra said the problem in her view is unrealistic expectations on the part of both many of those trying to sell their home, who believe their house is worth far more than what a check of comparable properties in their neighborhood are actually selling for, as well as some buyers who believe the hype that Florida homes are selling at fire sale prices. “Is Florida overpriced? In some cases yes, but in some causes homes are actually underpriced,” she said. “I just bought one in Spring Hill for $260,000 that’s going to sell, once I fix it up, for well over $400,000.” Florida Realtor questions the accuracy of Parcl Labs’ report Brenden Rendo is a Realtor with NextHome Neighborhood Realty in Winter Springs who co-hosts a weekly podcast about the Orlando real estate market. While he himself has voiced concerns about Florida’s cooling housing market relative to the COVID boom years, he takes exception to the claims in Parcl Labs’ report and Lewris’s posts on X in particular. “Their ‘1 in 10 homes are SELLING for less than the owner paid’ claim misquotes their own map,” Rendo told USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA. “Their legend says ‘asking price below purchase price (unrealized loss).’ Asking is not selling. Median sale prices are up statewide.” Intrigued by the report and its claims, Rendo said he researched Lewris’s past posts on X, which he said uniformly painted a bleak picture of Florida’s housing market, including a characterization of sellers here as having a desperate “fire sale” mentality. “I ran fresh MLS (Multiple Listing Service) numbers Sunday for the fourcounty Orlando market (Orange, Seminole, Lake, Volusia),” Rendo said. “There were 161 active short-sale listings in the entire region, and only 11 short sales closed in all of June. If Florida sellers were ‘fire-selling,’ it would show up here first. It doesn’t.” Rendo also noted: “Parcl Labs own X bio says it powers Parcl, a crypto exchange where traders short housing indexes with up to 10 times leverage, and it sells $50/month subscriptions marketed around finding ‘motivated sellers.’ That doesn’t make the data wrong, but readers deserve the disclosure.” Parcl Labs co-founder defends his report’s findings In an email responding to questions from USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA, Lewris provided more details regarding his company’s findings on the Florida housing market and defended its accuracy. “We do count townhomes, new construction and condo units in our total for sale supply,” he wrote. “As of today (July 6), we are seeing 1,587,702 for sale units nationwide with 38.3% of these current units for sale undergoing price cuts. In Florida, we are seeing 215,447 units for sale with 44.9% of these current units for sale undergoing price cuts. “However, I would recommend our motivated seller index as a primary measurement of seller motivation vs. price cuts alone. This index accounts for not just price cuts, but price cut velocity as well as price cut depth. We have a detailed methodology regarding our motivated seller index (MSI) metric, which covers both the depth and breadth of price cutting behavior. It’s a measurement from zero to 10 with zero being the lowest and 10 being the most extreme case of seller motivation. “Currently, the U.S. is sitting at 5.1 while Florida is at 5.8 ... with Tampa leading major Florida metros at 7 while Miami is sitting at a 4.7. Tampa is currently ranked second amongst major metro areas nationwide for this measurement, sitting behind Sherman, Texas.” Lewris added, “Our data is trusted and used frequently by the WSJ (Wall Street Journal), CNBC, NYT (New York Times), and other national and local housing outlets to break emerging housing stories. “We were early on issues in Florida housing, including The Great Florida Migration is Coming Undone (WSJ), The Worst Housing Market in America is Now Florida’s Cape Coral (WSJ), and Trouble in Florida’s Real Estate Paradise is a Grim Warning for All of America (Business Insider). “We’re an objective third party. Our mission is to provide transparency on U.S. housing, not to advance any industry group, interest, or narrative other than what the data shows.” Clayton Park is a journalist for the USA TODAY NETWORK FLORIDA. He covers everything from insurance, utilities and home prices to groceries, gas and auto prices as the Florida consumer pocketbook reporter. text: Strategy just sold 3,588 $BTC to fund its digital credit dividends — and Michael Saylor isn't done. Reports point to him aiming for around $1.5B in total sales. Let that sink in. The man who spent years telling everyone to NEVER sell their Bitcoin… is selling Bitcoin. So is this the moment to panic? Our answer at CapitalFronts is the opposite — we think this is the moment to get IN. Here's why. He started selling near 74k, and between his pressure and the broader market, $BTC bled down to 58k. That drop already absorbed the MicroStrategy dumping. The proof? This latest sale of 3,588 BTC barely moved price — 62k to 61k. Compare that to the 74k → 58k slide earlier. The so-called "selling strength" is exhausted. They simply cant push it much lower anymore. And serious investors saw this coming. How did the market know roughly how much he'd need to sell? The $STRC chart. Strategy's Variable Rate Series Perpetual Stretch Preferred — the one paying ~13% — has to cover dividends. From Jun 26 it dumped from $92 to under $72, because the market realised he only had about 8 months of coverage left. To pay dividends he needs somewhere north of a billion a year, and he was sitting on roughly $500M in reserve — only about 7 months of runway. He needed to sell BTC just to keep more than 12 months of fiat on hand. By end of June, people were openly doubting whether he could even pay. Around $91 STRC he first sold ~$2.5M — a drop in the ocean — and we knew a much bigger sale was coming. STRC cratered to 72, then V-bounced back to 91. We think it pushes to $94 or higher. But here's the twist: he still hasn't sold that full billion. He's moved just $216M so far to fund the dividends, and claims $2.5B+ in fiat reserves. So the real question — if 95% of the market already knows he's going to sell more, who do you think is buying while retail panics? Whales. They're positioning between 55k and the low 60s, ready to catch the retail flush and ride it back up. The last time Saylor sold it was pure panic. This time? It's calm. That tells you everything. Our BTC view hasn't changed since our last post: one more fear-driven dip toward 55k, and then we go straight up. Now the macro. $SPX : if we close this week above 750, we're in a V-shape recovery targeting new all-time highs, maybe 2–3% above. We're also posting our Z-Score chart of the S&P CAPE ratio vs EPS. It measures how stretched the market is versus standard deviations — CAPE (the price/earnings side) in one line, EPS (actual earnings per share) in red. In the 2000 dot-com bubble, EPS was decent but CAPE was WAY higher — that gap is what signals a crash. Right now the gap is small, so the chart says "no bubble." But we don't fully buy that read. The 1929–early-40s depression also had CAPE sitting close to EPS, and it was the worst crash in history. The dot-com crash isnt even explained by this measure. Post-war through the late '60s, stocks were flat while CAPE and EPS hugged too. So it's not an honest standalone signal — it just tells us we're NOT in a dot-com setup. It doesn't tell us we're safe. And here's what worries us — our hyperscaler free cash flow chart. Since ~2012, when earnings rose, cash flow rose with it. Not this time. The red line has crashed. Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Google, Meta — total free cash flow is down hard. Why? They've poured it all into AI, semis, NVIDIA, SanDisk, Micron, energy. They used to hold ~$300B in cash flow and have now spent it — over $1.5 TRILLION in capex. So ask yourself: if the biggest names in the index are burning this much cash to invest, how sustainable is this earnings season really? Gold — same call as last time. We're watching for a third bottoming tail. We think $GOLD dips to around 3980 again, then bounces, maybe by Friday. If we get three bottoming tails, that's a strong signal for an upcoming uptrend. That's our read for today. One more thing — when our platform launches (mid-July), members get every one of these calls 24 hours BEFORE we post them publicly. So — are you panicking with retail, or positioning with the whales? NFA, just our analysis. Charts below 👇

text: 27-year-old Elon Musk paid $200 a month for a leaky roof office and slept in it because it was cheaper than an apartment. Summer of 1995, no money, no income, so he showered at the YMCA for 4 months and worked out of the nastiest place you can imagine. The office had 1 hidden advantage an internet provider sat on the floor below, so he drilled a hole in the concrete and plugged straight into their server for near-free bandwidth. He couldn’t afford a Cisco T1 router either, so he read a white paper and wrote an emulator, skipped the web server entirely to save CPU cycles, read port 8080 directly, and coded the first national maps, directions and yellow pages on the internet that summer in C with a little C++. The company was Zip2 online city guides, where to eat, how to get around. By 1998 CBS came to film the vintage Jaguar, the 6-figure salary, the dog, the house, the girlfriend, and a market Microsoft had tried to enter and failed. Then the reporter asked the standard 1998 question where is the internet going? The 27-year-old answered like he’d already seen the ending: “The internet is the superset of all media. Print, radio, broadcast all of it folds into the internet. It’s the first two-way medium that’s intelligent, where consumers choose what they see and when they see it.” That was 28 years ago and he was describing a feed. A year later Zip2 sold for $307M, the money became X com, X com became PayPal, and PayPal became rockets. It all started with a drill and the server downstairs.

text: Notes from Rick Schwartz’s conversation with Ishmilly in Ish’s domain investing space on X on Saturday, 7 February 2026: AI․com just sold for $70M. Ish said LasVegas․com sold earlier for 90M and like AI․com, it was sold just as a domain, with no business entity attached. Rick Schwartz said that the original asking price for AI․com was probably $100M. “How did the other CEOs miss it?” Rick said. The sale buys the buyer a seat at the table, whether the incumbents like it or not. It is not because it’s a LL․com, but because it defines the sector. Amazing power. Rick’s message to the other AI CEO’s: “Wake up.” They shouldn’t have missed it. The buyer knew what he was doing, Rick said. Other CEOs have to pay for ads, so they’re merely renting those ad spaces, whereas the buyer of AI․com now owns the ground they’re standing on. Rick’s advice: don’t negotiate on price. “The moment you start with price, you lose with price,” he said. Get into a conversation, he said. “The best way to do that is to not open with price. Have an intelligent conversation.” He doesn’t answer most inquiries because he can’t qualify them. Rick heard “smart glasses” mentioned on a news media site. Then he ran to Huge Domains and bought the .COM for $3500. Rick doesn’t sell inventory, he sells dreams. Rick negotiated $8.5M for porno․com, but then buyer started to play with the deal and asked Rick to be allowed to try it for a month. Rick told them to fuck off and never contact him again. The buyer’s CEO immediately wrote to him, saying the money will be in Rick’s account in 48 hours. Don’t let buyers play with the deal, Rick said. Non-COMs aren’t marketable, Rick said. .AI is the only non-COM that has earned a place in the ecosystem, Rick said. It’s marketable because people accept it, he said. Rick says 36-48 months should be the most popular LTO period for domains. “Approved use” an LTO buyer has to agree to, Rick said, before he’ll approve an LTO deal. You gotta know an LTO buyer, which can take weeks. He doesn’t do LTOs on adult domains. Domains are valuable because they enable customers to find you, Joseph Çiprut said. “Every digital strategy starts with a name,” Joseph said. Rick contrasted domains with collectables such as baseball cards. He owns some collectables. He said a $30M baseball card needs to be protected with an insurance policy that could cost $300,000 per year. Like NFTs, baseball cards don’t produce income and the owner can’t use such an investment to expand. The card is practically useless and has to be kept locked in a vault. Like NFTs, baseball cards and other stores of value can never serve as the world headquarters of a business. They don’t earn income. They cannot do anything. Rick has started allowing a few people to represent a small number of his domains for a period of 1-2 years. He describes these representative arrangements as “slow burns.” He sets a price minimum for each domain, and everything above that Rick will split with the rep who sells it. He chooses his reps on the basis of their connections in the industry vertical that each domain represents. Alex Verdea is representing property․com and properties․com. In representing Rick’s names, Alex will protect the asset, Rick said. Betty is the name Rick gave to his AI agent advisor. He named her Betty because the name is associated with Betty Flintstone and Betty Boop, who are seen as trustworthy mom types. Rick bought Betty․ai, which has a PPC lander. The AI runs on ChatGPT and cannot be reached from the lander. “She” read everything about him and is his AI agent. He bounces ideas off her. Betty isn’t publicly available, but Rick might lease her out so she could answer questions from others, using Rick’s voice. “She’s indispensable.” He urges everyone to train their own AI agent. He uses Betty to introduce him to other AIs. The introductions that Betty prepares are one to two pages long. We’re 1-3 years away from being able to put an agent like Betty into a robot. The adult sector will soon figure this out and exploit it first, he said. Rick currently has about 6500 domains. 700 are meaningful, super high-value ones. Some of the others are moats, which protect a primary, high-value domain in his portfolio. One of his moat domains was Teem․com that he bought by mistake, but which he ended up selling for $1.5M “My job is to collect intersections. It’s impossible to know when it (the domains) will be needed.” Domain flippers often don’t understand their inventory, he said. They don’t know the value or potential applications. He can’t always estimate the value of brandables, he said. Parking is down but not out, he said. He said most businesses advertise by going to FB and Twitter and making easy ad buys without really understanding the value of each customer or click. The adult industry is far advanced in terms of metrics for ads and parking. For a new domain, he puts it on a lander with PPC ads to see what’s going on with a domain and whether it gets traffic. If you’re going to build out a domain, you need someone to buy your leads or you need a cash register yourself, i.e., something you’re selling. Regarding WHOIS data, “make sure you’re not on privacy” he said. The telephone number he uses for his WHOIS records sends everything to voice mail. Google is fantastic on spam handling. He doesn’t want GoDaddy to get his leads. “Be vague when you’re negotiating,” he said. Fractionalization needs to be monetized 100% immediately in his view. He’s not bullish on fractionalization because it can lock up a domain forever. There’s not enough activity in the domain space for fractionalization. To make fractionalization work, he said you need to get collectors involved. In regard to estate planning, Rick set up a foundation with three executors who will decide how to manage and sell his domains. “The day I die, everything goes up 300%.” He stressed the importance of having domains that are relevant. If your site (or domain) isn’t relevant, you won’t get traffic. He buys .AI names not as an investor, but as an end user. In the adult industry, back a decade or more, if you used clickbait, you’d be banned. Now Rick says that’s all Fortune 400 companies clickbait use to attract traffic. Rick advises against using minimum offers. “A minimum offer becomes your maximum offer,” he said. “Take off your minimum offers.” Look for fingerprints (clues) to see who submitted the offer, then decide how to proceed. He doesn’t receive a huge number of inquiries for his domains, which he attributes to his names being very high quality. The guy selling VWs has more foot traffic than the guy selling Ferraris, he said. He’s never had to pitch a domain. The buyers always come to him. “Stop selling the domain name...it’s a self-explaining entity.” He’s never done outbounding. Don’t use outbounding to try and make a sale, he advises. The key is to create awareness and to simply make it known that a domain is available. A domain is most valuable when it’s the buyer’s idea to buy it. So you might have someone come back in a year (after they’ve found out about your domain) and seek to use your domain as the keystone of a comprehensive corporate initiative. Every buyer is unique, which is why it’s important to communicate with them. It’s like two people sitting down at a table, showing their cards, and trying to create the best deal with the available cards. “What are you trying to achieve, what’s your strategy to get there?” are initial questions he often asks people who inquire about his domains. Everyone lies in negotiations. You can’t lie about anything material though. Other than misrepresentation, there are no rules in negotiations. You can call people names, for example. People enjoy the back and forth. “Nobody wants the easy girl,” said Ish. Most people say stupid things in verbal conversations. This can kill a sale. A seller may not even know they’ve killed the sale. He takes no phone calls for negotiations. Everything is by email. Email records are admissible in court. Email is one of the strongest contract forms you can have. $10k-$20k is the usual cost of having his lawyer prepare a sales contract, Rick said. He asks buyers to pay it, and said that the money spent (on having a contract developed) can be applied to the purchase price if the deal goes through. If it’s a straight lease-to-own, he will use email to define and execute a contract. In negotiations, an email response by a seller should be 3-4 sentences maximum. “All our domains start in the six figures and go up from there,” is an example of Rick’s reply to an initial price inquiry. “That gets rid of 99% of the fish right away.” “If you want to be a millionaire, you have to act like one.” He expects interest rates to fall by 2-3% in the next year or two, which could drive home prices to double. More money will be flying around in the next 36 months than ever before, Rick said, which will be good for the domain industry. Rick invested in crypto by investing in Coinbase. He likes Seattle but is rooting for the Patriots in the Superbowl. [End]

text: AI.com just sold for 70 million dollars, now the highest publicly reported domain sale ever. That number is huge, but the real story is what it represents about the future of digital ownership.. We are still early in how the world prices digital assets. Entire businesses, audiences, and revenue streams now live online, yet the core pieces of digital real estate that control access, trust, and brand authority are often valued like afterthoughts... A strong digital asset can influence customer perception, reduce marketing costs, drive organic traffic, and compound brand equity for decades, all without the physical limitations of traditional property. Look at where the global economy is heading. Trillions of dollars in commerce, services, and innovation are flowing through the internet. Artificial intelligence, online education, fintech, media, remote work, creator economies, all of it sits on digital foundations. Compared to the scale of value being created, the price of owning key digital positions is still shockingly low. People will spend fortunes on office space that employees barely use, yet hesitate on assets that operate as permanent storefronts to the entire planet. Companies spend that much on ad campaigns that are forgotten in months. A domain like this becomes the foundation of a brand, the front door, the first impression, and a permanent trust signal. It works every day, in every country, without media buying or algorithms deciding your reach. As artificial intelligence becomes the backbone of everything, owning the exact word match .com is long term strategic dominance at a price that may look laughably cheap a decade from now. This is the kind of asset that pays you back over time through brand power, reduced marketing costs, and perpetual visibility. Anyone who walks away from this as an expense probably does not understand the value of digital positioning yet, but the person who made this purchase absolutely does. Congrats to both the buyer & the seller.

text: Elon's ex Justine Musk wrote an essay describing herself as a "starter wife." The phrase went viral because of its precision. Not an ex wife. A starter wife. As if she was the beta version of a product that was tested, iterated on, and eventually replaced by a newer model. She described watching Elon transform during their marriage from a passionate entrepreneur into someone she didn't recognize. The money arrived and the sweetness left. Not simultaneously. Gradually. Like a dial being turned so slowly that you don't notice the room getting darker until you can't see. She said the power dynamic shifted with each financial milestone. When they were equals in college the relationship was balanced. When he sold Zip2 for $22 million the balance tilted. When PayPal sold for $1.5 billion the balance broke. The same ambition that attracted her to a nervous college student in Canada became the force that made her invisible in her own marriage. She described dinners where Elon would read a book at the table instead of talking to her. Not to be cruel. Because the book was more efficient than conversation and his mind was optimized for efficiency in every domain including the one where efficiency destroys intimacy. The phrase "starter wife" carries a brutality that Justine intended. It frames the relationship not as a love story that ended but as a phase in a man's development that was always going to be temporary. She was the person who loved him when he was nobody. The reward for that love was becoming nobody to him once he was somebody. Every ambitious man should read Justine's essay. Not as a warning about Elon specifically. As a mirror for the version of ambition that consumes everything in its path including the people who were there before the ambition had a name.
name: Space Tourist

text: The million dollar webpage... Owner sold a 1,000×1,000 pixel page a pixel at a time for a dollar per pixel. In August 2005, 21 year old British student Alex Tew came up with an unusual way to pay for college. He created The Million Dollar Homepage, a website consisting of exactly one million pixels arranged in a 1,000 by 1,000 grid. Businesses and individuals could purchase advertising space for $1 per pixel, with a minimum purchase of 100 pixels, which formed a 10 by 10 square linking to their own websites. The idea spread rapidly through word of mouth, blogs, and news coverage. Companies large and small rushed to secure a permanent place on what became one of the internet's earliest viral sensations. By January 2006, every pixel had been sold, earning Tew exactly $1 million before taxes and transaction fees. More than two decades later, the website remains online as a time capsule of the early internet, preserving hundreds of advertisements exactly as they appeared during the height of the dot com era. The final 1,000 pixels were not sold directly. Instead, Alex Tew auctioned them on eBay, where they sold for $38,100, bringing the total revenue from the project to more than $1.03 million. #archaeohistories
name: Archaeo - Histories

text: Doma Protocol: Bringing the World's Largest Digital Asset Class On-Chain @domaprotocol For decades, internet domains have been among the most valuable digital assets in the world. Premium names like voice.com , chat.com , or business.com have sold for millions of dollars, yet the domain market has remained largely illiquid, slow, and dependent on brokers and escrow services. Doma Protocol is changing that. Rather than creating a new naming system like ENS or Unstoppable Domains, Doma focuses on something far more ambitious: bringing real internet domains (.com, .ai, .xyz, and other ICANN-compliant domains) onto the blockchain as programmable assets. This is the foundation of an entirely new financial ecosystem known as DomainFi. Not Another Domain Protocol Many people mistakenly compare Doma to ENS or Unstoppable Domains, but they solve completely different problems. ENS creates blockchain-native identities such as .eth. Unstoppable Domains introduces crypto-native extensions like .crypto. Doma, on the other hand, tokenizes existing internet domains that already power websites, businesses, and brands around the world. That means a domain such as software.ai or yourcompany.com continues functioning exactly as before while simultaneously becoming a blockchain asset that can be traded, financed, or integrated into DeFi applications. No browser extensions or alternative DNS infrastructure are required. DomainFi: Unlocking Liquidity for Internet Domains Traditional domain ownership has always suffered from one major limitation: Domains are valuable, but they are difficult to monetize without selling the entire asset. Doma introduces DomainFi, allowing domains to become productive financial assets. Through tokenization, domain owners can: Trade ownership instantly on-chain Use domains as DeFi collateral Fractionalize premium domains into thousands of tradeable tokens Provide liquidity Participate in decentralized financial markets Instead of waiting weeks for escrow services and paying high broker commissions, ownership can be transferred within seconds on blockchain networks. The Dual-Token Architecture One of Doma's most innovative designs is its dual-token model. Every tokenized domain generates two independent assets: DOT (Domain Ownership Token) Represents the legal ownership and transfer rights of the domain. Whoever owns the DOT owns the domain itself. DST (Domain Service Token) Controls DNS records, website hosting, email routing, and operational management. This separation creates possibilities that traditional domain systems cannot offer. For example: Sell ownership while keeping the website running. Lease operational control without giving away ownership. Separate investors from operators. Enable institutional management of valuable digital assets. This architecture is a core innovation behind DomainFi and distinguishes Doma from virtually every other blockchain domain project. Fractional Ownership Changes Everything Imagine a premium domain worth $1 million. Historically, only one buyer could own it. With Doma, that domain can be fractionalized into thousands of ERC-20 tokens, allowing anyone to purchase a small percentage of the asset. The well-known example is software.ai , which was transformed into thousands of tradeable tokens that investors could buy and sell on decentralized exchanges while the underlying website continued operating normally. This dramatically lowers the barrier to entry and brings liquidity to an asset class that has historically been available only to wealthy investors. Built for the Existing Internet Unlike projects attempting to replace DNS, Doma works alongside today's internet infrastructure. The protocol collaborates with established registrars, enabling traditional domains to be tokenized without disrupting ICANN compliance or existing registration systems. Its architecture connects: Traditional registrars Blockchain infrastructure DomainFi applications This allows businesses to continue operating exactly as they do today while gaining access to blockchain-native financial capabilities. Why This Matters The internet has hundreds of millions of registered domains representing billions of dollars in value. Yet until recently, these assets were largely static. Doma transforms domains from passive digital property into programmable financial assets capable of: Generating liquidity Supporting lending markets Powering decentralized trading Enabling fractional investment Expanding cross-chain interoperability Rather than replacing the existing internet, Doma is building a bridge between Web2 infrastructure and Web3 finance. The Bigger Vision Doma is not simply creating another blockchain application. It is creating the infrastructure for DomainFi—an ecosystem where internet domains become fully composable blockchain assets. By combining traditional DNS infrastructure with decentralized finance, Doma unlocks entirely new economic possibilities for one of the internet's oldest and most valuable asset classes. As tokenization continues expanding into real-world assets, domains represent a natural next frontier. And Doma aims to become the protocol powering that transformation.

text: 🚨 The AI Bubble Scare Is a Con Job - Here's The Receipts 🚨 If you know, you know. But do you? **November 29, 2025** Peter Thiel just sold $100 million worth of Nvidia ($NVDA). Stanley Druckenmiller dumped his entire position - both Nvidia and Palantir ($PLTR). Michael Burry took out over $1 billion in puts against AI stocks. SoftBank exited $5.83 billion in Nvidia shares. Then suddenly - SUDDENLY - everyone's screaming about AI bubbles. Jeff Bezos warns it's an "industrial bubble" on October 3. Sundar Pichai tells the BBC on November 18 there's "irrationality" everywhere and "no company will be immune when it bursts." Sam Altman admitted back in August that investors are "overexcited" and someone's going to "lose a phenomenal amount." And the media? They're eating it up. Chip stocks down 11% in November. Nvidia lost over $500 billion in market value. Meta ($META) down 21%, Microsoft ($MSFT) down 13%, Oracle ($ORCL) cratering 24%. By the way is Microsoft going the way of SAS with AI, it's only real assets data centers? If they're Advanced AI lab catches up, now that they're Unshackled from openai, it's. Still a long bet. In my humble opinion. Everyone's calling this the dot-com crash 2.0. Except here's what they're not telling you: These guys weren't warning about bubbles when they were BUYING. They were warning about bubbles after they SOLD. Let me show you the timeline, because once you see it, you can't unsee it. The 13F Receipts: They Sold At The Top, Now They're Talking It Down Peter Thiel started buying Nvidia in Q4 2024. Added more in Q1 2025. More in Q2 2025. By mid-2025, he's sitting on 537,742 shares - about $100 million worth - representing 40% of his entire fund. That's not a casual bet. That's an "I'm all-in on AI" position. Then Q3 2025 hits. He dumps every single share. Stanley Druckenmiller? Same story. Held 214,060 Nvidia shares and 769,965 Palantir shares through most of 2024 and early 2025. Then between July 1 and September 30, 2025 - gone. Sold everything. Michael Burry - the guy who shorted the housing market - took out massive put positions against both Nvidia and Palantir in Q3 2025. Over $1 billion notional value betting AGAINST AI stocks. SoftBank sold its entire Nvidia stake in October 2025. 32.1 million shares. $5.83 billion. Out. Now here's the kicker: When were these guys warning retail investors about the bubble? Not in Q4 2024 when they were buying. Not in Q1 2025 when they were accumulating. Not in Q2 2025 when they were loading up. They started warning in Q3 and Q4 2025 - AFTER they sold. You see what's happening here? They rode it up for 12-18 months, made their money, rotated out, and NOW they're concerned about YOUR portfolio. That's not prophecy. That's profit-taking with PR. This Is Literally The DeepSeek Playbook All Over Again Remember January 2025? DeepSeek drops a model claiming GPT-4 performance for $6 million in compute costs. The market absolutely loses its mind. Nvidia crashes 17% in ONE DAY. Biggest single-day market cap loss in U.S. history. $589 billion evaporated. Analysts declared AI investments dead. Why buy $30,000 H100 chips if some Chinese lab just cracked the code with pocket change? 🚨Then people actually tested DeepSeek.🚨 And... it wasn't GPT-4-level. The cost claims were misleading. The compute estimates ignored inference. It was good optimization, not some fundamental breakthrough that made expensive infrastructure obsolete. Within weeks, the panic faded. Nvidia recovered. AI development kept accelerating like nothing happened. We're watching the ⚠️EXACT ⚠️same movie right now. Insiders sell. Media panics. Retail freaks out. And six months from now, we'll realize the technology never stopped advancing. Don't be the person who panic-sold and missed what happened next. Meanwhile, In The Actual Real World Where Technology Gets Built While everyone's losing their minds about bubbles, let me tell you what actually launched in November 2025. Google ($GOOG) dropped Gemini 3 on November 18. Not incremental - transformative. PhD-level reasoning benchmarks that would've seemed impossible six months ago. Compared to Opus 4.5 it's slow. I also have to use Claude to correct it left and right. Especially in anything to do with research. Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.5 on November 24. And I need you to understand what this model actually did, because this is where the entire bubble narrative falls apart. Opus 4.5 scored 80.9% on SWE-bench Verified. That's a test of real GitHub issues that stumped human developers. Gemini 3 Pro hit 76.2% on the same test. That 4.7 point gap is massive in this domain. But here's the part that breaks the bubble argument completely: Anthropic dropped prices from $15/$75 per million tokens down to $5/$25. That's a 67% price cut. While IMPROVING performance. At the same time. 👀 Read that again. Better results. Lower costs. Simultaneously. That's not bubble behavior. That's Moore's Law on steroids. YouTuber Alex Finn tested Opus 4.5 by asking it to build a complete 3D first-person shooter from scratch. The model generated the full dev plan, wrote all the code, and executed the entire project in one attempt. Previous models would create a task list and fail halfway through. Internal testers at Anthropic reported the model scored higher on their engineering assessment than any human candidate in company history. Every single person who ever applied to work at one of the world's leading AI companies - outperformed by software. And this dropped SIX DAYS AGO while everyone was busy writing bubble think pieces. The Efficiency Revolution Nobody's Talking About Critics say AI needs infinite capex. Unsustainable energy. Eventually the house of cards collapses. They point to Microsoft targeting $120 billion in capex, Amazon over $100 billion, Alphabet $85 billion, Meta $72 billion. Those are big numbers. Scary numbers if you squint. But while capex surges, efficiency is exploding FASTER. Opus 4.5's 67% price cut isn't marketing spin. It reflects genuine compute efficiency gains. The model uses fewer tokens to solve the same problems. At scale, that compounds. This is the opposite of bubble dynamics. In a real bubble, valuations rise while fundamentals stagnate. Here? Capabilities rising, costs plummeting. That's not irrational exuberance. That's technological progress working exactly how it's supposed to work. Let's Talk About What These Insiders May Actually Be Afraid Of Bezos warns about bubbles on October 3 at Italian Tech Week. Says AI is like the dot-com era where "every experiment gets funded." You know what Bezos didn't mention? Amazon ($AMZN) just spent years building AI infrastructure. AWS is seeing explosive AI-driven growth. They're investing in nuclear power plants to support future compute needs. But sure Jeff, it's all a bubble. Sundar Pichai warns about "irrationality" on November 18. Says "no company will be immune if the bubble bursts." You know what else happened in 2025? Google battled OpenAI and Anthropic all year. Poured tens of billions into AI development. Launched Gemini models that represent their entire strategic future. But sure Sundar, let's talk about how irrational everyone else is being. Here's what they're really afraid of: Missing the next wave. Looking stupid if they sold too early. Justifying their exits if the stock keeps climbing. If you dump $100 million in Nvidia in Q3 and it moons in Q4, you look like an idiot. But if bubble warnings intensify after you sell and the stock corrects 15-20%? Now you're a genius who saw it coming. They're not warning you. They're covering their own asses. The Media Made This Worse Once the insider exits became public, financial media went into full panic mode. Every billionaire exit got breathless coverage. Every bubble warning became a headline. Every stock decline became proof the collapse was imminent. What got buried? The actual technology breakthroughs happening in real-time. Claude Opus 4.5 - the biggest coding model leap in years - launched November 24. Barely registered outside tech circles because everyone was too busy writing "AI Bubble About To Pop" takes. Gemini 3 launched November 18 and should've been front-page news. Instead it got overshadowed by Pichai's same-day bubble warnings to the BBC. The negativity creates a self-fulfilling cycle. Stocks drop because of bubble fears. Stocks dropping becomes evidence of the bubble. More warnings follow. More selling follows. But strip away the noise and look at what's actually being built - it's the exact opposite of a bubble bursting. It's innovation accelerating. The Nuclear Tell: They're Planning For Decades, Not Quarters You want to know the real tell that this isn't a bubble? Microsoft committed to restarting Three Mile Island. Amazon invested $500 million in small modular reactors. Nuclear power plants. You don't invest in nuclear for a two-year AI fad. You invest in nuclear for a 30-year technological transformation. These are 20-30 year infrastructure plays. You don't make those bets if you think AI is about to crash. The hyperscalers with the most money on the line - the ones actually building the infrastructure - are betting on decades of exponential growth. But sure, let's listen to the guys who just sold their positions about how this is all going to collapse. What Actually Happens Next Sundar Pichai said something interesting buried in that BBC interview. He acknowledged potential overinvestment but noted that looking back at the internet, there was clearly excess investment, yet no one questions whether the internet was profound. He expects AI to follow the same pattern. That's the right framework. Yes, there will be overinvestment. Yes, some companies will fail. Yes, investors will lose money. That's not a bubble - that's how technology transitions work. Amazon lost 95% of its value in the dot-com crash. It was still the right company. It still revolutionized retail. The stock just got ahead of fundamentals temporarily. Five years from now, we'll look back at November 2025's bubble panic and laugh at how obvious it was that AI was going to transform everything. The technology is advancing too fast. The use cases are too real. The efficiency gains are too dramatic. The competitive intensity is too fierce. 43 out of 48 analysts rate Nvidia as Buy or Strong Buy, with average 12-month price targets around $254.50. Those aren't bag-holders hoping for recovery - those are analysts modeling the actual business seeing continued strength. Stifel analyst Ruben Roy just raised his Nvidia price target to $250 from $212, citing CEO Jensen Huang positioning the company as the backbone of AI infrastructure with over $500 billion in cumulative orders for their next-gen chips spanning 2025-2026. $500 billion in ORDERS. Not projections. Not hopes. Contracted revenue. 👉The Bottom Line: Don't Get Played The market can stay volatile. Stocks can correct. Valuations can compress. None of that changes the fundamental reality: AI capabilities are advancing at unprecedented speed while simultaneously getting cheaper and more efficient. Three frontier models dropped in one week in November 2025. Each pushing different boundaries. That's not the release cadence of a technology hitting a wall. That's fierce competition driving rapid iteration. ChatGPT now reaches 700 million weekly users - 4x growth year-over-year. That's not speculation. That's measured demand. Jensen Huang reported $500 billion in orders for 2025-2026. That's not hypothetical. That's contracted business. The capex isn't speculative. It's responding to massive demand that's already here. Sam Altman said some investors will get burned as hype unwinds, but the long-term value created by AI will outweigh short-term losses. He's right. Some investors will get burned. They always do in technology transitions. But the people getting burned won't be the ones who stayed focused on technological progress. They'll be the ones who panic-sold because billionaires who already made their money suddenly got concerned about retail portfolios. Peter Thiel rode Nvidia up for over a year, made a fortune, sold at the top, and now everyone's supposed to freak out about bubbles. Stanley Druckenmiller did the same thing. SoftBank did the same thing. They're not prophets. They're traders who timed their exits and are now managing their narratives. Meanwhile Claude Opus 4.5 delivers frontier reasoning through 30-minute autonomous coding sessions at 67% lower prices than previous models. That didn't exist six months ago. It's here now. And it's already becoming commoditized. The fourth industrial revolution doesn't care about your stock portfolio. It's happening whether the market believes it or not. Wedbush analyst Dan Ives has been right about this from the start: This IS the fourth industrial revolution, with trillions being spent on buildout, and while there's froth in private markets, this isn't a bubble. The real risk isn't that AI progress will stall. The real risk is panic-selling at the bottom of a correction and missing the next decade of exponential growth because you confused market volatility with technological plateau. Don't be the person who sold Amazon in 2001 because everyone said dot-com was dead. Don't be the person who sold Nvidia after DeepSeek in January 2025. Don't be the person who sells AI in November 2025 because insiders who already cashed out are suddenly worried about bubbles. Watch what they do, not what they say. And what they did was accumulate for 18 months, sell at the top, and then start warning everyone else. You're getting played. Don't fall for it. Not again...

🚗 $OUST : Strong Results + Utah Expansion Fuel 7.7% Move

 $OUST (Ouster) is up 7.7% today, driven by strong Q2 results, continued lidar demand and a major expansion of its Utah traffic-management contract. Ouster reported Q2 revenue of $55M, up 56% YoY, while product revenue has now grown for 14 consecutive quarters and shipments exceeded 17,000 lidar and camera units. Q3 guidance is $54.5M–$57.5M, suggesting demand remains strong.

The latest catalyst came on August 11, when Ouster announced a multimillion-dollar Utah expansion covering another 160 intersections, bringing its total contracted Utah footprint to nearly 300 deployments. This is important because Ouster’s BlueCity traffic platform is moving toward larger-scale deployments.

💰 Balance Sheet

Ouster ended Q2 with approximately $263M in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and short-term investments. A July equity offering strengthened the balance sheet further, although investors should consider the potential dilution. The market currently appears more focused on revenue growth, improving margins, liquidity and execution.

🏦 Institutional Activity

Institutional activity is mixed. 210 institutions increased their OUST positions, while 112 reduced them. Major additions included JPMorgan +728,688 shares (~$45.6M), Sixth Street Partners +533,951 shares (~$33.4M) and Morgan Stanley +510,920 shares (~$31.9M). Mirae Asset also added approximately 491,332 shares. On the other side, Tao Capital Management sold 845,316 shares (~$52.8M), Slate Path Capital exited 829,000 shares (~$15.2M) and Handelsbanken reduced approximately 514,325 shares (~$32.2M).

⚠️ Insider Selling

The biggest caution is insider activity. Over the past six months, insiders reportedly made 50 open-market transactions: 1 purchase and 49 sales. CTO Mark Frichtl sold approximately 884,279 shares worth ~$30.0M, COO Darien Spencer sold 83,497 shares (~$3.44M), CFO Kenneth Gianella sold 54,337 shares (~$2.11M) and CEO Charles Angus Pacala sold 54,454 shares (~$1.73M). One notable purchase came from Virginia Boulet, who bought 6,500 shares for ~$136K. Insider selling isn’t automatically bearish because shares can be sold for compensation, taxes or diversification, but 49 sales versus 1 purchase is worth watching.

🎯 Analyst Targets

Reported analyst targets remain significantly above the current trading area, with a median target of approximately $48. Recent targets include $53 from Rosenblatt and $43 from Amerx. Targets aren’t guarantees, but they show that some analysts see substantial upside if Ouster continues executing.

🧠 My Take

The bullish case is becoming stronger: $55M Q2 revenue (+56% YoY), 14 consecutive quarters of product-revenue growth, 17,000+ units shipped, $54.5M–$57.5M Q3 guidance, 160 additional Utah intersections, nearly 300 total Utah deployments, ~$263M Q2 liquidity and meaningful institutional buying.

The risks remain insider selling, equity dilution, competition and the need to convert strong revenue growth into sustainable profitability and cash flow.

Overall, $OUST is becoming an increasingly interesting AI/automation infrastructure play, not just an autonomous-driving company. Its lidar and BlueCity technology can support smart cities, traffic management, infrastructure monitoring and industrial applications.

The key question now isn’t today’s +7.7% move — it’s whether Ouster can sustain strong revenue growth while improving margins and expanding deployments. If it can, today’s valuation could look very different over the next few years. 🚀

🎓 QUESTION: Is your university degree still worth what you paid for it?

AI is starting to challenge something universities have sold for centuries:

Access to knowledge: lectures, explanations, tutoring, research assistance, feedback.

You can increasingly get all of that from an AI, personalized to you, available 24/7, for almost nothing.

So what are you actually paying $50,000+ a year for?

The degree itself or the the professors, maybe the network, could be the reputation of the institution?

The signal to future employers that you were good enough to get in?

Because those things don't disappear when knowledge becomes cheap.

And that's why I suspect AI won't affect every university equally.

Harvard, Stanford or MIT aren't valuable only because of what they teach.

They're also valuable because of who gets admitted, who you meet there and what graduating from them signals.

But what happens to universities without that powerful network or brand?

If an AI tutor can teach you the same material — potentially better and completely personalized — the value proposition becomes much harder to explain.

AI probably won't make education worthless.

But it may force us to finally separate two things we've bundled together for centuries:

Learning and credentials.

JULY 2026 PORTFOLIO UPDATE:

Sorry for the late update. I've been underwater working on a few things lately.

Numbers first. Then the breakdown.

YTD PERFORMANCE

MONTHLY PERFORMANCE

Performance is strictly common stock. Zero leverage, zero options, zero margin. Conviction and patience are my only leverage.

July was terrible for all of us exposed to AI. It was really two months stitched together. The beginning rode the disinflation relief from the June CPI print, the biggest monthly drop since 2020. The back half got ugly: a sharp month selloff tore through the entire AI-infrastructure complex, and a lot of my book sits right in the middle of it. The trigger was not a broken thesis anywhere. It was forced selling, most visibly the implosion of 360,000 retail investors wiped out in South Korea and Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness fund unwinding its whole book into a thin summer tape.

When a crowded trade gets liquidated like that, correlation goes to one and the good stuff gets sold with the bad. Step back though. The long-term book is still +50.62% YTD. The short-term book still up 133.67% YTD. Nothing in the July tape changed a single thesis I hold. Reset, not break.

Let me walk the whole thing.

LONG-TERM PORTFOLIO: POSITION REFLECTIONS

 $NBIS · 23.2%
Still my largest position. My conviction anchor and I have no interest in trimming it. July was mostly noise. The neocloud complex chopped around and NBIS got dragged into the late-month selloff despite zero company-specific bad news. The story is the same one that got me here: contracted backlog north of +$40B, a power target that keeps climbing, and revenue growth that does not care about a two-week sentiment swing. Up about 200% on my average. The Q2 print in early August is the next real test. Holding.

 $OUST · 18.2%
Quietly becoming of my largest position, and like last month that is price doing the work, not me adding. July was a giveback month. The stock ran hard into late June on the Build America Buy America clearance for Rev8, then priced a roughly $200M equity raise at $55.22 on July 2 and settled back into the low $40s. The raise looks like dilution at first glance. It funds the Rev8 ramp and still leaves the company with about $263M in cash and no debt, which is exactly the balance sheet you want going into a capacity build. Rev8 got qualified for NVIDIA's DRIVE Hyperion platform and BlueCity lidar went live around MetLife for the World Cup. I'm up roughly 100% on the position. Thesis intact, sizing comfortable.

 $IREN · 15.2%
The reason I own this got louder in July even as the stock stayed volatile. Sweetwater 1 is operational, the NVIDIA DSX partnership from May keeps Sweetwater slated as the flagship AI factory site, and the ARR ramp got raised to roughly +$4B by late 2026 is contracted, not hoped for. IREN also caught the late-July AI-infra downdraft. I'm up about 25% on my cost. The vertically integrated power-to-compute thesis is stronger than it was a month ago, especially with recent handover of Horizon 1 to $MSFT . Holding.

 $RKLB · 11.1%
Choppy month. RKLB drifted to its late-July lows in the high $60s as the space sector cooled, then started clawing back on another clean Electron mission. The signal under the noise was all positive: mission success on the Space Force VICTUS HAZE responsive-space flight, the pending Iridium acquisition moving forward, and fresh launch contracts stacking. Neutron is the whole long-term inflection and it is still targeting a Q4 pad delivery. Up about 20%. Holding, conviction unchanged.

 $ONDS · 9.1%
This is the disconnect of the month. The stock consolidated and gave back part of its prior run in July, drifting into the mid-$6s to low-$7s, while the actual business had one of its loudest months yet. Ondas closed the roughly $876M DZYNE acquisition and stood up its Sentinel division, raised full-year revenue guidance to at least $525M (well above the ~$395M the street was modeling), added Cyberhawk for recurring inspection revenue, and brought in the former head of Mossad to run Ondas Defense. Order flow keeps landing: Army Lethal Unmanned Systems awards past $240M, an Australian counter-drone order, World Cup airspace-security contracts. I'm basically flat on the position, up about 1%. Price and fundamentals have come apart here, and I've seen this before. Holding.

 $CIFR · 8.1%
Rough July on the tape. CIFR pulled back from its late-June highs near $28 into the high teens by month end, and the late-month AI-infra selloff did most of the damage in a couple of sessions. Underneath, the story kept improving. BTIG took its target to $35, KBW to $32, and the New York data-center moratorium noise actually helps a builder sitting on power in friendlier states. The Fluidstack colocation model, backstopped by Google and AWS, is the thesis and it is intact. Up about 15% on my average. Holding into the Q2 print.

 $AAOI · 8.1%
One of the cleaner months in the book. AAOI broke ground on a nearly 400,000 square foot, roughly $300M expansion of its Pearland campus on July 14, specifically to scale 800G and 1.6T transceiver output, and Rosenblatt named it a top pick for the back half of the year. The stock spent July high and volatile (there are now leveraged single-stock ETFs on both sides amplifying every move) and finished the month around the mid-$120s. Capacity ramps precede revenue ramps, and this is the ramp. Up about 40%. Holding.

 $KRKNF ($PNG.V) · 7.1%
The one real drawdown in my book. I'm down about 18%. Here's the frustrating part: July was arguably Kraken's most important month ever. It closed the roughly C$615M Covelya acquisition on July 2 (Sonardyne, EIVA, Forcys, Voyis, Chelsea) and nearly doubled full-year revenue guidance to C$290-320M, then added another $35M in fresh orders on July 20. The stock stayed weak in the low C$6s anyway, which is what small-cap defense names do when a big deal brings dilution into a risk-off tape. The subsea sonar and pressure-tolerant battery thesis is intact, and Covelya makes the platform broader, not thinner. Holding.

SHORT-TERM PORTFOLIO: POSITION REFLECTIONS

3 positions now. Weighted heavily toward space, with a photonics name and a placeholder.

 $ASTS · 47%
July was a sell-the-news, execution-is-boring kind of month, and the stock took it on the chin, down roughly 18% into the high $50s before it found a bid. Nothing about the buildout slowed. BlueBird 8, 9 and 10 are in orbit from June, production is running through satellite 42, the Midland manufacturing expansion got teed up, and the next launch (BlueBird 11-13) got locked for early August. The market got impatient with a company that is executing exactly to plan. After the recovery I'm down only about 4% from my average. Still my highest-conviction short-term hold.

 $PL · 25%
My laggard, and I'll say it plainly: down about 17% here. Planet got caught in the broad space-sector unwind that started when the SpaceX post-IPO froth came out in June, and July gave it no relief even as the contract wins kept coming (a Scottish Government AI-monitoring selection, an Isar launch agreement, a new London office). The fundamentals are not the problem: record revenue up 42% year over year, defense and intelligence demand growing more than 65%, guidance raised, EBITDA turning positive. Against a roughly $40 street target this looks cheap. I expected it to grind back toward its highs faster than it has. Holding.

 $SIVE · 27%
The photonics bottleneck bet in the short book. July was a lock-up month: the April placement's lock-up expired on July 16 and a holder (Headwaters) sold into it, which capped the stock. It held up fine against my cost, down under 1%. The reason to own it is unchanged: III-V lasers and external light-source modules for AI data centers, a pending US dual listing that would open it to American institutions, and a Northland top-pick tag in photonics. This is a volatile Swedish micro-cap (the 52-week range runs from under 3 SEK to 110 SEK), and the production timelines with $POET and O-Net are the risk to watch. Holding into the August 27 report.

 $SPCX · 1%
Still a 1%-share placeholder, not a conviction bet, and it is red: down about 13%. SpaceX joined the Nasdaq-100 on July 7, which forced a wave of index buying into a stock with barely any float, but the post-IPO air kept coming out through July and the stock drifted back toward its $135 offer price. The business is not the question (Q2 revenue was $7.8B, Starlink is past 10 million subscribers, and it is cash-flow positive). The entry price is. I bought on the IPO-day to tell my grandkids a story in 30-years from now. Holding the position. Might add in the future.

MACRO THOUGHTS FOR AUGUST

July was two months in a trench coat. The first half traded off genuine disinflation relief, with June CPI printing its biggest monthly drop since 2020 and the market briefly believing the Fed was done. The back half was a forced-selling event in the AI complex, and the clearest fingerprint on it was the Situational Awareness fund blowing up and liquidating its entire book into a thin late-summer tape. When a crowded trade unwinds like that, quality gets sold alongside the junk. Most of my book got sold for reasons that had nothing to do with my book. I even made a post about this, where I wrote; July is technical, not fundamental.

That is the distinction that matters. This was positioning, not fundamentals. The structural demand under AI infrastructure, power, photonics, launch and defense did not change in the last week of July. Contracts did not get cancelled. Guidance got raised, not cut, across the whole sector.

August is all about earnings. So far earnings across AI sector confirm that capex is still converting into revenue and backlog, meaning the names that got liquidated in late July are the ones that snap back hardest which is also what we've seen.

On the macro, the one number that matters is inflation. The debate this year is a hike versus a hold, not a cut, and every cool print pushes the September FOMC further toward a pause. CPI for July came out in line. This is the KEY things I'm watching going forward the next couple of months. September is mid-term month. As of now I'm still 100% in the market. I'm considering raising 10-20% in cash. But I haven't decided fully yet. I expect FED to hold the rates when September is coming as things are looking right now.

My positions have not changed. My overall conviction has not changed. July shook out the tourists.

Quick note before you go:

Nothing in this update is financial advice. I share what I'm seeing, thinking, and doing, but your situation is different from mine.

Please do your own research, size your positions to your own risk tolerance, and never invest more than you can afford to lose.
