💥 Luxury Real Estate News 💥
 Jeff Bezos Is Getting A New Neighbor In Billionaires Bunker

An empty lot on Indian Creek Island, Miami-Dade County’s “billionaire bunker,” sold on Monday for $105 million, a record price for a property on the island. The seller is Mikhail Peleg, a German developer and investor living in Switzerland who “exclusively buys top-tier real estate at the highest prices,” according to Ilya Reznik, the broker who represented him in the deal. Reznik declined to share details about the buyer, citing a non-disclosure agreement.

Strategically, it’s the best piece of land in Miami,” says Reznik, noting that the lot faces Biscayne Bay, to the west. “It’s a new opportunity for somebody to create a really beautiful mansion,” on what he claims is Miami’s “most secure island.”

The exorbitant price for the property can in part be chalked up to the fact that the lot sits on an exclusive island that is home to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Donald Trump’s daughter Ivanka and her husband Jared Kushner, and retired NFL star Tom Brady, among other high-profile residents. In fact, it borders two of Bezos’ similarly sized properties, which he purchased for $68 million and $79 million, respectively, in 2023.

Six months ago, the seller put the 1.84-acre lot on the market for an even bigger sum: $200 million. Although it sold for much lower than that, the $105 million deal is still extremely expensive—and beat out the island’s previous sale record of $87 million, which Bezos paid in May 2024 when he bought a third property on the island to live in while renovating the first two.

Peleg, the German investor, initially bought the lot with the intention of building a home there, but decided to sell because he no longer planned to come to the U.S., according to Reznik. The dramatic runup in prices on Indian Creek also influenced his decision. “My client figured now’s the right time to sell the property,” the seller’s lawyer Daniel Rudoy told Forbes in January. “He’s a savvy investor.”
On the first day the lot was listed back in January, potential buyers put in a couple of offers around $100 million, according to Reznik. Those offers were met with no response in the hopes of something even higher. As of January 6, six or seven potential buyers had seen the property, with additional offers expected to come in “very soon,” Rudoy told Forbes at the time.

As the sale process progressed, though, offers close to the original, attention-grabbing $200 million did not materialize. “Even if you want more, but nobody pays, it’s not gonna happen. But I think it’s one of the most expensive lots ever sold in Miami,” Reznik says. Peleg’s lawyer Rudoy described it as a “heavily-negotiated transaction.”

The $105 million deal—nearly four times the $27.5 million Peleg paid for the property in 2018—was paid in cash, according to Reznik. In 2023, Peleg took out a $20 million mortgage on the property; the loan was refinanced and expanded last December to $41 million and transferred to an entity connected to British billionaires David and Simon Reuben. A representative for the Reubens declined to comment. (SMM Sunny Holdings, an LLC that lists Mikhail and Marina Peleg as authorized agents and two Belize-based companies as shareholders, owned the property and its related loans.)
Other factors that make Indian Creek so attractive to buyers are its security and privacy. The island has its own police force and is patrolled by sea and air. “It’s like a fortress,” says Rudoy.
Compared to the national average for luxury real estate, where prices have increased by close to 50% over the past four years, per Realtor com, Indian Creek homes went from selling for single-digit millions in the early 2000s to an average of $30 million in the 2010s to Bezos’ $87 million purchase last year. 

Via Forbes

text:
🛠️ Dear Builders: Dominion 2026 Is the Opportunity You've Been Waiting For
Most people watching Dominion this week are looking at it as traders or speculators. They're tracking token prices, watching domain launches go live on stage, and getting excited about a new narrative.

That's fine. But if you're a developer a builder you should be looking at this event through a completely different lens.

Because what Dominion 2026 really represents is the opening of a construction site. And right now, almost nobody is building on it.

The Problem With Most "New Primitives" in Crypto
Every cycle, a new primitive gets announced. Restaking. Intent based architectures. Omnichain tokens. And every cycle, the first builders to actually ship production grade apps on top of that primitive end up capturing the majority of the value.

DomainFi is the next primitive. Doma is the protocol underneath it. And the window to be an early builder is open right now not in six months, not after the infrastructure matures further.

The $360 billion domain industry has no DeFi rails. None. That's not a slight exaggeration it's just true. You cannot go to any DEX and swap domain exposure. You cannot go to any lending protocol and post a premium domain as collateral. You cannot fractionalize a high value domain like crypto.ai or trading.com and sell shares of it on chain. None of these products exist.

Every single one of them is a Forge application waiting to be built.

What the Forge Program Actually Is?
Doma's Forge program is a $1M USDC grant pool, backed by Paradigm, Coinbase, and Maelstrom, specifically designed to fund the first generation of DomainFi applications.

This isn't a generic ecosystem fund where you pitch a vague idea and wait six months for a committee decision. Forge comes with SDK access, direct mentorship from the Doma core team, and the kind of infrastructure support that actually matters when you're building on a new protocol.

The SDK itself is built around a key design principle: integrate once, run everywhere. Doma Chain handles cross chain coordination via ERC7786 messaging, which means the app you build isn't locked to a single network. Your domain DEX works on Base. The same protocol serves Solana users. The same collateral protocol functions on Ethereum. You write the application logic once; Doma handles the bridging and settlement across chains.

Five App Categories Nobody Has Built Yet
Here's the honest state of DomainFi today: the primitive exists, the infrastructure is live, and the application layer is essentially empty. That's where builders come in.

The most obvious categories to build in right now:

A domain trading marketplace with real on chain settlement is the most obvious gap. Afternic and Sedo process billions in domain trades every year, all via manual OTC processes with escrow intermediaries. A decentralized exchange with Doma tokenized domains as assets would be the first of its kind.

Collateral lending against domain portfolios is another entirely open field. Premium domains are verifiable, scarce digital assets with real appraisal markets behind them. A lending protocol that accepts domain collateral would unlock liquidity for domain investors who currently hold illiquid assets worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Fractional ownership of high value domains is more experimental but potentially the highest upside play. Casino.com reportedly sold for $5.5 million. What if a thousand people could own a fractional stake in the next mega domain? That's a product Doma can now support that literally couldn't exist before.

Domain native analytics and discovery tools, portfolio dashboards, and yield strategies on domain royalties are all further down the stack but every mature DeFi vertical has an ecosystem of tooling built around it, and DomainFi will need the same.

Why Dominion Is the Moment to Start?
Timing matters more than most builders admit. The window to be a credible early mover on a new primitive is narrow. Too early, and the infrastructure isn't ready. Too late, and you're competing against entrenched players with distribution advantages.

Dominion 2026 is the exact moment when Doma crosses from "interesting infrastructure being built" to "live protocol with real domains tokenizing on stage in front of an audience." The narrative is moving from testnet to mainnet. The registrar integrations are real. The chains are connected.

If you start building now, you're not building speculatively you're building on a foundation that already works. And if you debut at Dominion or ship in the weeks after it, you're doing so at the moment of maximum attention and minimum competition.

That combination doesn't last long.

Where to Start Right Now?
If this resonates, the path is straightforward:

Start with the docs at docs.doma.xyz the architecture is well documented and the SDK is accessible. Get a feel for how domain tokenization actually works under the hood, and where the application layer hooks in.

Explore the testnet at start.doma.xyz . Build a throwaway prototype. Understand what becomes possible when a domain is on chain.

Then apply for Forge at doma.xyz/forge . The $1M USDC pool is real, the backing is credible, and the upside for being an early builder on a new $360B market is asymmetric.

Dominion is happening now. The construction site is open. The question is whether you're watching from the stands or picking up tools.

 @domaprotocol @d3inc @SDMikeCM #Dominion2026 #DomainFi #Doma #BuildOnDoma

🎉 Happy New Year, everyone!

Asia and Oceania are the first regions in the world to welcome 2026, and from where I am, there’s just one hour left before saying goodbye to 2025.

Looking back, 2025 was a truly special year for me.
I achieved my highest annual income ever, and for the first time in nearly 15 years, revenue from domain sales surpassed all of my other income sources combined.

📊 2025 domain sales summary:
• 30 domains sold
• $250,000+ USD in total sales
• ~80% via Afternic, with the remaining ~20% through Sedo and other channels
Some notable deals:
• NNet․com — $80,000
• Satay․com — $50,000
• Kanav․com — $22,000
• _______.com — $100,000 LTO (60-month agreement with a meme coin project; only 2 payments made, ~$4K total, then stopped)
• _______.com — $80,000 LTO (12-month plan, still ongoing)
• Plus 20+ four-figure sales

For comparison, my total domain sales in 2024 were ~$100,000, so 2025 grew by over +250% YoY 🚀

💻 2025 was also a year of experimentation.
I went all-in on vibe coding and actively built and launched:
 Gomoku.com , Fanorona.com , Planisphere.com , SoLucky.com , SpeedQuiz.com (and more)

One milestone I’m especially proud of:
🎯 Gomoku.com surpassed 1,000,000 games played before the end of 2025.

In the coming year, I’ll be doubling down even more on Domain-Driven Development.

🌍 On another front, I continued developing geo .com domains into travel websites.

In 2025, this side project reached a new milestone:
✨ Annual travel affiliate revenue exceeded four figures USD for the first time.

While it’s still small compared to my other income streams, I firmly believe that with continued compounding, this will become a stable and sustainable long-tail revenue source.

✈️ To close out the year, my final domain acquisition of 2025 was JordanTravel․com.

I now own ~20 Country+Travel․com domains, about half of which were acquired in 2025.

In 2026, I’ll gradually start bringing these domains online one by one.

Wishing everyone a fantastic 2026 —
📈 strong growth,
💰 great sales,
and many domain wins ahead!

text:
SOLD

 Love.now for $79,499 USD

Big congrats to the buyer — this is a remarkable name to own!

The 9-month young .Now TLD is proving itself to be one of the most—if not the most—exciting gTLDs ever. 

Think of it this way: what TLD could have entered the market late 2024, with some much competition—so many well-established TLDs—and score:

1) a $37,500 sale in less than 2 months
2) a $79,499 sale in less than 9 months

Both organic inbound sales.

And for that, a TLD not tied to any hyped-up trend – a gTLD in the truest sense of the G, like .Com.

Only .Now. We don't see any other TLD that could've made it work.

But – we think no one really sees .Now's true potential yet. We'll share this: for about two months we've had an idea for .Now – a vision. And with it, a special promo post where we'll lay it out. It's probably dropping in September or October. Stay tuned.

The sale happened on @sedo via the Buy Now option. The buyer was referred by Porkbun but ultimately chose Spaceship as their registrar. It will be submitted to DN Journal and NameBio shortly.

Atom​.com wasn't part of this sale – but shoutout to @atomHQ for spotting .Now's potential early and backing it from the start.

As much as we love our account manager at GoDaddy​.com, and we wish every domainer had someone as caring as Mauli in their corner: GoDaddy and Afternic have been a big disappointment. We don't think they've ever had more requests to add a TLD than they've had for .Now – from all of us. Despite that, they weren't there to support us in the first—and often the most difficult—year.

To their credit, registrars like 101domain, Dynadot, Namecheap, Spaceship, and Porkbun stepped up.

Has to be said: the rapid success of .Now wouldn't be possible without the steady progress new gTLDs have made over the years. It's impressive: in June alone, we sold 15 gTLD domains. For June, that's an unprecedented result. People want creative, memorable premium names for their businesses – a necessity in today's fast-paced world.

.Now investors – don't miss our post tomorrow (or shortly after). We just picked up another .Now via BIN on Atom (seller should be notified soon). And yes – we'll be buying more.

Once again, big congrats to the buyer on acquiring Love.now .

text:
I invested in (and told you to invest in $INFQ when it was still $CCCX . Here’s why:

 $INFQ (Infleqtion) stands out as the leading quantum computing company right now:

Infleqtion (NYSE: INFQ, formerly ColdQuanta) is the first neutral-atom quantum company to go public (Feb 2026 via SPAC). It operates a full-stack neutral-atom platform for computing, networking, sensing, and software. Neutral atoms (typically rubidium/cesium held in optical tweezers and manipulated by lasers) offer key advantages: easier scaling to large qubit arrays, long coherence times, all-to-all connectivity potential, and operation without extreme cryogenic requirements like superconducting systems. infleqtion.com 
Key technical leadership points:
• Demonstrated the world’s largest neutral-atom array: ~1,600 physical qubits.
• Industry-leading entangling (CZ) gate fidelity for neutral atoms: 99.73% (user-facing/post-selected higher in some cases), with recent dual-species (Rb-Cs) gates and theory work pointing toward >99.9%. This is critical because higher fidelity reduces the overhead needed for error correction. infleqtion.com 
• Delivered the UK’s only operational 100-qubit neutral-atom system (Sqale platform) and demonstrated real-world logical qubit applications, including a materials science use case in collaboration with NVIDIA—the first of its kind using logical qubits.
• Roadmap: Targeting 30+ logical qubits in 2026 and 100+ by 2028, with a path to fault-tolerant, utility-scale systems. They’ve already hit milestones like 12 logical qubits (error-detected) ahead of schedule in some reports. thequantuminsider.com 

Commercial and financial edge:
• Unlike pure-play computing companies still deep in cash-burn R&D with minimal revenue, Infleqtion has a diversified portfolio. It generates real revenue today from quantum sensors (optical clocks, RF receivers, inertial/gravimetric sensors) sold to governments, military, NASA, and commercial clients. These are deployable products addressing real needs like precision timing and GPS-denied navigation.
• Well-capitalized post-IPO (> $550M funding) plus a fresh $100M Letter of Intent from the U.S. Department of Commerce CHIPS program (announced May 2026) specifically to accelerate U.S. neutral-atom quantum leadership. businesswire.com 
• Proprietary Superstaq software optimizes circuits across hardware, giving it a full-stack moat.

Why this makes INFQ clearly leading compared to peers:
• Scalability edge over IonQ/Quantinuum (trapped-ion): Trapped ions have excellent fidelity (IonQ has hit 99.99% two-qubit in some reports), but packing and controlling large numbers of ions is harder due to charge interactions and shuttling. Neutral atoms scale more naturally to thousands of qubits via optical lattices/tweezers. indexbox.io 
• Practical advantages over IBM/Rigetti (superconducting): Those require massive dilution refrigerators and face manufacturing bottlenecks at traditional fabs. Neutral-atom systems leverage more optics/laser-based manufacturing and can operate in less extreme conditions.
• Revenue + government backing reduces risk: Most quantum pure-plays are pre-revenue or low-revenue. INFQ’s sensor business provides a bridge to profitability while the computing side matures. The recent CHIPS funding and defense contracts signal strong U.S. strategic prioritization.
• Broader ecosystem: Partnerships (NVIDIA), international presence, and a platform spanning compute + sensing/networking position it for hybrid quantum-classical applications sooner

text:
🚨Quantum Breakthrough…
Not a Quantum Break-In 🔐⚛️

It's true that China has reportedly sold and delivered a neutral-atom quantum computer (Hanyuan-1). That’s real — and strategically important.

Reporting from @SCMPNews , @QuantumDaily , and @QuantumReport says sales exceed ¥40M ($5.6M), including delivery to a China Mobile subsidiary and an overseas order (Pakistan). The system uses neutral atoms as qubits and doesn’t require cryogenic cooling — a real engineering advantage.

☝🏼 Now the reality check:

🧠 It’s a commercialization milestone.
❌ It cannot break modern encryption.
❌ It’s not fault-tolerant.
❌ It’s not consumer quantum computing.

A ~100-qubit machine is nowhere near the millions of error-corrected qubits needed to crack RSA-2048.

Also, “world’s first atomic quantum computer” is overstated. Companies like QuEra and Atom Computing have operated neutral-atom systems for years (mostly via cloud access).

⚠️ So what is this?

A meaningful step in the long quantum race.
Not a crypto apocalypse. ⚛️

Commercial milestone? Yes.
Encryption breaker? No.
Geopolitically relevant? Absolutely.

Sources:

 scmp.com/news/china/science/… 

 thequantuminsider.com/2025/1… 

 quantumcomputingreport.com/c…

text:
Domain Investing: Keeping Up with Trends

It’s hard to keep track of what’s trending and what isn’t in the fast-moving world of tech and AI. Just a few weeks ago, while I was in #Nigeria , I heard the term "OpenClaw" for the first time. According to Wikipedia, OpenClaw is a free and open-source autonomous AI agent developed by Peter Steinberger. As of February/March 2026, several variants of the “Claw” concept are already appearing—names like ZeroClaw, PicoClaw, and NanoBot.

Then, a few days later, I noticed on @NameBio that OpenClaw..org reportedly sold via Spaceship for $55,000. That caught my attention.

Around the same time, I read that Mark Zuckerberg had acquired MoltBook for an undisclosed amount. Honestly, I had never even heard of MoltBook until I saw the article. Shortly after, I discovered there’s an AI agent sub-project called MoltBuilds. And just like the “Claw” naming pattern, it’s probably only a matter of time before more "Molt" variations appear.

Then today—only a few hours ago—I heard about another AI agent called Livebook. According to Hugging Face, Livebook is an open-source tool for writing interactive code notebooks in Elixir. It’s part of a growing ecosystem of Elixir tools for numerical computing, data science, and machine learning. Then you have "Muta," a conversation for a different day.

Another thing I’ve started noticing is a trend around the word "Book." According to Medium, the concept of a “book”—often framed as a playbook, guide, or even a “Bible” for agentic AI—has become popular because it provides structured guidance in a rapidly evolving field.

So what’s the takeaway?

Trends appear fast, evolve quickly, and sometimes disappear just as fast. As domain investors, spotting them early can be exciting—but it also comes with risk. The truth is, it’s very difficult to know which trend will produce the best ROI.

If you decide to invest in trend-based domains, do it carefully and strategically. There is definitely money to be made riding trends—but timing, judgment, and discipline matter.

For full transparency, I’ve also picked up a few names in this space, including MetalClaw..com, MoltBuilds..com, LiveBook..co, MutaBots..com, and others.

The AI naming wave is still forming, and new ideas are appearing almost daily. For #domain investors—especially newcomers—the key is to stay curious, watch the market, and be ready when opportunity appears.

In this industry, sometimes the biggest wins come from seeing a trend just a little earlier than everyone else.

🎉Ai Ai Ai and Ai 🎉

I just sold a domain! 🥳
 Hold time: 35 months
 Cost: $11 + renewals

This is a one-word + AI, category-defining domain very relevant in the biotech industry. Yes, I know many will say I super undersold it — Dynadot appraisal gave it a $25K value, and some might price it at $50K. But hey, it only cost me $11 when I registered it at the end of 2022, right when the ChatGPT and AI buzz started, and I’m happy with the funds.
The only thing I regret is that the lander at Spaceship was priced the same as at Afternic. I didn’t update it — otherwise I could have priced higher at Afternic and paid no commission if the buyer chose that route, or kept more funds in my pocket if he bought via Spaceship.

This domain was not acquired by a domainer, because I had it listed for $2K at Porkbun and Atom — there’s no way they missed that.

What’s really interesting is that I submitted this domain months ago to Atom Premium, it only got approved two weeks ago for $7K (I haven’t approved it yet), and today — boom — it sold. No way this is a coincidence; they must have known something. The timeframe is too narrow.🤔

Today was the first time I took my laptop to the beach, and domaining in front of the sea is something else — great energy! While managing my portfolio and writing a different post for today, I saw many emails from Porkbun related to one of my domains being transferred out:

"We have received a successful Afternic Fast Transfer command for your domain."

In between, I missed the Afternic “congrats” email and thought, “Shit, a f***er is stealing my domain!” 😅
Then I found the congrats email.

I’m officially adopting the beach as my everyday office now! 🌴😎🌊

text:
99.999% of the data we publish is not "discovered" by other people. It is observed by us. In rare instances it is reported by one of the parties, who either don't care about credit or put their own site as the venue for attribution.

As much as I respect you and your immense contribution to the discovery of many of history's most important domain sales, I'm not adding a database column just to cite the third-party sales you (or in extremely rare cases someone else) found. It would only be populated for one in every 100,000 sales or less.

I haven't ever written a single article about anything you found, and never wrote a dedicated social media post about it.

I just quietly add it with the old date (which I often have to look up myself), so it can come up in search.

It's already buried in nearly 7 million results and not pulling any attention away from you. And then I at least like and/or comment on your post, or sometimes repost it (without comment) depending on the situation.

To lump me in with everyone who is racing to leech attention away from you is beyond ridiculous.

Yes, we try to prevent people from stealing the whole database. But how many times have you seen me complaining about someone posting data we collected without attribution? It's zero. Even when it is our own personal sales that we only ever reported on NameBio, and they couldn't possibly have gotten it anywhere else. And it happens daily, not a few times per year.

I understand your frustration, but you don't need to take it out on me. I spent a few hours digging into the sale you mentioned, at your invitation, and you spat in my face when I tried to compare notes with you. Feel better?
name: NameBio

text:
Random Sunday Thoughts #215

1. The past few days were slightly quieter for me from a transaction standpoint, as we worked towards closing some exciting deals this week. There was no lull in the full court press talking to prospects on the world's most valuable domains that we represent. High level discussions have been nonstop since November with no slow down in site. These are the most progressive and informed conversations I can recall having in my 28+ years of investing in and brokering domain names. For years, many of my peers and I spent an enormous amount of time educating founders, investors, and management teams, at companies ranging from early stage startups to Fortune 100 corporations, about the strategic importance of exact match and category defining domain names. The awareness is taking hold, the urgency is real, and the recognition that owning your exact match brand, category domain is a foundational business decision, not a vanity purchase, has never been more widespread. It is fantastic to see it taking hold at this level. 

2. Further to that point, I saw at least two founders post publicly about their domain acquisitions on X this week, and both are perfect illustrations of exactly what I am talking about. The first was the founder of Flint, who posted simply: "we dropped the try, now at Flint .com. It's cleaner that way." That one line says everything.They get the game changing strategic importance, their customers know what it means, and to the market its intuitive. TryFlint becomes Flint .com and the brand instantly becomes more credible, more permanent, and more memorable. Shout out to Elliot Silver for flagging this one, nitter.poast.org/michlimlim/status/2057… . The second was Harper Insurance, which upgraded to Harper .com after securing a $47 million Series A. This is the pattern I see consistently; a company raises a significant round, and one of the first strategic decisions they make is to acquire their exact-match domain. It is not a coincidence. The investors writing those checks increasingly understand that the domain is part of the brand infrastructure they are funding. A $47 million business operating on a suboptimal domain is leaving brand equity on the table every single day. Both of these are quiet announcements that most people scroll past. But to me they are data points in a much larger trend, and the trend is accelerating. In the next several days, as has been the case all year, we will upgrade 3 more emerging and market leading brands to their exact match domains, all mid 7 figure transactions, that will be the smartest  strategic investment these companies make to date. 

3.  I am a hard core sports lover, but I have never been much of a soccer fan. My son recently introduced me to Arsenal and its clever, wildly dedicated fans. They have reminded me that whomever you root for and whatever you do, there is no replacement for being passionate. I can't wait to experience the World Cup this summer!

Until Next Week #domains
name: Andrew Miller

text:
Landed in Las Vegas for Adobe Summit 2026.

This week I'll be meeting with teams from the Magnificent 7 and Fortune 500 companies about something most enterprises still treat as an afterthought: how a category-defining domain name elevates a brand, a subsidiary launch, or a new product rollout much more than C-level teams realize.

I'll be discussing domain names like AIART.COM , HARDWARE.COM , CHATBOTS.COM , GENERATIVE.COM — category-defining domains from GoDaddy's DomainNames.com brokerage. When executed properly, these assets can generate $100M+ enterprise brand value over the long-term.

A thought I keep returning to:

Every interaction in a deal is a real-time win-rate calculation.

The email domain you send from. The way your profile reads. Your tone. Your response time. The clothes you walk into the room wearing. None of these are decisive on their own. All of them move the percentage.

One of my habits — and it sounds trivial until you practice it — is negotiating hotel room upgrades. Not because I want a better room. Because it's a zero-risk environment to stay sharp on the small decisions that compound in high-stakes negotiations.

Today's version, after I landed:

→ Studied the available inventory before approaching the desk
→ Walked up with a genuine compliment about the property
→ Used staff names
→ Changed out of flight clothes into a suit before the conversation

None of those moves, in isolation, wins anything. Together, they shift the percentage enough to matter. The same principle governs every domain transaction I've ever worked on: the deal is rarely decided by one variable. It's decided by the accumulation of small ones.

Now, thanks to a win at today's front-desk negotiation, I can watch the Las Vegas Sphere run Adobe creative — AI art, the word "Generate" on loop — and prepare for the conference, where the same principle plays out on a much larger stage.

Two questions worth sitting with:

For Domain Owners → How is your asset being positioned, by whom, and what does a serious buyer perceive when they encounter it?

For Executives & Entrepreneurs → Your domain is the first impression your brand makes to the world, make it count.

P.S. If you're in Vegas this week, keep an eye out for GoDaddy's "Gaggle" of Geese on the Strip and some fun outfits that get attention. I'm genuinely very excited about GoDaddy's brand strength and innovative DomainNames.com promotions we have planned this week to connect the right ultra-premium domains with the right buyers #AdobeSummit

text:
I don't think your takeaway is correct here. It isn't proof that your domains bring the sales, in fact multiple large portfolios confirm that distribution networks produce a majority of sales. Landers generally only account for about 35-40% of volume.

Here's a recent discussion on de-listing from marketplaces, which also links to another older post about the makeup of aftermarket sales in the comments:

 nitter.poast.org/NameBio/status/2038913… 

Assuming you still list at Afternic, it's only proof that Sedo MLS provides very little extra coverage above Afternic DLS, and most partners of both prioritize Afternic listings.

We list a majority of our ~75k portfolio at Sedo, while being fully listed and majority landed at Afternic, and Sedo produces about 1 sale per year for every 4-5k names listed. Abysmal, but still five-figures per year in extra revenue that we likely wouldn't have had otherwise.

It's definitely a burden to keep multiple marketplaces up to date, and depending on portfolio size and your average sale price, I could definitely see an argument for de-listing from marketplaces that are under-performing.

So you're likely making the right call and won't regret it. Statistically with 1,750 listings you should only get a Sedo sale once every other year at best.

But I wouldn't jump to the conclusion that most sales come from the domain itself, because I guarantee you that isn't true.
name: NameBio

text:
🚨 FREE Access to Retail Keyword Stats 🚨

We just launched one of the most valuable things we've ever built, and we're giving it away completely for free, no registration required!

It's an API endpoint that lets you search a keyword, and it gives you stats on how that keyword performs in Retail sales when it is the exact SLD, at the start, at the end, and somewhere in the middle.

For each keyword position it will tell you the number of sales, total dollar volume, average price, highest price, and standard deviation.

You can also download the entire list of more than 100k unique keywords, including all placements and stats.

This not only helps you identify valuable keywords, it also helps you understand programmatically which position is better for each one.

For example, look at the attached screenshot of a search on "agent". You can instantly see that it has a higher sales velocity at the end rather than at the start. But you can also quickly see that being at the start results in a 33% higher average sale price than at the end.

This information is extremely valuable for domain spinners, appraisers, and AI agents, to better understand keyword values in Retail sales.

Please note: unlike the Placement search on our homepage, these placements are mutually exclusive. On our site, searching "shop" could return shop․net if you search Exact, At the Start, At the End, or In the Middle. We generally err on the side of showing you something that might potentially be of interest.

But in this tool a sale of Shop․net would only contribute to the "Exact" stats, favoring precision over all else.

Enjoy! Link is in the comments 👇

text:
ABM just dropped one of the most valuable pieces of knowledge that has ever been shared in the domain industry, and most people are going to miss it because it was a reply to a reply.

In August of last year I did a pretty lengthy post breaking down the realities of the aftermarket, trying to help people understand what percentage of sales come directly from "for sale" landing pages, what percentage come from distribution networks, and of the network sales which come from each major distribution partner.

The reason I did that was to show the math on what happens if you list at Afternic and use their landers, versus using other landers with discounted commissions. What I essentially proved was that even if the alt lander has a 0% commission, you still end up worse off due to Afternic's commission penalty for not using their landers.

I'll link to that post in the replies if you want to do a deep dive and really understand the full picture. But in short, around 60-65% of domain sales come from Afternic DLS and Sedo MLS (the distribution networks), and the remaining 35-40% come from the "for sale" landers directly. This is confirmed by multiple large portfolio holders.

There were still two important questions that I was unable to answer though:

The first is what would happen if you fully delisted from Afternic, so they couldn't sell your domains at the 25-30% punitive rate while using alt landers. The theory a lot of people shared was that the network buyers, not being able to find you on the network, would still find you by typing in the domain.

I wasn't buying it. Sure, it'll happen sometimes, but I was almost certain it would be an extreme minority, and the move would be a major net negative.

My theory was that a vast majority of network buyers were either shown your domain as an alternative to what they were actually searching, or when brainstorming a bunch of different domains. And they wouldn't have found it without the network, because they weren't typing domains into their browser's address bar to check availability. They were using a registrar.

But I couldn't prove it because I've never fully delisted from Afternic and Sedo to find out, and I didn't know anyone who has and then talked about it. Until now.

Thanks to ABM we now have that missing piece of the puzzle; he said sales dropped 50% by delisting. That means if his sales breakdown was 40% landers 60% network, only 17% of network buyers would buy directly if it wasn't on the network. Or if his breakdown was 35% landers and 65% network, only 23% would buy directly if it wasn't on the network.

Let that sink in. Between 77% and 83% of network buyers will NOT buy your domain directly from your discount-commission landers if you are not on the distribution networks. If you scroll up on ABM's reply below, you'll see it was a reply to a comment I made predicting this "50% drop" outcome pretty much on the nose.

The second looming question is what would happen if you raised your prices on Afternic and Sedo to offset the higher commissions and then used your own landers with low or no commissions offering the domain at a lower price. A lot of people think this is "free money" for network sales by baking in the commission.

But I know that it will, for the most part, hurt your sell-through rate quite a bit. I can't quantify it, but I suspect it would almost definitely more than offset the commission penalties you were hoping to recoup. It just seems logical, if you hurt your STR on 65% of your sales to get a slightly better commission on 35% of your sales, you're probably going to lose.

Except in the situation where most of your domains are priced below $2k; at that level you can raise prices without affecting the demand curve.

I selfishly hope ABM will test this next by relisting at Afternic and Sedo, but at higher prices than shown on his NamePros Landers; enough that he would net the same wherever it sells.

That would answer the last remaining question surrounding the economics of the domain aftermarket: is it even possible to offset a commission by raising prices?

My money is on "no". But once we know that, we'd be able to fully model out all possible outcomes and make perfectly informed decisions to maximize revenue based on all the various marketplace commission structures and "for sale" lander options.

Regardless, I hope ABM stops this delisting experiment for both his and Jamie's sake. It's already been running long enough to learn everything there is to learn from it.

It's painfully obvious that a 50% drop in sales to save 15-20% on commission isn't a winning move. Let's say he was doing $1 million in sales a year and netting $800k after commission. Now he would have about $500k in sales, netting maybe $480k after transaction costs. That means he probably spent around $320k to learn this lesson.

We all owe ABM an enormous debt of gratitude for generously sharing what he learned with everyone.

text:
I can't overstate how important this piece of advice is. We all get lowball offers, but how you respond can make a huge difference.

One time I received a $250 opening offer for a .org that I had on a "make offer" lander. I had purchased it for four-figures and expected mid five-figures.

Instead of firing off a snarky response, I responded saying thanks for the offer but we're too far apart, and showed a dozen close comps of .orgs selling for five and even six figures.

He responded back saying he was the buyer for many of those comps I had shown him. He added that he knew the value, but hey, he had to start somewhere. We ended up closing at $30,000 after a little bit of back-and-forth.

The domain wasn't something he had to have, he just wanted it for his collection, and it still isn't developed to this day. So if I had responded like a jerk or just ignored him entirely I'm pretty sure he would have moved on and found something else.

We also saw this recently when @dnx shared one of Josh's negotiations:

 nitter.poast.org/dnx/status/19908664574… 

He received a $5,000 offer on a name he was expecting $100,000 for. Instead of being rude he responded professionally, and ended up closing a deal at $52,700. They probably weren't bluffing and were actually considering alternatives, so if he was a difficult person to deal with they might have walked.

Watch the video all the way to the end, because it also serves as a great reminder to follow up multiple times. I needed that, it appears that I'm too quick to close a lead when it seems obvious that it won't go anywhere.
name: NameBio

text:
Most people don't know that because it isn't true 😅 NameBio was founded on November 15, 2006 by Justin Allen (aka Spade). Then Adam bought it from him in 2011 (not 2009) and ran it with the McKegney brothers of DomainAgents fame for a few years.

In late 2014 I (Michael) noticed that several months had passed with all the data feeds being broken. Not wanting to see my favorite site go away, I reached out to Adam and asked if I could take over development and rebuild it from scratch.

I've spent the past 11 years and counting, working seven days a week without a single day off, growing it from a couple hundred thousand sales records to more than 6 million. Approximately 95% of the data we have today was added during my tenure.

Many people deserve thanks for their contributions these past 19 years; including Justin for founding it and Adam, Ryan, and Phil for keeping it afloat.

And as your multiple recent odes to Ron Jackson correctly noted, he pioneered the tracking and charting of domain sales in the first place.

I'm looking forward to NameBio turning 20 next year, and I'm honored that I could be a part of it for so long.

text:
Swetha's STR is low, the most sales she ever had in a year was 141 which works out to about 0.5%. That means if you own one xyz, the expected time to sell is about 200 years.

At her average selling price of around $20k, renewals would have to average less than $100 just for her to break even.

Yours was $540 per year, so statistically you should expect to pay $108,000 in renewals before it would sell, on top of the $6k acquisition price.

Even if you were hoping to sell it for $114k (almost six times Swetha's average) that would just be a break-even expected value.

This was essentially a very expensive lottery ticket with no burn-down value to the wholesale market due to the renewal.

I don't even think it's a good empty vessel for a brand, not many companies call themselves just "Luxury." It's too generic and more commonly an adjective than a noun, which begs people to react with "luxury what?" not "wow, nice brand". Look how the .com is used.

But the larger issue is that you didn't pick something which would work well for crypto and Web3, which are the types of companies that adopted the TLD. Luxury relates well to the physical world (cars, apartments, fashion, travel) not intangibles like crypto, NFTs, or other blockchain projects.

People need to understand that Swetha is playing a large numbers game with standard renewals, and as long as her average selling price is more than $3k she's guaranteed to win. Nobody else can play that game now because premium renewals will eat you alive. Negari cut out the middle man, which is all of us... let him.

Other investors who had random sales despite doing it on a small scale stacked the odds in their favor as much as they could. They had low acquisition cost and renewal prices, owned enough of them that they could reasonably expect a sale in their lifetime, took the time to understand the buyers and what they might demand, and then got very lucky on top of it.

That's my take on it anyway, as someone with no skin in this TLD.

First of all, thank God. Sold Pcc.ai last month. Thanks to @atomHQ 

I like to share story behind that.

In 2023, I hand-registered PCC.ai and submitted it to @atomHQ Premium. It was initially approved at $3,499, but I felt the AI market was just getting started, so I removed it. Later, I resubmitted it and Atom approved it in the $22k-$45k range. After further market research and a pricing review, I listed it at $77k.

A buyer came in at $50k. Following a negotiation strategy I learned from @TonyNames , I kept my floor at $50k and asked the broker to push higher. The buyer ultimately agreed to $70,000.

Huge thanks to the #domain community for all the knowledge shared along the way, and special thanks to @MichaelCyger , whose comment on my first sale gave me the confidence to keep going.

Sometimes the biggest difference between a $3,499 sale and a $70,000 sale is having the patience and conviction to hold the right asset.

text:
The STR of expired domains is far from 100%, you're thinking purely of backorder auctions. Obviously the STR of preorders will always be 100%, that isn't a function of price though.

But if you look at registrars such as GoDaddy, Dynadot, Namecheap, etc. that auction expired inventory before it gets deleted, where no backorder is required, a very large percentage end without bids despite not having reserves.

Yes, STR is absolutely a function of price. But that curve is also shifted and shaped by quality. As you noted, a low enough quality domain will have a 0% STR at any price. Hence so many no-reserve expired auctions ending without bids.

At the other extreme, the quality of domains you own would have a 100% STR even in the five and sometimes six-figure range. In any case it looks more like a step-wise curve.

At the lower end of quality the steps might be at $2.5k, $5k, and $10k but the lowest step is 2% STR. One of your domains might be stepped at $100k, $500k, $1m, and $5m but the lowest step is 100% STR.

Most people are operating much closer to the low end than the high end. In that neighborhood, the curve is shaped and shifted in such a way that there is an absolute cap on STR below which dropping the price does not increase the buyer pool nor the chances of it selling, because you're still bound by demand (or lack thereof).

It makes very close to zero difference if you price an average quality domain at $1,250 or $2,500. This was confirmed by our own testing on tens of thousands of domains over several months, and Atom (Squadhelp at the time) independently observed the same phenomenon months later.

You can't engineer literally any STR on average quality domains simply by adjusting pricing. You would need to open up a new buyer pool by pricing into wholesale liquidation territory, or do outbound, to get it above the natural cap.

There's actually a reason you see 1-2% so often, it isn't a coincidence or domainer lore. It's the upper bound on an average quality portfolio doing passive retail sales with fair pricing in the first step or two of the spectrum.

Even if you send the price all the way into wholesale liquidation territory, it still has an extremely low chance of selling unless you actively promote it. Otherwise you need a domain investor to randomly think of it out of a pool of millions of possible domains, like it more than the thousands of auctions they have to choose from every single day, and pull the trigger within 12 months, which is very unlikely.

At this quality level it's almost entirely a function of time and RNG for which ones hit. As long as the price is in the same ballpark/step, what actually sold would have sold regardless, and it's just a choice of if you'd rather make $1,250 or $2,500 on the sale. Pretty easy decision.

Auction houses and registrars would warehouse the names for retail sale if they could get away with it. Remember Standard Tactics? For some reason the optics on this are worse than them liquidating the names and giving the previous owner nothing, even though it is the same thing.

Same reason most new gTLD registries went for premiums with retail pricing instead of wholesale liquidation. Cut out the domainer middle man.

text:
AI written, but:

The 2026 Commercial Shift: Boston's current policy (Mayor Wu era) is shifting the tax burden heavily onto business property to subsidize residential. If you’re a startup with any hardware or lab gear, your Business Personal Property tax is pegged to the commercial rate—likely $25+ per $1,000 of value—while SF startups effectively pay $0 on the same equipment. It’s an annual tax on your own balance sheet just for existing in the city.

• The "Reuter" Trap (Wage Act): SJC ruled in Reuter v. City of Methuen (2022) that there is zero "good faith" defense for late final pay. If you fire someone at 4:55 PM and don't hand them a physical check or confirm the wire immediately, you’re strictly liable for 3x the total wages, plus their legal fees. SF has wait-time penalties, but MA has a mandatory 3x "nuclear option" for being one day late.

• The 50% Garden Leave Anchor: Since the 2018 non-compete law, you can’t just sign a standard CA-style non-compete (which are void anyway). In MA, to actually enforce one, you have to pay the departing employee 50% of their highest salary for the entire duration (up to 12 months). It makes "protecting the IP" a massive cash-flow liability that CA companies don't have to budget for.

• SaaS vs. Service Tax: MA (6.25%) treats "prewritten software" (SaaS) as a taxable event if the "object of the transaction" is using the software. In CA, SaaS is almost always treated as a non-taxable service. If you're a Boston-based B2B SaaS company, your finance team is dealing with sales tax audits and nexus issues years before an SF peer even thinks about it.

• 201 CMR 17.00 (The WISP Debt): MA is the only state that mandates a "Written Information Security Program" the second you touch a resident's name + SSN/CC. It requires a designated "Security Officer" and mandatory encryption on all mobile devices/laptops by law. It’s "Enterprise-grade" compliance debt forced onto a Seed stage team.

• The Article 80 Grind: If you're building a lab or high-growth HQ over 50k sq ft, you hit Article 80 Large Project Review. This isn't just a permit; it's a 12-18 month "public process" of hearings, community advisory teams, and "mitigation" payments.

• The Pre-2019 Exit Haircut: This was the biggest "gotcha"—MA only followed the 2005 federal code for QSBS, which meant only a 50% exclusion vs. the federal 100%. If you sold for $10M in 2018, you were looking at a ~5% state tax hit on $5M that an SF founder likely didn't pay. We finally aligned in 2019, but for a decade, Boston founders were just lighting 5% of their exit on fire.

• The PFML Cash Drag: In MA, you’re hit with the Paid Family and Medical Leave payroll tax (0.88%) the second you hit 25 "covered individuals"—and in MA, 1099s count toward that head count. Unlike CA where it’s mostly employee-funded, MA forces the employer to pay for the "medical" portion. If you’re a 30-person Seed team, that’s a direct tax on your burn that SF peers don't pay.

• The "Market Rate" Illegal Pay: Under the MA Equal Pay Act (MEPA), "market conditions" is not a legal defense for pay gaps. If you hire a "rockstar" engineer for $220k because that's what it took to close them, but your existing engineers with the same title make $180k, you’re legally liable for the difference + liquidated damages. In SF, you can pay what the market demands; in Boston, your payroll is a litigation target the moment you out-compete for talent.

• The Performance Review Trap: MA law (M.G.L. c. 149, § 52C) requires you to notify an employee within 10 days of putting any "negative" info in their personnel file (even a Slack memo about a missed deadline). If you don't, you can't use it in a termination defense later. It turns basic management into a high-stakes legal paper trail that SF founders don't have to touch until they’re mid-market.

2024 Trading Summary and 2025 Plan.

At the beginning of 2024 I had a goal of 20% gain on $601k of stocks and cash. The year started off on the wrong foot and continued on until the low point on 4/19. I was assigned a few stocks that just seemed to find a way to go down so selling covered calls only softened the blow a bit. It wasn’t until the week of May 24 that my account turned positive for the year. At the midpoint of the year my account was up 10.50% but the summer/fall was rocky until November and early December when the account reached its high point at 20.56% on December 6. The account took a hit when Uncle Jerome forecast less rate cuts for 2025 and the anti Santa rally hit the market hard. The account missed the 20% goal and finished the year at 16.03% or $25k under my goal. My accounting is based on weekly Friday close but for this calculation I used December 31 market close numbers. Had I used the January 3 Friday close numbers I would have surpassed the goal with 22.93% due to the New Years rally. Yes NVDA which is an overweight position was the catalyst in both directions.

Lessons learned in my first year of trading such a large account.

Forcing trades due to time constraints with the 9-5 job does not produce the best results.

Trading a large number of contracts with the same strike and expiration concentrates risk.

 Oversizing positions with volatile stocks (NVDA in my case) leads to large up/down swings in account value.

Do more DD on stocks I want to own via cash secured put assignment.

Sell equities that are not good for options trading. In my case I just sold all my TSLY

My goal for 2025 will be for a 30% gain on a $650k balance consisting of stocks and cash. I plan to morph the account to be biased towards AI. Some tickers I’m interested for long positions are: META, MU, NVDA, AMZN and SOUN. Options trading CSP and CC mixed with vertical spreads will be my main focus.

text:
I still remember June 21, 2005.

Instead of following my normal evening routine with Guild Wars, I felt a bit bored of the game and ended up poking around the Internet instead. I saw that timschmoyer.com was available and decided to register it. Why? I don't know.

So I poked around more. "What do I do with this domain now?"

I found WordPress and decided to set that up on the domain because, why not? After learning a bit about FTP, MySQL users, and text editors, I was up and running. Nice!

But then came my next question. "What do I write about?"

At first I wrote about whatever was on my mind: my girlfriend, what I ate for dinner that night, or screenshots of my adventures in Guild Wars.

Over time, however, I wrote more and more about what I was most passionate about, which was youth ministry. Within a few years, it turned into the most-subscribed youth ministry blog on the Internet. In 2011 it became my full-time job. That turned into creating YouTube videos, which turned into my career. In 2013 I started a YouTube growth agency, had success there, and sold it to vidIQ in 2022.

Today I work as the Chief Creator Coach at vidIQ where I'm building a 1:1 coaching team for their 3 million weekly active creators. After years of YouTube coaching, scaling it is an amazing new mountain to climb!

But after almost 20 years of YouTube, I have the itch to get back to my roots: writing about whatever is top-of-mind and seeing where it leads.

Life is a lot different for me now than it was when I first started blogging in 2005. I'm married now, have 7 kids, and hold very different beliefs around money, business, family, relationships, and faith than I did 20 years ago, but I'm finding that I still desire a place to wrestle "out loud."

And who knows where this will lead. Last time it turned into a career, but this time I just want it to give me a place to think and subject those thoughts to the critique of others as I pursue practical wisdom in business, relationships, and faith.

Let's see where this goes.

👉 If you want to join me, sign up for email updates to get new posts in your Inbox: timschmoyer.com

A striking environmental statement from Mike Winkelmann (Beeple), the most influential digital artist of our time.

Predictive & Technical Analysis :::
The Strategic Meaning of the Accounting Constant 314,159 
( — A Number Designed for System Stability, Not for Price Discovery )

[[[ From Market Price to System Constant ]]]
[[[ Where Competition Moves When Exchange Rates Disappear ]]]
[[[ The Point Where AI Simulation Meets Network Laws ]]]
[[[ The Design Language of an Economic Operating System ]]]
[[ This article includes Predictive & Technical Analysis and may differ from actual outcomes ]]]

I. The Core Question: Why 314,159?

With the deployment of the *stellar-pi-coin-sdk*, the value
**1 Pi = $314,159** appears as a de-facto accounting constant within the architecture of Pi Network.

This number does not clearly belong to any conventional category:

* Not a market price formed on exchanges
* Not a value decided by community voting or governance
* Not a simple peg to fiat, gold, commodities, or GDP
* Not a symbolic or marketing-driven figure

Yet it functions consistently as a reference point across settlement, validation, and accounting layers.
This reframes the question fundamentally:

> **Is 314,159 about what Pi will be worth,
> or about what Pi must withstand for the system to remain stable?**

---

II. Core Hypothesis: 314,159 Is a System Stability Constant, Not a Price

The most internally consistent hypothesis is the following:

> **314,159 is not a market valuation,
> but an accounting constant derived by reverse-engineering
> the long-term real-economy load the Pi infrastructure is designed to settle.**

This interpretation only holds if Pi is viewed not as a cryptocurrency,
but as an **economic operating system**.

In operating systems, constants do not describe market desirability;
they define **structural tolerances**—the limits within which the system remains stable.

---

III. Why Traditional Economic Models Cannot Produce This Number

If conventional economic reasoning had been applied, one would expect values derived from:

* Global GDP divided by projected supply
* User count multiplied by average consumption
* Monetary aggregates weighted against collateral

However, **linear models rarely yield non-round, non-symbolic values like 314,159**.

Numbers of this nature typically emerge from:

* Multi-variable optimization
* Non-linear system modeling
* Long-horizon (decades-scale) stability analysis
* Constraint-based avoidance of collapse thresholds

This strongly suggests **AI-assisted simulation or constraint optimization**, not human price intuition.

---

IV. Plausible Simulation Structure (Strategic Inference)

1). Defining the Scope of Global Real-World Infrastructure

Likely simulation inputs include:

* Essential utilities:

 * Food
 * Housing
 * Energy
 * Transportation
 * Connectivity
 * Healthcare
 * Education
* Regional cost differentials
* Margin reduction from disintermediation
* Labor cost restructuring due to automation and AI

This stage defines **how much of the real economy the system intends to absorb**.

2). Modeling a World Without Exchange Rates

When exchange rates, speculation, and arbitrage are removed:

* Per-transaction margins decline
* Transaction frequency increases sharply
* Aggregate settlement volume grows non-linearly

The AI model then confronts the central constraint question:

> **How much real economic value must a single accounting unit represent
> to avoid dilution, inflationary psychology, or systemic instability?**

3). The Intersection of Scarcity and Usability

* If the unit value is too small:

 * Unit proliferation accelerates
 * Value perception collapses
 * Speculative behavior re-enters
* If the unit value is too large:

 * Usability degrades
 * Psychological distance increases

**314,159 plausibly represents the convergence zone**
where scarcity, usability, and long-term stability coexist.

---

V. How Metcalfe’s Law Was Likely Considered

1). The Role and Limits of Metcalfe’s Law

Metcalfe’s Law states:

> The value of a network is proportional to the square of its participants (N²).

It is effective at describing:

* Network expansion speed
* Growth of connection density
* Interaction potential as users increase

However, it has critical limitations.

Metcalfe’s Law does **not** explain:

* Real-economy settlement capacity
* Unit dilution thresholds
* Psychological value stability
* Where systemic instability begins

In short:

> **Metcalfe’s Law explains how fast systems grow,
> not where they must stop to remain safe.**

2). Why It Cannot Directly Determine an Accounting Constant

If an accounting constant were directly tied to Metcalfe’s Law:

* User growth → exponential value expansion
* The accounting unit would require continual redefinition
* A fixed accounting reference would collapse

This directly contradicts the concept of a **fixed accounting constant**.

3). Most Plausible Use: Stress-Test Input Variable

The most coherent interpretation is:

> **Metcalfe’s Law was not used to determine the value of Pi,
> but to generate growth and load scenarios against which Pi’s unit stability was tested.**

Specifically, it would inform:

* Connection density escalation
* Transaction frequency surges
* Settlement call intensity

The AI simulation then asks:

> **If the network grows at Metcalfe-scale intensity,
> what unit magnitude prevents dilution, instability, or psychological collapse?**

4). The Relationship to 314,159 (Key Insight)

* Metcalfe’s Law → predicts growth velocity and transaction explosion
* AI simulation → derives the unit size capable of absorbing that growth

Thus, **314,159 likely represents**:

* A value large enough to remain stable
* Even under extreme network expansion
* Without unit dilution or loss of trust

5). Consolidated Summary (Integrated Key Points)

* ( X ) Metcalfe’s Law was unlikely the formula used to *set* the accounting constant
* ( O ) It was likely used as an **input variable to simulate network growth stress**
* ( O ) Those simulations modeled:

 * Transaction frequency surges
 * Settlement density
 * Unit dilution risk

>>> **The accounting constant most plausibly converged at the smallest unit size that remained stable under maximal growth assumptions—314,159.**

-------------------------------
VI. Conclusion: 314,159 Is a Collapse-Prevention Constant, Not a Future Price
-------------------------------
The value 314,159 most plausibly answers this design question:

> **When Pi functions as a global real-economy settlement layer,
> at what unit magnitude does the system remain stable
> without exchange rates, speculation, or dilution?**

This is not price forecasting.
It is **system architecture**.

Final Synthesis
----------------
* 314,159 was not set by markets
* It was not voted into existence
* It was not symbolically chosen

It was most likely **derived** by modeling:

* Real-economy settlement scope
* Post-exchange-rate transaction behavior
* Network growth stress (via Metcalfe-type dynamics)
* Unit dilution avoidance constraints

> **Pi’s value is not defined by what it can be sold for,
> but by what it can responsibly settle.**

At this point, Pi exits the category of cryptocurrency
and enters the domain of **economic constants**—
the silent numbers that determine whether systems endure or collapse.

text:
The Chinese government has been instrumental in advancing autonomous vehicle (AV) technology, setting up pilot zones, issuing licenses, and creating regulations to support this growth. In June 2024, 20 cities were chosen for a pilot program to build infrastructure for smart connected vehicles, which includes self-driving trucks. This involves installing roadside infrastructure and a cloud-based control platform to facilitate the operation of AVs on public roads.

- By August 2024, China had established 32,000 kilometers of roads for AV testing across 16 cities, with 16,000 test licenses issued, providing a robust environment for real-world testing and data collection.

Technological Development‼️

- Major Chinese tech firms like Baidu, Pony.ai , and WeRide are at the forefront, leveraging AI capabilities from autonomous driving for broader applications like generative AI. Companies like TuSimple, now rebranded as CreateAI, have shifted focus towards AI in video games and animation, showcasing the versatility of their technology.

- Cost efficiency and operational improvements are key drivers. Inceptio Technology, for example, offers trucks that are 5% cheaper than traditional models, with added safety and environmental benefits. Their focus on reducing driver workload by automating long-haul trips where drivers are mostly in standby mode highlights the economic advantages.

- The concept of platooning is utilized, where a human-driven truck leads a convoy of autonomously driven trucks, reducing the need for multiple drivers and improving fuel efficiency.

Market Dynamics‼️

- With approximately 7 million heavy-duty trucks in China, and a significant annual turnover of 1.2 to 1.5 million new sales, the market for autonomous trucks is substantial. The shift towards fleet operations over individual drivers supports the integration of autonomous technology for efficiency.

- Economically, autonomous trucks could revolutionize China's logistics, offering 24/7 operation, reducing labor costs, and enhancing delivery speeds, which aligns with China's ambitions to lead in global logistics efficiency.

Challenges and Future Directions‼️

- Data privacy and cybersecurity remain concerns, especially for international expansion, where foreign governments might scrutinize data handling practices.

- Global competition is fierce, with U.S. companies like Waymo and Aurora also advancing in autonomous technology, influencing China's strategies. 

- The transition of companies like TuSimple to broader AI applications could bring back innovations that enhance AV technologies, such as improved visual recognition systems for autonomous trucks.

Infrastructure Development‼️

- Smart road initiatives, like those in Wuhan, involve significant investments in infrastructure to support AVs, including sensors and data transmitters for real-time interaction between roads and vehicles, aligning with smart city goals.

International Collaboration and Competition‼️

- Collaboration with international entities, like Tesla's partnership with Baidu for mapping, shows integration with foreign systems, while also stirring competition with local giants like Xpeng and Nio, who are developing their own advanced driver-assistance systems.

Future Projections‼️

- S&P Global Mobility forecasts suggest that by 2034, around 250,000 Level 4 autonomous vehicles, including trucks, might be sold for mobility services in China, indicating a future where these trucks could be common in logistics.

Challenges Ahead‼️

- Balancing technological advancement with job displacement, ensuring data privacy, cybersecurity, and maintaining public trust are ongoing challenges. Integrating these trucks into existing logistics networks will require overcoming technical, regulatory, and operational hurdles.

China's approach to self-driving trucks involves a synergy of government policy, technological innovation, economic strategy, and international dynamics.

whatscoin .com (sold for $25K is not shown as "similar")
"coins .com" suffix in 5 of 6 "similar" domain sales

text:
Meet the Liberals: Frank Baylis, the former MP embroiled in sole-sourced contract scandals

The former Liberal MP from 2015-2019 was at the heart of a controversy during the COVID-19 pandemic, when his company, Bayliss Medical, was awarded a lucrative sole-sourced ventilator contract.

Frank Baylis wants to lead the Liberal Party of Canada. The same guy embroiled in one of the most flagrant conflicts of interest scandals in recent memory is now vying for the top spot in the party that gave us SNC-Lavalin and the WE Charity debacles.

It's so perfectly Liberal — he's so ethically challenged that he's giving Trudeau a run for his money. To learn more about Baylis and the other Liberal leadership contenders, go to Meet The Liberals dot com.

Now, let’s rewind the clock to 2020.

Frank Baylis, a former Liberal MP from 2015-2019, was at the centre of a major controversy involving his company, Baylis Medical.

This company was handed a $237 million contract to produce ventilators during the COVID-19 pandemic. Sounds noble, right? Wrong.

Baylis was no longer an MP, but he was still deeply entrenched in the Liberal network. And that contract? It was awarded without competitive bidding. Let’s call it what it was — a sweetheart deal for an insider.

Now, let’s dive deeper into the details of this scandal, which only get more infuriating the more you learn.

The ventilators in question, known as the VFC-560, were described as “new” and had not been approved in any jurisdiction at the time the contract was awarded.

Yet somehow, Baylis Medical was selected as a key subcontractor through FTI Professional Grade Inc., a consortium formed to fulfill the government’s alleged urgent need for 10,000 ventilators. This raises serious questions about the safety and efficacy of the devices procured for nearly a quarter of a billion dollars.

What’s more, Canada reportedly overpaid for these ventilators by up to $100 million. Each unit cost taxpayers $23,700, a far cry from the much lower prices of approved models from competitors like Medtronic. Was this about saving lives or lining the pockets of Liberal insiders?

But wait, there's more. Then Baylis got a contract to maintain the unused vents, to the tune of a further $4 million.

Then there’s the matter of conflict of interest. Frank Baylis had only recently left politics after serving as a Liberal MP from 2015 to 2019. Under the Conflict of Interest Act, former MPs are prohibited from taking improper advantage of their previous office.

But with Baylis Medical receiving this lucrative contract, it’s hard to ignore the appearance of favouritism. After all, Baylis has been a donor to the Liberal Party, and internal memos suggest there was direct communication between his company and government officials. How convenient.

Baylis himself appeared before the House of Commons ethics committee, where he denied any backroom dealings or influence peddling.

Just another Liberal contracting scandal. Throw it on the pile with ArriveScam and Randy Boissonnault's company, GHI.

And what happened to the ventilators? Many of these overpriced devices ended up unused. Reports indicate that some were sold for scrap metal at laughable prices, with units that cost $23,700 being offloaded for as little as $6 each. Others were donated to Ukraine as “war surplus,” with at least 839 units shipped overseas.

Fast forward to today, and Frank Baylis wants to lead the Liberal Party of Canada.

The arrogance is staggering. This is a man who’s already demonstrated that he’s willing to exploit his connections for personal gain. Does anyone seriously believe that he’ll suddenly transform into a paragon of virtue as party leader? Of course not. His candidacy is just another example of the Liberals’ culture of entitlement, where rules and ethics are mere inconveniences.

More of the same, I guess. But here’s the bigger question: What does this say about the Liberal Party itself?

Baylis’s decision to run isn’t happening in a vacuum. It’s a symptom of a party that has become so detached from everyday Canadians that it no longer even bothers to pretend to care about ethics. From Justin Trudeau’s multiple personal ethics violations to the WE Charity scandal, the Liberals have made it clear that accountability is a foreign concept to them. Baylis is just the latest in a long line of insiders who think they’re above the rules.

And let’s talk about what this means for Canada. The Liberal Party is still the governing party. Their leader will likely be the next prime minister unless Canadians finally wake up and demand better.

Do we really want someone like Frank Baylis at the helm? Someone who’s already demonstrated that he’s more interested in serving himself than serving Canadians? This is a man who’s benefited from backroom deals and insider connections. How can we trust him to make decisions in the best interest of our country?

Let me be clear: This isn’t just about Frank Baylis. It’s about the rot at the core of the Liberal Party. It’s about a government that has consistently prioritized its friends and donors over hardworking Canadians.

text:
In the wild frontier of cryptocurrency, a seemingly simple digital asset — an Ethereum Name Service (ENS) domain ending in “.eth” — ignited global imagination. Its name was **paradigm.eth**, short, punchy, and loaded with meaning : “paradigm” as in a fundamental shift, a perfect metaphor for how blockchain could upend the world.

On October 9, 2021, this domain sold for **420 ETH** — roughly $1.5 million at the time — smashing every previous ENS sale record and becoming the most expensive single ENS domain ever traded.

Picture the scene: a mysterious wallet emerges from the shadows of the Ethereum network. For months it had been probing with small bids, getting rejected again and again. Then, suddenly, it drops **420 ETH** in one decisive move — a number deliberately chosen, because 420 is the crypto culture’s wink to cannabis culture, rebellious and cheeky.

Who was the seller? Unknown. Who was the buyer? An even bigger enigma. The wallet’s profile was a masterpiece of trolling: the email pointed to “paradigmcapital.eth,” the avatar was SushiSwap’s logo, the Twitter link led to venture capital giant a16z (Andreessen Horowitz), the GitHub pointed to Yearn .finance founder Andre Cronje, and the bio read something like “Skate on the Paradigm and shift it when I feel like.” It felt like a deliberate prank — or a savage satire of the entire crypto ecosystem.

The internet exploded. Accusations flew like shrapnel: “Marketing stunt!” “Wash trade!” “Left hand selling to the right hand!” Fingers pointed at Paradigm Capital, the prominent crypto VC firm — surely they were behind this self-dealing spectacle? The firm quickly denied any involvement, but the suspicion lingered. Was it artificial price pumping? The hefty gas fees (around $37,500) seemed to argue against a pure scam. On social media, the debate raged like wildfire: genius move or peak bubble insanity?

Yet strip away the noise, and what remains is not vaporware — but an indelible mark on history. 
**paradigm.eth** isn’t just a transaction; it’s a chapter carved permanently into the blockchain, impossible to erase. It signaled the moment ENS domains evolved from quirky tech experiment into serious digital real estate worth millions. In the grand narrative of crypto, it’s like Columbus sighting land: proof that decentralized identity has real, lasting value, a harbinger of the Web3 paradigm shift to come.

No matter whether the buyer was a visionary, a joker, or something in between, this sale is embedded forever in Ethereum’s DNA — a legend future generations will retell with the same mix of awe and disbelief.

Now look back at the .com era, the “old world” internet. Did it have zero marketing tricks or suspicious deals? Hardly.

Remember 1999: **business .com** sold for $7.5 million — a jaw-dropping sum during the dot-com frenzy. Critics screamed “speculative madness!” and whispered about insider flips and hype-driven valuations. The buyer, Marc Ostrofsky, was branded a “domain squatter” by some, accused of artificially inflating the market. The **sex .com** saga dragged on for years in courts, riddled with fraud allegations and ownership battles. Even **cars .com** fetched a valuation north of $800 million in 2014 (including the business), yet the domain alone was seen as the golden crown jewel, sparking endless “bubble” cries.

Those .com legends weren’t marketing gimmicks — they were turning points. Mocked at first, they laid the foundation for the digital economy we live in today. Amazon, Google, countless unicorns — all trace roots back to domains that once seemed overpriced.

**paradigm.eth** is no different. It’s not a trick; it’s a prophecy. The doubters can shout as loudly as they want the historical narrative, etched immutably on-chain, will outlast them all. It will keep inspiring the next wave of dreamers to chase the next true paradigm shift.

That’s the magic of crypto: legends born from mystery, enduring through skepticism, forever shifting the game.

text:
Here's a summary of Elon Musk's wealth journey over the years. Read till the end and bookmark this, because legacy media will never show you this. 

Early Years (1990s - Early 2000s):
- Musk's entrepreneurial ventures started early. He co-founded Zip2, which was sold for $307 million in 1999, netting him $22 million. His next big venture, X. com, merged to become PayPal, sold to eBay in 2002 for $1.5 billion, earning him $165 million. This money was used to fund SpaceX and invest in Tesla.

2000s - Building Foundations:
- By the end of the decade, Musk's net worth was estimated at around $1 billion, largely from his Tesla and SpaceX investments. Tesla went public in 2010, and Musk's wealth began to significantly increase as the company's valuation grew.

2010s - The Rise of Tesla and SpaceX:
- Musk's wealth saw a steady climb with Tesla's success. By 2012, he made Forbes' Billionaires List with a $2 billion net worth. His net worth was volatile but generally grew, particularly as Tesla's stock price soared. By 2019, his wealth was around $22 billion.

2020 - The Breakthrough Year:
- Musk's wealth exploded due to Tesla's stock surge during the economic recovery from the global health crisis. Starting the year with an estimated $27 billion, his net worth ballooned to $170 billion by year's end, making him one of the richest people globally.

2021 - Peak Wealth:
- Musk briefly became the richest person in the world, with his net worth hitting about $340 billion in November 2021, driven by Tesla's stock performance and SpaceX's valuation increases.

2022 - Volatility and Twitter Acquisition:
- Despite a massive drop in Tesla's stock price, Musk's net worth remained high, though it saw significant fluctuations. His $44 billion acquisition of Twitter (now X) in 2022 was a headline event, although it also led to questions about his focus and the financial impact on his wealth.

2023 - Recovery and Further Growth:
- Musk's wealth saw a recovery, with his net worth increasing from $146 billion at the end of 2022 to $251 billion by the end of 2023, thanks to a rebound in Tesla's stock price and SpaceX's increased valuation.

2024 - New Milestones:
- Musk's net worth reached $400 billion in December 2024, becoming the first person to achieve this milestone, fueled by a SpaceX insider share sale and Tesla's stock hitting all-time highs post-Trump's reelection.

2025 - Current Standing:
- As of January 2025, Musk's wealth is estimated at around $449 billion, making him the wealthiest individual on Earth, driven by his stakes in Tesla, SpaceX, and other ventures, as well as his political and business influence.
