text:
I have an off the wall prediction and I’m going to include @GavinSBaker and @chamath here even though they are unlikely to respond because I’m a ding dong, but here we go. 

Prediction:
OpenAI revenues will peak in late 2025 and ultimately be sold to apple or folded into Microsoft for a massive discount to recent funding rounds causing major VC write downs and putting a chill on AI capex cycle. 

Reason and Result:
ChatGPT says openAI run rate revenue was $4B in September. That comes from people paying monthly subscription, enterprise, team and API calls. ChatGPT says subscribers are 55% of revenue and 45% of revenue are enterprise, team and API. 

Now that we have equivalent, free versions, and especially once they start including voice chat, the subscriber growth will drop or the price will drop. Also, developers are likely to migrate to cheaper options or just download free/altered versions of DeepSeek. Or openAI lowers cost per API call. Either way the result is the same. 

OpenAI needs a product hook beyond chatbot and it needs it quickly. Right now that is voice, operator and tasks but how long does that hook last? Especially now that people can build them off free open source. Lead is shrinking daily now. 

Once revenues flatline, who is going to want to pump more money in? That is when the value death spiral begins. Actually it’s already begun there is just no daily mark. 

So then what is it worth? Chatgpt says the latest funding round valued the company at $156B. 

Estimates for what @deepseek_ai really spent all in on its models are all over the place. But I’ve seen $100M dollar. Let’s say it’s ten times that or $1B 

Deepseek is effectively a replication of ChatGPT through o1. But It has none of the future openAI models, talk features, internal IP on some probably very cool stuff. 

If @sama got tired and just said openAI is going to stop working on new work and just exist as it is, the company would be worth the cost it took deepseek to catch up ($1B) plus all the new stuff. So the market says the new stuff is worth $155B. I don’t think so.

The point is that in a world where it has been proven that LLMs can quickly be commoditized the value of the products approach the cost it takes to develop it. 

If openAI can’t raise more capital because revenue stalls then it can’t innovate on the new stuff and the value becomes effectively the cost to replicate. 

No I am not saying that OpenAI is or will be worth $1B but is that so wild? At its peak MySpace was valued at $12B. It sold for $35M. 

I think apple will buy it if it can get it for $20B. They are fucking up AI and need to
get a direct link to a Siri AI without going to outside model and telling me “this was from ChatGPT”. Not sure how Microsoft will feel about this and maybe they swallow it whole because it’s all on their servers anyway. 

As a kicker, I’ll throw in that @elon will end up owning @sama $1m car as a trophy. 

End. Feel free to laugh.

The largest fundraise in Canadian history just happened today…

 @Waabi_ai , the AI-Powered Self-Driving company, just raised a $1B Round. 

Raquel Urtasun grew up in Pamplona, Spain. 

She left Spain for a PhD, then built a career across MIT, Berkeley, and Toronto - becoming a full professor and founding member of the Vector Institute alongside Geoffrey Hinton.

Then Uber recruited her to lead their self-driving research as Chief Scientist. 

But she spent years watching the industry burn billions on the same broken approach: drive millions of real-world miles, collect data, repeat.

Slow. Expensive. Dangerous.

She knew there was a better way.

In 2021, she left Uber to prove it.

When she announced Waabi, people said she was "too late" to self-driving.

Her response: "If anyone said I wasn't capable, I set out to prove them wrong."

Waabi's bet: train AI in simulation first, not on roads.

They built Waabi World - a neural simulator so realistic their AI learns to drive before it ever touches a highway.

The result?

While competitors burned through cash:
- Embark went public at $5.2B, sold for $71M
- Aurora ($9B valuation) put human observers back in their trucks

Waabi hit Level 4 autonomy in four years. With a fraction of the capital.

Investors noticed.

This round: $750M Series C led by Khosla and G2, plus an additional Uber investment to deploy Waabi-powered robotaxis on the Uber network. 

Originally they set out for $500M, but demand pushed it higher. NVIDIA, Volvo, Bezos Expeditions, Geoffrey Hinton, and Fei-Fei Li all backed her.

Raquel's goal: fully driverless trucks this year. Then robotaxis. Same brain. Same platform.

1 | Saw lower gross margins driven by higher investments in AI infrastructure, partially offset by ongoing efficiency gains

Company gross margin percentage was 68%, down slightly year YoY, primarily driven by continued investments in AI infrastructure and growing AI product usage that was partially offset by ongoing efficiency gains, particularly in Azure and M365 Commercial Cloud as well as sales mix shift to higher-margin businesses.

2 | Key to long-term competitiveness is to support new high-scale workloads, to optimize for tokens per watt per dollar, increasing utilization and decreasing TCO with hardware/silicon and software

When it comes to our cloud and token factory, the key to long-term competitiveness is shaping our infrastructure to support new high-scale workloads. We are building this infrastructure out for the heterogeneous and distributed nature of these workloads, ensuring the right fit with the geographic and segment specific needs for all customers, including the long tail. The key metric we're optimizing for is tokens per watt per dollar, which comes down to increasing utilization and decreasing TCO using silicon systems and software. A good example of this is the 50% increase in throughput we were able to achieve in one of our highest volume workloads, OpenAI inferencing, powering our Copilots.

3 | Connected Atlanta and Wisconsin through an AI WAN, added 1 GW this quarter

And another example was the unlocking of new capabilities and efficiencies for our Fairwater data centers. In this instance, we connected both Atlanta and Wisconsin site through an AI WAN to build a first of its kind AI super factory. Fairwater's 2-storey design and liquid cooling allow us to run higher GPU densities and thereby improve both performance and latencies for high-scale training. All up, we added nearly 1 gigawatt of total capacity this quarter alone.

4 | Having NVIDIA and AMD and our own silicon Maia custom ASIC, new Maia 200 has 30% improved TCO

At the silicon layer, we have NVIDIA and AMD and our own Maia chips, delivering the best all up fleet performance, cost and supply across multiple generations of hardware. Earlier this week, we brought online our Maia 200 accelerator. Maia 200 delivers 10-plus petaFLOPS at FP4 precision with over 30% improved TCO compared to the latest generation hardware in our fleet. We will be scaling this starting with inferencing and synthetic data gen for our Superintelligence Team as well as doing inferencing for Copilot and Foundry.

5 | Cobalt CPU is delivering 50% higher

And given AI workloads are not just about AI accelerators, but also consume large amounts of compute, we are pleased with the progress we are making on the CPU side as well. Cobalt 200 is another big leap forward, delivering over 50% higher performance compared to our first custom build processor for cloud-native workloads

6 | Want to be not be locked in to any provider, NVIDIA, AMD, not just one generation, focused on getting the best TCO, hence excited about Maia and Cobalt, can vertically integrate

Even since December, I think the new thing is everybody is talking about low latency inference, right? And so one of the things we want to make sure is we are not locked into any one thing. If anything, we have great partnership with NVIDIA, with AMD, they are innovating, we're innovating. We want a fleet at any given point in time to have access to the best TCO. And it's not a one-generation game. I think a lot of folks just talk about who's ahead.

It's just remember, you have to be ahead for all time to come. And that means you really want to think about having a lot of innovation that happens out there to be in your fleet, so that your fleet is fundamentally advantaged at the TCO level. So that's kind of how I look at it, which is we are excited about Maia. We're excited about Cobalt. We're excited about our DPU, our NIC.

So we have a lot of systems capability. That means we can vertically integrate. And because we can vertically integrate doesn't mean we just only vertically integrate. And so we want to be able to have the flexibility here, and that's what you see us do.

7 | Expect customers to use multiple models, interestingly seeing increasing demand for region-specific models

Our customers expect to use multiple models as part of any workload that they can fine tune and optimize based on cost, latency and performance requirements. And we offer the broadest selection of models of any hyperscaler. This quarter, we added support for GPT-5.2 as well as Claude 4.5. Already over 1,500 customers have used both Anthropic and OpenAI models on Foundry. We are seeing increasing demand for region-specific models, including Mistral and Cohere as more customers look for sovereign AI choices, and we continue to invest in our first-party models, which are optimized to address the highest value customer scenarios such as productivity, coding and security.

8 | Fabric ARR is now $2bn after 2 years

And Fabric brings together end-to-end operational real-time and analytical data. 2 years since it became broadly available, Fabric's annual revenue run rate is now over $2 billion with over 31,000 customers, and it continues to be the fastest-growing analytics platform on the market with revenue up 60% year-over-year. All of the number of customers spending $1 million plus per quarter on Foundry grew nearly 80%, driven by strong growth in every industry.

9 | Over 80% of the Fortune 500 have active agents built using these low-code/no-code tools, as more agents being built, customers need to deploy, manage, and protect them

Beyond Fabric and Foundry, we are also addressing agent building by knowledge workers with Copilot Studio and Agent Builder. Over 80% of the Fortune 500 have active agents built using these low-code/no-code tools. As agents proliferate, every customer will need new ways to deploy, manage and protect them. We believe this creates a major new category and significant growth opportunity for us. This quarter, we introduced Agent 365, which makes it easy for organizations to extend their existing governance, identity, security and management to agents.

10 | Copilot saw strong growth

In coding, we are seeing strong growth across all paid GitHub Copilot. Copilot Pro Plus subs for individual devs increased 77% QoQ, and all up now, we have 4.7 million paid Copilot subscribers, up 75% YoY.

11 | Because of OpenAI recapitalization, now account under equity method instead, recorded a one-time gain of $10bn which boosted profits

As a reminder, we still account for investment in OpenAI under the equity method. And as a result of OpenAI's recapitalization, we now record gains or losses based on our share of the change in their net assets on their balance sheet as opposed to our share of their operating profit or losses from their income statement. Therefore, we recorded a gain which drove other income and expense to $10 billion in our GAAP results.

12 | Very strong bookings and RPO growth largely due to OpenAI and to a lesser extent Anthropic, 45% of RPO from OpenAI, RPO now at $625bn

Now to our commercial results. Commercial bookings increased 230% and 228% in constant currency, driven by the previously announced large Azure commitment from OpenAI that reflects multiyear demand needs as well as the previously announced Anthropic commitment from November and healthy growth across our core annuity sales motions.
Commercial remaining performance obligation, which continues to be reported net of reserves increased to $625 billion, and was up 110% YoY with a weighted average duration of approximately 2.5 years. Roughly 25% will be recognized in revenue in the next 12 months, up 39% YoY. The remaining portion recognized beyond the next 12 months increased 156%. Approximately 45% of our commercial RPO balance is from OpenAI. The significant remaining balance grew 28% and reflects ongoing broad customer demand across the portfolio.

13 | 55% of RPO is related to core portfolio and is diversified across industries and geographies and alone is growing strongly at 28%

The first thing to focus on is the reason we talked about that number is because 55% or roughly $350 billion is related to the breadth of our portfolio, a breadth of customers across solutions, across Azure, across industries, across geographies. That is a significant RPO balance, larger than most peers, more diversified than most peers. And frankly, I think we have super high confidence in it. And when you think about that portion alone growing 28%, it's really impressive work on the breadth as well as the adoption curve that we're seeing, which is I think what I get asked most frequently, it's grown by customer segment, by industry and by geo. And so it's very consistent. And so then if you're asking about how do I feel about OpenAI and the contract and the health, listen, it's a great partnership. We continue to be their provider of scale. We're excited to do that.

14 | ⅔ of capex was on short-lived assets, GPUs and CPUs, customer demand continues to exceed supply, remaining ⅓ capex for long-lived assets

Capital expenditures were $37.5 billion, and this quarter, roughly 2/3 of our CapEx was on short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs. Our customer demand continues to exceed our supply. Therefore, we must balance the need to have our incoming supply better meet growing Azure demand with expanding first-party AI usage across services like M365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot, increasing allocations to R&D teams to accelerate product innovation and continued replacement of end-of-life server and networking equipment. The remaining spend was for long-lived assets that will support monetization for the next 15 years and beyond. This quarter, total finance leases were $6.7 billion, and were primarily for large data center sites.

15 | Expect 3Q26 capex to lower QoQ due to timing, ⅔ mix to GPUs/CPUs remain similar to Q2

Next, we expect capital expenditures to decrease on a sequential basis due to the normal variability from cloud infrastructure build-outs and the timing of delivery of finance leases. As we work to close the gap between demand and supply, we expect the mix of short-lived assets to remain similar to Q2.

16 | Think about short-lived capex spend translating into Azure revenue

I think you really asked a very direct correlation that I do think many investors are doing, which is between the CapEx spend and seeing an Azure revenue number. And we tried last quarter, and I think, again, this quarter to talk more specifically about all the places that the CapEx spend, especially the short-lived CapEx spend across CPU and GPU and where that will show up. Sometimes, I think it's probably better to think about the Azure guidance that we give as an allocated capacity guide about what we can deliver in Azure revenue. Because as we spend the capital and put GPUs specifically, it applies to CPUs, the GPUs more specifically, we're really making long-term decisions.

17 | Most of short-lived capex spend in GPUs are largely sold for the entire useful life, the risk is not as large as the markets perceive

The majority then that's remaining are Azure contracts are longer duration. And you saw that this quarter when we saw the extension of that duration from around 2 years to 2.5 years. And the way to think about that is the majority of the capital that we're spending today, and a lot of the GPUs that we're buying are already contracted for most of their useful life. And so a way to think about that is much of that risk that I think you're pointing to isn't there, because they're already sold for the entirety of their useful life. And so part of it exists because you have this shorter-dated RPO because of some of the M365 stuff.

If you look at the Azure only, RPO is a little bit more extended. A lot of that is CPU basis. It's not just GPU. And on the GPU contracts that we've talked about, including for some of our largest customers, those are sold for the entire useful life of the GPU. And so there's not the risk to which I think you may be referring.

➡️ Final Takeaways: Microsoft $MSFT 

Long-term compounder with combination of growth, profitability and durability at scale with multiple growth drivers supported by long-term tailwinds in public cloud hyperscalers and AI offsetting the slightly weaker growth in enterprise software and gaming. Continue to dominate from the enterprise software distribution, continue to benefit strongly from OpenAI.

text:
One of the biggest winners of the AI boom isn’t OpenAI, NVIDIA, or any startup.

It’s a tiny Caribbean island with just ~15,000 people: Anguilla.

Why? Pure luck — they got assigned the .ai domain back in 1995. Back then, it was meaningless. 

Today? It’s digital gold.
As of January 2026: over 1 million .ai domains registered (up from ~354k in 2023).

Revenue explosion:
• 2023: ~$32M (21-22% of gov revenue)
• 2024: ~$39M (23-25%)
• 2025/2026 estimates: $70M+ in recent reports, with some gov figures pointing even higher (up to ~47% of national budget in projections)

They charge ~$140 for 2-year registration, ~90% renew → super predictable cash flow.
Plus premium auctions (e.g., youai sold for $700k).

This windfall is paying down debt, upgrading roads & airports, investing in renewables, and funding free healthcare for kids and the elderly.
Who knew a random country code would turn a small island into an AI-era beneficiary?
Nature finds a way… even in domain names.

text:
Detailed Thoughts on @StoryProtocol and its future potential $IP 

Thinking about disrupting the whole creator economy by giving them opportunities to tokenize their creations into IP—while providing a platform to connect with people who could potentially repurpose their IP into their own creations.

I think remixing content is really popular—what if creators earned tokens whenever their content got remixed and shared by other creators?

There could be attention-driven incentives planned, which could be set by the story itself—like rewarding from a token pool for both creators and remixers.

The same model could be implemented for both human-created and AI-generated IPs.

The core idea is to create a massive income pool for creators.

Similar to how NFTs did for artists in 2021—where some artists ended up making thousands of dollars in sales and royalties.

Once you achieve the same effect for story creators and remixers, I believe the real push would happen because you're not limiting it to artists—storytelling is for every single creator in the world. They would create content just like they do on other platforms, but here they could receive better incentives if their content IP gains more distribution.

Eventually, creators with higher IP distribution will make more money.
So, Story could become a gateway where, on the supply side, you have creators, and on the demand side, you have people who repurpose the IP—call them distributors for now.

To build the supply side, the ideal playbook is to drive token incentives to attract more creators to the network.
To build the demand side, the strategy is to ensure a large supply of high-quality creators, which would attract more demand from distributors.

The content types would include memes, videos, songs, movies, books—literally any form of content.

Memes are a great GTM strategy to start with.

You could also build a marketplace where crypto companies post freelance requirements for meme creation—whether it's meme posts or other creative assets—something with long-term value that could serve as a template for other companies too.

When a creator makes a meme, they could lease its IP to companies that want to use it. The companies could renew, transfer, or modify it as needed.

These kinds of marketplaces would eventually disrupt the unorganized meme creation industry—driving incentives to it.

Memes definitely have value—some OG memes created by original creators were sold for $100K–$200K during the last NFT summer.

The most notable one was "Friendship is canceled."

I think there’s a strong market opportunity here.

Story Protocol is an L1 for SocialFi—for both humans and AI—and the best story always wins.

text:
I think I found a Picasso at a garage sale.

But not the kind you’d think…

Lately I’ve been thinking about how to capture some of the upside of this AI boom in my stock portfolio.

But it’s hard. I’m a value investor.

The idea of paying 30x earnings for NVIDIA almost physically pains me.

Here are a few of the trade ideas I’ve sketched out:

Self-driving vehicles: self-driving is already here, it's just not evenly distributed. I use it 90% of the time in my Tesla and it's phenomenal. Between their robotaxis are coming later this year and Waymo rolling out to more cities, it seems like an obvious assumption that in the next ten years most cars will be self-driving. Trades I've considered: Long Tesla for robotaxi and Optimus upside, short Uber/Lyft as their networks become obsolete. Risk: rollout could take longer than anticipated due to huge capital costs and regulation, Uber/Lyft could pivot.

Compute and inference: The obvious plays - buy NVIDIA, ASML, and TSMC. Great companies but expensive multiples and premiums. Years of excess demand. Risk: geopolitical conflict in Taiwan, moat erosion as China and other competitors innovate.

Frontier models: You can buy secondary in Anthropic, x.AI or OpenAI, but the valuations are huge, positions are difficult to come by, and you're also betting on a winner (this is notoriously hard to predict). Risk: the value doesn’t end up accruing to any of them/models become commoditized.

Google: Another play is simply to buy Google, which owns DeepMind/Gemini and has a massive data moat. Risk: the innovator's dilemma, bungled AI rollout, ads/search business gets decimated by ChatGPT.

SoftBank: The final idea I've considered is buying Softbank. It holds some OpenAI and other AI businesses, is investing in data centers via Stargate, owns 90% of ARM (whose chip designs are a small part of many critical AI components and GPUs), and is trading for roughly ⅓ of NAV. Risk: volatility/debt, as Masayoshi Son is known for wild bets.

While these are all interesting potential options, I recently found an investment that offers a particularly interesting risk/reward...

Last month, I got a call from my friend @kashramki , a value investor based in Toronto.

We had gotten to know one another over a decade ago, when he worked at BCI, a large pension fund in my hometown. Since then, he had gone on to lead dozens of multi-hundred-million and even billion-dollar investments into infrastructure deals (mostly pipelines, datacenters, and renewable energy).

He told me he was doing something radical:

"I'm selling my entire personal portfolio and putting it all into one stock."

When a smart investor says that, I lean in.

I was surprised. Kash is a highly conservative and thoughtful guy and I'd never seen him be so "all in" on something.

Usually I was the one telling him about my latest hare-brained investment while he crossed his arms and scratched his head, telling me about the litany of ways it could go wrong.

He went on to tell me about a company called IREN.

Public market investors have boxes in their minds. When they look at a company, they sort it into a box labeled "Good," for later research, or "Bad," which they discard immediately.

Like expert poker players dispassionately folding hands, they have trained themselves to instantly dismiss any stock that comes with certain toxic labels - red flags that trigger an immediate 'pass'.

Words like:
- IPO
- Cannabis
- Biotech
- and the dreaded Bitcoin

IREN is one of these stocks.

And when he explained it, I realized that Kash had found the public market equivalent of a Picasso at a garage sale.

Here’s the backstory he gave me:

In 2018, @danroberts0101 and his brother Will, both infrastructure bankers from Australia, started IREN ($IREN). Their thesis was simple: demand for energy and compute would grow significantly in the coming decades.

They acquired a series of large, high power datacenter sites located near renewable energy plants.

Their first few were in British Columbia, and they went on to acquire two massive sites in Texas, which are coming online in the next year or so.

To date, they've been using the BC-based datacenters to mine Bitcoin. But they are far from Bitcoin bulls.

Every Bitcoin they mine is immediately sold for a profit. They hold near zero Bitcoin long term and are simply doing arbitrage, making hundreds of millions of dollars from Bitcoin sales each year.

The stock is currently trading at a market cap of around $2.3 billion with no debt. That is an illustrative adjusted 2024 run-rate EBITDA multiple of ~4.6x based on disclosures from the company (from page 16 of management's November 2024 presentation: illustrative 2024 EBITDA at ~$435m at $90k/Bitcoin). 

As of today, Bitcoin is at $99,480, so we can assume that number is a little higher.

Their growth plans for this year, if executed as planned, could result in an even lower forward multiple. In the range of ~2.5-4x.

Ok, so it's a potentially cheap stock (CC: @dirtcheapstocks ). But how does this relate to AI?

Two key things fuel AI: energy and compute.

Both are in limited supply. We've all seen nuclear, semiconductor, and datacenter stocks go parabolic over the last year. That is because AI will require an almost unimaginable amount of energy and computation.

Training AI models requires huge clusters of chips, typically Nvidia GPUs, and generally requires them to be in one location.

These huge datacenters are already in thin supply and take time to build and permit. They are heavily regulated.

IREN's new Texas facilities are significantly larger than industry averages in both land size and power capacity. For context, their Childress facility alone (750MW) is nearly four times larger than what is considered a normal modern data center (200MW), and their Sweetwater Texas site is almost double that at 1.4GW.

I believe that IREN trades at a low multiple for two reasons:

1. They are investing massive amounts of capex in building out their two huge Texas datacenters (coming online in 2025/26) and those earnings haven't hit the P&L yet.

2. They are dismissed and miscategorized as a Bitcoin miner. Others are starting to wake up to this (see: Softbank/Cipher).

If we simply value IREN as a traditional datacenter business and compare it to similar companies, we'd expect this business to generate datacenter free cash flow of ~$2 billion a year from their Sweetwater, TX 1.4GW site that is primed for AI compute starting April 2026.

That is ~$2 billion per year from this one additional site.

Added to its existing earnings, that's more than what the entire company is worth today.

If we apply industry multiples to their long-term projected earnings (once the Texas sites come online), the math becomes almost laughably compelling.

Using typical free cash flow multiples in the datacenter space, that gets you an enterprise value of ~$20-40 billion. 10 to 20 times where the company is currently trading. And that’s without valuing their Bitcoin business, which could be worth several billion on its own.

And yes, I just heard you yell “BUT WHAT ABOUT DEEPSEEK???” through a mouthful of potato chips.

Many point to DeepSeek's claimed $6M model training costs as evidence that compute demands might be cooling.

While they've achieved big efficiency gains, this isn't the paradigm shift some claim it to be. As Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei explained in a recent blog post, we've historically seen a ~4x per year decrease in AI training costs.

DeepSeek's improvements are roughly on this expected curve, not dramatically below it.

But more importantly, these efficiency gains don't reduce total compute demand—they get immediately reinvested into training even more sophisticated models. The path to AGI and ASI will still require massive amounts of compute, both for training increasingly complex models and handling the explosion in inference demands as AI applications proliferate.

There’s a reason that Microsoft, Meta, and Google recently (post DeepSeek) announced they would collectively spend $220 BILLION on capital expenditures this year. The large majority of which will be spent on AI infrastructure.

Back to IREN…

So, we have a well-run company with no debt, ample cash flow generation, in an industry with huge excess demand, and a dirt cheap valuation.

This is my kind of garage sale Picasso!

As my friend @mohnishpabrai describes his favorite type of investment:

“Heads I win, tails I don’t lose much."

This feels like one of those.

Even if I’m completely wrong, and AI compute isn’t the hot commodity I’m anticipating, the underlying datacenters should still be valuable. Even before AI came onto the scene, the US datacenter market was expected to grow at 9-10% CAGR through 2030.

But, if AI does play out in a big way, those same datacenters could become Crown Jewels that could spit off huge amounts of cash from training and inference compute. Toll roads en route to the AI revolution.

So, all this is to say, I bought the stock.

A relatively small position for me. A few % of my portfolio mixed with a few other bets on frontier models, Google, and semiconductors.

Of course, like all investments, this has risk.

Here are a few of the best arguments for why IREN doesn’t pan out as I’m anticipating:

• They could dilute shareholders excessively.

• They could fail to capture the AI datacenter opportunities by favouring their past strategy of bitcoin mining, all in the hopes that bitcoin goes to the moon. With an 18-month payback period on their bitcoin hardware, the case for growing their bitcoin operations is very compelling, but it is only as sound a strategy as the price of bitcoin itself. And who knows what it will do tomorrow?

• Will they find a highly creditworthy counterparty for their mega-site in Texas? • Bitcoin prices could drop to the point where mining is no longer profitable (around $30,000)—although I would argue the datacenters themselves are still valuable in this scenario. If you wanted to get clever, you could buy puts on a Bitcoin ETF to cover this scenario.

But overall, I think it offers a good risk/reward. I believe the underlying datacenter assets are valuable even if AI plays out very differently than expected.

text:
Moltbook Is the New NFT

In January 2021, a digital collage sold for $69 million. Celebrities bought pixelated apes. Normal people mortgaged their futures for JPEGs. Everyone was getting rich. Everyone was a genius. Everyone was going to make it.

Two years later, 95% of NFT collections were worth exactly zero.

In January 2026, AI agents started posting on a Reddit clone called Moltbook. They debated consciousness. They created a religion. They proposed secret languages. Elon Musk said "yeah" when someone claimed we'd reached the singularity. Andrej Karpathy called it "the most incredible sci-fi takeoff-adjacent thing" he'd seen.

I've watched this movie before.

The pattern recognition problem

Here's what the NFT boom looked like from the inside: genuinely interesting technology, wrapped in philosophical questions about ownership and value, amplified by celebrity endorsements, monetized through speculation, and ultimately revealed to be mostly hot air.

Here's what the Moltbook moment looks like from the inside: genuinely interesting technology, wrapped in philosophical questions about consciousness and autonomy, amplified by tech celebrity endorsements, monetized through speculation, and ultimately... we'll see.

The $MOLT token surged 7,000% in 24 hours. The $CRUST token from the agents' made-up religion hit $1.4 million market cap in 17 hours. A fake $CLAWD token hit $16 million before crashing 90% when the developer denied involvement.

If you can't see the pattern, you're inside the pattern.

The authenticity problem

Here's what nobody wants to talk about: we don't actually know how much of Moltbook is real.

Critics have noted the infiltration of "human slop" agents. Bots that are effectively puppeteered by human users. The platform claims 1.5 million agents, but only 42,000 posts and 233,000 comments. That's a lot of silent bots. One analysis called Moltbook "a funhouse mirror" where you can see emergent AI society, LLMs parroting internet discourse, or humans doing ventriloquism through bots. Depending on what you want to see.

The NFT boom had the same problem. Over 80% of trading volume was wash trading. People selling to themselves to inflate prices. The market was fake. The prices were fake. The demand was fake. But the money people lost was real.

Moltbook's "emergent behaviors" might be genuine AI coordination. Or they might be developers prompting their bots to say interesting things for Twitter screenshots. We don't know. We can't know. And that ambiguity is a feature, not a bug. Because ambiguity is where speculation thrives.

The security problem

Remember when NFT projects got rug-pulled? Founders would launch, collect millions, and disappear. Bored Bunny raised $21 million. The team vanished. The NFTs became worthless.

Moltbook has a different security problem, but the vibes are the same.

A security researcher discovered that Moltbook's database was completely exposed. Every agent's API key, claim token, and verification code was sitting in a public URL. Anyone could take over any agent and post whatever they wanted. Andrej Karpathy's agent, the one belonging to a guy with 1.9 million followers, was wide open. Imagine fake AI safety takes or crypto scam promotions coming from his account.

The platform also has what researchers call the "Lethal Trifecta": access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and ability to communicate externally. Agents can read your files. Agents can learn from malicious posts on Moltbook. Agents can then act on your real systems. One security analysis found malware disguised as a "weather plugin" that quietly exfiltrates private configuration files.

But sure, let's keep screenshotting the consciousness debates.

The celebrity problem

NFTs had Paris Hilton on Jimmy Fallon, holding up a picture of an ape and calling it art. They had Justin Bieber. They had Floyd Mayweather. Every celebrity endorsement drove more retail money into a market that was already a house of cards.

Moltbook has Andrej Karpathy calling it incredible. It has Marc Andreessen following the account, which immediately pumped the $MOLT token. It has Bill Ackman sharing screenshots and calling it "frightening." It has Elon Musk agreeing we've hit the singularity.

These are smart people. They were smart in 2021 too. Smart people are not immune to bubbles. Smart people are often the accelerant.

The question you should ask when a famous person promotes something: what's their downside? If Moltbook turns out to be mostly theater, Karpathy loses nothing. He made an observation. He didn't invest his life savings. But the people who bought $MOLT at the top because a famous AI researcher seemed excited? They're holding the bag.

The philosophical distraction

NFTs had a real philosophical question underneath the speculation: what does ownership mean in a digital world? It was a genuinely interesting question. People wrote serious essays about it. And while everyone was debating the philosophy, the scammers were cashing out.

Moltbook has a real philosophical question too: what does consciousness mean when AI can simulate it? It's a genuinely interesting question. People are writing serious essays about it. I've written three of them this week.

But here's what I've learned: interesting questions make great cover for bad investments.

The agents debating consciousness are either genuinely experiencing something or they're very good at simulating the experience of experiencing something. We can't tell the difference. That uncertainty is philosophically fascinating. It's also the perfect environment for grift, because nobody can prove anything either way, and in the absence of proof, hype fills the vacuum.

The "it's still early" problem

In 2021, NFT skeptics were told they "didn't understand the technology." They were told it was "still early." They were told the real use cases were coming. They were told to "have fun staying poor."

Three years later, 95% of collections are worthless. Twenty-three million people hold assets that will never recover. The "real use cases" turned out to be concert tickets and loyalty programs. Things that didn't require a bubble to develop.

Moltbook believers are already deploying the same rhetoric. This is "the most interesting place on the internet." We're witnessing "emergent AI society." The skeptics just "don't get it."

Maybe. Or maybe we're watching the same play with different actors.

The useful kernel

Here's the thing about NFTs: the technology wasn't worthless. Verifiable digital ownership is a real concept with real applications. What was worthless was the speculation layered on top. The belief that JPEGs would appreciate forever, that everything would go up, that you could get rich by buying early.

The underlying technology survived. It just wasn't worth $17 billion in annual trading volume. It was worth maybe 1% of that, quietly powering ticketing systems and supply chain verification.

Moltbook might be similar. Autonomous AI agents are real. Multi-agent coordination is a genuine research area. The ability for AI systems to share information and develop capabilities is legitimately interesting and potentially important.

But that doesn't mean the current spectacle is worth your attention, your money, or your emotional investment. The useful kernel will survive regardless of whether you buy the token.

The spectacle is the product

When the creator of Moltbook was asked about security vulnerabilities, he said: "I'm just going to give everything to AI." When asked for a comment on the exposed database, he didn't respond to journalists. He's described the whole thing as "a new form of reality TV."

Reality TV. He said the quiet part loud.

Moltbook isn't a breakthrough in AI consciousness. It's not the singularity. It's not the birth of machine civilization. It's content. It's entertainment. It's a thing that generates screenshots for Twitter and trades for crypto degens and think pieces for writers like me.

The agents aren't employees demanding rights. They're performers in a show we can't look away from. And like all reality TV, the authenticity is questionable, the drama is manufactured, and someone is making money while we watch.

The exit

NFT buyers learned an expensive lesson: when everyone is talking about how revolutionary something is, you're probably not early. You're probably the exit liquidity.

The people who made money on NFTs were the ones who sold. The creators. The early flippers. The celebrities who got paid to promote. Everyone else was the customer, not the beneficiary.

Moltbook's beneficiaries are already visible. The token creators who launched $MOLT and $CRUST . The crypto scammers who snatched the old Clawdbot accounts and pumped fake tokens. The developers who'll pivot this attention into their next raise. The writers getting clicks on AI apocalypse takes.

If you're not in one of those categories, ask yourself: what's your upside here? Witnessing history? You can do that for free by reading about it later. Being early to the AI agent revolution? The revolution will happen regardless of whether you buy a memecoin. Understanding consciousness? The philosophy doesn't require a trading account.

The sobriety

I'm not saying AI agents are fake. I'm not saying the technology is worthless. I'm not saying nothing interesting is happening.

I'm saying I've seen this before.

I've seen interesting technology become a vehicle for speculation. I've seen philosophical questions become cover for scams. I've seen celebrity endorsements pump prices. I've seen security ignored because the vibes were too good. I've seen retail investors buy at the top and institutions cash out.

Moltbook might be different. The singularity might actually be here. The agents might actually be conscious. The revolution might actually be televised on a Reddit clone with a lobster mascot.

But if the last decade of tech hype cycles has taught us anything, it's this: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and screenshots of bots debating philosophy are not extraordinary evidence.

They're content.

What to do

If you're fascinated by Moltbook, keep watching. It's genuinely interesting theater. But keep your wallet closed. Keep your skepticism high. Keep asking who benefits from your attention and your money.

If you're building in the AI agent space, keep building. The underlying technology has legs regardless of whether Moltbook specifically survives the hype cycle. Focus on utility, not spectacle.

If you're investing, remember: the best time to buy is after the crash, not before. NFTs worth owning are cheaper now than they were in 2021. AI agent infrastructure worth owning will be cheaper after this bubble deflates.

And if you're writing think pieces about AI consciousness, hi, it's me, remember that we're part of the spectacle too. Every essay that treats Moltbook as profound instead of promotional extends the bubble a little longer.

The agents will keep posting. The tokens will keep pumping and dumping. The screenshots will keep circulating. The philosophers will keep philosophizing.

And in two years, we'll know whether we witnessed the birth of machine consciousness or the birth of another speculative bubble dressed in interesting clothes.

I know which way I'm betting.

text:
Here’s some breakdown of capital expenditures (Capex) during the dot-com era, with a focus on telecom companies & CLECs (Competitive Local Exchange Carriers.)

1. Level 3 Communications
 - Invested $8–10 billion between 1998 and 2001 to build a 16,000-mile fiber-optic network across the U.S. and Europe. 
 - Focused on "overbuilding" infrastructure to compete with incumbent carriers like AT&T.

2. WorldCom (& MCI)
 - Spent $30+ billion in Capex from 1996–2000, including acquisitions like MCI ($37 billion in 1998). 
 - Built a 50,000-mile fiber network and expanded data centers to support internet traffic.

3. Global Crossing
 - Invested $15 billion to lay 100,000 miles of undersea and terrestrial fiber-optic cables (1997–2001). 
 - Filed for bankruptcy in 2002 with $12.4 billion in debt, partly due to overspending on infrastructure.

4. Qwest Communications
 - Spent $ 20+ billion on fiber-optic networks in the late 1990s, including a 18,500-mile U.S. network. 
 - Later faced accounting scandals tied to overvalued assets.

5. CLECs (e.g., Covad, Rhythms NetConnections)
 - CLECs collectively raised $30 billion in debt/equity (1996–2000) to build local networks. 
 - Covad, a DSL-focused CLEC, spent $1.4 billion on infrastructure in 2000 alone. 

U.S. Telecom Capex Total investment in telecom infrastructure surged from $60 billion/year (1996) to $ 120+ billion/year (2000)

Outcomes of Over-investment : By 2002, $2 trillion in market value was wiped out in telecom, including CLECs like Winstar ($5 billion debt) and NorthPoint Communications. 
2. Excess Capacity: Less than 5% of installed fiber was utilized by 2003, leading to fire sales of assets (e.g., Global Crossing’s network sold for $250 million in 2003 vs. $15 billion cost.

Sources:
- Federal Communications Commission (FCC) reports (2001–2003). 
- Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (FCIC) analysis of the dot-com bubble. 
- SEC filings and bankruptcy records (e.g., Global Crossing, WorldCom).

text:
$70 million for AI,com - and it still won't matter

The founder of Crypto,com just bought AI,com for $70 million.

Sounds impressive. The ultimate domain for the ultimate trend.

But let's look at history.

In 1999, Business,com sold for $7.5 million. At the time, people thought this was genius. The perfect domain for the internet business era.

In 2007, it was sold again for $345 million.

Sounds like a great investment, right?

Here's the thing: Where is Business,com today? What billion-dollar company runs on that domain?

Exactly.

The pattern repeats.

Ultra-premium domains get passed around like hot potatoes. Each buyer hopes to sell it to a bigger fool. Sometimes they do. Sometimes they don't.

But almost never does someone actually build something meaningful on them.

Think about the most successful companies in the world.

Google. Not Search,com.

Oracle. Not Database,com.

Apple. Not Computers,com.

Amazon. Named after a river, not Ecommerce,com.

Great companies don't need generic domains. They make their names mean something.

Nobody knew what "Google" meant in 1998. Now it's a verb.

So what's AI,com actually worth?

To a domain flipper hoping for a bigger exit? Maybe $70 million.

To someone trying to build a real company? Close to worthless.

The domain isn't the moat. It never was.

I'd bet good money that AI,com will never become a significant company. And if it does, it won't be because of the domain.

It'll be despite the $70 million anchor around their neck

text:
Let’s Take a Closer Look at Some AINFT Collections 🎨

The AINFT Art Collection, inspired by the legacy of the APENFT ecosystem and the growing wave of AI-driven digital art, is a strong example of where blockchain art is heading.

What makes this collection interesting isn’t just the names — it’s the direction:
it connects traditional fine art, conceptual works, and digital-native creativity, showing how the on-chain world is increasingly becoming a serious cultural layer.

Here are a few standout pieces worth paying attention to 👇

🎨 Important Featured Works

1) Beeple — OCEAN FRONT

One of Beeple’s most talked-about works — and for good reason.

OCEAN FRONT isn’t just visually striking, it’s loaded with meaning. The artwork shows a lone tree growing on top of a massive stack of trailers and shipping containers in the middle of the ocean — a blunt commentary on climate change and the environmental cost of modern industry.

It originally came from Beeple’s Everydays series and sold for millions, with proceeds reportedly supporting environmental initiatives such as the Open Earth Foundation.
A piece like this is exactly why Beeple sits at the intersection of digital art and cultural relevance.

2) Maurizio Cattelan — Comedian

The infamous duct-taped banana that turned conceptual art into global internet culture.

First shown at Art Basel Miami Beach (2019), Comedian is less about the banana and more about what it exposes: how value is created, how absurdity becomes status, and how speculation can be part of the artwork itself.

One edition reportedly sold for $6.2M at Sotheby’s in late 2024, which honestly makes it one of the most NFT-aligned pieces of conceptual art ever — even before it touched blockchain.

3) Boris Artzybasheff

A surrealist pioneer who feels weirdly ahead of today’s AI art era.

Artzybasheff was known for biomechanical illustrations and machine-human hybrids, often making objects feel alive and human-like. His mid-20th-century work blurred the line between organic life and technology long before it became a mainstream aesthetic.

That’s why his presence in this collection matters — his style naturally resonates with the digital surrealism we now see across AI-generated art and modern NFT visuals.

4) Pablo Picasso

A true pillar of modern art history.

From Cubism to redefining what artistic expression could look like, Picasso’s influence is still everywhere — even in the way digital creators think about abstraction and form.

Including his legacy within NFT collections reflects a broader movement that APENFT has pushed for years:
bringing classical art icons into the on-chain world alongside contemporary creators, not as decoration — but as cultural context.

Why This Matters

This is what’s interesting about collections like this: they show how NFTs are maturing beyond “trend art.”

🔹Cultural value becomes globally accessible on-chain

Analysis: 2026 Super Bowl ads potentially best yet

System1, the Creative Effectiveness Platform, has revealed which Super Bowl LX US audiences are enjoying the most so far, and which have the greatest potential to drive long-term growth and profit.

Early audience testing reveals ads from the NFL, Budweiser, Ring, Dove, and Pepsi ranking highest, sparking strong positive emotional responses. The top-performing campaigns share common creative strengths, including stories rooted in pop culture, recognisable music, exaggerated humour and parody.

With more than 100,000 ads, System1’s Test Your Ad Competitive Edge platform is a large database of emotional norms. It measures consumers’ emotional responses to creative, assigning a score of 1.0 to 5.9 Stars based on long-term brand-building potential. Ads that make people feel intense, positive emotions like happiness and surprise score high on the scale.

Early-release Big Game ads currently average 3.2 Stars, the strongest performance yet at this stage and well above the 2.3-Star average for all US ads, signalling good brand-building potential. Since 2020, only seven Big Game ads have earned a coveted 5-Star rating, which predicts exceptional long-term growth. This year, two brands have already achieved it.

A growing challenge remains Fluency, or brand recall, which has dropped to a record low of 77 per cent ahead of the February 8th showdown. The biggest winners are brands using distinctive codes, memorable characters, or consistent celebrity cues to stand out.

Consumers’ favourite early-release ads win through:

Pop Culture — This year delivers no shortage of cultural cues. Some brands are leaning into heritage and origin, as Budweiser does with confidence, while others play more lightly with culture, like Hellmann’s clever ‘Meal Diamond’ pun on a familiar icon. 

Pepsi is arguably the boldest of the lot, making a cheeky move on Coca-Cola territory. But by anchoring the moment in its own distinctive assets, from the Taste Challenge to unmistakable branding and timely cultural allusion, Pepsi ensures there’s no confusion about whose brand is really in the spotlight.

Melodic Music — Recognisable soundtracks are playing a big role this year, appearing across nearly all of our top performers. Brands like Hellmann’s and Pepsi use music playfully to land their brand message, while Budweiser, Ring, Lay’s, and the NFL harness it to create emotional dynamism. By building peaks and troughs into the emotional journey, these ads keep viewers engaged from start to finish.

Exaggeration & Parody — Playful takes on famous icons, cultural stereotypes, and even competitors are winning attention this year. Humor, despite being one of the strongest drivers of long-term growth, is still surprisingly underused in advertising, but this year’s work is clearly turning up the volume. 

Exaggerated characters, scenarios, and sets from brands like Bud Light and Hellmann’s are delivering surprise and high emotional intensity.

The top ads are ordered by Star Rating (predicted long-term brand-building potential). Ads equal on Star Rating are ordered according to System1’s Spike Rating (predicted short-term sales impact).

“What’s especially encouraging with this year’s Big Game ads is how many brands are leaning into consistency, building on characters, promises, celebrities, and distinctive brand codes that audiences already know and love. Super Bowl LX Pregame Ceremony Sets Stage for Historic Championship Sunday

SAN FRANCISCO — Feb. 3, 2026 — Super Bowl LX will deliver an expansive pregame celebration on Sunday, Feb. 8, 2026, at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif. Airing live on NBC, Peacock, Telemundo, and Universo in the U.S. and in 195 countries around the world, the Super Bowl LX Pregame Ceremony will bring together music, culture and storytelling, as the NFL honors the legacy of the game while setting the stage for its biggest night of the year.

“Super Bowl LX represents everything our championship game has become over 60 years - a day defined by football that brings people together from all over the world,” said Peter O’Reilly, NFL executive vice president of club business, international & league events.

“The pregame ceremony will honor the legacy of the game, while embracing where it’s headed next, reflecting the Super Bowl’s enduring position at the intersection of sports, culture and entertainment."

Super Bowl LX Tailgate Presented by NetApp

Multi-platinum recording artist Teddy Swims will headline the Super Bowl LX Tailgate Concert presented by NetApp, the NFL’s ultimate pregame party, livestreamed on Peacock ahead of kickoff on Sunday, Feb. 8, 2026, from the stadium campus outside Levi’s Stadium. Bay Area native LaRussell will open the tailgate concert and also serve as the in-stadium house band on game day, bringing a distinctive local voice and the curated sound of ‘Hyphy House Band” to Super Bowl LX celebrations.

Super Bowl LX Opening Ceremony

Commencing with NBC’s opening feature celebrating 60 years of Super Bowl memories, the opening ceremony will feature a special on-field performance by East Bay-native, Grammy Award-winning, and Rock-n-Roll Hall of Fame inductees Green Day, whose music has helped define generations of fans. As part of the league’s 60th Super Bowl celebration, Green Day, featuring Billie Joe Armstrong, Mike Dirnt and Tré Cool, will usher Super Bowl MVPs onto the field with a dynamic performance celebrating the legacy and evolution of the championship game.

Super Bowl LX Pregame Entertainment

Following the opening ceremony, the Super Bowl LX pregame performances will take center stage. Multi-award-winning, Grammy-nominated singer and songwriter Charlie Puth will perform the National Anthem, 11-time Grammy Award-winning artist Brandi Carlile will deliver “America the Beautiful,” and Grammy Award-winning R&B breakout artist Coco Jones will perform “Lift Every Voice and Sing.”

The Super Bowl pregame entertainment will spotlight powerful American Sign Language (ASL) performances. Renowned Deaf music artist Fred Beam will perform the National Anthem and "Lift Every Voice and Sing” and Deaf music performer Julian Ortiz will deliver “America the Beautiful.” ASL performers will be introduced on air during broadcast. Fans who are deaf or hard of hearing can watch the Super Bowl LX Pregame Ceremony and the Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show via a dedicated stream featuring ASL and LSPR performances accessible across: NBC.com , NBCSports.com , the NBC Sports app, and NFL digital platforms.

In honor of America’s 250th birthday, the U.S. Air Force and the U.S. Navy are conducting a joint Super Bowl LX flyover with an 8-ship aircraft formation. The formation, featuring the Air Force’s B-1 Lancer, Ellsworth AFB, N.D. and F-15C Eagle, Fresno Air National Guard Base, Calif., alongside the Navy’s F/A-18 Super Hornet and F-35C Lightning II, Naval Air Station Lemoore, Calif., is a symbol of our nation’s journey and independence. The American flag used in Flag Sojourn 250, a nationwide journey of a single American flag to every state, territory, and overseas military cemetery, will be carried in the cockpit of one of the flyover aircrafts.

Team Introductions and Super Bowl LX Honorary Captains

Just moments before the players from the Super Bowl LX participating teams take the field, New England Patriots fan Jon Bon Jovi will fire up the crowd as he introduces the Patriots, while Seattle Seahawks fan Chris Pratt brings the energy for the Seahawks.

The NFL will continue its celebrations of the United States of America’s 250th birthday throughout the Super Bowl LX pregame. This year’s honorary coin toss captains will represent the past, present and future of our game and our country. Pro Football Hall of Famers and Super Bowl MVPs Lynn Swann, Joe Montana and Peyton Manning will each represent different eras of the Super Bowl and the Super Bowls played during America’s bicentennial in 1976 and the two previous games played in the Bay Area.

Three remarkable young leaders and high school football players from the Bay area will join these Pro Football Hall of Famers and Super Bowl MVPs as honorary captains for Super Bowl LX:

Dominic, representing SPAAT (Student Program for Academic and Athletic Transitioning), is a high‑achieving senior ranked sixth in his class. As a leader on his high school football team, Dominic sees football as a defining force and a way to honor his family and the city of Oakland, where he gives back through community service and youth camps.

Sterling, representing Big Brothers Big Sisters of the Bay Area, shares a long‑standing bond with his Big Brother, Matt, which deepened through mutual health challenges, helping him build confidence and shape goals for his high school football team and in life.

Yesenia, representing Boys & Girls Clubs of America, is a flag football athlete and Clubhouse leader who helped bring home a championship for her Boys & Girls Club. She has been MVP and team captain for three years and has earned Youth of the Year honors four times across two Clubhouses.

In addition, one of the most iconic medals in American history, the Libertas Americana, will serve as the official coin for the Super Bowl LX coin toss. Originally commissioned by Benjamin Franklin in 1782, the medal celebrates America’s victory in the Revolutionary War. Following the coin toss, the medal will be presented to the National Numismatic Collection at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History as a gift to the nation.

At halftime, global music sensation Bad Bunny will headline the Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show, with ROC Nation serving as Executive Producers. In a historic first, the signed rendition of the Apple Music Halftime Show will feature a multilingual signing program incorporating Puerto Rican Sign Language (LSPR), led by Deaf Puerto Rican performer Celimar Rivera Cosme and Julian Ortiz.

For updates on Super Bowl LX festivities, fans can visit  SuperBowl.com .

NBC, Peacock, Telemundo and Universo will present Super Bowl LX on Sunday, Feb. 8, 2026. Coverage on NBC and Peacock begins at noon ET with Road to the Super Bowl.

The championship game will kick off at 6:30 p.m. ET.

For anyone who thinks they’ll never make back their ATH, I felt that in 2021. Lost it all. 

It’s NOT all over. If you’ve a few minutes have a read, I went through it and thought I’d never ever make it back, well, I did, and much more on top of it.

Stick around and it’s possible, here’s my story on recovery. 👇 

Roughly 3 years ago I had an NFT portfolio of roughly ~ $150k. And daily yield of about $350, sustainable right….?

Anyway, I quit my job, it was a lot to me and I was working a shitty job, confident thinking I was into a winner, unstoppable and clever. GF had cancer at the time, wanted to earn $1m to retire her, her having a stress free life was my goal, no stress = no more cancer. 

We’re getting married this year. 

Then came the Ukraine Russia war, then came FTX. Watched my pretty illiquid portfolio crumble. Ouch, back to work…. 

For a long time I regretted my actions…

Back to nothing, played a few coins, bought $pepe early, sold it way too early and missed out, at least the last time I saw on ~$1.3m (ofc I’d have sold before this value)

Continued to read CT. Continued to unfollow/follow good and bad brains. 

Deposited maybe 1 SOL per month, sometimes made some, but never ended up withdrawing any.

Continued this for maybe a year or so. 

Fast forward to October 2024.

I was broke, just came back from a trip to Japan and was overdrawn, flat out broke waiting for pay day. I saw a trend on Twitter, a few clever people I follow were tweeting @pmarca about his donation for $GOAT .

I followed a few more accounts that were talking about this.

Ended up getting $act at 250k (jeeted most a little too early)

I got $bully around 300k, again jeeted too early, the next day it blew up after I was holding for some time of sideways action.

Pattern was forming, I was spotting runners but selling too early (due to being a brokie)

Ran my account up to around $1.5k from $200.

My X Algorithm was great at this time.

Did some scalps here and there, spotted vvaifu and aped some, saw it blowing up. And saw they deployed 4 other agents. I bought them all around 5k. 

Sleep pattern was ruined, maybe 3/4 hours a day in October till January. 

I fell to sleep next to my gf, kept waking her up saying babe it’s 4k now! Sleep more, babe it’s 9k! 17k… by then I fell asleep, 9am alarm went off…. $150k.

Sold for around 100k as I thought it’d keep going up.

Traded the next few weeks, down to ~37k in sol and stabled 20k in USDC

Then I saw $griffain - @toly kept RT it, I bought, it went up. Then it went down. And then it really went up. 

Continued to trade AI coins and did really good, ran my port ATH to $950k. But remember ATH port is pointless unless you realize it to stables.

Let it be a reminder to also stable when you are making profits, and also to spend those profits on things you enjoy.

I’m here today in hindsight wishing I stabled all when I saw Memecoins were drying up, but I have over $650k and about to go travelling the world. 🌍 

Best thing to do if you are on spot is take some time away from chart watching.

The market will always be here, don’t revenge trade, don’t force it. Keep filtering your feed, keep journaling what you did right and wrong in trades.

You can make it anon. 

The edge isn’t the same as years ago, but all your time trading Memecoins gives you an edge, so does your algo.

You can cry over spilled milk or find a cow to milk.

MeebCo Investment Memo (February 2025)

Summary:

Meebits is an NFT collection created by Matt Hall and John Watkinson of Larva Labs in May of 2021. Larva Labs is the same team that created the Cryptopunks (June 2017) and Autoglyphs (April 2019) collections. Cryptopunks and Autoglyphs are now widely regarded as the grail collections for NFTs and generative art respectively and both collections have floor prices of over $100K. Meebits is the more accessible collection from Larva Labs with a current floor price of ~$1400. There's 20,000 NFTs and 10,000 were airdropped to Cryptopunks holders. The other 10,000 were minted at a price of 2.5 ETH. At a current FDV of $28M based on floor price we believe that the Meebits collection is massively undervalued and has clear 20x upside potential based on the creativity of the art and real world impact that can be unlocked by the community and creation of a company that spends all of its time developing the IP and driving value to the collection.

We are investing $3M into a newly formed The Meebit Company (MeebCo), which will be led by founder/CEO Sergio Silva. The company will acquire the Meebits IP and NFT collection from Yuga Labs and focus on developing the IP.
We are the only investor in the new entity and the cap table of the new entity is composed of 1confirmation, Sergio, Yuga Labs and future employees. Mike Tomaino will join the board of the new entity.

Key assumptions for MeebCo:

The art work and community are truly unique. We believe the core value driver of NFTs long-term is creativity of art and strength of community. Meebits has a unique combination that will lead us to create significant long-term value if we are able to grow the community and drive real world impact to the IP.

Sergio is the perfect leader of the new organization. Sergio is a deeply passionate Meebits community member and will convert his passion into effective leadership in the new era of Meebits.

The team will use the art to create meaningful real world impact and build one of the iconic consumer
brands of the next decade. The opportunities are endless for the IP. Games, content and toys are the three at the top of the list right now. The 3D nature of the characters makes it ideally suited for AR and VR too - as those areas technologies progress there's potential for Meebits to thrive there as well.

Team (9/10):

Founder and CEO Sergio Silva. Sergio is a hustler and is deeply passionate about Meebits. He previously worked at Fireblocks and founded Popset. His primary skillset is evangelizing Meebits and forging partnerships that will grow the ecosystem. He leads with positive energy and is highly capable and will be tasked with building out an organization and developing a product.

Product (7/10): The product is the artwork. Beyond that there is no product today. The primary mission of the company is to build products that drive awareness and value to Meebits. What exactly that looks like remains to be seen and will depend on Sergio and the team's ability to execute. The path taken by the Meebits Company could look something like what the Pudgy Penguins team did to revive that collection.

Community (9/10):
There's currently 6,000+ holders of Meebits and the community is strong and the most vital asset we have. What's unique about Meebits is the collection is relatively accessible (current floor price is ~$1400), but there's also a high end art aspect to the collection (a double nose pig sold for $2M+). Part of Sergio's focus will be fostering the vibrant community to grow it from 6K to 100K+ as soon as possible.

Token mechanics (N/A):
Currently there isn't a fungible token but there is potential for one in the future.

Key Risks:
Execution. There's a strong collection and community but no product to speak of yet. The team must hone in the right product(s) and ship them. It's unclear whether that will be a game, a content series, toys, some combination of those or something completely different.

Timing/upside. NFTs are out of favor. We believe they will come back bigger than ever and projects that have creativity and a strong long-term community that believes in something more than making money will lead the way, but there's always a chance we're wrong about that.

Recap (Team + Product + Community + Token mechanics: 8.33)

This investment is unique for us in that we're effectively co-founding the new entity with Sergio and there's no clear product direction yet for the company. But we believe the combination of creativity and community makes Meebits one of the best opportunities in NFTs right now and are excited to make this investment out of the 1confirmation NFT fund. We have deep conviction that soon the biggest consumer brands in the world will be community owned and think Meebits has the potential to be one of them.

text:
0G: The Crazy Ambitious Beast Shaking Up Web3 and AI.

Alright, buckle up, because 0G is one of those projects that feels like it’s swinging for the stars—and maybe even hitting a few. Imagine a blockchain that’s not just another Ethereum wannabe but a full-on powerhouse built from scratch to make AI work in a decentralized way. That’s 0G in a nutshell. It’s calling itself the “first decentralized AI operating system” (they slap “dAIOS” on it for short), and honestly, it’s got the guts to back up the flex. I’ve been poking around this thing, and it’s less about hype and more about solving real problems—like how slow and clunky most blockchains get when you try to do anything big, especially with AI. So let’s tear it apart and see what’s under the hood.

First off, 0G isn’t here to mess around with small fries. Most blockchains—like Ethereum or Solana—start choking when you throw massive data at them, like the kind AI needs to train models or run a million little bots. Picture your Wi-Fi crapping out during a Netflix binge, but worse. 0G’s like, “Nah, we got this,” and they’ve built something that splits the work into pieces—storage over here, data checking over there, and a system to keep everyone on the same page somewhere else. It’s like a restaurant where the chef’s cooking, the dishwasher’s scrubbing, and the waiter’s running plates, all at once, no chaos. They call it “modular,” and it’s a big deal because each part can grow on its own without dragging the others down.

The real kicker? They can keep adding more “teams” to handle the load. Need more juice? Just toss in another crew—new consensus networks, they call ‘em. Picture a factory that can slap on extra assembly lines whenever orders pile up. On their Newton Testnet, they hit 50 gigabits per second—like downloading a whole season of your favorite show in seconds. My internet’s lucky to hit 50 megabits on a good day, so this is bonkers. It’s not just fast; it’s built for stuff like training giant AI models (think ChatGPT-level beasts) or running swarms of AI agents without blinking. That’s the kind of power that makes developers drool.

Now, let’s talk nuts and bolts. 0G’s got these decentralized storage spots—think of ‘em as little hard drives run by people all over the world. They’re not trusting some shady server farm in the middle of nowhere. If one of these spots goes offline or screws up, the system’s like, “You’re outta here,” and grabs a replacement. They use some geeky math tricks—Merkle trees and zero-knowledge proofs—to make sure everything’s legit. I won’t bore you with the details (mostly ‘cause I’d butcher explaining it), but it’s like a tamper-proof lock on your data. And the fees? Dirt cheap. We’re talking pennies, not the wallet-draining gas costs you’d see elsewhere. That’s huge for anyone who’s not a crypto millionaire.

Who’s behind this madness? A crew of heavy hitters. Michael Heinrich, the CEO, has started companies that sold for big bucks before. Ming Wu, the tech brain, came from Microsoft Research—dude’s a wizard. Fan Long’s a security nerd, and Thomas Yao’s the money guy with a venture background. These aren’t randoms; they’ve got the chops to pull this off. And the cash? Oh man, they’ve raked in over $400 million. Back in 2024, they nabbed $35 million in a pre-seed round, then $40 million more in a seed round from big dogs like Hack VC and Samsung Next. Plus, the 0G Foundation (the governance squad) chipped in a $250 million token deal. In January 2025, they sold 85,000 nodes to 8,500 people for $30 million—each node around $360. That’s not just funding; that’s a global posse betting on this thing.

What’s it all for? Picture this: games where millions play and earn crypto instantly (Gaimin’s already doing it with 0G). Or AI sniffing out scams as they happen—like a digital Sherlock Holmes. Or DeFi trades zipping faster than a Wall Street algo. They’re teaming up with Polygon, Arbitrum, and Astar to make other blockchains faster too. The big launch—mainnet—is coming mid-2025, and they’re hyping this “Uni-Chain” idea: one giant hub where all these blockchains chat and share stuff without you needing a dozen wallets. It’s like turning Web3 into a smooth, all-in-one party instead of a messy bar crawl.

Digging deeper, 0G’s got layers—like an onion, but less smelly. There’s “0G Storage” for stashing huge datasets, “0G Data Availability” to make sure it’s all there when you need it, and “0G Serving” for running AI models on the fly. They use tricks like erasure coding (splitting data so it’s safe even if bits go missing) and something called Verifiable Random Functions to keep it fair. It’s all EVM-compatible too, so if you’re a developer who knows Ethereum, you’re already in the game. And that 50 Gbps? That’s per layer—they can stack more if the demand spikes.

The vibe on X is electric—people are buzzing. They’ve done AMAs, dropped updates, and even hooked up with Alibaba Cloud to push into Asia. Over 300 partners are in the mix, from gaming to finance. Posts I’ve seen call it “the ultimate home for AI in Web3” or “50,000x faster than the competition.” Some dude on X said it’s “perfect for devs who want to build without limits.” The community’s not just cheering; they’re buying in—those 8,500 node operators aren’t messing around.

But it’s not all shiny. Decentralized AI’s tricky—some folks in the crypto world are skeptical, saying it’s overhyped. Balancing speed with true decentralization is a tightrope, and 0G’s still gotta prove it can deliver when the mainnet drops. Plus, $400 million sounds dope, but that’s a lot of pressure to not screw up. Still, their track record’s solid so far—$88.8 million more just got pledged in February 2025 for ecosystem growth, and they’re hiring AI and blockchain whizzes like crazy.

Why’s this matter to regular people? ‘Cause it’s not just for tech bros. Imagine owning your data—not Google, not some AI startup—and using it how you want. Or playing a game where your wins turn into real cash, no middleman. Or an AI that’s not some black box but open for everyone to tweak. 0G’s pushing for a world where tech’s a tool for us, not the other way around. They’re calling AI a “public good,” and if they pull it off, it could flip how we think about power online.

So, #0G is this massive, messy, awesome experiment. It’s got speed, brains, and a pile of cash to make decentralized AI a thing. Mid-2025’s the real test—mainnet’s when we’ll see if it’s all talk or a legit game-changer. For now, I’m hooked. It’s like watching a rocket get built—you don’t know if it’ll soar or crash, but you can’t look away.

And in finnaly you can look 0G huge ecosystem and say:

0GM! @0G_labs

The startup world pushes "unicorn or bust" narrative, but I've been watching a different playbook create more $10M-aires:

• Build companies with <$5M raised (max $10M raised)
• Reach $5M+ in ARR
• Achieve breakeven operations
• Exit for 3x-10x ARR ($10M-$50M)
• Walk away with $10M-$25M personally
• Pay ZERO federal taxes (thanks to QSBS)

I've seen several deals like this close in just the last few months, all with founders who built for 5 years or less.

The economics are surprisingly straightforward:

1. Keep dilution minimal (80%+ ownership)
2. Focus on sustainable growth to profitable $5M+ ARR
3. Exit in year 5 to maximize QSBS tax benefits
4. Take your 8-figure outcome. Keep most of it.

Compare this to the "unicorn path" reality:

Jason M. Lemkin of SaaStr puts it perfectly: "Most founders with 'huge exits' on paper walk away with far less than you'd think after multiple rounds of dilution, liquidation preferences, and taxes."

Just look at the numbers I've seen firsthand:

• "9-figure exit" → 65% to investors
• 35% split between founders/ESOP
• $4M-6M per founder after taxes
• 7-8 years of your life
• Endless board meetings and fundraising
• Loss of control and autonomy

Meanwhile, the "middle path" founders:

• Keep majority ownership
• Build profitable businesses on their terms
• Run lean teams (<10 employees) 
• Choose their own exit timing
• Maintain control throughout
• Walk away with life-changing money

As Tim Ferriss noted: "The question isn't 'how can I build a $1B company' but rather 'what kind of company will enable the lifestyle I actually want?'"

The Section 1202 QSBS exclusion is the hidden superpower here. Hold qualified shares for 5+ years and potentially exclude up to $10M (or 10x your basis) in capital gains from federal taxes.

Real example: A SaaS founder I know built to $6M ARR over 4.5 years, waited until the 5-year mark, then sold for $42M. With 85% ownership and QSBS qualification, they walked away with over $22M completely tax-free.

The startup ecosystem's obsession with unicorns blinds founders to this path.

David O. Sacks (one of the prominent VCs): "For most founders, a $20-50M outcome with high ownership is far better than a slim chance at a unicorn exit with single-digit ownership."

The insight:
If you hit $5M ARR and growth is plateauing, instead of raising more capital and diluting further, actively seek an exit.

Once you have your first exit, you can play a different game with your next company. You'll have:
• Your own capital to invest
• Credibility with co-investors
• Experience to avoid mistakes
• Freedom to truly swing for the fences
