text:
"Blockbuster turned out to be the worst investment I ever made" - Carl Icahn. Oh, was it? [Part 1]

First, I want to thank everyone for taking my poll about the main reason for Blockbuster's demise. There was only one person who voted for what I think was most conclusively the real main reason for Blockbusters demise and should have discussed more broadly over two decades ago. I will explain why I think so later. This post includes speculation. And we'll hammer this speculation home.

Topics:
** The mainstream reasons why Blockbuster failed
** Blockbuster's history, from inception to its IPO
** Blockbuster's IPO in 1999 and Viacom cashing in
** Blockbuster from 1999 until the Viacom spin-off in 2004
** Viacom's second dividend; shareholder deception '99 all over again
** Side quest: Removing late fees probably costing Blockbuster several $100m in operating income per year
** Carl Icahn enters the game: The acquisition attempt of Hollywood Entertainment
** Carl Icahn as new shareholder; the person and his plans
** Blockbuster's planned murder? (This is speculation)
** Carl continuing the former board's path...
** The business behind the business (speculation)
** The very roughly estimated value for a third-party dealmaker
** Interlude: About cigar butts and real value vs balance sheets
** Looking back at Hollywood
** Ending thoughts

** The mainstream reasons why Blockbuster failed

Asking grok for former deep dives into Blockbuster's demise and grouping them it comes up with the following:
* Failure to Adapt to Digital Technology and Innovation (8 sources)
* Poor Strategic and Management Decisions (6 sources)
* Financial Mismanagement and Debt (4 sources)
* Customer Dissatisfaction and Changing Preferences (2 sources)
( nitter.poast.org/i/grok/share/45449cf97… )

While the list is by far not comprehensive and the sources of varying quality, this pretty much reflects the public opinion from all I know. Grokipedia as of today (January 2026) reads that "failed attempts to adapt [...], compounded by heavy debt and [losses], led to bankruptcy filing in 2010 with only 1,700 corporate stores remaining" ( grokipedia.com/page/Blockbus… ).

Carl Icahn said: "It failed because of too much debt and changes in the industry" ( forbes.com/sites/stevenberto… ).

What you are about to read is another perspective and I invite any discussion since I may have made mistakes and formed wrong conclusions. However, it is interesting as fuck and includes lessons from $AMC , $GME and other companies I investigated over the last two years.

** Blockbuster's history, from inception to its IPO

Blockbuster was founded on October 19, 1985, by David Cook in Texas, after his software business as his wife suggested he should rent out videos for oil workers. He created a software for checkout, inventory tracking and even tracking customer preferences.
Oil workers? Well,... uh, no clue what genre the first videos were mainly, but, ah, uh,... that doesn't matter here, right?
In 1987 he sold part of the business and Wayne Huizenga took control, moving its headquarters to Fort Lauderdale in Florida. He grew it to over 1,000 stores and internationalized it before selling it in 1994 to Viacom ( history.com/this-day-in-hist… ). Viacom acquired Blockbuster through a stock-swap merger which was valued at $8.4bn ( latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-… ), including that Blockbuster bought Viacom shares for $1.25bn ( nytimes.com/1994/01/08/busin… ).

This acquisition looks super interesting. We also find QVC in this bid. Maybe it is worth another post at some point in time. We'll continue for now. This sets the stage for Viacom's role in Blockbuster's next phase.

** Blockbuster's IPO in 1999 and Viacom cashing in

In August 1999 Blockbuster IPO'd $465m by selling a 18% stake, with Viacom as the remaining majority holder with 82%. The shares were sold for $15 per share, $1 under the previously set range of $16-$18. Putting the valuation of Blockbuster to $2.63bn, way under what Viacom paid for it ( latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-… ).

Maybe Viacom wanted to use the halo of the dot-com valuations, which were at the height then. Even while their free cash flow was pretty much negative with roughly -$40m in 1999 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). But they had a positive overall cash flow of $137.2m that year. Nice, right?
By undercutting the range we can assume there just wasn't enough demand for the IPO as investors were said to already worry about new technology.
Uh, and ... not sure but, maaaybe investors were also worried about Viacom paying itself a cash dividend of $1.4bn in December 31, 1998 masked as debt (same as above, "Note 8--Notes Payable to Viacom") and paid by a new $1.9bn unsecured credit agreement with a syndicate of banks on June 21, 1999 ($700 long-term revolver due 2004, $600m term-loan due 2002 and $600m short-term revolver). The repayment to Viacom totaled to $1,576m. The timing was either a coincidence or deliberately done, giving people the chance to not realize the impact during the IPO in August.

Hypotheses 1: Blockbuster used the timing of the debt paid dividend to deceive share buyers with a temporary better looking balance sheet.

Probably, Viacom would have sold even more shares if they had a buyer. They already tell us that they plan to sell the rest (see latimes above).

We can assume the banks at the time had reasonable belief that their loan will pay off, or would they lean into the hype of a rosy future?

Question 1: What was Blockbuster's security entering the deal and allowing reasonable interest rates from the banks?

** Blockbuster from 1999 until the Viacom spin-off in 2004

We see positive free cash flow until 2005, but instead their cumulative operating income before taxes from 2000-2004 was roughly $-4bn. Even if we would add impairments and dividends on top, we end up at $-168m cumulatively.
But hey, what really matters is cash flow, right? If you want to save some taxes you'll probably on paper reduce your operating income anyways.

Thus, let us look into their cash flows. Free cash flow adds up to $6.6bn from 1999 to 2004. In 2006 we learn that Blockbuster is reclassifying their rental library as current instead of non-current and their purchases as operating cash outflows instead of investing cash outflows after months of discussion with the SEC ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). They state that it doesn't affect "revenues, net income, total assets, shareholders’ equity, total cash flows, current cash or liquidity position" and adjust the cash flow for 2004 and 2003. Further they say the original statements for those years should no longer be relied upon.

We won't stop here but adjust the free cash flow for 1999-2004, which leaves us with a total discrepancy of $5.1bn and a restated free cash flow of $1.5bn. Anyone experienced with financial accounting and the rather fast-lived nature of the movie industry, digging into their financial statements could have done this adjustment before.

Would you think this was a surprise for someone like Carl Icahn? Probably not.
Do you think this was a surprise for the banks with their $1.9bn unsecured credit agreement?

Hypotheses 2: The bank feels Blockbuster has enough security for a $1.9b loan.

[CHART 1: Financial performance of Blockbuster]

Next we can see major impairments from 2002 to 2004, cumulating to $4.6bn.

"In mid-December of 2002, the Company issued a press release stating that it would have lower than anticipated earnings for the quarter and the year due to softness in sales during the holiday season. In addition, the press release cited unanticipated competitive factors contributing to the Company’s earnings shortfall. As a result of this information, the Company’s stock price declined" ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Note 2—Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets") and so they impaired $1.82bn.

In 2003 these were justified by "Company’s performance during the holiday selling season [...] caused by increased competition. [...] Additional risks included implementation risks associated with the Company’s new initiatives and risks associated with certain of the Company’s international operations, such as increased competition, two-tiered pricing and piracy". They conclude that this "adversely affected Viacom’s negotiations with third parties regarding their possible disposal of their investment in the Company" ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Note 3—Impairment of Goodwill and Other Long-Lived Assets").
Yes, they were trying to sell Blockbuster in late 2003 for $2.5bn, but didn't get a deal ( nytimes.com/2003/12/15/busin… ).

During Q3 2004, the management believed the planned divesture needed an impairment test where they concluded that accelerated decline in the in-store rental industry, accelerated investments in initiatives and other growth opportunities and increased competition in the online movie rental industry needed another huge impairment ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Note 2—Impairment of Goodwill and Other Long-Lived Assets").

End of 2004 their goodwill position was down to $1.1bn from $6.8bn in 2000, caused by these major impairments and former depreciation. Leaving a book value of $1bn.

We know a lot of example where impairments were used for allegedly undervalued asset sales ($QVCGA with Zulily - nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/2… ; $TCS - nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/1… ; $GME , $BBBY - nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/1… ; $LUMN - nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/1… ). Thus we'll form a hypotheses.

Hypotheses 3: Blockbuster used the $4.6bn impairment to prepare an undervalued asset sale.

On February 10, 2004, Viacom announced that it wants to sell its 81.5% Blockbuster stake. 

On March 15, 2004 we learn that the board intents a special dividend in the case of a split-off ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "BLOCKBUSTER OVERVIEW").

June 18, 2004 Blockbuster adds that the special dividend will be a cash distribution of $5 per share. Totaling $905m, whereof 738m would go to Viacom, financed by a new $1.45bn credit facility from JPMorgan, Citigroup and Credit Suisse First Boston, also replacing the old facility ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ), which was paid down by the time besides $50m.

** Viacom's second dividend; shareholder deception '99 all over again

On August 20, 2004, they announced the dividend for everyone holding stock August 27, 2004 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ), which brought Viacom's cash from Blockbuster dividends to a total of 2.314b. They ended up financing the deal with $300m 9% senior subordinated notes due 2012 and a $650m loan under the now $1.15 credit facility, both done that day.

On October 27, 2004, Blockbuster Inc. issued a press release announcing its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2004. A copy of the press release is attached hereto as exhibit 99.1.
 sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… 

The tender offer ran from September 8 to October 5, 2004 and offered 5.15 Blockbuster shares (2.575 Class A and 2.575 Class B) received per tendered Viacom share at the time representing a 19.2% premium ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). The offer was oversubscribed and participants received about 9.2% of the shares they tendered for ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). Viacom class B were at $35.32 and the Blockbuster package value was $40.27 (5.15 x $7.82), reducing the premium to 14% at the time of the transaction.

Like in 1999 it was either coincidence or deliberately done, giving people the chance to not realize the impact of the dividend and debt.

Oh, that pretty much adds to Hypotheses 1: Blockbuster used the timing of the debt paid dividend to deceive share buyers with a temporary better looking balance sheet.

While the 10q on September 9 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ), at the start of the tender offer, was looking good in terms of shareholder equity of $3.4bn, assets of $4.8bn and total debt of $1.4bn those numbers changed significantly.

On November 11, the 10q after the tender offer ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ), we learn that for September 30 shareholders were left with $1.1bn equity, assets of $3.4bn and total debt of $2.3bn, a significantly weaker balance sheet. Those flipping the shares for cash potentially made a good deal but long-term holder were obviously worse off.
This may have been legally fine, but morally in my opinion was a deception of shareholders ... but maybe for some a useful deception? We'll see why.

** Side quest: Removing late fees probably costing Blockbuster several $100m in operating income per year

There were some lawsuits with Blockbuster, but the biggest was certainly a class action lawsuit for Extended Viewing Fee Policies filed in February 1999. It claimed that Blockbuster defrauded and/or deceived its customers who didn't return their products in time using unlawful penalties which resulted in unjust enrichment ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Item 3. Legal Proceedings").

June 2001, Blockbuster proposes a settlement offer, paying the attorney fees ($9.25m) and giving all customers a refund for extended viewing fees between 1992 and April 1, 2001. This totalled to $450m in value ( abcnews.go.com/Business/stor… ).

The settlement was approved in January 2002 and included the refund in form of coupons for the 38m people affected ( chiefmarketer.com/blockbuste… ). Thus we could expect a revenue drop of roughly the value in 2002. Interestingly, their revenue even increased by 8%, where also their store count growth by 7% could have played in.

They changed the rules for late fees several times and closed the last lawsuit on them in a Quebec Superior Court, ruling in their favor in September 28, 2004 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). Right before Viacoms tender offer for their shareholders ended (to exchange Viacom with Blockbuster shares), giving buyers probably one more reason to accept the offer.

January 1, 2005 Blockbuster got rid of the late fees and instead sell the product to the customer after a 30-day return window ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Domestic Operations", "Revenue Recognition"). They started to report "Extended Viewing Fee" already in 2004, also backwards for 2002-2004 and "PRP" (Previously Rented Product) in 2005, backwards beginning 2003.
Also during the lawsuit we learn that late fees are in my opinion a surprisingly high part of revenue, e.g. with reportedly $800m being 16% of revenue in 1999 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , "Comparison of 1999 to 1998") and with no additional costs assumed, driving up gross margin by 6% (average for 2000;2002-2004) and gross profit by on average $721m per year (same timeframe).

Remember, when we summed up the restated free cash flow from 1999 to 2004 to $1.5bn? That would be roughly $253m free cash flow per year. Even if we would assume only 50% of the late fee gross profits went into operating income, that would still be $360.5m per year. More than their free cash flow!

First, I thought that cannot be true. Late fees cannot be billions of dollars with probably no additional costs. Comparing Hollywood Entertainment their late fees were between 10% and 13% (2000-2003; sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). 

The gross margin between 2000 and 2004 for Blockbuster (only rental, PRP, w/o extended fees) and for Hollywood Entertainment (only rental; already including late fees) were both 62%, thus Blockbuster's late fees really seem like a competitive edge. And even while the late fees went down from 16% in 2000 to 13% (2002, 2003) to 10% in 2004, they are a big profit driver.

We could understand if the company turned late fees off in 2002 after the big settlement. But since they didn't and we can see that revenue didn't go down 2002-2004 and also Extended Viewing Fee revenues were relatively steady, we can assume that customers were rather okay with the new late fee model. Psychologically, I assume that the late fees actually may have made some customers unhappy, but under the assumption that they are known beforehand, they might have accepted them. Because of Blockbuster's store locations being convenient for them and because "being late" could be psychologically accepted as "ones own fault". Moreover, because of the latter I assume that customers mentally didn't attribute the late fees to their costs, which made the perceived rental price less expensive and could explain consistent high rental and late fees.

Thus, Carl Icahn was right in calling them out for their removal, "which has cost the company from $250 million to $300 million in operating income [per year]" ( latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-… ). In my opinion he could have easily said $500 to $600m.

Yet, Carl later didn't bring them back. Was it just an argument for his proxy fight? Did something else change?

Question 2: Why did the Blockbuster management cut the Late Fee in 2004 and didn't reintroduce it when they saw gross profit and revenue suffer?

I still got an odd feeling about those late fees, maybe I'll look back again later.

text:
Why didn’t the black hole join $LUMN’s party? It knew no value could escape the company’s M&A mess.

This is not financial advice. Just a nice bedtime story for @DOGE_SEC to read. There may be errors in it. Feel free to point them out.

Further, this post is super boring to read in most parts, but really explains a lot of the fraud and deception going on with mergers & acquisitions. Also, for $LUMN shareholders this should be interesting to read and try to understand everything, question everything you learn here.

TL;DR:
* $LUMN’s M&A Mess: Opaque deals have screwed small investors twice in 8 years—maybe more to come.
* Act 1 (2017): Level 3 merger doubled shares, cut value 25%, added $19B debt—shareholders lost big.
* Act 2 (2021-22): Sold Latin American and ILEC for $10B (below value), EMEA for $1.8B—cash flow tanked.
* Act 3 (2024): PCF and a $2.2B cash boost mask revenue drops; shaky future looms.
* Takeaway: Debt-heavy M&A and questionable moves leave $LUMN’s stock—and shareholders—on thin ice. Many M&A make actually just generate cash for Wallstreet and banks, not shareholders

Well, well, well. During the research for the RoBB Grade ( nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/1… ) I saw a lot. But $LUMN is really something special. $LUMN an American telecommunications company that provides a range of services including internet, voice, and managed IT solutions through its extensive fiber optic and copper networks. The level of lack of transparency with their M&A is staggering and in the last eight years they’ve screwed over small investors twice and might do it again.
Two of three times were M&A. Ahh, M&A, the art of either leveraging assets or just earn a shit ton of money without creating additional value.

---
Your wifes boyfriend explains: M&A
Imagine your wifes boyfriends business is renting apartments in New York. This will create some decent cash. But let’s say he sells the real estate, and he is getting like 15-20 annual rents in cash immediately.
Now, what if he could sell the real estate, let’s say to your wife and continue to collect half of the rent? Sounds too good to be true, right?
Now imagine your wife doesn’t pay for the real estate but takes on a bank loan. Oh, and her friends (lets call them shareholders) which gave her money for her company and formerly owned 100% of it, now own only 50% after the deal.
The other 50% go to your wifes boyfriend. See, he got the money (15-20x annual rent) and still gets 50% of the rent? 69!

Being your wifes boyfriend you really like what’s going on. But being your wifes friends (aka shareholders), oh wow… wouldn’t you be pissed?
---

M&A as net positive or negative?
Not all M&A are good. In fact, half or more of them maybe bullshit.
Sometimes M&A can leverage assets, transform them, and make them more valuable. Now, I am far from an expert in the field, but you might argue that in the case of $LUMN high speed (fiber) connection infrastructure might not appreciate due to an M&A.
So, you might buy businesses or merge to grow. But doing so with purely debt, may increase value for banks and actually decrease value for shareholders since the assets are not leveraged.

Wallstreet cheat sheet: Execute M&A to create several times the cash flow the asset would yield in a given time on the back of a company and its shareholders.

I will lead you through 3 acts of recent $LUMN history. I think there is much more before, but for now we’ll focus on those. Here they are:

Graph 1: Certain metrics for $LUMNs Financial Performance, like using impairments to make the company look worse than it is.
You see that operating income without (dotted green line) impairments, dividends and share buy backs looks way different than operating income with (green line). That cash flow from operations tells another story and also shareholders equity, book value is off the chart before 2023.

Act 1: The 2017 Level 3 merger doubled shares, slashed per-share value by 25%, and added $19B in debt—hardly a win for shareholders.

Starring: Glen F. Post, III as your wife, who served as Chief Executive Officer from 1992 to May 2018 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… )
Guest star: Temasek Holdings as your wifes boyfriend, with about 18% in ownership in Level 3.

Cash Flow from operations increased for four years by roughly $2 bn p.a., which would be $8 bn. Now of that, they spent $7.6 bn on dividends and share buy backs. Sounds good, right? Let us see how they paid the merger:
“Our preliminary estimate of the amount of aggregate consideration of $19.617 billion is based on:
> the 517.3 million shares of CenturyLink’s common stock (including those issued in connection with the Converted RSU Awards) issued to consummate the acquisition and the closing stock price of CenturyLink common stock at October 31, 2017 of $18.99;
> the cash consideration of $26.50 per share on the 362.1 common shares of Level 3 issued and outstanding as of October 31, 2017, and the cash consideration of $1 million paid on the Converted RSUs awards;
> the estimated value of $136 million of the Continuing RSU Awards, which represents the pre-combination portion of Level 3’s share-based compensation awards assumed by CenturyLink; and
> the estimated liability of $60 million for the dissenting common shares issued and outstanding as of October 31, 2017.” ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… )

Okay, so beside the cash they also issued 517 million new shares to Level 3 stockholders. That’s roughly double their total shares outstanding at the time. So besides increasing the total Cash Flow from Operations if one looks on a per share basis they actually decreased their CF from Operations by a quarter. Oh wow.
Also, the book value per share went down by 25%, from $24.5 to $18.3.

How did $LUMN debt change?
Long term debt increased by $19bn.
10.6bn assumed from Level 3 and 8.3bn for the acquisition in addition to the shares Level 3 stockholder received ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… , sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ).
Not only did their debt rose, but also their interest expense from $1.37bn in 2016 to $2.23bn in 2018 by roughly $1bn a year. This surely ate into their additional cash flow from operations of $2 bn.
However, interest expense was lowered the following years, 2019: 2bn, 2020: 1.7bn, 2021: 1.6bn, 2022: 1.3bn.

For Act 1 we can conclude that each individual share was worse off after the merger. Further, cash flow from operations minus increased interest expense would leave $1 bn p.a. which would lead to a payback time of about 19 years, uh?
The whole company assumed a lot more debt and total shareholder equity, reduced by goodwill, decreased from roughly $11 bn in 2016 to $-19 bn in 2018. Bad, right?

The question remains how the company intended to leverage the acquisition, pay back the debt and create long term value for its shareholders. The market cap fell off a cliff after 2018, from $23 bn in Aug 2018 to $12 bn one year later. Well, done, well done.
However, looking at the cash flow from operations, the performance of the business itself looks good.

Act 2: After four years of $LUMN bEiNg BaReLy PrOfItAbLe (same tactic using impairments to reduce operating income as with $GME and $BBBY ), now sell of all your good assets for peanuts and leave shareholders holding the bag

Starring: Jeffrey K. Storey as your wife, who should have taken over the CEO role on January 1, 2019 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… )
already took it on May, 2018 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ).
Guest star: Apollo, Stonepeak and Colt

---
Your wifes boyfriend explains: Making a deal on the back of shareholders
Remember your wifes boyfriend? Yes, exactly, the one with the brilliant idea of selling the real estate and still keeping 50% ownership and renting profits, while your wife who bought it didn’t use her own money, but 50% disowned shareholders and took on debt.
Its 2021 and he is back with three friends. Let’s just call them Apollo, Stonepeak and Colt. She tells them about their business, offers to sell the most profitable real estate to them for peanuts in turn for some favors. Her friends (shareholders) don’t feel comfortable after they saw how bad the last merger played out and are wary. Your wife just decides to sell the real estate and telling them as little as somehow possible for the first two sales and barely anything about the third. Of course, that’s just a nice story I just made up…
---

2021/22, the sale of Latin American and ILEC Business for $10bn.

In Q3 2021 $LUMN reported the planned divesture of the Latin American and ILEC Business ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ).

I didn’t find a stated reasoning for the sale. But looking at their reported operating income (EBIT) this doesn’t look good at first sight. At second sight its clear that the company only reported bad operating income through impairments. This was the strategy used for $GME (see here: nitter.poast.org/beyond_mythos/status/1… ) and $BBBY to justify selling stores and reducing inventory, bringing the business into a downward spiral. Here it seems like it could have been used as justification to sell three parts of the business, Latin American, ILEC and EMEA.

 ir.lumen.com/files/doc_finan… 
On slide 5 we find information for the acquisition which is equally sparse. ILEC here is mentioned with a 5.5x multiple. We know that ILECs net income for 2021 was $851m, so a 5.5x would be $4.68 billion adding net assets of $4.75bn this would mean a selling price of $9,43bn and not $7.5bn, right?
Also doing this for Latin America they state a 9x multiple which would be $1.93bn ($214m net income in 2021), adding net assets of $1.8bn this would be $3,73bn instead of $2.7bn. Or I am getting something wrong here?

For those multiples the selling price would rather be $13.16 bn instead of $10 bn, right?
So, they sold their Latin American and ILEC Business for roughly $10 billion. $7.6bn from Apollo for ILEC and $2.7bn from Stonepeak for Latin America. Those two generated $1.1 billion pre-tax net income in 2021, they say. The assets minus liabilities were $6.6 billion (the equity).
This would give us rather a multiple of 3 ( ( m&a price minus equity ) divided by pre-tax net income), right? That doesn't sound like a good deal.
We can further assume a return on assets of 12% (net income / total assets = $1,065m/$8,809m). Now, this isn’t the end of the story …

2022/23, the sale of EMEA Business to Colt for $1.8bn.

The information for the sale of the Latin American and ILEC Business was sparse, but this sale is even more obscure (see “(2) Divestitures of the Latin American and ILEC Businesses and Planned Divestiture of the EMEA Business”, sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… )

I skimmed through all other investor presentation and must say, I never ever have seen less information for such a big or even for smaller deals. Maybe I just didn't open the right presentation??

They don't tell us the revenue and not even like with Latin America or ILEC the net income. Hello?
They only tell us the balance sheet for EMEA for one year (2022), showing assets minus liabilities of $1.377 billion. And this Business should be sold for $1.8 billion? So, $423m premium?
Assuming the same 12% return on assets this would be $165m net income, an even lower multiple of 2.6.

I even went through some earnings calls and couldn’t find any meaningful information, like the one for Q4 2022 ( events.q4inc.com/attendee/43… ) where only once the m&a came up in the q&a section at minute 53. Guess what, no additional information was given.

Now you notice in graph 1 that the cash flow from operations, while being stable for years, drops dramatically in 2022 and 2023.
The drop of $2.6 billion in 2023, following a $1.6 billion drop in 2022, is "largely due to the impacts of the 2022 and 2023 divestitures" ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ). $LUMN sold assets generating allegedly around $1.2 billion net income, but the cash flow from operations drops 2x that? Interesting.

Looks like $LUMN maybe only left with debris, nearly no book value (check out how it crushed down in graph 1) and the stock price is reflecting just that.

Act 3: I call bullshit, Kate. A $2.2B cash bump from PCF and a tax refund masks a shaky future.

Starring: Kate Johnson as your wife, appointed as CEO September, 2022 ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ).
Guest star: PCF … uh PCF?
“Last week, we announced Lumen’s Private Connectivity Fabric (or PCF for short), a custom network that includes dedicated access to existing fiber in the Lumen network, the installation of new fiber on existing and new routes, and the use of Lumen’s new digital services. This AI-ready infrastructure will strengthen the connectivity capabilities between datacenters by providing the network capacity, performance, stability, and speed that customers need as data demands increase.” ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… )

AI-ready infrastructure? What is an AI-ready infrastructure? I thought about letting this explain to you by your wifes boyfriend, but he was embarrassed by this bullshit.

---
Your wifes boyfriend explains: PCF
Picture your wife waltzing in as CEO with a dazzling new sidekick, PCF. She’s flaunting a sudden cash boost—like finding $2.2B in the couch cushions—thanks to some shady advance payments and a tax refund. But while she’s busy dazzling the market with this rebound, the books are quietly crumbling, and shareholders are left wondering if this is just another fling that’ll end in a pricey breakup.
---

We see that the stock price recovered mid of 2024. Why is that?
On graph 1 we see indeed while cash flow from operations went up, operating income (adjusted for impairments, the dotted green line) went down!

Why did operating income go down?
While we had an increase in revenue in Act 1 of about $5 bn p.a., we had a decrease of $7.6 bn from 2020 to 2024. In this timeframe revenue went down 35%, while costs of goods sold only decreased 21% and SG&A only 14%.
Looks like with the sale of those three businesses we lost way more revenue than we lost costs, right? In the investor presentation you'll find the revenue bridge, going down. Interestingly, only a very small fraction is attributed to the divestitures but like 10% (1Q24) is organic declines?
So, we can cross out that this happened because of the business sales? I don’t think so.
Okay, now we know why operating income went down. But why did cash flow from operations go up??

Checking the section for net cash provided by operating activities we learn that the $2.2bn increase is mainly due cash payments for PCF solutions and federal income tax cash refund of $729m ( sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… ).
“Net cash provided by operating activities increased by $2.2 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024 as compared to the year ended December 31, 2023 primarily due to (i) cash payments received in the third quarter of 2024 pursuant to our recent sales of PCF solutions and (ii) our federal income tax cash refund of $729 million.”

They write that “[a]lthough our recent PCF agreements have significantly increased our near-term liquidity, we cannot assure you our future cash flows from operating activities will be sufficient to fund our capital investments, debt obligations or any other long-term cash requirements”. And that “[d]uring the second half of 2024, we began receiving advance payments under these agreements, which increased our net cash provided by operating activities reflected in our consolidated statements of cash flows and our deferred revenue reflected in our consolidated balance sheets”.
Now we see that the change in deferred revenue is $1.76bn. Adding deferred revenue and the tax refund that would be $2.5bn. Reducing cash flow from operations by this number we would have a reduction of $300m in 2024 to 2023.
If… and I mean only if $LUMN cannot deliver on their PCF promise they could have to pay back those $1.76bn which never, ever, ever will happen, right Kate? Right? Because they are in the PCF business for actually ah… where did I have my notes, ah here, right. They first reported about PCF in August 2024 and had two filings mentioning PCF with 5 attachments mentioning PCF. So that sounds like they know what they are talking about. Wow, I hope they do. I hope they do.

I hope I don’t have to say RIP $LUMN in the next year or two.

Slowed down this year. 

I first caught wind of NFTS in 2019 before most, because art forums were mind blown over works selling for 10 bands. I gave it no second thought.

My ex-girlfriend (now wife) borrowed my PC one night and bought a picture of a house and was offered 20k for it. It took me months to relent and finally dive in deep.

Flipped my first Webbland L apartment for 1.8E. Shocker. Won Murakami raffle and sold for 6.7E. Wow.

Then CloneX, Azuki, Doodles..
Then memecoins..
Then ordinals..
Then farming 20 over airdrops protocols..
Then HYPE..

Some meta I caught, some I simply could not. Since then, I am no stranger to missed chances. Right now, I am feeling the same gut instincts in 2019 about AI and the suite of evolving AI models. 

The age of intelligence is here. It was first optimized for codes, now it's coming after the creative industry. 

Parents of my students remain oblivious to the threat looming ahead. Graduates of animation degrees are growing despondent. 

The community at large is coping with well wishes and comfort that human art will not be displaced. "AI Slop!" they scream - Cognitive dissonance is at all time high..

No. If AI continues to grow at this rate, it will completely wipe out the industry in less than 5 years time. The lines will be blurred. Mangakas will employ agentic AI as editors because the human ones simply cannot match the well of knowledge it possesses.

Art directors will spawn by thousands; ones who understands creative intent, artistic vision and brilliant prompters - they will lead a shell studio from their homes, managing a headcount of 100 agents furiously working 24/7, each with a role of their own.

Established artists who have already built a following today will exist as a relic to be enamored over, just like Van Gogh or Leonardo Da Vinci. Their value proposition will not be the output, but the historical mileage they clocked in their careers. Think of Togashi, Yusuke or Horokoshi sensei. No kids will aspire for art school anymore.

Do I sound pessimistic? Maybe a little. But all that might be only a hint of what is to come. My creative endeavors are on a chopping block - I have skin in the game so I can't help but to scare myself into observing, adapting and experimenting.

At the end of the day, we all will feel the pain. But we get to choose; either we endure the pain of trekking into this emerging frontier, or we choose the pain of scrapped knees, getting dragged around because the world has moved on without us.

I will continue to create fearlessly, but with every stroke now comes with massive opportunity costs. RIP to my ex-student enrolling into her Diploma in Furniture & 3D design though, she is officially cooked.

- A frightened artist

text:
🚀How Domaining came to be an industry - Journey of 40 years ! 🚀

The first-ever domain name symbolics.com was registered on March 15, 1985—exactly 40 years ago today. It was registered by Symbolics, Inc., a computer manufacturer based in Cambridge, Massachusetts. However, this wasn't a domain sale but rather a registration since domain names were initially free before commercial registrations started in the 1990s.

▶️Evolution of Domaining: From Free to a Billion-Dollar Industry.

✔️1985-1995: The Dawn of the Internet and Free Domains

In the early days, domain registrations were handled by DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) and later by Network Solutions, which was contracted by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF).

Domains were free until 1995, when Network Solutions started charging $100 for a two-year registration.

✔️1995-2005: The Birth of Domaining & the Dot-Com Boom

The commercialization of the internet led to a surge in demand for domain names.

Companies and individuals began buying domains as digital real estate, realizing their potential resale value.

The late 1990s dot-com boom saw massive domain acquisitions, including high-profile domain flips like business.com , which sold for $7.5 million in 1999.

✔️2005-2015: Rise of the Domain Marketplaces & New TLDs

Sedo, Afternic, and GoDaddy Auctions became major players, allowing domainers to list and sell domains easily.

Generic and premium domains (like hotels.com , insurance.com ) started selling for millions.

The introduction of new gTLDs (e.g., .tech, .club, .xyz) expanded domaining opportunities.

✔️2015-Present: AI, Crypto, and Web3 Domains

The rise of AI, blockchain, and Web3 changed domaining trends, with demand shifting to short, brandable names (e.g., .ai, .xyz, .eth).

Crypto-related domains like voice.com sold for $30 million (2019), and nft.com fetched $15 million (2022).

AI and automation tools have also changed how domains are bought, appraised, and traded.

🚀The Future of Domaining

🔺AI-generated brandable names are gaining traction.

🔺Web3 and decentralized domains (ENS, Handshake, Unstoppable Domains) may disrupt traditional domaining.

The premium domain market remains strong, with one-word .coms, AI domains, and ccTLDs still holding significant value.

👁️‍🗨️Final Thoughts

From a free registration in 1985 to billion-dollar sales today, domaining has evolved into a highly lucrative digital asset market. 

The next frontier may be AI-driven domain valuation, blockchain-based ownership, and even fully autonomous domain marketplaces.

97% of ecom brands are using AI completely wrong.

Here’s what the 3% are doing differently…

Imagine two painters in New York City competing in the annual Chelsea Art Fair.

The winner gets a $50,000 prize.

The goal?

To create the painting that sells for the highest price.

And they both have exactly one week to complete their masterpiece.

The first painter is Thomas.

He immediately sets up his canvas in his Brooklyn studio and spends the first day brainstorming ideas and sketching concepts.

Then dedicates the remaining six days to creating what he believes is his masterpiece.

The second painter, Sophia, takes a completely different approach…

She spends the first 5 days visiting the Museum of Modern Art, analyzing auction data from Christie's and Sotheby's, and studying the last 200 paintings that sold for over $100,000.

She's hunting for patterns.

What styles do high-end buyers actually want?

Which design elements consistently sell?

What colors, themes, and techniques are bringing in the highest bids right now?

Once she felt she had solid insights into what was actually selling and why, she spent only the final two days in her Manhattan loft executing her painting.

The night of the auction arrives.

Which painting do you think sold for the most money?

Sophia’s.

Her work went for triple the price because she understood what her buyers actually wanted and what they were already purchasing – not what she thought they should want.

Most ecom brands are like the first painter.

They think of an idea and ask AI to create it.

The genius approach?

Be like the second painter.

Ask AI to analyze thousands of data points and reveal patterns in what actually works.

AI isn't about replacing humans.

It's about amplifying what works.

Tomorrow I’ll be posting a full breakdown sharing the 3 genius ways we're using AI like the second painter to blow up our clients' brands.

text:
Yet another case of someone hallucinating upstream numbers with AI with no knowledge to fact check them against. 

Some errors that should be obvious to anyone:

1) ARC’s market value is shown as $14B CAD which is their market cap and excludes debt, the EV is $17B CAD

2) Ovintiv’s US volumes are shown after royalties while their Canadian volumes are shown pre royalties, this meaningfully skews flowing barrel comparisons 

3) Because of the gross working interest volume adjustment up to 108 MBOE/d, Ovintiv’s flowing valuation on the sale was US$27,650/BOE/d

4) You can’t compare LTM volumes for Ovintiv and NTM guide for ARC. After correcting the EV to US$12.45B their flowing valuation is US$30,450/BOE/d (even using guidance it’s US$30,200). 

This is an awful phenomenon and if you’re going to opine on equities either way have some self respect and check the numbers your chatbot generates. 

The infrastructure that ARC owns is offset by the shitty gas market they produce into. On a cashflow basis it would have sold for ~5x cashflow and a 10-11% FCF yield. Of course flowing barrel valuations when adjusted reflect that ARC is more expensive

text:
Seems to be evidence of the investment 'crowding out' effect (e.g., @pkedrosky ) many pointed to in terms of AI data centers vs. residential housing at least.

Data centers are outbidding homebuilders for land in Northern Virginia. Between 2022-2024, data center development jumped 50% above the prior nine-year total. The region already faces a 75,000-home shortage. Makes the math on residential building economically impossible.

-Amazon paid $700M for land acquired for ~$50M - a 14x markup in a few years. Separately, NTT paid $257M for a single vacant parcel, and a garden store sold its land for $160M.
-In Elk Grove Village, IL, Stream Data Centers bought and demolished an entire 55-home subdivision to build data centers paying nearly $1M per house.
-Land along US Route 67 near Dallas that sold for $20K-$40K/acre three years ago is now fetching $350K+/acre in some spots - a 10-15x increase.

text:
Did you know Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI in 2023?

Within three days, over 700 employees signed a letter demanding his return.

Five days later, he was CEO again.

Here's how a startup kid became the most powerful person in AI:

Picture this. It's 2005. Sam is 19 years old. Drops out of Stanford University after two years.

Most parents would lose their minds. His didn't.

He had an idea for a location-based social networking app called Loopt. Sounds basic now. Back then it was wild.

That app got him into Y Combinator's very first batch. 8 startups total. He was the youngest founder in the room.

Loopt never became huge. Sold for $43 million in 2012. Not a home run. But here's what mattered.

Paul Graham noticed him.

The guy who built Y Combinator saw something different in Sam. Not just a founder. A connector. Someone who could spot talent before anyone else.

By 2011, Sam was already investing in companies like Airbnb, Stripe, Reddit. He wasn't even 30 yet.

Then Paul Graham did something crazy. Handed Sam the keys to Y Combinator in 2014.

Think about that. The most influential startup accelerator in the world. Given to a 28-year-old.

Sam didn't just run it. He transformed it.

Grew the number of funded startups by 10x. Launched YC Research. Started experimenting with basic income studies.

But he kept getting distracted by one thing. AI.

In 2015, he sat down with Elon Musk. They talked about a problem.

Google was dominating AI research. One company controlling that much power felt dangerous to both of them.

So they started OpenAI. A nonprofit. The mission was simple.

Build AI that benefits everyone. Not just shareholders.

Sam wasn't even CEO at first. He was just a board member and donor. Had his hands full with YC.

Then 2019 happened.

Sam stepped down from Y Combinator. Went all-in on OpenAI. Became CEO.

Most people thought he was crazy. 

Leaving a proven success for a research lab that hadn't shipped anything mainstream yet.

Here's what he understood that others didn't.

AI wasn't a feature. It was a platform shift. Bigger than mobile. Bigger than the internet.

He restructured OpenAI. Created a capped-profit model. Brought in Microsoft's billions. Hired the best researchers he could find.

November 30, 2022. ChatGPT launches.

1 million users in 5 days. 30 million in 2 months. Fastest-growing consumer product in history.

Sam went from tech insider to household name overnight.

Then came November 2023. The board fired him.

No warning. No clear reason given publicly. Just gone.

What happened next showed something about Sam that numbers can't capture.

Satya Nadella offered him a job at Microsoft within hours. Could've taken it. Would've been the safe move.

Instead he negotiated his way back into OpenAI. Got the board restructured. Came back stronger.

That's not luck. That's leverage built over 20 years of relationships.

Here's what I learned studying his path:

Sam didn't have some master plan at 19. He just kept putting himself in rooms where interesting things happened.

Y Combinator. Silicon Valley dinners. Research labs.

He asked better questions than most people. Listened more than he talked. Connected dots others missed.

And when the moment came, he was ready.

The guy who dropped out of Stanford now advises world leaders on AI policy. 

Testifies before Congress. Shapes how billions of people will interact with technology.

Not because he was the smartest. Because he positioned himself at the center of the right revolution.

That's the playbook.

Find the biggest wave forming. Get there early. Build relationships before you need them.

Sam's still just 40. The AI story is barely starting..

text:
In 2020, the art NFT market was still in its infancy. Sales were relatively modest, with estimates suggesting a total market value of around $100 million for the year, according to some blockchain analytics. This was a period of early adoption, with projects like CryptoKitties laying the groundwork, but the broader art NFT boom had not yet taken off.

By 2021, the market exploded. The total sales value of art-related NFTs surged, peaking at approximately $2.9 billion (sources: Art Basel and UBS) This was driven by high-profile sales, such as Beeple’s "Everydays: The First 5000 Days," which sold for $69.3 million at Christie’s, marking a watershed moment. Monthly sales volumes reached their height in August 2021, with around 117,400 transactions in a 30-day period, and the aggregated value of sales hit nearly $881 million in September 2021. The market was fueled by speculative fervor, cryptocurrency appreciation (notably Ethereum), and a rush of new collectors and artists entering the space. Comparatively, the conventional art market saw sales of about $50 billion in 2020, meaning NFTs were rapidly closing the gap, reaching an estimated $41 billion across all categories by year-end 2021 according to Chainalysis.

Fast forward to 2025, and the art NFT market has experienced a dramatic downturn. Recent data indicates that in Q1 2025, trading volumes for art NFTs dropped to just $23.8 million, a stark contrast to the $2.9 billion peak in 2021—a decline of over 99%. Transaction numbers have also plummeted, with sales falling from tens of thousands monthly in 2021 to around 2,100 in a 30-day period by November 2024. Platforms like Art Blocks and SuperRare, once leaders in the space, have seen trading volumes drop by 95% and sales decrease by 88% or more from their highs. This suggests a significant cooling of the speculative "JPEG trading" bubble that characterized 2021.

Compared to 2020 and 2021, the art NFT market in 2025 is a shadow of its former self in terms of volume and hype. However, some perspectives suggest this isn’t necessarily the "death" of the market but rather a shift. The decline from 2020’s nascent stage to 2021’s boom was a massive upward trajectory, while the drop-off since reflects a stabilization or correction after unsustainable growth. Current sentiment on platforms like X and analyses from sources like DappRadar hint at a potential rebirth, possibly driven by new technologies like AI or Bitcoin Ordinals, though this remains speculative. The market in 2025 appears to be settling into a niche, with fewer but potentially more mature collectors focusing on utility and intrinsic value rather than quick profits, unlike the frenzy of 2021 or the quiet potential of 2020.

text:
When the Noise Fades
On AI Art Hate and the Search for Real Audience

A murmur circles among those of us creating with AI. Two questions drift between posts and private chats. They hang behind every new drop. Will the hate toward this work ever soften? Is it hard to find an audience that truly embraces it? Not just tolerates it. Seeks it. Feels it. Claims it?

These aren’t abstract musings. They’re the pulse beneath every prompt we write. Every piece we refine. Every strange and beautiful thing we share with the world.

If you’re making AI art consistently and sincerely you’ve felt the resistance. The sneers say “soulless” and “mechanical.” Gatekeepers would rather frame a napkin sketch than a generated masterpiece. Silence buries a piece before it gets a chance. Still something in you keeps going.

So what’s underneath all this noise? Let’s look closer.

This Has Happened Before and It Always Starts with Resistance

Every shift in art history begins with a wall. A hard “no.” A declaration that this (whatever this is) isn’t real art. Why do they fight it? Fear. Of losing control. Of machines outpacing hands. Of change. But that wall always cracks.

• Photography terrified painters in the 1800s. A machine could capture likeness in seconds. Heresy. Paul Delaroche famously declared “from today painting is dead.” But photography didn’t stop. It evolved through daguerreotypes and portraiture and photojournalism and surrealist experimentation. Over time it earned not just a place but an irreplaceable one. In 2023 a Midjourney-generated piece sold for $50,000 in a digital auction. Critics scoffed (echoing Delaroche). The buyer saw something else. Vision.

• Digital art was dismissed throughout the 1980s and 90s. Photoshop was a toy. Vectors were for designers not artists. Some museums were slow to embrace it though pioneers were already reshaping the field. Artists like Jenny Holzer turned LEDs into poetry. Casey Reas (a co-creator of Processing) coded generative works. Refik Anadol turned data into vast immersive environments. Today they exhibit globally and define the digital avant-garde.

• Impressionism (now a staple of museums) was once ridiculed. Monet’s brushwork was sloppy. His atmosphere unfinished. “Impressionist” was originally a jeer. But they kept painting. They found each other. They opened their own exhibitions. They sold to collectors who saw. Now their work defines a century.

The pattern repeats. New mediums face backlash not because they lack value but because they ask people to look differently. Discomfort comes first. Acceptance later. Legacy after that. Every shift proves the hand still guides.

Will resistance to AI art soften? Yes. It already is. But the point isn’t to wait. The point is to push because that’s how the story changes.

Digital Space Makes It Easier to Be Seen If You Know Where to Look

We don’t need to beg gatekeepers anymore. The old art world still prizes resumes and recommendations. But digital space moves differently.

Platforms like Objkt and Foundation and SuperRare have cracked the door open. These aren’t just marketplaces. They’re living ecosystems (messy and chaotic and full of potential).

• Foundation’s Spaces let artists curate entire collections. Don’t just mint. Tell a story. Collectors there often buy narratives not just pixels. I’ve seen bids double because the description pulled people in.

• Objkt thrives on experimentation. It rewards frequency and voice and engagement.

• SuperRare moves slower. More curated. More exclusive. But when it works it works hard.

None of them care about your degree. They care about style and voice and vision.

You can grow fast. But only if you show up like you mean it. No shortcuts. No mimics. Drop work that feels like yours. Build a world. Build a lane. And engage. Don’t mint and vanish. Collectors remember presence. Consistency breeds curiosity. Curation earns trust.

Beyond the platforms culture is forming. X and Instagram and Discord and Farcaster (each holds micro-scenes with their own cadence). Weekly rituals like Tezos Tuesday and Thirsty Thursday and Caturday and Nunday aren’t gimmicks. They’re rhythms. A heartbeat for discovery.

Lost in the scroll? Search #AIArt or #TezosTuesday . Filter by Latest. Dive into the replies. That’s where the real talk happens.

A single post can reach Berlin and Lagos and Seoul by midnight. What matters is clarity. Does it cut through? Does it speak with intention?

The Audience Is Not Just Real It’s Growing

The loudest lie? That AI art has no audience. It does. It just doesn’t look like the old one.

These are people raised on game concept art and Tumblr surrealism and anime keyframes and glitch loops and vaporwave and fashion edits and photorealistic fantasy. Ten years ago they were teens on DeviantArt. Now they’re adults with wallets curating their own feeds and collecting on Tezos and building Discord galleries.

They’ve grown with the tech. AI meets them right where they are.

They don’t care how it was made. They care how it feels.

Some are coders. Some are collectors. Some are scrolling through curated feeds reshaping their taste in real time.

They’re not asking “is this valid?” They’re asking “does this stop me cold?”

Look at Objkt. Thousands of AI pieces are traded monthly (up from hundreds just a year ago). The numbers whisper what critics still won’t.

And when it hits they follow. They stay.

The best AI artists I know? Most aren’t famous. But they grow every day. Quietly. Intentionally. Through curated portfolios and recognizable aesthetics and emotional depth.

The current is real. If you’re paying attention you can feel it pulling.

Why the Hate Feels Loud and Why It Won’t Last

It feels loud because the language hasn’t caught up.

People see a finished piece and assume it was instant. They don’t see the failures. The prompt revisions. The post-edits. The trained eye behind it. Next time someone says “instant” show them your rejects. Ten or twenty or fifty. Let the work speak.

They don’t realize we’re mid-process. Still naming our tools. Still shaping the vocabulary.

Photography gave us exposure. Digital art gave us render. What’s ours?

Prompting is our brushstroke (part chance and part intent). Post-editing is our chisel (shaping raw chaos into clarity).

Call it what you want. Just name it yours. We’re building the language now.

And every week the gap grows clearer. Scroll Objkt. Scroll Foundation. You can see the difference between shallow noise and intentional voice.

The copies collapse. The originals endure.

We keep making. And that clarity keeps rising. Let the rest catch up.

When the Noise Fades the Work Will Still Be Here

Yes the hate will fade. The skepticism will soften. Some critics will shift. Others won’t. Doesn’t matter.

The work matters. The audience already arriving matters.

They’re building taste outside the old rules. That’s who we’re here for.

Finding fans isn’t about hype. It’s about building something people come back to.

A voice. A style. A feeling they remember.

Make work that sharpens with time. Make work that outlives the noise.

Pick one piece this week. Make it truer than the last. Share it where they’ll see.

That’s how the signal grows.

The smoke will clear. The signal will stay. And when it does your voice is what they’ll hear.

Hate fades with time. History shows it. Audiences grow where artists persist. Keep creating. The noise doesn’t win.

text:
Hi friend 👋🏼

This week feels like a mix of collectibles mania, market nerves, and big-picture thinking. A Pokémon card just reset the record books. Bitcoin is flirting with a pattern we haven’t seen since 2018. A macro thinker is comparing markets to physics. And inflation? It might finally be behaving.

Let’s get into it.

The Weekly Fun Fact 🤔 

A single Pokémon card just sold for $16.4 million, and no, that’s not a typo.

Logan Paul’s PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator card became the most expensive trading card ever sold, officially surpassing the 1952 Mickey Mantle rookie card record. The Illustrator card wasn’t sold in packs, it was awarded to winners of a 1997 Japanese Pokémon art contest, with only 53 copies known to exist today.

What makes this specific copy extraordinary is its condition. It’s the only one graded PSA 10, meaning it’s essentially flawless, a level of rarity within rarity that collectors obsess over. In collectibles, condition isn’t a detail. It’s everything.

Then there’s the theater around it. Paul didn’t just store it in a safe. He wore it as a diamond-encrusted pendant during his WWE debut. The custom piece includes over 60 carats of diamonds, turning what was already a grail collectible into a cultural spectacle.

The buyer, AJ Scaramucci of Solari Capital, purchased it live at auction via Goldin. The sale says something bigger than “Pokémon is hot.” It reflects how nostalgia, scarcity, and celebrity amplify value in today’s market. We’re seeing collectibles behave more like fine art, where provenance, storytelling, and media exposure move prices as much as intrinsic rarity.

If you want the full breakdown of the sale and the card’s backstory, it’s covered in detail here.

Onto this week’s topics🚦

🔴 BTC hasn’t done this since 2018 📉

Bitcoin just printed four consecutive red monthly candles, something it hasn’t done since the depths of the 2018 bear market.

For context: the worst monthly streak in Bitcoin’s history was six straight down months between August 2018 and January 2019. If February closes red, this will be only the second time BTC has pushed beyond four consecutive losing months.

That matters because long monthly streaks often reflect structural pressure, not just short-term volatility.

On top of that, altcoins are under even heavier stress. CryptoQuant data shows 13 consecutive months of net selling pressure in altcoins (excluding BTC and ETH). In fact, cumulative sell pressure is now roughly three times worse than at the peak of the FTX collapse.

So what are investors debating?

The bearish case:

-Post-halving cycles historically include painful drawdowns.
-Analysts see potential downside toward $40K–$50K.
-Breaking the 200-week moving average could mean a prolonged sideways grind.

The bullish case:

-February 5th may have marked the bottom.
-Bitcoin appears to be consolidating rather than accelerating lower.
-If macro conditions loosen in the second half of 2026, risk assets could rebound.

Right now, $74K is the line in the sand. A decisive reclaim could confirm strength; rejection opens the door to further downside.

This isn’t a panic moment, but it’s definitely a “pay attention” moment.

🟡 Physics + markets = one code? 🧠

Raoul Pal’s latest thesis, “The Universal Code,” attempts something ambitious: tying physics, AI, markets, and civilization into one framework.

The core idea is that everything is computation, not metaphorically, but literally. Systems that extract more intelligence per unit of energy survive. That’s why life outcompetes chemistry, civilization outcompetes biology, and AI now threatens to outpace human cognition.

Progress accelerates because intelligence compounds.

Where do markets fit?

Markets compress massive amounts of distributed information into one output: price. Capital becomes stored energy. Price becomes the signal directing that energy.

Pal argues that modern economies are constrained by shrinking demographics and rising debt. As organic growth slows, policy becomes more interventionist, more liquidity, earlier responses, more stimulus. That’s not chaos; in his view, it’s the system adapting.

The boldest part of the thesis is the “Economic Singularity”:

-Intelligence scales without population growth.
-Automation replaces demographics.
-Productivity decouples from employment.

Capital accumulation decouples from human labor.

If intelligence becomes abundant, then meaning, not productivity, becomes scarce. And scarcity defines value.

You don’t have to agree with it. But it’s an attempt to explain why everything feels like it’s accelerating and destabilizing at the same time.

🟢 Where is inflation heading next? 

Inflation is slowly cooling, and for the first time in a while, the trend looks consistent rather than fragile.

The latest U.S. CPI print came in at 2.4% year-on-year, down from 2.5% the month before. That’s the lowest headline inflation reading since 2021. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, held steady at 2.5%.

What’s encouraging is where the softness is coming from.

Core goods inflation (think physical products) is slowing again, suggesting that earlier tariff-related price spikes may be largely behind us. Supply chains are normal. Shipping costs are stable. Inventory levels aren’t stretched. In other words, we’re not seeing fresh cost shocks feeding into the system.

The stickier problem remains services, especially shelter (or housing data).

Shelter accounts for a huge portion of CPI, and it’s notoriously lagged. Today’s official rent data still reflects pricing decisions made 12–15 months ago. Meanwhile, private rental data and home price indices have already cooled meaningfully.

If those leading indicators continue to feed through, shelter inflation should keep drifting lower, pulling headline CPI down with it.

There are, however, two forces worth watching closely:

Wages: Real average weekly earnings rose 1.9% year-over-year, the strongest growth since early 2021. That’s good news for households, but sustained wage strength can eventually support services inflation.

Energy prices: Crude oil has started to firm up again. Oil is deeply embedded in the cost structure of the economy, transportation, production, logistics. If energy spikes, CPI can reaccelerate quickly.

Market expectations reflect cautious optimism. One-year and two-year inflation swaps are pricing roughly 2.4% average inflation over the next couple of years.

So what does this mean for rate cuts?

Interest rate traders are currently pricing more than two Fed cuts in 2026.

If inflation keeps trending down while growth remains resilient, we’re in what markets love most: a “Goldilocks” setup, growth intact, inflation fading, and rate cuts ahead.

That combination historically supports equities, credit, and risk assets.

.BOT domain SOLD via $23,399 LTO @afternic 

In this post we'll talk a bit about the sale—but mostly about the .BOT TLD in general, and why we predict it will be one of the most established gTLDs in the near future.

.BOT, a TLD from the Amazon Registry, began its existence in a different era. Calling it a non-AI or non-robotics era might be a stretch, but you get the point—December 2017 was a very different time.

Back then, .BOT was a restricted TLD, unavailable through standard domain registrars – making it a niche extension that domain investors couldn't even consider.

When ChatGPT came along, Amazon realized the times had changed and, in early 2023, ended the restricted period to prepare for the general launch of .BOT.

On October 30, 2023, .BOT was officially reborn as a standard ICANN gTLD – available to anyone through standard domain registrars, with no limitations.

Still, the launch wasn't heavily promoted by Amazon, and so what really happened is that the natural—hype-free—life cycle of .BOT has begun.

Here's why we predict it will become one of the major gTLD players in the near future. Let's start with the basic characteristics of a TLD:
● It's a 3-letter TLD, which is optimal – a standard set decades ago by .com, .net, and .org, which is visually the most pleasing, feels most secure, and is generally the easiest to pronounce.
● It's super easy to say and sounds modern and sleek – in this regard, it belongs alongside top-tier TLDs with clear, easy pronunciation—like .com, .app, .now, .bet, or .dev.
● It looks distinctive—creating unique names—and adds a futuristic touch.
● It is backed by a solid registry within the ICANN program.

Here are some potential use cases for .BOT:
● AI-driven projects and web apps.
● AI companion—ranging from on-chain and finance to romance.
● Automation, which will define our era.
● AI Agents – with actual use cases already in action.

And here's a very interesting one:
● Robotics. Elon Musk predicts that by 2040, there will be more humanoid robots than humans. And that's just humanoid – imagine the total number when you include all types of robots. We're about to be living in a robot world. So, what's the perfect TLD for robotics? Of course, it's .BOT. The hypothetical .ROBOT, though it would still be a strong one, has two syllables and it's a bit too heavy to be an ideal TLD.

Given its optimal TLD structure and futuristic potential, .BOT is, in our book, destined to succeed on a larger scale. The only question is when.

What about downsides? One potential issue is that the word "bot" still carries some negative connotations. We've all heard terms like "bot attack", which likely originated in the 1990s with the rise of Internet Relay Chat (IRC), where automated scripts—early bots—were used for both benign and malicious purposes. While the idea of 'bad bots' still exists, public perception of the word "bot" has been steadily shifting in a more positive direction. A major turning point was the emergence of ChatGPT, a chatbot that helped people associate bots with advanced, helpful AI.

That could get anyone hyped… but remember, these wallets aren’t buying to make you money.

1 hour later, the same wallet sold for a loss – $19.23K gone.

This is why it pays to think like a trader, not a fan. 

Tools like Stalkchain let you watch smart (or reckless) money in real time. 

Use that info to make better entries, exits, and avoid becoming exit liquidity.

How can you use this info to make better entries and exits?

If you see a wallet just ape in with a big amount (like $49K into $AVA ), don’t rush in. That buy might already have pushed the price up.

If multiple wallets follow up and the price holds or climbs gradually → it's building momentum. Right time to buy in.

If the wallet starts selling shortly after (especially at a loss) → it was likely a failed scalp or a trap.

text:
The Ethics of Monetizing Patient Data

In the digital age, patient data is a goldmine. Every blood test, diagnosis, and prescription generates a breadcrumb trail of information—valuable not just for care delivery but for research, marketing, and innovation. By March 2025, the global healthcare data market is projected to exceed $70 billion, driven by pharmaceutical companies, insurers, and tech giants eager to tap into this resource. Monetizing patient data—selling or licensing it, often in de-identified form—promises to accelerate medical breakthroughs, optimize treatments, and fund healthcare improvements. Yet, this practice raises profound ethical questions: Who owns this data? What constitutes consent? And where do we draw the line between societal benefit and exploitation? This article delves into the ethics of turning patient information into profit, exploring the tension between progress and privacy.

The Case for Monetization

Proponents argue that monetizing patient data is a win-win. For healthcare organizations, it’s a lifeline—revenue from data sales can offset shrinking margins, subsidize care for underserved populations, or fuel technological upgrades. A 2024 study by Deloitte found that hospitals reinvesting data profits into infrastructure saw a 15% improvement in operational efficiency. Beyond finances, the data itself drives innovation. De-identified records power AI models that predict disease outbreaks, refine drug development, and personalize medicine. Pharmaceutical firms, for instance, use aggregated patient data to identify candidates for clinical trials, slashing R&D timelines by years.

The societal good is compelling: when a biotech company leverages millions of patient records to develop a rare disease treatment, lives are saved. Advocates also note that HIPAA allows de-identified data to be sold without explicit consent, provided identifiers like names or Social Security numbers are stripped. In theory, this protects privacy while unlocking value—an ethical bargain, they say, where the greater good justifies the transaction.

The Ethical Fault Lines

Beneath this optimism lies a web of moral dilemmas.

Consent and Autonomy 
Patients rarely know their data is being monetized. A 2023 Kaiser Family Foundation survey revealed that 70% of Americans were unaware their de-identified health information could be sold, and 60% opposed it when informed. Consent forms, buried in fine print, often fail to disclose commercial uses explicitly. This opacity erodes autonomy—the right to control one’s own information. Critics argue that even de-identified data isn’t truly anonymous; advanced AI can re-link it to individuals, as demonstrated in a 2022 MIT study that re-identified 85% of a “scrubbed” dataset using public records.

Equity and Exploitation 
Who benefits from the profits? Too often, it’s not the patients whose data fuels the system. A low-income diabetic contributing data to a drug company’s insulin breakthrough may never afford the resulting medication. This imbalance raises justice concerns: marginalized groups, already overrepresented in public health datasets, may be disproportionately exploited without seeing returns. Meanwhile, corporations rake in billions, amplifying healthcare’s profit-driven disparities.

Trust in Healthcare 
Monetization risks eroding patient trust—a cornerstone of medicine. If individuals suspect their data is a commodity, they may withhold critical information from providers, fearing downstream misuse. A 2024 JAMA study linked privacy concerns to a 20% increase in incomplete medical histories, undermining care quality. Once trust fractures, the ripple effects—missed diagnoses, delayed treatments—could outweigh monetization’s gains.

Purpose Creep 
Data sold for noble aims (e.g., cancer research) can end up in less savory hands. Insurers might use it to deny coverage based on predictive risk profiles, or marketers could target vulnerable patients with unproven therapies. A 2023 scandal saw a telehealth firm sell behavioral health data to advertisers, who then bombarded patients with mental health product ads. Such “secondary use” blurs ethical lines, turning a tool for healing into one for manipulation.

Ownership Ambiguity 
Legally, patients don’t own their medical records—providers or systems do. Yet, morally, many argue that data derived from a person’s body and experiences belongs to them. Monetizing it without compensation or input feels like a theft of agency, especially when patients bear the risks (e.g., breaches) but not the rewards.

Real-World Stakes

The ethics play out in stark examples. In 2022, a major health system sold de-identified genomic data to a biotech firm, leading to a patented therapy that cost $2 million per dose—unreachable for most contributors. Patients cried foul, but the transaction was legal. Conversely, a nonprofit hospital in 2024 shared data with researchers under a transparent revenue-sharing model, funding free clinics and earning community praise. The difference lies in intent, execution, and equity—variables that define the ethical tightrope.

Navigating the Dilemma

Can monetizing patient data be ethical? Experts suggest guardrails:

Transparent Consent: Patients should opt in, not out, with clear disclosure of how data will be used and who profits. A 2025 pilot in California tested “data consent dashboards,” letting patients choose research-only sharing, boosting participation by 30%.

Equitable Benefits: Revenue could fund public health initiatives or patient subsidies, ensuring contributors share the gains. Models like data cooperatives, where patients co-own and profit from their data, are gaining traction.

Strict De-identification: Robust standards, audited regularly, could minimize re-identification risks. Blockchain might track data use, preventing unauthorized resale.

Regulatory Oversight: Laws must evolve. The EU’s GDPR fines companies for mishandling health data, a model the U.S. could emulate beyond HIPAA’s limits.

Purpose Limits: Contracts should restrict data to health-related uses, barring commercial exploitation like targeted ads.

The Future: Profit vs. Principle

As healthcare digitizes—think wearables, telehealth, and AI diagnostics—the volume of monetizable data will explode. Tech giants like Amazon and Google, already eyeing health markets, could escalate the stakes, blurring lines between care and commerce. Patients may demand “data dividends” or boycott providers who prioritize profit over privacy. Meanwhile, innovations like synthetic data—AI-generated datasets mimicking real ones—could reduce reliance on actual patient records, sidestepping some ethical quagmires.

Conclusion

Monetizing patient data teeters between promise and peril. It’s a catalyst for progress, funding cures and cutting costs, yet it risks commodifying the human experience, undermining trust, and widening inequities. The ethics hinge on execution: transparency, fairness, and respect for autonomy can tilt the scales toward benefit, while opacity and greed tip it toward harm. In an industry built on “do no harm,” the challenge is clear—patient data’s value must never eclipse the dignity of those it represents. As we navigate this frontier, the question isn’t just what we can do with this data, but what we should.
name: Hapogy
