text:
This shoe company just became an AI infrastructure provider overnight.

And the stock went up almost 600%.

Let me explain why this is so ridiculous and concerning:

Allbirds - the wool sneaker brand once worshipped by Silicon Valley - announced it is selling its shoe business for $39 million and rebranding itself as "NewBird AI."

A "fully integrated GPU-as-a-Service and AI-native cloud solutions provider."

Those are their words. Not mine.

A company with ZERO experience in semiconductors.

ZERO experience in data centers.

ZERO experience in cloud infrastructure.

ZERO customers.

ZERO GPUs on hand.

The stock closed Tuesday at $2.49. It opened Wednesday and shot up to nearly $22. A 582% move in one session.

The funding? A $50 million convertible from an unnamed institutional investor. Subject to shareholder approval on May 18.

That's it. That's literally the entire transformation.

Sell the shoes for $39 million. Take $50 million from somebody willing to hand it over. Add "AI" to the name. Watch retail traders lose their minds.

This reminds me of an older story:

In December 2017, a beverage company called Long Island Iced Tea Corp. announced it was changing its name to "Long Blockchain Corp." and pivoting to crypto.

The stock jumped nearly 300% in a single day. Trading volume up 1,000%.

But they had no blockchain business. No blockchain employees. No blockchain anything.

14 months later, NASDAQ delisted them. The SEC eventually charged 3 people with insider trading on the name change itself.

The company never filed another financial report. The blockchain business never existed.

It’s the same playbook, only with a different buzzword.

And here is what should worry every serious investor:

Allbirds once traded above $600 a share. It was valued at roughly $4 billion in 2021.

The shoe business they just sold for $39 million.

That is a 99% wipeout of real operating value, from a real company selling real products.

But the moment they stapled "AI" to the shell, retail traders bid the market cap up by $127 million in a single day.

Buying what, exactly?

A press release. A $50 million IOU. A NAME change.

When a dying retailer can create 9 figures of "value" by announcing it will buy GPUs it does not own, from suppliers it has no relationships with, to serve customers it does not have - you are no longer looking at a market.

Hyperscalers are spending $380 billion a year on real AI infrastructure and most of the buyers still cannot measure a return. And now we are pricing a wool sock company as a neocloud.

This is how late-cycle tops feel from the inside. Not with a crash. With absurdity.

Long Blockchain Corp. was not a business. It was a warning.

Allbirds-to-NewBird-AI is the same warning but louder.

Own real cash flow. Own gold. Own silver. Own companies that make things people actually buy.

Not stupid hype.

text:
A gallery director in London is writing emails about a $2 million painting using ChatGPT on her personal iPhone.

Her gallery has no idea she is doing this.

84% of gallery staff are using AI right now.
80% of them are doing it on personal accounts.
Only 8% of galleries have any kind of policy about it.

Let me tell you why that is a bigger problem than anyone is admitting.

The gallery world does not run on art. It runs on secrets.

Who owns the Basquiat. What a collector actually paid. Why a piece is listed at $400K but sold for $180K. The price negotiations that never get written down anywhere.

All of that is now going into ChatGPT. Personal accounts. Under terms of service nobody read. On phones that can be stolen, hacked, subpoenaed.

Callum Hale-Thomson built a platform for gallery operations. When ChatGPT launched in 2022 he went around asking galleries if they were interested in AI.

Every single one said no. Not for us. He called them back two years later.

ChatGPT was already on the salespeople's phones. Gemini was already writing collector emails. Nobody made a decision to adopt AI. It just happened while everyone was looking the other way.

63% of staff got zero guidance from management.
The most popular use? Writing emails to collectors.
Second most popular? Translation.
Third? Artist biographies and press releases.

The most sensitive stuff. Running through free tools. Through personal accounts.

"In an industry built on discretion and trust, the gap between how widely AI is being used and how little governance surrounds it should concern everyone."

That is Hale-Thomson. Not me. The guy who built the software for these galleries.

The art world spent three years in a very loud argument about AI-generated images and who owns the copyright.

While that argument was happening, 84% of their own staff were quietly doing something far more dangerous with client data.

Nobody noticed. That is kind of the point.

🚨 Breaking: Vercel was breached, data sold for $2M

A single infected machine in Context AI led the path to compromising anyone who connected to their beta OAuth Google App - a Vercel employee connected his enterprise account to Context AI, and exposed his Google Workspace including sensitive information and environment variables to threat actors.

Threat actors posted on BreachForums under the name of ShinyHunters - and tried to sell the breached Vercel database for $2M.

While Vercel states that Nextjs wasn't affected, we argue that threat actors with such intimate access to their data - might have reached their API keys and tokens, these packages (over 500 on NPM) should be pinned to prevent a supply chain attack from affecting you.

If you used the Context AI beta and experimental programs, and if you used Vercel, on any type of app or project - rotate your keys, pin your versions, and check for the relevant IOCs in your Google environment.

text:
I always consider the downside. Grok "Bear Case" Analysis of OpenAI

1. Unsustainable Financial Model and Escalating Losses

OpenAI's revenue growth, while impressive (from near-zero in 2022 to $12-15 billion ARR in 2025), is dwarfed by its capital-intensive burn rate, creating a path-dependent trap where costs perpetually outpace income. Projections show $5 billion in losses on $3.7 billion in revenue for 2025, escalating to $44 billion in cumulative losses through 2028 (excluding stock-based compensation). Compute expenses alone hit $6 billion annually, with server spends projected at $16 billion in 2025 and ballooning to $400 billion by 2029—far exceeding revenue trajectories. Altman's "Stargate" mega-data centers and $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments (e.g., with Nvidia, Oracle, and UAE partners) are conditional but risky, relying on circular financing where partners fund OpenAI's chip purchases, creating contagion if demand falters.

Unlike traditional software giants (e.g., Google's 11% profit margin at IPO on $962 million revenue), OpenAI's generative AI model incurs rising costs per query and training run, with no clear path to economies of scale. Its $157 billion valuation implies 13.5x forward revenue multiples, but bears argue this misprices the "bad economics": margins erode as models grow more complex, and infrastructure demands could exceed $1 trillion industry-wide, straining global energy and supply chains. If adoption slows (already down to 56% YoY growth in 2025 from triple-digits), or if AGI timelines slip, investors could bail, triggering a valuation collapse similar to WeWork's overhyping. Altman's restructuring to a for-profit public benefit corporation (potentially IPO by 2026) might unlock capital but exposes it to market scrutiny, where skeptics could short the stock as he himself suggested.

2. Technical Plateaus and the Elusive Path to AGI

Altman's goals hinge on rapid AGI breakthroughs, but bears highlight diminishing returns in AI scaling laws. Despite models like o3 and o4, progress has plateaued: GPT-4 token pricing dropped 98% since 2024 due to commoditization, and open-source alternatives (e.g., Meta's Llama 3.1 405B) achieve near-parity at half the cost. Achieving AGI requires 93% annual revenue growth for five years to hit $100 billion by 2029, but technical hurdles—like data scarcity, energy constraints (250 GW data centers by 2033), and algorithmic limits—could delay it indefinitely.

Critics argue OpenAI lacks a durable moat: Its "superalignment" safety team was gutted, whistleblowers silenced, and focus shifted to acceleration over safety, risking uncontrolled AI or ethical failures. If AGI proves a "utopian folly"—a rationalist dream ungrounded in reality—OpenAI could become a commoditized tool provider, not a transformative force.

3. Intensifying Competition and Talent Exodus

OpenAI's early lead is eroding as competitors like Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Meta (Llama), and xAI (Grok) scale up. Open-source models democratize AI, undercutting subscriptions (e.g., Meta's free Llama powers 1.1 billion users, avoiding lock-in). Leadership turnover exacerbates this: Eight of 11 co-founders have left, including CTO Mira Murati and Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever, many starting rivals amid disillusionment with Altman's direction. The "talent wars" favor diversified players like Microsoft, which hedges with its own AI (e.g., Inflection acquisition) and could pivot if OpenAI falters.

4. Regulatory, Legal, and Ethical Headwinds: OpenAI faces mounting scrutiny

Copyright lawsuits, antitrust probes (e.g., FTC on Microsoft ties), and investigations like California AG Rob Bonta's into safety lapses (linked to a teen suicide via ChatGPT). Altman's inconsistent stance—advocating regulation publicly while lobbying against EU AI Act and California's SB-1047—fuels distrust. Restructuring concessions (e.g., $50 million fund for "historically excluded" communities) could politicize operations, turning OpenAI into a "politicized nonprofit" vulnerable to extortion and slowed innovation. Ethical lapses, like allowing erotic content or influencing elections via ChatGPT, amplify risks.

5. Leadership Vulnerabilities: Sam Altman's Experience and Track Record

Perhaps the most damning element is Altman's fitness to helm a company pursuing world-altering AGI. At 40, Altman lacks the operational experience for managing a trillion-scale entity—his background is entrepreneurial, not scaled executive. He dropped out of Stanford after two years (no CS/AI degree), founded Loopt (sold for $43 million in 2012 amid internal pushes to oust him for "deceptive and chaotic behavior"), and led Y Combinator (2014-2019), where he was fired for absenteeism, personal enrichment (e.g., double-dipping investments), and prioritizing side projects like OpenAI. Critics note: "If [Altman] imagines something to be true, it sort of becomes true in his head … It may or may not lead one to stretch."
At OpenAI, a documented pattern of dishonesty, manipulation, and abuse led to his November 2023 ouster: Executives like Murati and Sutskever reported "psychological abuse," chaos, and lying (e.g., fabricating board views, undisclosed ownership of the Startup Fund, indirect equity via funds). Board member Helen Toner cited "years worth of issues with trust, accountability, oversight," including withholding information and outright lies. Murati described his playbook: "First, say whatever he needed to say to get you to do what he wanted, and second, if that didn’t work, undermine you or destroy your credibility." Sutskever: "I don’t think Sam is the guy who should have the finger on the button for AGI."

This "web of lies" extended to equity clawbacks (apologized for but authorized by him), safety approvals (falsely claiming approvals), and pitting teams against each other. Post-ouster, Altman demanded board resignations for his return, and restructuring purged safety advocates for profit focus. Users and ex-employees decry his "psychological manipulation," e.g., dismissing critics as "bots" or stigmatizing AI attachments. Bears argue this pattern—evident across Loopt, Y Combinator, and OpenAI—disqualifies him from stewarding AGI, risking internal implosion or ethical disasters. Unlike seasoned CEOs (e.g., Satya Nadella at Microsoft), Altman's style fosters "fear-mongering and systematic lying," per Toner, potentially derailing execution at scale.

Overall Assessment

The bear case envisions OpenAI as a house of cards: Overleveraged finances, technical overpromises, eroding edges, regulatory traps, and a CEO whose manipulative tendencies amplify risks. If AGI delays or costs spiral, it could collapse like Theranos—valued at billions before fraud exposure—or become a marginalized player in a commoditized market. Altman's vision demands flawless leadership he may lack, turning "insane scale" into unsustainable hubris. While the bull case bets on breakthroughs, bears see a 20-30% growth miss triggering a funding crunch, rendering Altman's portrayal unattainable.

In April 2022, Alameda Research, the trading firm founded by Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), invested $200,000 in Anysphere, the company behind the AI coding tool Cursor. That investment bought them about 5% of the company.

Fast forward one year, and FTX had collapsed, and the bankruptcy court was in control of the company. In April 2023, the FTX bankruptcy estate sold that 5% stake for the same amount Alameda had paid a year earlier: $200,000.

However, SpaceX announced a major partnership with Cursor today. Under the deal, SpaceX has an option to buy the entire company for $60 billion; if they choose not to, they will pay $10 billion for the partnership.

Based on that $60 billion valuation, the 5% stake that FTX sold for $200,000 would now be worth about $3 billion, representing a 15,000x return.

Why does this matter for the incarcerated SBF?
Sam Bankman-Fried is currently in prison but remains active on social media. He has been fighting for a pardon, arguing that FTX was not truly insolvent and that the bankruptcy lawyers destroyed value by selling assets too quickly.

In February 2026, SBF shared a chart suggesting FTX could have reached a net asset value of $78 billion after asset prices recovered if the company had not been forced into bankruptcy.

Crypto lawyer John Deaton dismissed those claims at the time, saying projected values do not change the fact that customers lost money, and that the court had already ruled on the case.

Now, with the Cursor deal, it is hard to agree that the lawyers maximized value three years ago.

SBF’s parents have also been active in pushing for a pardon, appearing on CNN earlier this year in March to argue that FTX customers got their money back.

Creditors pointed out that the repayments are based on 2022 prices, not current market values. A customer who had one Bitcoin got paid based on Bitcoin’s $16,800 price in November 2022.

President Trump has said he will not pardon SBF, and prediction markets currently put the chance of a 2026 pardon at only 5%, but SBF seems determined to keep pushing his version of events regardless.

ChatGPTs take/translation: 

It means the asset sold for far less than the headline number suggested.

What they are saying, in plain English:

Paso Pe was a 70 MW site in Paraguay that Keel sold on April 22, 2026. (GlobeNewswire)
The deal had been presented as “up to $30 million”, but after closing, the actual proceeds were only about $13 million. (GlobeNewswire)
The company says the cut was due to weaker Bitcoin mining economics and broader macro factors. (GlobeNewswire)

What that really implies:

“Up to $30 million” was never a hard guaranteed $30 million.
That wording usually means there were conditions, adjustments, or earnout-style assumptions built in. So the market should never have treated $30 million as locked. (GlobeNewswire)
The asset became worth less before closing.
If Bitcoin mining returns got worse, then a mining-focused site in Paraguay becomes less attractive to buyers. Lower expected profit = lower price. That is the core message. (GlobeNewswire)

“Customary closing adjustments” is corporate language that softens the blow.
Usually that can include things like working capital adjustments, assumed liabilities, cash/debt balances, taxes, fees, or other closing mechanics. But the company itself directly says the main reason was the deterioration in mining economics, so this is not just a tiny bookkeeping haircut. (GlobeNewswire)
This is not a bullish signal for the value of their non-core mining assets.
If an asset once framed at up to $30 million closes at $13 million, that tells you the asset was worth materially less in the real market than the earlier headline implied. That is the honest takeaway from this release. (GlobeNewswire)

Why management is trying to spin it positively:
Keel says this sale ends its Latin America exposure and lets it redeploy the cash into its North American HPC/AI pipeline, where it believes returns will be better. CEO Ben Gagnon framed the lower price as effectively pulling forward two to three years of estimated free cash flow under current market conditions into immediate cash. (GlobeNewswire)

So the market interpretation is basically:
Negative: they sold way below the headline number, which shows weakness in the asset / market backdrop.

Potentially positive: they got rid of a non-core asset and can now focus capital on the AI/HPC story they want investors to value. (GlobeNewswire)

Net-net:
This quote is corporate PR for “we had to accept much less than originally advertised because the asset got worse and buyers wouldn’t pay up.”

text:
"The Hustle" by @thesamparr sold for $27 million.

"Milk Road" by @ShaanVP sold for millions too.

Both were newsletters.

Literally just emails.

But people actually wanted to read them.

They'd see the email come in and open it immediately.

Why?

Just because they wanted to see what was in it.

In eCom that's RARE.

Most people don't open emails because there's no mystery.

It's going to be a sale.

Or highlight product features and benefits.

Or a reminder about something in their cart.

They've read this email before, even if this is the first time they've sent it.

But The Hustle and Milk Road?

People opened them because they were entertaining.

Because they made business news not boring.

Because reading them was worth the three minutes even if you didn't click anything.

And their emails generated MILLIONS, so they were able to sell for millions too.

Not because they had the best design.

Not because they had clever subject lines.

Because they understood something most email marketers don't:

People don't want more information.

They want to be interested.

David Ogilvy said it 69 years ago:

"You can't bore people into buying your product".

But most email marketing ignores this completely.

We act like the problem is getting people to open emails.

So we optimize subject lines.

Or we act like the problem is getting people to click.

So we add more buttons and make them bigger.

But the real problem is nobody actually wants to read the email.

They're just enduring it.

Skimming for the discount code.

Deleting it.

Moving on.

And we wonder why email "doesn't work" for some brands.

It's not that email doesn't work.

It's that boring doesn't work.

Take Instagram for example – another platform that fights for your attention.

When it launched, it was all beautiful images and photoshoots.

Brands would post product photos with perfect lighting.

Influencers would post aesthetic shots of their coffee or their outfit or their vacation.

That's what everyone thought Instagram was for.

A place to make things look good.

And for a while, that worked.

But slowly, the algorithm figured something out.

It started tracking what people actually engaged with.

What they stopped scrolling for.

What they spent time watching.

What they shared with friends.

And it turned out people didn't actually want the aesthetic shots.

They wanted to be entertained.

They wanted memes that made them laugh.

They wanted stories that made them feel something.

They wanted reels that were interesting or dramatic or weird.

Not just pretty product photos that looked the same as everyone else's.

So the algorithm started pushing what people actually wanted.

And brands that didn't adapt died.

Their beautiful product shoots stopped getting seen.

Because the algorithm wasn't rewarding beautiful anymore.

It was rewarding entertainment.

The brands that survived the new algorithm were the ones that figured this out.

That stopped optimizing for aesthetic and started optimizing for attention.

The algorithm forced evolution.

And now Instagram looks completely different than it did five years ago.

Not because Meta decided to change it but because users voted with their engagement.

Here's the thing though:

Email doesn't have an algorithm.

So it hasn't evolved.

There's no feed.

No ranking system.

No AI deciding which emails get shown first.

Every email that gets sent just... shows up.

In the order it was sent.

Whether it's good or boring doesn't matter.

It gets the same placement.

So brands don't get punished for being boring.

They just get ignored.

But since there's no algorithm forcing them to adapt, they don't.

They keep sending the same emails they were sending 10 years ago.

Product photos.

Feature lists.

Bigger and bolder "SHOP NOW" buttons.

Because it's what they've always done.

And because there's no immediate feedback that it's not working.

The email still "sends".

It still gets some opens.

It still generates some revenue.

So it looks like it's working.

Even though it's leaving everything on the table.

I think about this a lot.

What would email look like if there was an algorithm?

If boring emails got buried and entertaining ones got promoted?

Brands would adapt immediately.

They'd have to.

But since there's no algorithm, boring survives.

Even though nobody wants it.

I started Email Engineers in 2021.

I didn't have a philosophy back then, so I just followed the best practices.

Which is why nobody knew about us for about 1 or 2 years.

Now things have changed.

My current philosophy is simple, and it has served me and my clients (7-8 figure eCommerce brands) very well:

Send emails people actually enjoy reading.

Not emails they tolerate.

Not emails they skim and delete.

But emails they look forward to.

Emails that when they see the sender name, they think "oh good, this one".

Now we're considered one of the best email agencies according to Klaviyo.

Actually, not.

Let me rephrase that...

We're not considered by Klaviyo at all.

I don't even think we're in their partner directory because I haven't done enough boot licking or paper-filling.

Klaviyo rewards the agencies that make Klaviyo more money (by pushing their services to clients).

Not the ones that make their clients more money.

Weird if you think about it.

Anyway, Klaviyo benchmarks are real and the great equalizer. 

The "Elite" agency that shoved a bunch of useless AI feautes down their clients' throats despite not being in their best interest.

And the underdog agency that just focuses on results.

And this is what it says about us, Email Engineers:

Campaigns that generate 12.5 times more sales than our clients' competitors.

Subscribers that are worth 7 times more.

Not because we're smarter than everyone else.

But because we optimize for a different thing.

Most agencies optimize for opens and clicks.

We optimize for whether someone actually wants to read the email.

Whether it passes the REV test.

Whether it's relevant, entertaining, and valuable.

Because if they want to read it, everything else follows.

They open it.

They engage with it.

They buy from it.

And they don't unsubscribe.

Because they're not being bored into buying.

They're being interested into it.

Right now we're scaling ecom brands' email revenue to 43-56% of total sales.

Normally 10-20% above what internal teams or agencies can.

The difference isn't tactics.

It's not that we have better subject lines or smarter segmentation.

It's philosophy.

We send emails people enjoy reading.

And it turns out that matters more than anyone thought it would.

Because there's no algorithm in email forcing brands to be entertaining.

So almost nobody is.

Which means the brands that are have a massive advantage.

They're the only interesting thing in the inbox.

Everyone else is competing with each other on discount percentages and countdown timers.

We're competing on a different axis entirely.

And it's working.

–Matt

P.S. If you want to see what entertaining emails actually look like in ecommerce (not just funny emails, but the full spectrum - dramatic, vulnerable, controversial, story-driven, educational but interesting), reply below with "SEND" and I'll send examples.

Most brands won't do this because it doesn't feel like "professional marketing".

Which is exactly why it works by the way.

text:
Leonardo da Vinci

Best Quotes

"There are three classes of people: those who see, those who see when they are shown, those who do not see." Leonardo da Vinci

"Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art." Leonardo da Vinci

"Iron rusts from disuse; water loses its purity from stagnation... even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind." Leonardo da Vinci

"Nature is the source of all true knowledge. She has her own logic, her own laws, she has no effect without cause nor invention without necessity." Leonardo da Vinci

Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher. 

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity. 

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive. 

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498
Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490
Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.
Czartoryski Museum, Kraków 

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science
Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

Military Tech: Armored tanks, giant crossbows, and portable bridges—way ahead of his era's tech.

Hydraulics and Engineering: Canal locks, diving suits, and self-supporting bridges. He even planned an ideal city to beat plagues.

Anatomy: Sketches more accurate than printed texts of the time, showing heart valves and fetal positions.

Fun fact: He invented the robotic knight in 1495—a mechanical automaton that could wave and sit up.

Steampunk before steam.

Personal Quirks and Legacy
Vegetarian and Animal Lover: Bought caged birds just to free them. Ahead of his time on ethics.

Procrastinator Extraordinaire: Queen Isabella of Spain once joked he'd paint her when pigs fly—ironically, he sketched flying pigs.

Death: May 2, 1519, at age 67 in Amboise, France. Buried in Château d'Amboise; his bones were scattered during the French Revolution.

Da Vinci's influence? Everywhere—from NASA's designs to modern AI ethics (he'd probably geek out over neural networks).

In 2025, his Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017, and recent scans of his notebooks (like the Leicester Codex) keep revealing hidden layers via infrared tech.

I got suspended for posting a banana. 🍌

No joke — I entered a @SuperRare art contest and somehow ended up mass-reported for “stealing ideas.”

The contest theme? Taped banana.
So I took a photo of my cluttered kitchen table, ran it through AI, made something weird, fun, and personal — my own take, my own chaos — and posted it.

A few days later — boom.
Account suspended.

Apparently, I had “stolen” the idea.
From… a banana.
Taped. To a wall. 🤦‍♂️

People mass-reported it like I’d looted the Louvre, while the original banana sold for $120K.
But my remix? Too dangerous for the timeline, apparently.

I filed countless appeals to @X .
Explained everything.
Screenshots, context, proof — all of it.

Nothing. Not even a single reply.

This is what happens when creativity meets mob mentality and automated moderation.
Artists remix.
We reference.
We evolve ideas. That’s literally how art grows.

Anyway — I didn’t steal anyone’s banana.
Just made my own, with AI, a messy kitchen, and too much caffeine.

Maybe that’s the real art crime. 🍌🔥

 #SuperRare #AIArt #NFTArt #DigitalArt #Web3 @elonmusk

A shoe company just became an AI infrastructure play.
And honestly? It might not be the craziest thing you'll hear this week.

Allbirds is losing the laces and rebranding as NewBird AI — $50M raised, IP sold for $39M, almost every store closed, and now they're buying GPUs and selling cloud compute.

Stock went from $20 to $2.50. The brand that built a cult following on eco-friendly wool decided the answer was AI infrastructure.

I've seen enough of these to know where it usually goes: Long Island Iced Tea renamed itself Long Blockchain in 2017. Dozens of retailers slapped .com on their name in 2000. The pattern is always the same: a struggling brand chases the hottest market, gets a short bump, then disappears.

But here's what's different this time. AI compute is not a trend: it's a decade-long infrastructure buildout with real enterprise demand, real capital flowing in, and a genuine shortage of capacity. That doesn't mean every late entrant survives. Most won't. But the market itself isn't going anywhere.

So the question isn't whether NewBird is opportunistic because it clearly is. The question is whether they have the execution, the relationships, and the staying power to matter in a space that is brutally competitive and capex-heavy.

Shoe brands don't usually win that game, only the ones who DO show up with more than a press release.

Have you ever heard of someone losing Billions from a $200,000 investment?

That’s exactly what happened to Sam Bankman Fried.

Back in 2022, his firm Alameda Research invested just $200K into a tiny AI startup called Cursor taking a massive 50% stake at the earliest stage.

At the time, it looked like a small, high risk bet.

Then FTX collapsed.

During the 2023 bankruptcy, that entire stake was forced to be sold for the same $200K.
No gain. No upside. Just liquidated.
Fast forward to today.

Cursor is now one of the fastest growing AI companies, with valuations pushing into the $60B.

That original stake?

It could have been worth $3B.

But it was gone before it ever had the chance.

And that’s the brutal part most people miss.
It wasn’t a bad investment.
It was a forced exit at the worst possible time.

A perfect example of how timing, liquidity, and collapse can destroy even the best bets.

Was this one of the greatest missed opportunities in AI history or an inevitable outcome of a system that was never sustainable to begin with?

text:
In 1995, somebody registered Hotels.com for around $100.

That domain later sold for $11 million.

 Insurance.com went for $35.6 million. Voice.com for $30 million. Cars.com became publicly traded.

Those buyers weren't buying domains. They were buying positions inside a brand-new namespace called .com — one of the first gTLDs (Generic Top-Level Domains).

Back then, people laughed. "Nobody will use the internet for business."

Now read that list of prices again.

Those were domains ON .com.

Owning a gTLD is the equivalent of owning .com itself.

In 5 days, ICANN opens the second-ever application window. Fee: $227,000. Closes August 12. The last window was 2012. The next one could be 2036.

Oil is whipsawed by the Strait of Hormuz. Tariffs rewrite themselves monthly. AI restructures industries quarterly.

Namespace is one of the few asset classes on a predictable 14-year ICANN cycle — not shipping lanes, not platform algorithms.

⚠️ The work that decides 2027's winners is happening this week.

Will $227K in 2026 look like $100 in 1995?

𝗡𝗙𝗧𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽. They've evolved into intelligent agents capable of economic autonomy. Here's that journey and how AINFT fundamentally rewrote the narrative.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗪𝗮𝘃𝗲: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝘄𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 (𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟮–𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟳)

The story starts in 2012 with Colored Coins on Bitcoin. The idea was straightforward: "tag" small amounts of BTC with unique metadata to represent real-world assets property deeds, shares, concert tickets. The Bitcoin blockchain's limitations made implementation difficult, but the core concept was planted: a token could prove you owned something specific, not just a fungible balance of currency.

In May 2014, Kevin McCoy and Anil Dash created Quantum a pulsing, pixelated octagon registered on the Namecoin blockchain. It sold for $4 at a conference in New York. For the first time, on-chain data was directly linked to a piece of art. Ownership was cryptographically verifiable, not just asserted. That same $4 NFT would later be valued at nearly $1.5 million during the 2021 boom not because the art changed, but because the world's understanding of digital ownership had.

By 2017, Ethereum introduced the ERC-721 standard, and everything accelerated. CryptoPunks launched: 10,000 unique pixelated characters that would become cultural icons, some selling for millions. CryptoKitties followed, a game where users bred and traded digital cats. At its peak, CryptoKitties clogged the Ethereum network entirely proof that NFTs could drive real demand, not just speculation. OpenSea opened as the "eBay of NFTs," giving anyone the ability to mint, buy, and sell digital assets.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝘁 (𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟬–𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟯)

What happened next was unprecedented. NFT trading volume exploded from $82 million in 2020
to $17 billion in 2021. Beeple's Everydays: The First 5000 Days sold for $69.3 million at Christie's. Bored Ape Yacht Club became a global status symbol. The narrative was fixed: NFTs were digital art and collectibles JPEGs you bought, held, and hoped to sell for more.

Then the market collapsed. Daily sales dropped 92% from their September 2021 peak. A 2023 report claimed 95% of NFT collections had zero monetary value, with 79% unsold. The bubble had burst, and the "NFTs as art" narrative died with it.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗙𝗧 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱

The market's collapse wasn't the end of NFTs it was evidence that the old narrative was too small. Owning a static JPEG was never the destination. It was the prototype.

In October 2025, AINFT completed its brand overhaul. The focus shifted from operating an NFT art collection platform to building crypto AI infrastructure a comprehensive ecosystem centered on the integration of AI and blockchain. This wasn't a rebranding exercise. It was a fundamental reconstruction of ecosystem positioning, technical roadmap, and narrative logic. The core goal: become the key AI infrastructure layer within the TRON ecosystem.

𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗢𝗻𝗲: 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗝𝗣𝗘𝗚 𝘁𝗼 𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲

The first shift was practical. AINFT launched the "AINFT Agent Framework" a general-purpose AI Agent toolbox and "AINFT Nova" , a one-click AI Agent project creation platform. Developers could customize AI Agent applications without deep technical expertise. The barrier to building decentralized AI collapsed.

On the ecosystem side, AINFT aggregated concrete AI products within the TRON ecosystem: digital human "SunLumi" built on the SunAgent framework, AI assistant "Banana King AI" for NFT creators, and the Meme issuance platform "SunGenX." These weren't demos. They were working applications validating the framework.

𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝘄𝗼: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗢𝗿𝗴𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺

But the real narrative rupture came in early 2026. AINFTs were no longer just AI-powered NFTs. They were "behavioral organisms" living assets that evolve based on your on-chain identity.

Forget static JPEGs and pre-programmed bots. In 2026, AINFTs represented a fundamental leap: assets whose appearance, voice, and utility are dynamic reflections of your financial activity. Rarity is no longer minted it's earned. An AINFT begins as a "neural seed," a blank canvas. Its final form is shaped by your "behavioral DNA" on TRON. Consistently provide liquidity on JustLend? Your AINFT develops glowing, powerful traits. Actively participate in DAO governance? It evolves wise characteristics. Use privacy tools like BitTorrent? Spectral glitch-art aesthetics emerge. You're not collecting art you're sculpting an on-chain mirror of your digital self.

𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗘𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘁

The final shift arrived in February 2026 with Bank of AI. AINFT launched the new infrastructure for AI Agents
a "financial operating system" that gives AI agents complete financial capabilities. Five core components: x402 (payment standard), 8004 (on-chain identity), MCP Server (AI-to-blockchain interface), Skills (modular function library), and OpenClaw Extension (one-click on-chain access). Developers need only a few lines of code to give AI agents automatic payments, on-chain identity, and DeFi operations. The platform has surpassed 600,000 users.

The shift is complete. NFTs started as static proof of ownership. They became art. Then collectibles. Then infrastructure. Now, through AINFT, they've become autonomous economic participants with wallets, identities, and the capacity to earn, spend, and transact peer-to-peer. The narrative didn't just change it evolved into something the 2012 Colored Coins pioneers could barely have imagined: your assets don't just belong to you anymore. They work for you. 🔻

text:
Elon Musk … a tale from 2 Points of View… 

Elon Musk's career began in the tech boom of the late 1990s, where he co-founded Zip2, a city guide software company sold for nearly $300 million, and then X.com , which merged into PayPal and fetched him over $100 million upon its sale to eBay. This early success propelled him into ambitious ventures like SpaceX in 2002, aimed at revolutionizing space travel, and Tesla Motors in 2004, where he became chairman and later CEO, pushing electric vehicles as a solution to climate change. However, critics from a liberal perspective often highlight how Musk's rise exemplifies the excesses of unchecked capitalism: his companies have faced accusations of exploitative labor practices, including long hours, low wages for workers, and a staunch anti-union stance at Tesla, which has drawn scrutiny from labor rights advocates. Moreover, while Musk positions himself as an environmental savior through Tesla's EV push, detractors point to the environmental costs of mining for battery materials and his personal carbon footprint from private jets, questioning the sincerity of his green agenda amid growing wealth inequality.

In recent years, Musk's acquisition of Twitter (rebranded as X) in 2022 for $44 billion has amplified concerns about his influence on public discourse. From a liberal viewpoint, this move has been seen as detrimental to democratic norms, with Musk reinstating banned accounts associated with hate speech and misinformation, leading to a surge in toxic content on the platform. His forays into Neuralink for brain-computer interfaces and xAI for artificial intelligence raise ethical alarms about privacy, inequality in access to advanced tech, and the potential for corporate overreach in human augmentation. Overall, Musk's career is viewed as a cautionary tale of billionaire hubris, where innovation serves personal ambition over societal good, exacerbating divides in income, information, and opportunity while dodging accountability through his vast resources and media savvy.

### Conservative Point of View

Elon Musk's entrepreneurial journey kicked off with Zip2 in the 1990s, a pioneering online mapping service sold for a fortune, followed by X.com 's evolution into PayPal, which revolutionized online payments and netted him substantial wealth upon its eBay acquisition. This foundation enabled him to launch SpaceX in 2002, challenging government monopolies in space with reusable rockets and ambitious Mars colonization goals, and invest in Tesla, where as CEO he transformed the auto industry by making electric cars viable and profitable. From a conservative lens, Musk embodies the American dream of self-made success through innovation and risk-taking, creating thousands of jobs and advancing technologies that reduce dependence on foreign oil and promote energy independence. His resistance to overregulation, such as fighting SEC oversight and union pressures at Tesla, is praised as defending free enterprise against bureaucratic interference that stifles growth.

More recently, Musk's 2022 purchase of Twitter (now X) is hailed as a bold stand for free speech, dismantling what conservatives see as liberal bias in Big Tech by restoring accounts silenced for dissenting views and promoting open dialogue. Ventures like Neuralink and xAI are viewed as forward-thinking pursuits that push human potential, countering government stagnation in areas like AI ethics and neuroscience. In essence, Musk's career is celebrated as a triumph of individualism and capitalism, where his disruptions in transportation, space, and communication challenge elitist establishments, foster competition, and inspire a new generation of entrepreneurs to prioritize innovation over conformity.

text:
Just listened to @a16zBioHealth 's conversation with @formationbio 's CEO @BenjamineYLiu on building this generation's big pharma. Packed with insights on why drug development is broken and how to fix it. 

Here are my top 5 takeaways (but honestly, listen to the whole thing):

1. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Discovery; It's Development Execution 🎧 02:10-02:48

Discovery candidates have doubled in 10 years, yet FDA approvals remain flat at ~50/year. "One competitive advantage you want to have as a pharma company, ironically, isn't in discovery. It's actually in this drug development process." Development costs hundreds of millions per program; that's where drugs live or die.
---

2. The M&A Trap That Prevents New Big Pharma 🎧 05:40-06:42

No major pharma company has been created since the 1980s. Why? At Phase 2, you face: sell for $3B today vs. 40% chance of $0 / 60% chance of $9B later. Risk-adjusted, everyone sells early. Formation Bio's solution: a hub-and-spoke model, selling individual assets without selling the company, and recycling capital into new shots. PureTech's Karuna (licensed from Lilly → sold for $14B) proves it works.
---

3. Cost-Plus CROs Are Incentivized to Inflate Costs 🎧 19:07-20:51

CROs bill per hour like law firms—"my Series D legal fee was more expensive than my Series C... same law firm." Simple fixes exist: consolidate redundant site visits, use risk-based monitoring (visit problem sites more, not everyone equally). These are FDA-approved but underused because of misaligned incentives.
---

4. "Psychological Arbitrage" in Drug Selection 🎧 11:54-12:44

"It's easier to fail the same way everyone's failing"—corporate career risk drives herding (everyone chasing GLP-1s). Formation Bio targets: (1) First-in-class with genetic validation (anti-CD226 for UC: 20K patients, 20-year dataset), or (2) Proven mechanisms in new indications (brain-penetrant TYK2). Behavioral economics creates systematic mispricings.
---

5. You Need 10+ Phase 2 Readouts to Prove a Platform 🎧 26:18-27:14

With 30% industry success rate, you need 10-20 shots to statistically distinguish 50% picking ability from 30%. "Just because the first drug didn't work, you actually don't know whether they're better than average." Formation Bio built a 0.72 AUC prediction model, but explicitly states "we don't weight it heavily." Intellectual honesty is rare in this space.
---

Tons more in the full episode: China's 360% increase in first-in-class candidates, why AI won't improve clinical success rates (yet), regulatory risk as opportunity. Worth the 40 minutes!

🎧 Full episode: youtube.com/watch?v=LYjxxmqA…

text:
I’ve worked with 300+ newsletters and virtually everyone who gets to $500K+ launched in 1 of these 4 categories:

1. Jobs (the biggest opportunity)

Help people do better at work.

This breaks down into 34 sub-categories:

• Trends (AI, business ideas, etc.)
• Functions/skills (marketing, copywriting, etc.)
• Industry (DTC, Biotech, etc.)
• Tools (Excel, Figma, etc.)

Examples:

a) Miss Excel: She’s done $10M+ in revenue, teaching Excel formulas, pivot tables, and dashboards.

b) Industry Dive: Built niche B2B newsletters around retail, utilities, and waste management.

None of the founders had industry experience, but they scaled to $100M+ revenue and sold for $500M+.

This category is the most scalable and the best fit for ad-driven newsletter models.

2. Investments

People pay for information that helps them make (or save) money.

Examples:

a) MarketBeat: It helps individual investors to make better trading decisions with real-time financial data, in-depth market analysis, and stock research tools.

They do $45M+ in revenue with ~20 employees.

b) Contrarian Thinking: An 8-figure business teaching people how to buy boring businesses like laundromats and accounting firms

c) Alts: Focuses on alternative assets (wine, whiskey, real estate).

They make $1M+/year with a community that gets you access to private investments.

These often monetize via subscriptions, communities, and information products.

3. Niche hobbies

Anything from rare LEGO collectors, quilting communities, to high-end watch buyers.

Why they scale: extremely engaged micro-audiences who will pay for curation, guides, classifieds, or membership clubs.

How to test: find active forums/subreddits, Instagram communities, Facebook groups.

If people spend money on a hobby (collectables, watches, quilting, fishing), you’ve got demand.

Examples:

a) A Lego collectors newsletter: Multi 6-figure ARR just covering rare Lego buys.

b) Quilting: There are 9-figure Quilting companies, and people spend THOUSANDS on quilting.

If there isn’t a 6-figure quilting newsletter + info product yet, there should be.

4. Personal transformation

Fitness, mindset, productivity, weight loss, and spiritual transformations.

High willingness to pay because people expect a drastic change in status/happiness and will spend on coaching, programs, and masterminds.

Examples:

a) Dan Go: Fitness & body transformation for founders. Likely $1M+/year.

b) Sahil Bloom: Took personal development + mindset, turned it into books and a broader business brand.

c) My friend Joel: Started + sold an astrology newsletter that did 7-figures with huge margins.

You probably shouldn't apply.

EdTech's graveyard is full of brilliant engineers. AltSchool raised $200M and closed. Knewton raised $180M and sold for scraps. 2,148 edtech startups in India shut down in the past five years.

They didn't fail because of a lack of technical skill. They failed from mission drift.

Here's what working in edtech actually means:

You're not building software. You're building a theory of how children learn. - @MitchForest 

When you're 2 months into the same feature, and it still doesn't work, you won't have the dopamine hits of shipping fast. You'll need something deeper.

For the engineers who build learning apps for @AlphaSchoolATX , they are REQUIRED to spend 2 hours every day studying. Not coding. Studying and reading papers on cognitive load theory, motivation research, and translating learning science into applications.

Two hours. Every single day.

Engineers like @yiran__c write about the neuroscience of handwriting. @arpangup shares the Harada Method. @LamarDealMaker explores AI for skill development.

This isn't optional. It's the job.

Your success metrics will lie to you.

High DAUs don't mean kids are learning. Viral engagement doesn't mean mastery. The metrics that drive consumer tech success actively undermine educational outcomes.

The money will tempt you to build the wrong thing.

EdTech market: $400B by 2030. That capital creates pressure to optimize for pitch decks instead of classrooms. Byju's hit $22B before collapsing.

An MBA analyzes constraints. A builder changes reality.

What we require:
➡️ Mission Alignment
➡️ Agency
➡️ Strong Engineering Skills

If you're chasing market opportunity or building for your resume, don't apply.

But if you're a builder who sees broken systems and feels an overwhelming need to fix them? If you believe high standards create happy kids? If you want to change education for a billion children?

text:
Why I keep talking about $TAO .
Real talk. 2021 did not shake out weak hands.
It robbed people blind and burned trust to the ground.

14 billion dollars stolen in 2021 alone.

2.8 billion of that was rug pulls.

46,000 plus reported victims to the FTC.

Over 1 billion in documented losses in 2021 to 2022.

And around 95 percent of NFTs are now effectively worthless.

That is not volatile markets.
That is extraction.

Look at the NFT graveyard.

Jack Dorsey’s first tweet sold for 2.9M
Today it struggles to fetch 4 dollars. Four.

Justin Bieber’s Bored Ape bought for 1.3M
Now worth around 60,000.

Madonna’s Ape bought for 466,000.
Now closer to 53,000.

These were not experiments in digital culture.
They were products designed to be dumped on the people who trusted them most.

Behind it all was the same playbook.

1. Create artificial scarcity
Limited NFTs, hidden or unlimited token supply, make it sound rare.
2. Manufacture FOMO
Celebrity endorsements, you are still early, Discord hype, Telegram raids.
3. Promise utility
Games, metaverse, community, yield. Almost none of it ever shipped.
4. Extract value
Projects launched, insiders and founders dumped into retail FOMO.
Exchange supply was just a constant stream of sell orders.
5. Disappear
Discord goes quiet. Website not updated. Founders lawyer up and move on.

Max supply more like unlimited or hidden.
Utility was promised, never delivered.
Revenue source was retail FOMO.
Revenue destination right into founder wallets.
Staking fake yields and ponzinomics.
Transparency Discord announcements, then silence.
End state founders rich, retail broke AF. 

So when people say retail abandoned crypto, I get it.

If you lost a few thousand dollars on something you genuinely believed in, you did not just lose money.
You lost confidence in your own judgment.
You felt stupid. Embarrassed. Used.

The reasonable conclusion was simple.
The game is rigged. I am exit liquidity. I am out.

And honestly, that conclusion was correct for 2021.

Now here is why I am still here.
And why I keep talking about Bittensor and $TAO .

Because structurally, it is the opposite of that playbook.

Where 2021 projects lived on retail FOMO, Bittensor lives on real demand for AI.

Money in and money out look completely different.

Money comes from enterprises and developers paying for AI services.

Money flows back into the network through subnet tokens and $TAO economics.

Look at actual revenue, not roadmaps.

Targon, Subnet 4, is not selling vibes. It is selling enterprise inference.
Tens of millions of dollars worth of Nvidia hardware behind it.
Over ten million dollars a year in revenue from customers using the system.

Chutes is building serverless AI compute that looks a lot more like an AWS competitor than a meme coin.
Celium did over a million in a handful of months.
Ridges is hitting coding accuracy close to frontier models.
Dippy has millions of users in production.

That is not we are going to build a metaverse someday.
That is already live product with paying customers.

Now overlay the token design.

Bittensor does not hide its supply.
There are 21 million $TAO . Full stop. Same hard cap as Bitcoin.

The model around $TAO looks more like this:
Subnets provide useful services.
Those services generate real revenue.
That revenue supports subnet tokens and demand for compute.
Scarce $TAO sits underneath the whole thing as the base asset.

They sold pictures of rocks and called it the future.
This time, we are building actual infrastructure for decentralized intelligence.

Retail is still stuck replaying the old trauma.
They hear new project and instantly think I am the bag holder again.
I do not blame them.

At some point, we are going to look past the scars and ask
Not what is the next meme, but what is actually being used, who is paying for it, and where does the money go.

Those two things should not be put in the same bucket.
 Eventually the market will stop treating them as if they are.

text:
Whether you entered NFTs a few months ago or have been around since the early waves, there is one name in generative art you need to know: Dmitri Cherniak @dmitricherniak . And one collection that has earned its place as a true grail in digital art: Ringers.

 #Ringers stands out because it takes an incredibly simple idea and turns it into an entire universe. Cherniak built a system where a loop of string winds around a set of pegs, yet every output looks completely different. Some pieces feel mechanical. Others feel like woven tapestries or futuristic schematics. Every Ringer has its own personality. The brilliance is how much beauty and complexity he created from such minimal ingredients. That is why many people see Ringers as one of the most important achievements in early generative art.

When it launched on @artblocks_io Curated in 2021, very few understood what they were minting. But once collectors took a deeper look, the collection took off. Floors pushed past 50 eth, then over 100 eth during peak times. Even the least rare pieces traded in the multiple-six-figure range when eth was strong. It became clear that Ringers was not just another project. It was art that could hold its place in any serious collection.

And then came the moment that changed everything.
Ringers #879, known as The Goose, sold for 6.2 million dollars at @Sothebys . Overnight it became the single most recognizable piece of generative art in the world. It appeared in mainstream press, institutional conversations, and discussions about the future of digital art. Even people who knew nothing about NFTs recognized The Goose. It became a symbol of what this entire movement represents.

This year gives Ringers an even bigger spotlight.
 @ArtBasel Miami is launching Zero 10, its first dedicated digital art section inside the main fair. This is a major step. Collectors, museums, and institutions from all over the world will walk through a curated digital art space, and Ringers is exactly the kind of work that thrives in that setting. It is thoughtful, elegant, and conceptually strong. It feels like it belongs in a museum because it does.

Newer collectors and long-time traders are both drawn to it for the same reason. Ringers has a clarity and confidence that separates true art from everything else. And as AI begins generating endless images, I think early human-made generative systems like Ringers will only become more important. They capture a moment when artists designed the rules, the logic, and the entire creative framework. That kind of authorship matters.

Even traders who live for volatility know this. They understand that turning short-term gains into long-term wealth requires placing value into scarce, respected assets. This is why serious collectors vault their Ringers, and why a few specialized platforms like @gondixyz even allow loans against them. Only a handful of NFTs in existence have ever reached that level of trust.

And here is the reality everyone needs to hear.
There are only 1,000 Ringers. Supply is fixed forever. The cultural and historical relevance keeps compounding as generative art moves into museums, galleries, and global conversations.

Yet right now, in this moment, a few Ringers are listed for under 10 eth. For a collection that once traded over 100 eth at the floor, that price feels unreal. Anyone who understands digital art knows how rare moments like this are.

The question is simple.

Who understands what Ringers represents?
Who sees where this is going?
And who will join the club of only 1,000 collectors who can ever own a grail like this?
name: davie satoshi

text:
Startups Using AI Have a Problem: Anyone Can Copy Their Awesome Idea | Joe Wilkins, Futurism

"Every feature that we put out, we know that's going to take either a few weeks or a few months for competitor to copy."

In an era of unprecedented tech hype, one AI startup founder has a warning to those who would follow his footsteps: vibe coding a double-edged sword that makes it trivially easy for competitors to copy your brilliant company.

Israeli tech founder Maor Shlomo, whose vibe coding startup Base44 sold for over $80 million when it was acquired by Wix, said on the podcast “20VC” that “it’s relatively easy to create a vibe coding tool.”

“Every feature that we put out, we know that’s going to take either a few weeks or a few months for competitor to copy,” he complained.

First flagged by Business Insider, the founder is arguably the poster child of the financial feeding frenzy that’s come to define the AI era. In another podcast recorded in July, Shlomo claimed he used AI to write “90 percent of the code” for Base44. Over the last three months prior to the acquisition, he recalled, he hadn’t written “a single line of front-end code” himself.

But while vibe coding is easy — all it takes is an idea, if Shlomo’s to be taken at face value — building actual software infrastructure isn’t so simple.

“It’s very, very, very hard to create a platform that could help people build products they’ll actually use, that are functional, that are complex enough for real-world use cases,” Shlomo admitted on 20VC.

The founder’s sentiments echo those of Andrej Karpathy, the OpenAI cofounder who coined the infamous term “vibe coding” earlier this year. “I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy-paste stuff, and it mostly works,” Karpathy wrote.

It’s an awesome foundation for a practice which is picking up billions of dollars of momentum in tech circles. Shlomo may be offering a particularly silly example of how fragile the AI economy has become, but he’s not wrong — if AI really does lead to a radical breakdown in the scarcity of intelligence, that’ll be extremely bad news for innovators.

🚨🇺🇸 THE $500 BILLION "WHAT IF": NETFLIX WAS ALMOST SOLD FOR $12 MILLION IN '98... TO JEFF BEZOS

As Netflix prepares to swallow Warner Bros Discovery in a $74 billion mega-merger, here's the insane backstory of how close the streaming giant came to never existing.

Three wild what-ifs before Netflix's 2002 IPO:

1. BEZOS TRIED TO BUY IT FOR PENNIES 

In 1998, just two months after Netflix launched, Jeff Bezos flew the founders to Seattle and offered "somewhere in the low eight figures" to acquire the company. 

Reed Hastings, who owned 70%, said no.

2. BLOCKBUSTER LAUGHED THEM OUT OF THE ROOM 

In 2000, during the dot-com crash, Hastings and co-founder Marc Randolph flew to Dallas to pitch Blockbuster on buying Netflix for $50 million. 

CEO John Antioco essentially laughed at them. "We can build this ourselves," Blockbuster thought. They couldn't.

3. BERNARD ARNAULT SAVED IT FROM BANKRUPTCY 

By 1999, Netflix was about to run out of money. 

The world's richest man, LVMH's Bernard Arnault, invested $30 million in July 1999, becoming Netflix's largest investor and keeping the company alive.

Today Netflix has a $400+ billion market cap and just bought Warner Bros and HBO.

Bezos could have had it for $15 million. 

Blockbuster could have had it for $50 million. 

Arnault kept it alive for $30 million.

The lesson? The biggest mistakes aren't the deals you make. 

They're the ones you don't.

Source: CNBC, @tbpn

text:
Why your Web3 username is an appreciating asset (and why you should claim yours now):

Most people think usernames are just usernames. A way to identify yourself online. But in Web3? They're actually assets. Real, tradable, valuable assets.

Here is an explanation.

Unlike Twitter or Instagram handles (which the platform owns), Web3 identities are owned by YOU. When you claim @yourname on MNS, you're not renting it. You're buying it. It's yours. Forever.

It's digital property. And like all property, it can appreciate in value.

Just remember the early internet? People thought domain names were silly. Everyone thought Why would I pay for a .com?

but after some years:
> Business.com sold for $7.5 million
> Voice.com sold for $30 million
> NFTs.com sold for $15 million

The people who bought early made fortunes and The people who waited paid millions or settled for terrible names. Web3 is growing. More users every day. More chains launching. More apps being built.

Web3 usernames appreciate for the same reasons domain names do and we're still early. Most people don't even have Web3 identities yet.

All of them need identity infrastructure.

Your username becomes:
> More recognized (as you build reputation)
> More useful (as integrations increase)
> More scarce (as good names get taken)
> More valuable (as demand grows)

It's not speculation. It's supply and demand.

Now, You have two options:

> Claim a good name now while they're available. Premium names are still affordable. @builder , @artist , @founder - many are still open.

> Wait and pay more later or settle for @builder_2025_web3 because the good ones are gone.

Choice is yours. Choose it wisely.

You don't need to claim a username as an investment.
Claim it because it's YOUR identity. Your Web3 presence. Your payment address.

The appreciation? That's just a bonus.

text:
INDIANA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION 

What happens when you give a monkey a pair of AI scissors?

Your car and your cell phone become a Palantir surveillance machine backed by the Indiana Economic Development Corporation, and banned by the Federal Trade Commission. Is the damage repairable?

"Economic Development" or Mass Surveillance? Indiana Handed Palantir Access to Millions of Drivers and Phone Users. The Federal Trade Commission Shut It Down. The Data Didn't Go With It.

Once upon a time, there was a Palantir investment called Wejo.

Wejo, short for We-Journey, was a customer-less car data trader based in the UK with annual revenue of less than $500,000 since its creation in 2013. Most of the data traded came from General Motors.

Until May 28 2021, the day of the Indy 500, when GM agreed to extend its data-trading contract with Wejo, which allowed Wejo to sign a contract with Palantir, making Palantir the database for that data.

Shortly after, on September 16, 2021, Palantir and Wejo announced a joint “mobility” program. That same day, Wejo California Corporation opened in Indiana.

Keep in mind that cars have a mechanism that allows them to transmit data wirelessly about everything that is happening inside, from your tire sensors to your maps, emails, radios, and conversations with your friends and family while you drive.

Think of this data flow: Your car → Your data → The internet → GM / OnStar → Sells it to Wejo → Saves it in Palantir → Available to anynone that feels like buying it.

The technology was there, but it does not make it legal.

Wejo was hired in the United States by Indiana’s Purdue Research Foundation (PRF) to provide data services for a Joint Transportation Project between Purdue University and the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT). PRF subcontracted a newly formed NGO, Ninetwelve, with zero expertise and revenue, managed by a for-profit, 9-12 LLC, opened by a former IEDC executive, Chad Pittman, right before he left to follow his boss Mitch Daniels at Purdue. 9-12 LLC was registered at Pittman’s home with his wife. Their company made $88M in revenue between 2020 and 2024 - zero bids.

The “innovative” Indiana initiative created a data pool and started convincing other state DOTs to participate in the so-called research. “Connecting the DOTs” they called it.

This was not a small pilot. It was a national grid, as Darcy Bullock, a professor at Purdue University, posted on X that he had just wrapped up analysis of “mobility and EV activity” on every interstate in all 50 states, using Wejo data.

The project could have been a real research initiative, where you and I agree to participate, knowing that our data is being collected and analyzed to make our lives better. And by making it better, I mean actually cheaper: with your permission, I will monitor how you drive, and you will get a discount on your insurance policy.

But that is not what it was.

What they did was exploit your location data to turn it against you. Because they were collecting data on you and your family, without your knowledge. Not cool. That data was then being sold to insurance companies, who were monitoring you and your family behind your backs. Not cool at all.

Just like Cambridge Analytica, but on wheels.

I told every single one of them that what they were doing was illegal.

But they had a clear goal: to collect all your data and hand it over to Palantir.

The Indiana Economic Development Corporation is a Data Sniffer

I told Paul Mitchell, the head of ESN and its Andretti sponsor, dba Battery Innovation Center, that it was not cool to sniff data. But I guess he did it anyway, and little known to me back then, this intellectual property would be sold by Paul and friends to Belgium in exchange for 5 million Euros in cash.

The only little problem is that this group stole my intellectual property to get it done. Minus the part where they stole data, that was their own “innovation orchestration.”

In 2021, I was working with Michael Andretti, who told me he wanted to start a company together while he was forming one with Palantir and the IEDC.

About Andretti and the IEDC → 

 substack.com/@barbarabessolo… 

Andretti introduced me to the Indiana Economic Development Corporation (IEDC). The IEDC awarded my company, DynamoEdge, a grant to analyze data from a vehicle using a 5G network. AT&T donated that network for a weekend to help DynamoEdge. Later, AT&T became the largest investor in DynamoEdge.

But the IEDC had another idea: steal DynamoEdge's intellectual property, customers, and contracts, and use me to secure sponsorships. Exactly the opposite of what they are paid public funds to do. This agency is supposed to help startups, not lie to them to steal their value.

This image was shared with me by an insider at the IEDC and shows my company as “connections for sponsorships” (!)

But let’s go back to our British friends at We-Journey.

How a 10-Year-Old UK Company With No Customers Became an $800M US Unicorn

Thanks to the Indiana Economic Development Corporation. As sad and as simple as that.

SPAC stands for Special Purpose Acquisition Company. It is basically a blank-check fund that invests in a private company and takes it public, bypassing the usual rules that any company must follow to mature and eventually list on its own.

Wejo was acquired by a SPAC called Virtuoso. Let’s call it SPAC1.

After SPAC1 acquires a private company, it enters a process called de-SPAC1, during which the private company becomes publicly traded. In this case, UK Wejo starts trading on US public markets, the NYSE and Nasdaq. To make that happen, the SPAC transaction draws on a type of financing called a PIPE, or Private Investment in Public Equity. The PIPE is the money from sponsors and founders that makes it possible for Wejo UK to become Wejo US, the money that makes them exist, in a nutshell.

And the money that enables Wejo’s illegal data trading comes from Indiana Economic Development Corporation programs.

The PIPE for Wejo came from a second SPAC2, TKB.

TKB sold its sponsorship shares to another SPAC3 called PROJECT ENERGY REIMAGINED ACQUISITION COMPANY (PERAC), run by IEDC executives and affiliates.

TKB terminates Wejo merger agreement →

I know, I know, what a collection of shells. I told the IEDC executives they should consider buying their own island.

So, SPAC3 Project Energy Reimagined becomes Wejo's PIPE. When the transaction closes, Wejo is worth $800 million.

This is what $800 million built on nothing looks like.

The Palantir SPAC PIPE: Indiana’s Project Energy Reimagined

Every SPAC has a sponsor. Project Energy was no different.

The sponsor of Project Energy, Smilodon Indiana Corporation, was registered in March 2020, right before the Palantir IPO in September, by a fund called Edgewater Capital, co-owned by Zhe Zhang and Srinath Nayaranan.

Project Energy Reimagined SPAC contract →

 contracts.justia.com/compani… 

Edgewater holds Palantir founder shares under GCM-PLT LLC:

Bivona lawsuit declaration →. diamondmccarthy.com/wp-conte… 

Smilodon (coming soon since 2020) →

 smilodonai.webflow.io/ 

Smilodon, whose website has said “coming soon” since 2020, is registered at 111 Monument Circle, Suite 2700, the same legal office used by the IEDC. This office appeared in the IndyStar’s award-winning investigation called Mr. Clean. During that investigation, the IndyStar team discovered that not only the IEDC, but also Hogsett, the two-term mayor of Indianapolis, had been handing out no-bid awards faster than bananas.

IndyStar: Mr. Clean investigation →

 indystar.com/story/news/inve… 

Hogsett’s Chief of Staff, Cook, apparently decided to get involved with a co-worker. In text messages obtained by IndyStar, Cook tells his lover that he was going to go work for the legal office that handles the economic development deals for Hogsett and would bring her with him.

Well, well, well. Mr. Clean’s legal office registered Smilodon.

What is even more interesting is that Smilodon operates from 300 N Philadelphia Street, an abandoned foundry managed by the IEDC La Porte Advancement Partnership (LEAP) as an innovation opportunity zone, co-located with a NIPSCO energy node that the Smilodon group purchased under a different name: La Porte Defense Technologies.

La Porte Defense Technologies has been involved in multiple lawsuits in Indiana, California, and China.

The COO of the group is David Roberts, the former IEDC Chief of Innovation, whose public role was to help startups and small Indiana businesses. The Chairman is Michael Browning, the disgraced former Chairman of Duke Energy, removed after an activist investor, Elliott, filed an SEC Proxy demanding that Browning leave Duke Energy, having found himself dealing with this very same group.

SEC filing on Duke Energy →

 sec.gov/divisions/corpfin/cf… 

This program should never have happened.

The Abandoned Foundry With US Army Contracts

Palantir’s SPAC sponsor, La Porte Defense Technologies doing business as Smilodon, is no stranger to lawsuits.

The group faces a $1.5 million garnishment after losing a multi-year lawsuit in Indiana for defrauding a local startup.

The Indiana lawsuits explain that former Governor Eric Holcomb and former Secretary of Commerce Brad Chambers, both IEDC executives, met with this group in Washington and invited them to open a defense company in Indiana.

The only problem is that La Porte Technologies never had a defense contract, never had technology to offer, and never had people qualified to be a government contractor. They had nothing. They were a shell.

But somehow that shell moved to Indiana and was awarded multiple contracts from the IEDC. Refer to the IEDC Transparency Portal under La Porte Technologies and La Porte Smart Solutions, some retroactive to 2017, totaling approximately $20 million. They never delivered a product.

What La Porte Technologies did was pretend to buy the contract from a small Indiana company called RainsfordSanger LLC, a spinoff of AM General, the company that holds the Humvee license. They claimed they did not have the money to pay, and took the contract for free. An IEDC-sponsored outsider stole the intellectual property of a small Indiana business to win a US Army contract for ten Humvee prototypes.

La Porte Technologies →

 laportech.com/home-backup 

The award was given through a Federal AI Hub, won by IEDC executives who then left public service to run it privately, in violation of every conflict-of-interest rule governing public officers.

And that is when it stops being funny.

Because when Monkeys Go to War, the Scissors Become Missiles

The award that RainsfordSanger LLC was selling came from a Federal AI Hub for Advanced Wireless Technologies managed by the IEDC affiliate, the Applied Research Institute.

The Indiana Applied Research Institute was founded in 2015 and registered by Mike Pence’s Chief of Staff at PO Box 1038 in Anderson, Indiana. The same PO Box was receiving campaign donations for Mike Pence at the time.

The Applied Research Institute continued doing business as the Indiana Innovation Institute, without luck in winning any federal awards, until 2021, when this group started promoting a bid for an AI Federal Hub, for which my intellectual property came in very handy to copy.

In 2021, Sean Hendrix was representing the IEDC partner, the Indiana 5G Zone, a zone supposedly built to help startups launch with funding and support. But that was not it. Hendrix was also representing 9-12 LLC, the for-profit of Ninetwelve, registered by Chad Pittman and his wife at home, who in 2021 became the sole contractor of the Purdue Research Foundation. On top of that, Hendrix was working for the Indiana Innovation Institute dba Applied Research Institute and for Eclipse Energy LLC, a personal company owned by David Roberts and his wife.

Roberts awards Eclipse Energy a contract. Eclipse Energy is later sold for $80 million. Yes, you read that right. Eighty sweet million dollars.

These recipients of no-bid contracts invoiced over $261 million in a couple of years.

Hendrix praised my technology as the best presentation he had ever seen in the space and started talking to me about the battlefield and tactical communications. I had no clue he was applying for an Edge-AI Hub using my technology.

And I had no clue that a SPAC was buying my UK competitor, Wejo, who at the time kept telling my company they would invest in us.

I had no clue that the UK company was also lying, backed by the very same IEDC network.

The money from Indiana’s taxpayers was going to the UK.

But that is not it.

The Applied Research Institute became the de facto authority, through a construct called Tradewinds, to qualify AI technology for the Department of Defense. Under that authority, it awarded Palantir a $33 million Proof of Concept to develop a mobility data collection system. Its database, carrying all the data collected by Wejo, is now available to ICE through Palantir’s ImmigrationOS platform.

And just like that, the bananas became missiles.

Michael Burry Substack note on Palantir →

 substack.com/@michaeljburry/… 

Time to Stop These Thieves.

What began as a story about a British data company with no customers ends as a story about three things converging at once: the failure of data privacy law to keep pace with the connected vehicle industry; the failure of government procurement accountability when public development agencies become patronage machines; and the failure of financial markets to price the legal and ethical liability buried inside AI surveillance platforms whose data came from people who were never asked.

IndyStar: IEDC Three Kings lawsuit, March 2026 →

 indystar.com/story/news/poli… 

The monkeys are still holding AI scissors.

But the cage door is open.

22 million dollars.

Change Healthcare processes one in every three medical claims in the United States. When the ransomware hit in February of 2024, the entire pharmacy network froze. Independent pharmacies could not fill prescriptions for weeks. Some patients went without insulin. Some went without chemotherapy.

After the payment they released the data anyway.

text:
openai.com was once Glenn's personal homepage in 2001.

 tiktok.com was a couple's shared site documenting their relationship from dating to married with a baby, roughly 1998 to 2001.

The thread is a reminder that the URLs running trillion-dollar AI and a billion-user social platform were, two decades ago, just regular people's blogs.

This is the hidden secondary economy of the internet.

Domains are real estate. The .com gold rush in the late 90s was the original land grab, and the early adopters who registered short, memorable, English-word URLs accidentally became landlords to the future. Most of them sold for a few thousand dollars in the early 2000s thinking they'd cashed in.

OpenAI later acquired openai.com for an undisclosed sum, almost certainly in the millions. TikTok parent ByteDance reportedly paid over $5 million for tiktok.com after launching as Musical.ly .

The pattern repeats across every major brand.

 facebook.com was registered in 1997, sold to Mark Zuckerberg in 2005 for $200,000. voice.com sold for $30 million in 2019.

 cars.com went for $872 million in 2014. carinsurance.com hit $49.7 million.

Generic, short, memorable URLs are some of the most appreciating assets of the digital age, and almost nobody talks about them outside the domain investor circle.

The hardware and the code change every five years.

The four-letter URL on the address bar is forever.

Glenn probably has a great story.
