text:
Leonardo da Vinci

Best Quotes

"There are three classes of people: those who see, those who see when they are shown, those who do not see." Leonardo da Vinci

"Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art." Leonardo da Vinci

"Iron rusts from disuse; water loses its purity from stagnation... even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind." Leonardo da Vinci

"Nature is the source of all true knowledge. She has her own logic, her own laws, she has no effect without cause nor invention without necessity." Leonardo da Vinci

Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher.

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity.

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive.

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498
Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490
Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.
Czartoryski Museum, Kraków

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science
Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

Military Tech: Armored tanks, giant crossbows, and portable bridges—way ahead of his era's tech.

Hydraulics and Engineering: Canal locks, diving suits, and self-supporting bridges. He even planned an ideal city to beat plagues.

Anatomy: Sketches more accurate than printed texts of the time, showing heart valves and fetal positions.
Fun fact: He invented the robotic knight in 1495—a mechanical automaton that could wave and sit up.

Steampunk before steam.

Personal Quirks and Legacy

Vegetarian and Animal Lover: Bought caged birds just to free them. Ahead of his time on ethics.

Procrastinator Extraordinaire: Queen Isabella of Spain once joked he'd paint her when pigs fly—ironically, he sketched flying pigs.

Death: May 2, 1519, at age 67 in Amboise, France. Buried in Château d'Amboise; his bones were scattered during the French Revolution.

Da Vinci's influence? Everywhere—from NASA's designs to modern AI ethics (he'd probably geek out over neural networks).

In 2025, his Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017, and recent scans of his notebooks (like the Leicester Codex) keep revealing hidden layers via infrared tech.

text:
$OUST 
The analysis I shared today when it was down -9% to -11% in pre-market 👇
Ouster reported Q1 2026 results that beat revenue expectations, showed strong growth in product revenue, and marked its 13th consecutive quarter of product revenue growth. Revenue increased roughly 50% YoY to $49M; product revenue came in at $48.2M; more than 12,600 lidar and camera sensors were shipped; and a new quarterly shipment record was also set on the lidar side. Despite this, the stock sold off by around -7% after ER. The most likely reason for this selloff is the combination of a good quarter, but a forward outlook that was not enough for the valuation: Q2 guidance implies only limited sequential growth, gross margin declined sharply on a quarterly basis, the company is still posting losses, and as emphasized in the 10-Q, risks such as integration, supply chain, customer concentration, tariffs/trade policy, and the path to profitability remain on the table. Still, the current data set does not show that the main investment thesis has completely broken. It points more to a divergence between short-term price expectations and the long-term platform story.

Main Picture of Q1 2026 Results

The company reported total Q1 revenue of $48.6M; $48.2M of this came from product revenue. Total revenue increased from $32.6M in the same period last year. Gross profit was $20.8M, while GAAP net loss was $17.5M. Loss per share came in in-line at -$0.28. Operating loss remained at -$19.2M. From an operational perspective, revenue growth is strong, but the company is not yet profitable on an accounting basis.

The management message was quite ambitious. The company positions itself as a unified sensing and perception platform for Physical AI; it emphasized that the Stereolabs acquisition is at the center of this and that the Rev8 native color lidar launch represents a new era in the product roadmap. Management said the strategic rationale of Stereolabs has quickly turned into operational reality and that customer feedback has been strong. It was also stated that Rev8 has started shipping and has seen early interest from many customers.

Operational Strengths

In Q1, product revenue increased 55% YoY and 18% QoQ. The company shipped more than 12,600 sensors; more than 8,300 of these were lidar units, which was presented as a new quarterly record. The lidar business grew approximately 44% YoY. On the Smart Infrastructure side, million-dollar agreements were announced for BlueCity in Arizona, Michigan, and the northeastern U.S.; deployment was expanded with the Georgia Department of Transportation at more than 30 intersections in the Greater Atlanta area. It was stated that BlueCity has more than 700 contracted site installations. On the Gemini side, millions of dollars of revenue were recorded from a meaningful customer renewal. These support the argument that the company is not just a lidar player selling individual products, but is transforming into a platform player trying to build a broader solution layer.

The first impact of the Stereolabs acquisition was also presented in a positive framework. Q1 revenue included roughly 7 weeks of Stereolabs contribution. Management said the camera portfolio delivered fast commercial contribution, and that demand was better than expected in foundational AI models, advanced robotics, autonomous delivery, precision agriculture, and manipulation use cases. The 10-Q also clearly states that this acquisition positions Ouster as an end-to-end platform combining lidar, cameras, AI compute, sensor fusion, and perception software.

Most Likely Reasons Why the Market Sold

For a triple upside reaction, three things were needed: revenue near the upper end, product-based margin resilience, and a management tone that gave confidence in the 2026 outlook. The first two largely arrived. Revenue came in at $49M, above the $46.15M expectation and also above the previously given $45M-$48M guidance. On the margin side, even though the Q4 royalty effect normalized, GAAP gross margin stayed at 43%, above the long-term 35%-40% framework. It was also specifically stated that royalty revenue was insignificant in Q1. So there is margin decline, but a major part of this is not quality deterioration; it is the disappearance of Q4’s unusually high-margin base.

So why did the stock fall?

Here, I think three main reasons stand out.

First, the market wanted to see not just a revenue beat, but earnings quality + acceleration. In the pre-analysis, I had said that expectations had risen, institutions had turned positive, and good results alone might not be enough. In this situation, the $49M revenue beat is positive, but the market likely expected a more aggressive forward outlook and a stronger profitability signal. Q2 guidance came in at $49.5M-$52.5M. This guidance is positive, but not explosive; especially when the Rev8, Stereolabs, and Physical AI narrative was built so strongly, the market may have looked for sharper momentum.

Second, the EPS and profitability side may not have looked as clean as expected. Although the company balanced this with strength on the revenue side, from a pricing behavior perspective, the perception may have formed as revenue beat, but losses are still high. Q1 net loss was -$17.5M, operating loss was -$19.2M, and adjusted EBITDA was -$7M. Also, adjusted EBITDA loss worsened by $20M sequentially. A significant part of this came from the loss of the Q4 royalty effect and integration expenses, but the market may have initially read this as profitability cadence is slow.

Third, although the Stereolabs and Rev8 story is positive, their contribution to financials may not yet have looked as large as the narrative. In Q1, revenue included only about 7 weeks of Stereolabs contribution. Operating expenses also rose to $40M, including $2.3M of acquisition/integration charges. So the market may currently be asking: the strategic direction is right, but how fast will financial leverage arrive? Especially even though management described very strong customer interest for Rev8, for this to immediately push the stock higher, investors need to see clearer monetization and mix impact.

Positive Side

Core product revenue did not deteriorate. On the contrary, product revenue accelerated.

Gross margin did not collapse. Once Q4’s roughly $21M royalty contribution was removed, margin normalization was already expected; 43% is still a solid level.

The balance sheet is not weak. The company ended the quarter with roughly $175M in cash and short-term investments, and no debt. The 10-Q also says current liquidity is enough to fund operations for at least 12 months.

Did the Main Investment Thesis Break?

My view: no, the main investment thesis does not appear to be broken.

Because if the main thesis is Ouster’s transformation from not just a lidar supplier, but into a Physical AI platform combining lidar, cameras, AI compute, sensor fusion, and perception software, this quarter does not weaken that thesis. The Rev8 launch, Stereolabs integration, BlueCity expansion, 12,600+ sensor shipments, record volume with 8,300+ lidar units, and strong cash position all support this main story. Also, as I emphasized in my pre-analysis note, sector consolidation and weakening competitors remain a framework that strengthens Ouster’s relative position.

But if the short-term expectation was this: after Rev8 + Stereolabs, the market would immediately move Ouster into a higher valuation band, this quarter did not clearly prove that. Because the market is still asking these questions: how much will growth accelerate, how much will the margin structure scale, how clean will the integration process be, and when will the company enter a clearer profitability stride? Management points to a clearer profitability threshold in 2027, but that may not be enough for impatient short-term investors.

🦇Batman Commentary
The main reason for the decline in OUST is not that the fundamental story broke; it is that elevated expectations, especially on profitability and forward momentum, were not fully met. Core product growth is strong, margin remains healthy when adjusted for the royalty effect, the balance sheet is strong, and the strategic platform story continues to live. That is why I do not think the main investment thesis has broken. But the stock is now being priced not only on good product and good story, but also on whether this story can produce faster financial output.

$TSLA & SpaceX are reportedly proposing a $55B investment to build Elon Musk’s “Terafab” semiconductor facility.

This figure could potentially rise to $119B.

Here's the crazy part:

Back in 1995, Elon Musk couldn't afford both an office and an apartment but now his companies are investing billions into semiconductors & AI.

Here is @elonmusk 's entire story:

His first company was Zip2 which was a software to help newspapers move their content online. He ran the whole operation with 6 people drilling a hole through the floor to steal internet from the ISP downstairs for $100/month.

Compaq bought it in 1999 for over $300 million in cash.

He then moved onto his next big idea: Paypal where you could email money to anyone like sending a message.

The feature took about a day to build. The growth took on a life of its own. One customer sent money to a friend. That friend signed up. That friend sent money to someone else. By the end of year two: 1 million customers.

He sold that to eBay for $1.5B.

Then Musk started asking a question nobody else was asking:

Why hasn't space improved since Apollo?

In the 1960s, we went from nothing to landing on the moon in a decade. Then 30 years of basically nothing. Every other sector of technology had transformed. Space just... stopped.

He flew to Moscow 3 times to buy a refurbished Russian ICBM. Couldn't get a deal that made sense. Flew home.

On the flight back, he decided: we should just build our own rocket.

SpaceX was founded with the goal of cutting launch costs by an order of magnitude.

The result: Falcon rocket.

$6 million per launch.

Nearest competitor (Orbital Sciences Pegasus): $25 million per launch, less capability.

Built by 30 people.

Fastest launch vehicle development in history including wartime.

The same playbook ran through all three companies:

- Small team, no hierarchy
- Best idea wins, not loudest title
- Obsess over product, not sales
- Simplicity = reliability + lower cost
- Run dependencies in parallel, never one at a time

The pattern that beat billion-dollar incumbents.

His first company sold for $300M. He used it to build PayPal. Then SpaceX.

text:
a tiny Caribbean island with 16,000 people accidentally became one of the biggest winners of the AI boom.

not through code, not through chips., but through two letters.

be Anguilla:

- British Overseas Territory
- 35 square miles
- economy built on beaches and tourism
- no tech sector
- no Silicon Valley connections
- no plan

1980s: the International Organization for Standardization assigned every country a two-letter code

- US gets .us
- UK gets .uk
- Anguilla gets .ai
- neighboring island Antigua gets .ag
- nobody thought twice about it

1994: an American software developer named Vince Cate moves to Anguilla

- he wants a domain name that ends in .ai
- reaches out to Jon Postel, the man in charge of all global top-level domains
- Postel tells him nobody is running .ai
- asks if Cate wants to run it
- Cate says yes
- that is literally how it happened

February 16, 1995: .ai officially goes live

- for the next 27 years, barely anyone cares
- mostly local Anguillian businesses
- a handful of niche companies
- 2018 total revenue: $2.9 million
- less than 1% of the island's government income

then ChatGPT dropped in November 2022

- registrations surge from 144,000 in 2022 to 354,000 in 2023
- perplexity, claude, X, meta, google, etc
- every startup that wanted to signal AI credibility needed a .ai

2023 revenue: $32 million 2024 revenue: $39 million nearly a quarter of the entire island's government budget

2025 revenue: $85.3 million government had projected $49 million actual revenue almost doubled their own forecast .ai domains went from less than 1% of state income to 47% in a single decade

over 1 million .ai domains now registered renewals kicked in on all the 2023 wave registrations in 2025 90% renewal rate that is when the real money started compounding

meanwhile the domain aftermarket went insane:

- bot.ai sold for $1.2 million in February 2025, the highest publicly known .ai domain sale at that point
- Dharmesh Shah, co-founder of HubSpot, paid $700,000 for you.ai 
- then in February 2026, AI.com sold for $70 million. the largest domain transaction ever recorded in history. the buyer was Kris Marszalek, founder of Crypto.com 

what is Anguilla doing with the money:

- paying down national debt, projected to fall to 19.9% of GDP by end of 2025, well below the Caribbean's 60% benchmark
- expanding airports and roads
- investing in renewable energy
- free healthcare for children under five and seniors over seventy

- in January 2025, Anguilla signed a five-year deal with US company Identity Digital to manage the registry. 
- Identity Digital takes 10%. Anguilla keeps the rest.
- compare that to Tuvalu, the Pacific island that made a similar bet with .tv when streaming took off. 
- Tuvalu gave domain registrations to a big foreign company and locked themselves in for 50 years. 
- most of the money did not go to the country. 
- Anguilla studied that playbook and refused to repeat it.

the Prime Minister still warns against complacency: - "you can't predict how long this will last.
- he is right to say that. the .ai boom depends entirely on whether those two letters stay synonymous with artificial intelligence as the industry matures. 
- so far, the association has only gotten stronger. the biggest AI companies in the world use .ai as product identifiers, not just domain names.

but the real story here is not just the money.
- in 1994, a developer on a tiny island emailed a man named Jon Postel and asked if he could run an obscure two-letter domain. 
- Postel said yes. nobody planned this. nobody strategized this. 
- the island of Anguilla did not outthink Silicon Valley.
- they just had the right two letters at the right moment in history. 
- and unlike most countries that stumbled into digital assets, they kept the bag and are doing something meaningful with it.

text:
One of the most iconic masterpieces in fantasy art: "A Princess of Mars" (1970) by the legendary Frank Frazetta.

This oil painting, created as the cover for the Doubleday reprint of Edgar Rice Burroughs' classic novel, captures John Carter triumphantly raising his sword over a defeated green Thark warrior, with the fearless Dejah Thoris at his side, set against the looming view of Earth and its moon from the red deserts of Barsoom (Mars).

Fun facts:

- Frazetta loved this composition so much that he painted two nearly identical versions: one for the publisher (fearing it wouldn't be returned, a common issue back then), and a personal "superior" copy with subtle refinements (more confident pose for Dejah, ornate jewelry, sharper details). The personal version, kept by his family for 50 years, sold for $1.2 million at Heritage Auctions in 2020.

- It's hugely influential, directly inspiring the original Star Wars poster style (Luke with lightsaber, Leia clinging, Vader/Death Star behind).

All credit to the master himself, Frank Frazetta, the godfather of fantasy illustration.

Now, for a modern twist: Using Grok's image generation and editing tools (powered by xAI), I reimagined this classic in a wildly different direction, transforming it into an extreme dramatic silhouette scene. The foreground figures (John Carter, Dejah Thoris, the fallen Thark, and a fiercer Komodo-dragon-inspired thoat) become near-black silhouettes with intense rim lighting from the massive glowing planet behind, while the background sky, planet Barsoom (now the dominant reddish-orange orb), moons, swirling clouds, and atmospheric haze/fog become hyper-photorealistic with volumetric god rays piercing the mist. It's a hybrid of Frazetta's painted heroism and cinematic sci-fi epicness, heroic romance meets alien apocalypse vibe.

Beeple is an American digital artist whose satirical, pop-culture–driven creations have positioned him as a central figure in contemporary digital and NFT art. 

Trained in computer science at Purdue University, he launched his Everydays project in 2007, creating and publishing a new artwork daily. These images are often dystopian, politically charged, and rendered through evolving techniques which built his reputation for blending humor, critique, and digital worldbuilding.

After his introduction to the medium in 2020, his works quickly became benchmarks in the crypto-art market: Crossroad sold for $66,666.66 and then for $6.7M on resale, and Everydays: The First 5000 Days became the first purely digital NFT sold by Christie’s, achieving $69M in 2021. He has since expanded into hybrid physical–digital installations, most notably Human One (2021), a generative sculptural portrait sold for nearly ~$29M, and The Tree of Knowledge (2024), a real-time data-driven environmental sculpture.

Operating out of Beeple Studios (a 50,000 square foot digital art hub in Charleston, SC) Beeple continues to explore how technology, politics, and culture intersect in a world increasingly influenced by screens and algorithms.

Beeple’s Regular Animals (2025) pairs a robotic canine with an NFT generated from the robot’s AI-interpreted photos. Satirizing tech power and machine-mediated vision, the work merges sculpture, performance, and blockchain, using humor and “dogshit” certificates to question authenticity and how AI and cultural icons shape what we see.

text:
🧠 Step 1 — Why I Acquired HealthStrategy .com for $3,000

In April 2024, I acquired HealthStrategy .com for $3,000. It wasn’t just a keyword play or a data-driven flip. It was a deliberate decision backed by clear reasoning, long-term vision, and flexible thinking.

When I came across the name, it immediately stuck with me.

Most people associate the word strategy with investing, marketing, or business consulting — but rarely apply that level of thinking to health, even though it's one of the most important areas of life and enterprise. That disconnect intrigued me.

I felt that HealthStrategy .com filled a critical gap. It wasn’t a gimmick or trendy mashup — it was:

==> Straightforward

==> Authoritative

==> Positioned for enterprise-level or institutional use

It had all the ingredients of a brand that could anchor a serious platform — whether for a corporate wellness consultancy, a strategic AI-driven health startup, a health planning app, or even a government or NGO initiative focused on public health policy.

📊 TLD Metrics vs Brand Potential

When evaluating domains, I often check how many other TLDs are registered using tools like DotDB.com . It’s a useful signal — and I believe in checking all key metrics.

In this case:

HealthStrategy .com had only 15 TLDs registered

By contrast, a domain I sold earlier — iSoft .com — had 152 TLDs registered

Yet the final outcomes flipped:

iSoft .com → Acquired for $9,000 → Sold for $60,000

HealthStrategy .com → Acquired for $3,000 → Sold for $100,000

This highlights an important truth in domain investing:

✅ TLD count is helpful, but not everything
✅ Every asset class is unique
✅ Brand clarity, context, and timing often matter more

🎯 Brand-First Decision Framework

Before I make a purchase, I always evaluate:

==> How the name sounds as a brand

==> Whether it makes semantic sense as a pair

==> How trustworthy or credible it feels in its industry

==> The strength of comparable sales in the niche

Only after those boxes are checked do I let gut instinct weigh in — and even then, it plays a supporting role, not a leading one.

In this case, I wasn’t influenced by how many TLDs were taken. I focused on the message the name delivers and how easily a serious company could build authority, trust, and inbound business using it.

Most of my best-performing sales in the high five to low six-figure range haven’t followed rigid, traditional investment playbooks. They’ve come from balanced judgment, thorough research, non-obvious positioning, and a willingness to wait.

That’s exactly what this was.

updated with new tips & tricks from the super survivors. 

---> the full guide from noob to survivor for @LootSurvivor beast mode on Starknet.

Quick Start Guide for the no-manuals guys

Connect @cartridge_gg controller at lootsurvivor.io or use the alternative client at death-mountain-coral.vercel.… . Have some $LORDS in your wallet. get them here @avnu_fi 

Before your first serious run, open the leaderboard and click the reel icon next to a top game. watch one full replay to copy tempo and shop discipline.

Upgrade Charisma first to make health potions cheap. if you ignore this you go broke on potions.

Buy a tier 1 weapon immediately. Do not use weak gear. item xp matters and level 15 unlocks the real bonuses.

Fill every armor slot fast. early game, tier 5 trash is fine. an empty slot gets targeted and you die.

Get Dexterity to level 3 so you can flee from nasty beasts early. flee chance drops deeper, but early it is your emergency exit.

Keep health over 100 always.

Kill beasts and collect their nfts.

Don’t die.

<<<>>>

The Full Guide: From Noob to Advanced

Settings and Focus

First thing you do is go to settings and turn off animations. you want to move fast. Another good way to learn is by watching replays of top games. open the leaderboard and click the reel icon next to a game to access a full replay.

Use the alternative client from @djizus_ . It is not cheating. It levels the playing field by showing you the deep math of the game. In an age of bots and ai your only edge is critical thinking and creativity. The alternative client handles the math so you can focus on the human strategy that bots cannot replicate.

The Early Game Foundation

You start by dumping your first points into Charisma. this keeps the market cheap. if you do not do this you will go broke buying potions.

Buy a tier 1 weapon on turn one if possible. Items gain experience and a tier 1 weapon at level 15 unlocks massive special bonuses. if you use a lower tier weapon early you are wasting experience on trash.

For armor, fill all five slots immediately. it does not matter if the gear is weak. if a slot is empty the game logic targets that area and you die. use cheap armor as a shield for your body until you find your real strategy.

Stat Benchmarks

Get Dexterity to level 3 early. this gives you very high flee chance in the beginning. be aware that this chance drops as you go deeper into the dungeon. anything above 50 percent is decent. it is your emergency exit.

Get Wisdom and Intelligence to level 2 plus. if you leave these at zero the game will punish you with constant fire storms and ambushes.

Strength is your pure offense but Vitality is the real secret. it is a mix of defense and offense because it keeps you alive long enough to actually finish a fight.

Bag Bonus Tech

This is the hidden tech people miss. bag bonuses are not universal.

Only Vitality and Charisma bonuses count when the item is in your bag. nothing else.
You only get those bonuses after the item reaches level 15.

So yes, you can farm items that give +3 Vitality or +3 Charisma, level them to 15, then keep them in your backpack for passive value. you do not need to equip them.

The Advanced Armor Flip

This is where creativity separates you from the midfield. Tier 1 armor is great but tier 3 armor with high experience is sometimes better for specific fights. for example if you are wearing tier 1 hide you are strong against magic but a beast with a katana will still kill you. in the alternative client you can flip to a tier 3 metal armor in one click.

Breaking the rules means not just sticking to one set. you integrate lower tier armor because of the material advantage. if you see a blade coming you switch to metal. if you see magic coming you switch to hide.

Hybrid Weapon Tactics

Advanced players do not just carry one weapon. a bludgeon and a book is a elite combo. you flip your attack gear depending on the beast type. this creates a game depth that bots struggle with. you are playing the math of the triangle in real time.

Jewelry and Strategy Direction

Rings and necklaces give you the kick you need for a legendary run. A gold ring early is sweet for the extra gold rewards. But the necklace is what defines your build.

If you find a pendant that buffs hide armor your strategy is now clear. you dump the trash and buy tier 1 hide armor. jewelry gives you the direction and you execute it with total focus.

The Target: The Beast Stable

The goal is to slaughter beasts and collect their nfts. these are not just jpegs. they will have massive utility in loot survivor 2. think of them like elite race horses.

Owning a tier 1 beast nft is like owning Fusaichi Pegasus, which sold for 70 million dollars, or Shareef Dancer, which went for 40 million. these horses were valuable because of their bloodlines and breeding utility. your beast nfts are the same. you are building a stable for the future of the ecosystem. NFA, FAFO.

The Human Edge

When you play this game it feels like a high stakes texas holdem tournament. your palms sweat because every choice matters. most players stay in the midfield because they play like bots. they just follow basic rules.

To win you have to be creative. use the tools to see the math then use your brain to break the game.

text:
I read every YC Request for Startups since 2016. The pattern nobody talks about is embarrassingly obvious in hindsight. - I will not Promote
Long post but I think this reframes how to think about startup ideas in a way that actually matters. Stick with me.

I spent three months going back through every YC Request for Startups published since 2016. Eight batches. Hundreds of problem descriptions from the most successful startup investors alive.

Here is what I found:

YC does not fund the most exciting ideas. They fund the most expensive problems.

That sounds obvious when you say it out loud. But I do not think most founders actually operate this way when they are generating ideas, and the difference in outcomes is enormous.

The pattern I have noticed is, Every single YC request, every year, every batch, without exception, follows the same structure:

Large established industry (healthcare, legal, financial services, manufacturing, agriculture)

Specific expensive problem inside that industry

Technology inflection that recently made the problem newly solvable

"Go build the company that solves this"

That is the entire formula. Large industry. Expensive problem. New solvability. Go.

To confirm above, Look at the companies that actually returned capital to YC, the ones that hit $100M ARR or got acquired for 9 figures. Almost none of them are the exciting ones.

Brex: corporate credit card

Gusto: payroll

Rippling: HR and IT administration

Segment: data pipelines between tools (sold for $3.2B)

Checkr: background checks

Faire: wholesale marketplace for independent retailers

These are not companies that dominated dinner party conversations in 2015 or 2017. They are companies that found large, expensive, underserved problems and built the solution at the moment when building it became technically feasible.

After this exercise I now apply one question to every startup idea I hear: what is this costing the economy right now, in dollars?

Not "how big is the market." What is this specific problem costing people this year?

If you cannot answer with a specific number in 60 seconds, you probably have not found the right problem.

Some examples from the 2026 YC batch:

Prior authorization in healthcare: estimated $35B per year in administrative cost for the US alone

Pesticide over-application: $18-24B in annual waste globally from imprecise application

Outside legal spend waste: US companies overpay estimated 18-22% on outside counsel, about $40-50B per year

Semiconductor supply chain opacity: $210B in vehicles not built in 2021 from one supply disruption

Inference compute waste: $30-40B per year in GPU compute wasted on agentic workloads running on hardware designed for batch inference

In every case: the "interesting" framing is about technology or environment or efficiency. The real framing is about cost.

Why founders keep missing this:

Three reasons.

1. Social reward. Telling someone you are building an AI assistant for drone swarm defense gets you follow-up questions. Telling someone you are building an AI insurance brokerage for small businesses kills the conversation. Founders respond to social reward the way everyone does.

2. Narrative. Building a company about a personal pain is a better story than "I noticed this was expensive and built the solution." The boring founding story does not attract press or conference invites. It attracts customers, which is the only thing that actually matters.

3. Technical glamour. Engineers like hard technical problems. Building an AI that reads insurance policy documents is not a hard technical problem. It is just an important one.

YC has built a system that filters past all three biases. They ask what is expensive, not what is interesting.

The three questions I now ask every idea:

What is this costing the economy right now, specifically, in dollars?

Why is this newly solvable in 2026 that was not solvable in 2024?

Who is currently absorbing this cost and what would they pay to stop?

If you can answer all three quickly and specifically, you have found a YC-pattern idea.

I believe, The best startup ideas are not the ones that keep you up at night with excitement. They are the ones keeping your potential customers up at night with pain.

Those two things your excitement and their pain are frequently not the same thing. When they align, you have a good idea. When they diverge, the customer pain wins every time.

YC has been publishing cost calculations disguised as funding requests for 8 years. Most founders read them as inspiration and move on.

The founders who treat them as a list of the most expensive unsolved problems in the economy, and then immediately call five potential customers to ask "how much is this costing you," are the ones who get funded.

Happy to answer questions. I went deep on the 2026 batch specifically and broke down the cost calculations behind each of their 13 stated priorities if anyone wants to dig into specifics.

Let’s look at some domain names sold with the suffix “Strategy,” including the recent sale by @qualitynames 

Using data from @NameBio , I reviewed the top five sales with this suffix. 

HealthStrategy/com sits at the top of the list with the price tag of $100,000, while RouletteStrategy/com sold for $20,000 in 2019. The gap between these sales is not only about timing; the real difference comes from the prefix.

Why HealthStrategy commands a premium: the word health carries strong commercial intent, consistent search demand, and serious enterprise spending power. It is immediately brandable for consultancies, health-tech SaaS companies, insurers, clinical platforms, and subscription-based content hubs. This translates into higher lifetime value, easier customer acquisition, broader advertiser interest, and stronger partnership potential, all of which justify significantly higher valuations.

In short, the suffix provides structure, but the prefix defines the market, and that is why two “Strategy” domains can be priced worlds apart.

Another useful comparison is MarketingStrategy/com, which sold for $14,500 in 2017. That price does not reflect a weak domain; it reflects the timing of the sale. Marketing is a broad, evergreen, and high-spend category with clear demand from agencies, SaaS platforms, consultants, and enterprise teams. 

In today’s market, with marketing budgets increasingly tied to data, automation, and strategy-led growth, a name like MarketingStrategy/com would be viewed as a far stronger and more valuable asset than its historical sale price suggests.

text:
An interesting winner of the AI boom: a Louisiana data center construction firm (Fibrebond) sold for $1.7B and the owner gifted $240m to 540 long-time employees (none had equity) as a thank you.

Great story from WSJ's Gregory Zuckerman:

◽️ in 1982, Claud Walker ran a 12-person company building structures for telephone and electronic equipment 
◽️ business boomed in 1990s with the company rebranding to Fibrebond and building concrete enclosures for cellphone towers
◽️ then, its factory burnt down in 1998 and the Dotcom Bubble burst crushed the business
◽️ Claud's two sons (including Graham Walker) took over Fibrebond in the mid-2000s after working their way up from doing "menial jobs"
◽️ over the next decade, they tried to find new infrastructure opportunities but it was tough sledding
◽️ the Walkers had to freeze salaries for a period (they had earned loyalty from employees for continuing to pay salaries after the factory burned down and also established an emergency fund)
◽️ Graham took over as CEO in 2015 and invested $150m "to expand capacity to build infrastructure for data centers, including enclosures for power equipment."
◽️ the data centre business zoomed during COVID and has kept going with the AI boom
◽️ sales are up 400% in the past 5 years
◽️ larger firms wanted to acquire Fibrebond but "Walker told suitors 15% of the proceeds of any deal would have to go to his employees, a reward for their loyalty and dedication."

When asked why 15%, Graham just said "it's more than 10%".

Power-management firm Eaton ($126B market cap) acquired Fibrebond for $1.7B in April.

The Walker family (5 siblings total) received ~$1B and the 540 employees were allotted $240m (those under the age of 65 earn the full sum over 5 years).

The average bonus is $440k but the most senior employees received more.

The only other large employer in Minden, Louisiana is Walmart, so this deal is a major W for the city.

Graham is exiting Fibrebond for good at the end of the year.

***

The full article from @GZuckerman has more great details (and employee reactions): wsj.com/business/fibrebond-e…

text:
Elon Musk: The Ultimate First-Mover Across Industries

Elon Musk didn’t just build companies — he repeatedly created products that were genuinely first-of-their-kind and changed entire industries forever. Here’s the definitive list of times he (or his companies) were truly the first:

✅ Zip2 (1995) – One of the very first online city guides and mapping/directions services on the internet. Basically the early ancestor of Google Maps/Yelp. Sold for $307 million in 1999.

✅ X.com → PayPal (1999–2000) – Musk founded X.com as one of the first federally insured online banks offering full digital payments and money transfers. After merging with Confinity, it became PayPal — the platform that made secure online payments mainstream worldwide.

✅ SpaceX Falcon 1 (2008) – The first privately developed liquid-fueled rocket to successfully reach Earth orbit. No government money. Pure private innovation.

✅ SpaceX Dragon (2012) – The first privately developed spacecraft to dock with the International Space Station. Changed space travel from government-only to commercial reality.

✅ Tesla Roadster (2008) – The first highway-legal production electric car to use lithium-ion battery cells and deliver over 200 miles of real-world range. Proved EVs could be fast, sexy, and practical.

✅ Tesla Model S (2012) – Introduced the world’s first mainstream over-the-air (OTA) software updates for cars. Your vehicle literally gets better while you sleep — a feature every modern car now copies.

It also featured a groundbreaking 17-inch vertical multi-touch touchscreen as the central control interface (replacing most physical buttons). This massive, tablet-like display (much larger than contemporary iPads) revolutionized car interiors and made the Model S feel like “an iPad on wheels” years before large touchscreens became standard in the industry. 

✅ SpaceX Falcon 9 booster landing & reuse (2015–2017) – First orbital-class rocket booster to land vertically after launch and be reused. Crushed the cost of spaceflight and made it routine.

✅ SpaceX Crew Dragon (2020) – First private crewed spacecraft to carry astronauts to orbit and the ISS. NASA astronauts now fly on American commercial rockets again.

✅ Starlink (2019–ongoing) – Created the world’s first large-scale low-Earth orbit mega-constellation delivering high-speed broadband internet from space to anywhere on Earth. Now serving millions globally.

✅ Tesla Full Self-Driving (FSD) (2021–ongoing) – The world’s first major production vehicle to deliver advanced autonomous driving capabilities using vision-only (cameras only) technology. Tesla removed radar and all other sensors, relying purely on Tesla Vision and neural networks — proving that camera-based AI can achieve generalized self-driving, just like human eyes.

✅ Neuralink (2024) – Successfully implanted the first wireless, high-bandwidth brain-computer interface in a human patient. The first step toward merging human brains with AI.

From online payments to electric cars, reusable rockets, global satellite internet, and brain interfaces — Elon Musk has a habit of being first where it matters most. He doesn’t follow trends. He creates them.

text:
Korean DRAM export prices just hit $64,000 per kilogram. The same chip sold for under $11,000 a year ago.

The hockey stick is what AI is doing to the global memory market.

HBM and conventional DRAM are built on the same fab lines. Every wafer SK Hynix and Samsung dedicate to high-bandwidth memory is a wafer they don't ship as DDR5 server modules or DDR4 desktop sticks. HBM also consumes roughly 3 wafers for every 1 wafer of equivalent DDR5 capacity. Supply gets eaten faster than the revenue line suggests.

NVIDIA accounts for roughly 90% of SK Hynix HBM output. SK Hynix sold out its 2025 HBM allocation by mid-2024, locked in all of 2026 by mid-2025, and is now pricing 2027. Samsung and Micron are sold out through 2026 too. AI alone is projected to consume 20% of total DRAM production in 2026.

Now the cascade.

Retail DDR5 prices climbed 123% in 2025. Another 45% increase is forecast for 2026. A 32GB DDR5-6000 kit that sold for $80 to $100 in early 2025 trades at $364 to $529 today. A 4x repricing on the same SKU, same speed, same generation.

Phones get the same bill. Xiaomi told investors its DRAM cost per device will rise 25% in 2026. Some OEMs are quietly engineering downgraded SKUs, 8GB laptops and 4GB phones, just to keep a product on the shelf. The Phison CEO warned that some consumer electronics manufacturers will exit product lines entirely by end of year.

Gaming GPUs caught the same wave. NVIDIA cut RTX gaming production 30 to 40% in the first half of 2026 because GDDR7 ships from the same Korean fabs that make HBM. Same factory floor, different SKU. HBM wins the priority queue.

Three companies set the price of every memory chip on earth. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron together control about 95% of global DRAM. Korean exports alone account for two-thirds. In October, OpenAI signed a letter of intent with Samsung and SK Hynix for 900,000 wafers a month for Stargate. Per month.

Memory was historically the worst business in tech. Cyclical, commoditized, single-digit operating margins through entire decades. SK Hynix now runs over 50% operating margin and just posted another record quarterly profit. SK Group's chairman said publicly that the wafer shortage will persist until 2030 because cleanroom buildouts take five years and nobody is willing to overbuild into an AI bust.

Memory stopped being cyclical the day NVIDIA wanted all of it.

𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 is the new oil… but 𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 are the pipelines. 🧯

Raw data has no value until it's refined, transported, and delivered to where it can be used. In Web3, that transportation layer is oracles – and without them, the entire DeFi economy grinds to a halt.

Here's why.

🔍 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺: 𝗕𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀

A blockchain is a deterministic machine. Give it the same input, it produces the same output. That's its strength – but also its weakness.

Without external data, a smart contract cannot know:

→ The price of ETH
→ Whether it's raining in a farmer's field
→ The outcome of a sports game
→ Who won an election

It's like a car with a perfect engine but no GPS. Fast, precise, and completely blind.

𝗢𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 are the windshield.

⚙️ 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗮𝗺𝗲

When an oracle delivers data on-chain, three things happen:

1. 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – Multiple independent nodes fetch the same data and sign their reports.
2. 𝗔𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – The contract removes outliers and computes a trusted median.
3. 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 – The final result is posted with cryptographic proof of origin.

Every DeFi protocol that uses price feeds – lending, borrowing, derivatives, stablecoins – relies on this pipeline. If the pipeline breaks, the protocol breaks.

📉 𝗔 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗕𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀

In March 2020, a lending protocol on Ethereum saw ETH drop 40% in one day. The oracle kept reporting falling prices. Liquidations fired. Some collateral sold for literal zero.

The oracle followed its logic perfectly. But its logic was incomplete – it had no cross-source verification, no anomaly detection, no way to ask "is this price plausible?"

Result: over $8 million in bad debt. The protocol had to mint new tokens to bail itself out.

That's not a smart contract failure. That's a pipeline failure.

🔐 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗸𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗙𝗶𝘁𝘀

By aggregating multiple independent data providers, WINkLink ensures accuracy, reliability, and manipulation resistance. Every data point is signed, verifiable on-chain, and resistant to single points of failure.

text:
San Francisco rents spike 22% in a year, far outpacing other US cities | Francesca Maglione, Bloomberg

In San Francisco’s latest real estate boom, renters are paying cash up front, multimillion-dollar houses are selling auction-style and AI company stock can buy a sprawling hilltop estate.

It’s a reflection of the new wave of wealth from the artificial intelligence industry, leaving even well-paid newcomers scrambling for a place to live.

For Jenni Lee, a Chicago tech worker seeking to join her boyfriend in the Bay Area, finding an apartment has at times felt more difficult than getting a job. She has spent six months searching for a San Francisco rental, flying in for tours and repeatedly losing out on offers, even after the couple almost doubled their budget to $6,500 a month for a two-bedroom. In Illinois, her friends were living in desirable places for less than half that.

At one point she showed up to what she thought was a private appointment just to wait in line and later find out someone had already signed a lease. One $7,000-a-month home didn’t have a washer-dryer — though the touring agent assured her there was a laundromat down the street. Lee recently applied for a place she liked, only to get a text an hour later saying someone else was willing to pay a full year’s worth of rent upfront in cash.

“My Chicago brain couldn’t compute that,” she said.

San Francisco’s new tech frenzy is reigniting home bidding wars and sending prices soaring in a city that just a few years ago was mired in post-pandemic malaise. With the AI industry paying hefty compensation to attract talent — and hometown startups OpenAI and Anthropic PBC commanding valuations approaching $1 trillion — the wealth effects are warping the entire residential market. And upcoming initial public offerings from the likes of SpaceX are set to unleash even more money into the market from early investors.

The city leads the US in annual rent growth, according to apartment-listing firm Zumper. Prices for two-bedrooms are now tied with New York for the most expensive in the country, with a median monthly rent of $5,500, the company said in a report this week. The median rent for a one-bedroom crossed $4,000 for the first time ever. Homebuyers also are facing soaring costs: The median price for a San Francisco house recently hit a record $2.15 million.

The surge is sharpening divides in a city defined by its extremes. San Francisco has long been mired in deep inequality, a place where a homeless encampment can be on the next block from houses owned by tech millionaires. Now, the real estate frenzy is colliding with broader wealth tensions across the state: Californians are facing a potential ballot measure to levy a tax on billionaires, while housing is a central issue in this year’s governor’s race.

And while the real estate market has been accelerating, the labor market tells a different story — suggesting the boom is concentrated among those benefiting from the AI fervor. While overall employment in the Bay Area is recovering after the pandemic, job creation has been modest. The San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont metropolitan area has added roughly 10,000 to 15,000 jobs over the past year, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

“One of the big mysteries in San Francisco is how can you have such a hot housing market when you have such a cold labor market,” said Ted Egan, chief economist for the city and county of San Francisco. “If you have some people moving in and nobody moving out and you don’t have any new supply, that can create a spike.”

‘What Inventory?’

For sellers, the frenzy has translated into windfalls. When real estate agent Butch Haze listed a four-bedroom home in the Marina neighborhood in March, he figured it would fetch around $4 million, netting the owner a profit from the $3.4 million they paid two years ago. Within days, the house drew five all-cash offers.

Instead of choosing one, Haze turned the process into an impromptu auction, asking buyers to bid against each other in $100,000 increments. The home ultimately sold for $4.9 million.

The competition has only intensified. Haze said a recent listing in the Central Richmond neighborhood drew seven showing requests almost immediately and an offer within an hour. The buyers of the four-bedroom, five-bath house paid $4.95 million, plus covered the broker commission for the sellers, pushing the total value of the sale to more than $1 million over asking.

The market has gotten so tight that many buyers are simply dropping out. Haze said he started the year working with about 20 clients; now less than five are still actively searching. His response when asked about the available inventory: “What inventory?”

With supply scarce and competition fierce, some sellers are getting creative — betting that the same AI boom driving up real estate prices can also unlock new ways to pay for homes. Storm Duncan, the founder and managing partner at a tech investment bank called Ignatious, is offering his roughly 13-acre estate in Marin County’s Mill Valley north of San Francisco in exchange for hard-to-get shares of Anthropic.

The four-bed, five-bath home, featuring an infinity pool, a putting green and a fruit orchard, is worth around $8 million, said Duncan, who was part of the wave of tech workers who moved to Miami during the pandemic. And although Duncan said he has never heard of anyone who has done such a transaction, he sees this as an opportunity to grow his investments in AI.

“I was sitting there thinking, how do I get invested here?,” he said. “And then I thought, maybe there’s someone else that has the opposite problem I have, which is they’re already invested, they started working there very early or they coincidentally got some seed shares or early shares as a VC and now they’re worth hundreds of millions of dollars, but it’s all illiquid.”

Duncan said he’s already fielded interest from potential buyers, such as a foreign investor looking to diversify out of concentrated tech holdings. Others have asked about replicating the structure with shares in companies like SpaceX, he said.

The turnabout in the market has been swift for prospective buyers. When Sedric Bailey and Michael Clery started looking for a home almost a year ago, they thought they had the upper hand. Bailey, a lawyer at a tech firm who has lived in San Francisco for seven years, already owned a condo in the Mission Dolores area, so the couple wasn’t in a rush. They were looking for a bigger home ahead of the birth of their first child — ideally a three- or four-bedroom that would also accommodate their German shepherd and French bulldog.

“We felt like we were basically in control,” Bailey said. “We would go see a property and say, ‘Look we’re only going to pay this amount,’ and if they take it, great, if they don’t it’s not for us. And that strategy has had to change starting this year.”

Several bids they made faced about 10 competing offers, Bailey said, including some in all cash. Some homes they tracked were selling for as much as double the asking price. After losing out several times, the couple eventually secured a home by viewing it before it officially hit the market and putting in an offer 25% over asking that same day.

“We saw a rapid big boom starting September and October and it caught everybody off guard,” said Frank Nolan, the president of Vanguard Properties. “There’s a house that somebody bought for around $4 million this fall that is probably worth $5 million right now.”

The demand is creating ripple effects: Many would-be buyers are turning to the rental market to secure a place while they find their home, driving apartment prices further up, said Rachel Swann, an agent at Coldwell Banker Realty.

Swann recently listed a two-bedroom home at the Four Seasons Private Residences for $15,000 a month and immediately had multiple people who were interested. She’s seen rentals that are 600 square feet with no parking go for $6,500 a month. With the sales market heated, one client who was “basically a billionaire” preferred to rent.

“For these people these payments are nothing,” Swann said.

All my failures and successes as an entrepreneur from age 7 to 27:

7 years old: Picked up coconuts that were treated as weeds in Miami, trimmed them and sold them to a guy who flew them up to NY and charged people $5 each. I got 25 cents a coconut and made up to $100 per truckload (my dad and brother helped).

19yo: skipped college to focus on tactical gear e-com shop STNGR that grew out of the eBay pilot and made $1.5M revenue

20yo: messed the business up, almost went bankrupt, lost $100k

– In April 2023 he opened ChatGPT and typed one sentence: "Help me create a successful meme coin with a budget of $69." He had zero coding experience.

– ChatGPT handed him everything. The name, the mascot, the smart contract code, the tokenomics, the whitepaper and the full launch strategy.

– His followers voted on the name and picked TurboToadToken. He fed the mascot description into Midjourney. Out came an orange cartoon toad in a space helmet. He named it Quantum Leap.

A detailed analysis of another cool AMA from @hanuveer_ We wish you a great reading the-open-network:native 

🎙 AMA: WHAT'S COMING NEXT FOR TON / GRAM

🎯 OVERALL THEME OF THE AMA

The central idea of the entire discussion was:

TON is currently in an accumulation and positioning phase before its next major growth cycle.

The strongest participants are positioning themselves early in:

• Memecoins

• NFT Gifts

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

• Telegram-native digital assets

Key themes repeated throughout the AMA:

1️⃣ Wealth is created before the hype arrives.

2️⃣ The biggest opportunities appear before mass adoption.

3️⃣ TON today resembles the early stages of other major blockchain ecosystems.

📌 TOPIC 1 — TON → GRAM REBRAND

Discussion:

The conversation began with the transition from TON to Gram.

Participants discussed:

• Why the market reacted positively

• What the return of the Gram name represents

• Whether Pavel Durov is directly involved

• Whether this is simply a branding change or something much larger

Participant perspectives:

🔹 Plug

His first reaction was regret that he had not accumulated more Gram-related assets earlier.

He believes:

• The return of Gram is an extremely bullish signal

• The project is returning to its original roots

• Regulatory changes are creating opportunities that did not exist during the original launch

🔹 Frag

Initially, he disliked the idea.

After further reflection, he concluded:

• It signals direct involvement from Pavel Durov

• Durov is actively pushing his own vision

• Investors see this as Telegram taking stronger control of its future

🔹 Sara

She emphasized the power of the word "Gram."

According to her:

• The name is familiar to billions of people

• It is easier to understand psychologically

• It is better suited for mainstream adoption

Conclusion:

Participants do not see the rebrand as a simple name change.

They view it as:

• A return to Telegram's original vision

• The beginning of a new development phase

• A bridge toward much larger adoption

📌 TOPIC 2 — HOW TON HAS EVOLVED OVER THE YEARS

Discussion:

Participants compared the ecosystem across:

• 2022

• 2023

• 2024

• 2025 / 2026

In the beginning:

According to Plug, the ecosystem was essentially empty.

It consisted primarily of:

• Basic infrastructure

• Early users

• Initial collectible assets

Today:

The ecosystem now includes fully functioning markets for:

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

• Gifts

• Memecoins

• NFT infrastructure

Conclusion:

Telegram has evolved from a messaging application into a digital economy.

Users can now:

• Own digital identities

• Own usernames

• Own anonymous phone numbers

• Build status through collectibles

• Invest in memecoins

• Use AI tools directly within Telegram

📌 TOPIC 3 — WHY TELEGRAM GIFTS BECAME A PHENOMENON

Discussion:

A significant portion of the AMA focused on Telegram Gifts.

Interesting historical detail:

When gifts first launched, users could not buy them for themselves.

They could only send them to others.

Why this matters:

Frag believes this helped create authenticity.

The feature was originally social, not speculative.

Why Gifts differ from traditional NFTs:

Traditional NFTs:

• Images can be copied

• Ownership is difficult to verify socially

Telegram Gifts:

• Assets are attached directly to profiles

• Ownership is instantly visible

• Collections become part of a user's identity

Conclusion:

Participants see Telegram Gifts as an entirely new category of digital assets rather than traditional NFTs.

📌 TOPIC 4 — WHY CORRECTIONS SHOULD NOT BE FEARED

Discussion:

The host asked how experienced investors handle 50%–60% drawdowns.

🔹 Plug's view

He used Plush Pepes as an example.

The collection experienced:

• Massive rallies

• Deep corrections

• Long periods of consolidation

Yet strong assets eventually recovered.

🔹 Frag's view

For him, gifts have become more than investments.

They function as digital social status.

Conclusion:

Corrections are viewed as a normal part of every cycle.

As long as the thesis remains intact:

• Panic is unnecessary

• Long-term positioning matters more than short-term volatility

📌 TOPIC 5 — WHY THEY ARE SO BULLISH ON TON MEMECOINS

One of the most important topics of the AMA.

Core thesis:

Participants believe memecoins remain the most undervalued sector in the ecosystem.

Argument 1️⃣

Most other categories have already appreciated significantly.

Examples:

• Gifts

• Usernames

• Anonymous Numbers

Argument 2️⃣

Memecoins have received very little liquidity compared with other ecosystems.

Comparison mentioned during the AMA:

• Solana memecoin volume ≈ $5.4B daily

• TON memecoin volume ≈ $4.5M daily

This represents roughly a 1,000x difference.

Conclusion:

If TON captures even a small portion of Solana's memecoin liquidity, participants believe the sector could experience explosive growth.

📌 TOPIC 6 — HOW THEY WOULD INVEST $50,000 TODAY

One of the most practical sections of the AMA.

🔹 Plug's allocation

He would invest in:

• Scared Cats

• Obelisk Cats

• Anonymous Numbers

• UTYA

• REDO

Remaining capital:

• TON

• Undervalued usernames

🔹 Frag's allocation

50%:

• TON memecoins

Remaining capital:

• Anonymous Numbers

• Strong usernames

• Gifts

• Plush Pepe

Why Plush Pepe?

Not primarily for investment potential.

Its value comes from access to one of the strongest private communities in the Telegram ecosystem.

📌 TOPIC 7 — WHY USERNAMES ARE CONSIDERED UNDERVALUED

Discussion:

Plug spent considerable time discussing usernames.

His thesis:

During the previous cycle, simple four-letter usernames sold for:

• $30,000

• $40,000

• $50,000+

Today many can be acquired for far less.

His expectation:

If Gram achieves broad adoption, rare usernames could appreciate dramatically.

Why?

Supply is permanently limited.

The number of possible combinations can never increase.

📌 TOPIC 8 — WHY THEY BELIEVE TELEGRAM IS STRONGER THAN COMPETITORS

Telegram vs Instagram

Participants discussed recent security concerns affecting Instagram.

Conclusion:

Telegram appears more secure and reliable.

Telegram vs Discord

Telegram is increasingly absorbing functions traditionally associated with Discord.

Examples:

• Communities

• Digital identity

• Asset ownership

Telegram vs X

Unlike X:

• Usernames can be owned

• Assets exist on-chain

• Identity cannot be removed by a simple centralized decision

📌 TOPIC 9 — LONG-TERM OUTLOOK FOR TON / GRAM

🔹 Plug's perspective

He believes TON remains dramatically undervalued relative to its long-term potential.

Reasons:

• Telegram already has a massive user base

• Pavel Durov continues expanding the ecosystem

• Core infrastructure already exists

• Competitors appear weaker

Expectations repeatedly mentioned:

• A return to previous highs

• New price discovery

• Significant ecosystem growth as mainstream users arrive

🎯 KEY TAKEAWAYS FROM THE AMA

1️⃣ The return of the Gram brand is being interpreted as the beginning of a new phase for the ecosystem.

2️⃣ Telegram Gifts have evolved beyond traditional NFTs and now function as a form of digital social status.

3️⃣ Usernames and Anonymous Numbers remain among the scarcest assets within the ecosystem.

4️⃣ Many experienced participants are actively accumulating memecoins because they view them as the most undervalued sector.

5️⃣ The largest gains are typically earned by those who position themselves before mass attention arrives.

🔥 THREE STANDOUT QUOTES FROM THE AMA

"We've been waiting two to three years for the shift back to Gram and for Telegram to go mainstream."

This captures the mindset of long-term ecosystem participants. They see recent developments as the realization of a thesis built over several years.

"The only area on TON that really hasn't been tapped yet is memecoins."

This was arguably the most important investment thesis discussed during the AMA.

"The biggest profits are usually made before the crowd arrives."

This quote summarizes the entire discussion.

The recurring message throughout the AMA was simple:

Position early.

Accumulate patiently.

Allow adoption to catch up later.

text:
A year ago, a six-month-old startup sold for $80 million in cash.

Bootstrapped. Eight employees. Zero outside funding.

Most people saw a lucky exit. I saw a playbook.

 @MaorShlomo , a 31-year-old developer, built @Base44 : a platform where non-programmers type prompts and get full applications, no coding.

No paid acquisition.
No sales team.

He posted his building journey on LinkedIn and Twitter. Word of mouth did the rest:

→ 10,000 users in three weeks
→ 250,000 by the time @Wix wrote the check
→ Profitable before the deal even closed

Then Wix bought it. Six months in. That was June 2025.

The real playbook underneath it:

1/ Bootstrapping isn't about discipline. It's about who's in the room.

No funding meant no liquidation preference to clear and no board's return math to satisfy. The buyer negotiated with one person: him.

And because he was profitable, he had no clock. He could say no forever, the strongest position in any deal.

2/ Building in public was free due diligence.

Buyers discount founder projections by default. Everyone inflates the deck.

Shlomo's growth was public and impossible to fake, on a timeline anyone could scroll back and verify. That turns "trust me" into receipts, which shortens the deal and lifts the price.

3/ He didn't sell revenue. He sold a hole in Wix's moat.

Wix owns no-code website building. AI app builders are the exact thing that could make it obsolete.

So $80 million on a company doing a few million in revenue had nothing to do with the P&L. It was defensive value: what it costs Wix to let a rival own this instead.

You get the highest multiples as the missing piece in someone's roadmap, not by growing your earnings. You're paid on the buyer's fear.

4/ He sold at the exact moment every instinct said keep going.

Most founders sell when they're stalled or tired. Worst possible position.

Shlomo sold while the curve was vertical and the category was on fire. Buyers pay a premium for trajectory, not the destination.

Wait six months and growth normalizes, and you're priced on a multiple of earnings like everyone else. He sold the rate of change, not the number.

5/ The repeat-operator edge is knowing what the other path costs.

He'd already built Explorium: $125 million raised, 100 employees, years of grind. So when he ran build vs sell, he wasn't guessing. He knew what scaling Base44 himself would cost.

First-timers romanticize the grind because they've never paid for it. The real question is always: what does it cost me NOT to sell?

The part that proves the thesis:

A year later, Base44 is reportedly near $150 million in ARR inside Wix. Shlomo is on track for another $90 million in earnouts. It even ran a Super Bowl ad.

The $80 million looks cheap now.

The lesson: profitable, fast-growing companies with clear strategic fit get acquired before they ever need to fundraise.

That window is wide open in AI right now.

It will not stay open forever.

text:
be Hugo Caselles-Dupré 

> born in 1993 in Paris, France - an engineer by training with a PhD in artificial intelligence

> co-founded Obvious in 2017 with his two best friends Pierre Fautrel and Gauthier Vernier - all three born the same year

> their shared belief: AI-generated images could have real artistic value - at a time when nobody took that seriously

> to prove it, they trained an algorithm on a dataset of 15,000 portraits painted between the 14th and 20th centuries

> the method they used was called a GAN - Generative Adversarial Network - two sides of an AI competing against each other, one generating images, the other judging them until something worthy came out

> the result was a blurry, unfinished-looking portrait of a fictional man in a dark frock coat; they called it "Edmond de Belamy"

> the name itself was a hidden tribute — "Belamy" means "good friend" in French, a nod to Ian Goodfellow, the man who invented GANs

> instead of signing it with a name, they signed it with the actual mathematical formula of the algorithm that created it

> they submitted it to Christie's New York with a modest estimate of $7,000-$10,000

> on October 25, 2018, a bidding war broke out - phone bidders, online bidders, people in the room; it lasted over 6 minutes

text:
A company built an actress who only exists as software. They gave her a name, Tilly Norwood, set up her Instagram, and walked her around Hollywood looking for a talent agent, the same as any rising star. The actors' union answered with one line: she is not an actor.

Flesh-and-blood movie stars get paid, get tired, take time off, and want a slice of the money a film makes. Software wants none of that. Emily Blunt saw a clip of the fake actress and said, "we're screwed." The same logic is already spreading through the rest of the movie business.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, just helped make a full-length animated movie for under 30 million dollars. The usual version costs around 200 million and takes three years. This one took nine months, with a crew of about thirty people. It is called Critterz, and it showed its first clips to buyers at the Cannes film festival a few weeks ago.

A big Wall Street bank, Morgan Stanley, figures AI could cut the cost of making film and TV by as much as 30 percent. Studios are chasing that number. Audiences never asked for any of it.

You can already see the cost in people's paychecks. The amount of filming in Los Angeles has nearly halved since 2022, and about 41,000 people left the film and TV business in just two years. Some of that is everyone watching shows on their phones now. A growing slice is software doing jobs that used to need a whole room of people.

Audiences still line up for big special-effects movies, though. The biggest film on the planet last year was Ne Zha 2, a Chinese cartoon with no human actors in it, now one of the five highest earning movies ever made. More than 300 million tickets were sold for it in China, almost one for every person in the United States. The new Avatar movie cost a reported 350 million dollars, one of the priciest films ever, and it still sailed past a billion. What flopped was special effects with no story behind them. For the first time in 14 years, not one Marvel movie made the year's ten biggest.

So the split came down to story. People pay for huge effects when there is a story worth sitting through, and they stay home when there isn't. The quieter fight is about money: who, or what, gets paid to make the thing. A 30 million dollar movie built mostly by AI and a 350 million dollar one built by hand are now going after the same ticket, the one you might buy this year.

A Japanese TV crew filmed a man for a feature on AI side hustles. He had earned 160 million yen in one year. He lived in a Tokyo high rise rented on AI income. He had built a YouTube channel with 1.4 million subscribers full of AI generated cat boxing videos.

The cat videos were obvious slop. AI cats in boxing rings. AI cats fighting octopi. 14 videos total. 1.4 million subscribers. He had sold the channel last month for 2 million yen and laughed at how cheap that was.

At 1:29 he says the phrase six year old girl. He says it once. He says it without looking at the camera. The TV crew kept the line because they did not know what it meant.

The six year old girl is his daughter. She prompts Claude for the cat videos. She picked the channel name. Her father is on TV because YouTube monetization requires the account holder to be 18.

She types into Claude in romaji because she has not learned all the kanji yet. The agent generates the cat boxing prompts. A second agent stitches them into shorts. A third uploads them on a schedule. The father cashes out the AdSense.

Someone pulled the upload metadata from the channel. Every video had been uploaded between 7 AM and 9 AM on weekday mornings. Every upload happened while the daughter was at primary school. The agent uploaded for her.

Six months ago a 14 year old in Shenzhen pushed an AI agent to GitHub. Judges said no real world application. 3,100 forks later. The daughter had been one of them.

He still has to be on camera because YouTube needs an adult account. He still does the TV interviews. He still signs the contracts when a channel sells. He still has not told his daughter what the last channel sold for.

He wanted to show TV viewers how he had earned 160 million yen on AI side hustles. He accidentally became the adult signature his six year old daughter needed to keep cashing out.

text:
a $2 product. $100k in profit. the product was not the variable.

the fidget gadget, the cheap phone stand, the $3 cable organizer. the product almost doesn't matter. the distribution does. here's exactly why.

the product cost $2 to source.

it was not innovative. it was not solving a problem nobody had solved before. it was not the result of months of product development or a proprietary manufacturing process. it was a physical object that cost $2 to make and could be sold for $20 if enough people saw it in their feed and decided they wanted it.

$100k in profit is not a product story. it is a distribution story. and the distribution story is the same every time regardless of what the product is.

here's the mechanism.

why the product almost doesn't matter

the assumption embedded in most ecommerce thinking is that the product has to be differentiated, innovative, or uniquely valuable to generate real revenue. the assumption is wrong.

what generates revenue is demand meeting distribution at the right moment. the product has to be interesting enough to stop a scroll and cheap enough to trigger an impulse purchase decision. it does not have to be useful. it does not have to be innovative. it has to be interesting in the feed for four seconds and priced below the friction threshold for a purchase decision made without deliberation.

a fidget gadget clears that bar. a $3 cable organizer clears that bar. a $2 phone accessory clears that bar. the question is never "is this product good enough." the question is "is there ugc that makes this product interesting enough in the feed that a viewer impulse-buys it before they have time to evaluate whether they need it."

ugc answers that question better than any other channel. because ugc delivers the product in the context of a real-seeming person's real-seeming life. the viewer does not see a product. they see a person who has the product and is implicitly endorsing it by using it. the purchase decision is not a rational evaluation. it is a social reflex. ugc triggers that reflex. polished ads do not.

the distribution stack that turns $2 into $100k

the product margin on a $2 item sold for $20 is high if the acquisition cost is low. the entire model depends on keeping the acquisition cost below the margin. performance ugc at $1–3 cpm is what makes the math work.

here is the stack:

the hook. claude agents. fifty variations. the pov is not "here is a product you should buy." the pov is "i found this thing and i cannot explain why i use it every day now." curiosity-based. specific. the viewer does not know what the product is until they are already interested.

the video. sora 2 pro inside kling. iphone color grade. ambient audio baked in via veo 3.1. the clip looks like someone filmed it in their apartment at 9pm because they wanted to share something they liked. it does not look like an ad. the viewer's threat detection does not fire.

the volume. 200 clips a week at under $2 each. fifty hook variations. the algorithm gets 200 shots at finding the audience for this product. some will find the fidget-obsessed corner of tiktok. some will find the desk-setup community. some will find the anxiety-management feed. 200 shots finds pockets that one ad creative never reaches.

the distribution. phone farm, openclaw, n8n workflows, residential proxies. fifty accounts posting simultaneously. staggered. the algorithm reads multiple independent sources posting about the same product as organic trend emergence. it amplifies without additional paid spend.

the performance layer. on top. 40,000+ creators applying to produce content about the product. brand pays only when clips hit the view threshold. zero risk. zero production cost. real human creators adding the social proof layer that ai ugc cannot fully replicate alone.

the math. $20 sale price. $2 product cost. $1.50 effective cpm on the ugc campaign. 1% conversion rate on ugc traffic — conservative for an impulse product with strong social proof. 100,000 views generates 1,000 sales. 1,000 sales at $18 margin is $18,000. $50k in ugc spend generates millions of views. the $100k profit is not a lucky outcome. it is the output of the math at scale.

why this works better for "uninteresting" products

the counterintuitive reality of ugc distribution is that it works better for simple, cheap, slightly absurd products than it does for sophisticated, expensive, genuinely useful ones.

sophisticated useful products require the viewer to understand why they need it before they buy. that understanding requires cognitive effort. cognitive effort breaks the impulse purchase loop.

a fidget gadget requires zero cognitive effort. the viewer sees it. it is interesting. it is $20. they buy it before they have time to decide whether they need it. the impulse loop closes in twelve seconds.

ugc accelerates that loop because the format is designed for the twelve-second attention window. the hook stops the scroll. the product appears in context. the creator's implicit endorsement provides the social proof. the price is low enough to bypass deliberation. the purchase happens.

the polished ad for the same product fails because the format signals "this is an ad" and breaks the loop before it closes. the viewer's rational brain engages. they decide they don't need a fidget gadget. they scroll.

ugc bypasses the rational brain entirely. the loop closes before the rational brain gets involved. that's the mechanism. the product being slightly absurd is an advantage, not a liability.

the ecommerce brands that haven't figured this out yet

most ecommerce brands are running meta ads at $15–30 cpm and wondering why the margins don't work on a $20 product.

they don't work because $25 cpm on a $20 product with a 2% conversion rate produces a $125 cac. the margin is $18. the math is negative before a single ad runs.

performance ugc at $1.5 cpm with a 1% conversion rate on a $20 product produces a $150 cac per 1,000 conversions — or $0.15 per conversion. the margin is $18. the math is extremely positive.

the product didn't change between those two scenarios. the channel did.

the brands paying $25 cpm are not running a worse version of the same model. they are running a different model entirely and the model doesn't work for low-margin physical products. performance ugc is the model that works. the $2 product at $100k profit is the output.

the product category doesn't matter. the distribution does.

phone accessories. desk gadgets. kitchen tools. pet products. fidget toys. cable organizers. the category is irrelevant. the variable is whether the ugc makes the product interesting in the feed for four seconds and the price is below the impulse purchase threshold.

if yes: the distribution stack above generates the volume of organic-seeming content that triggers the algorithmic amplification that reaches the audience that converts at the rate that produces the margin at the scale that gets to $100k .

if no: the product needs a different hook angle. fifty variations means fifty different ways to make the same product interesting. one of them will work. the algorithm picks the winner. you clone the winner into fifty more variations. the loop runs.

the product is $2. the distribution is the investment. the $100k is the output of the distribution, not the product.
