text:
🇬🇧 David Hockney, Britain's beloved painter of sun and joy, dies at 88 
Details Here: 
David Hockney, one of the most influential and widely loved British artists of the modern era, has died at the age of 88. According to a statement provided to CNN by his longtime publicist Erica Bolton, the artist died "peacefully at home" on Thursday, just one month short of his 89th birthday. Born in Bradford, England in 1937, Hockney rose to prominence in the 1960s as a leading figure in the Pop Art movement, though he always resisted the label. He moved to Los Angeles in 1964, and the city's light, space, and leisure culture became a lifelong inspiration. His iconic swimming pool paintings — including "A Bigger Splash" (1967) — captured frozen moments of California sunshine with a distinctive flat, bright style. In 2018, "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)" sold for $90.3 million, briefly making it the most expensive work by a living artist ever sold at auction. The following year, "Henry Geldzahler and Christopher Scott" went for $49.5 million, and "Nichols Canyon" fetched over $41 million. Beyond painting, Hockney worked in photography, printmaking, and stage design for ballet and opera. He also embraced new technologies, creating hundreds of iPad drawings and multi-camera video installations. He famously painted his two dachshunds, Stanley and Boodgie, in a series of intimate portraits. Despite his fame, Hockney remained approachable and endlessly curious — his mop of blonde (later gray) hair, large round glasses, and ever-present cigarette made him instantly recognizable. Major retrospectives of his work traveled to Tate Britain, the Pompidou Centre in Paris, and New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Hockney was openly gay at a time when homosexuality was still criminalized in Britain, and his work often celebrated queer love and friendship with warmth and honesty. He continued working well into his 80s, refusing to slow down. His death marks the end of an era, but his joyful, colorful view of the world will live on in every painting, drawing, and digital sketch he left behind.

I know it sounds backwards. it's the most reliable trick in business & you're too scared to use it

Some buyers don't even want the thing until it's expensive enough to prove they can afford it. lowering your price to close them is the exact reason you lost them

Look at what rich people actually pay for & the whole game stops being a mystery:

> the Amex Centurion = a $5,000 setup fee & $10,000 a year to use a metal card that does what a free debit card does. the fee is the entire point, it screams "I'm in a room you can't get into"

> the watch = a $120,000 Patek tells the same time as a $40 Casio & keeps it worse. nobody buying it cares, they're paying $120,000 specifically to wear $120,000 on their wrist

> the plate = a single license plate sold for around $15,000,000 in dubai. one letter, one number, no extra function. the price is the product, a number on a car that says I can set $15M on fire & not blink

These aren't idiots getting scammed. they're rational men buying STATUS, & status only works when it's expensive. for this buyer a high price doesn't scare him off, it's the whole reason he reaches for his card. economists have a name for the goods people want MORE of as the price climbs, & luxury runs on it

Now drop it onto your business, because this is where it gets stupid easy:

Charge $2,000 & you attract the buyer who counts every dollar, negotiates, churns, & emails you at 11pm asking for a discount. charge $25,000 & you attract the man who wants to be the kind of guy who hires the $25,000 option. he doesn't haggle, he brags. the price filtered him IN

the number alone changed who walked through the door

The play:

Step 1 = stop pricing for the broke version of your buyer. every time you discount to "make it accessible" you build a business out of the worst clients alive & lock out the ones who'd pay 10x with a tenth of the headache

Step 2 = raise the number until it makes YOU slightly uncomfortable to say. if quoting it doesn't tighten your throat, it's still too low. that discomfort is just the old broke buyer falling away

Step 3 = do NOT pile on more to justify it, because that's the tell of a man who doesn't believe his own price. a confident number stands on its own. extra bonuses make you look nervous, & nervous murders the status the high price was supposed to create

Step 4 = say the number & go silent. a premium price followed by an explanation turns into a negotiation. a premium price followed by silence turns into a fact

Your price isn't a measure of your cost, it's a signal of which room you belong in. go pick a higher room

Hagino Kamui O became a national sensation before he ever stepped onto a racetrack when he was sold for a record-breaking 185 million yen at the 1979 yearling sale.

His older sister was Hagino Top Lady, the champion mare who won both the Oka Sho and the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. From the very beginning, Hagino Kamui O carried the expectations of one of Japan's most distinguished racing families.

He lived up to those expectations brilliantly, winning six graded stakes races including the prestigious Takarazuka Kinen. His career earnings exceeded 200 million yen, establishing him as one of the most celebrated racehorses of the Showa era.

The family's legacy continued through Hagino Top Lady's daughter, Daiichi Ruby, another outstanding champion who left her own mark on Japanese racing history.

More than just an expensive horse, Hagino Kamui O proved his worth on the racetrack and captured the hearts of racing fans across Japan.

text:
Elon Musk: The Visionary Driving Humanity’s Multi-Planetary Future
Elon Reeve Musk, born on June 28, 1971, in Pretoria, South Africa, has become one of the most influential and polarizing figures of the 21st century. As the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, founder of xAI, and owner of X (formerly Twitter), Musk embodies the archetype of the bold entrepreneur who tackles humanity’s biggest challenges—from sustainable energy to space colonization and artificial intelligence. 
Early Life and Path to Entrepreneurship
Musk’s journey began far from Silicon Valley. The son of a Canadian model and dietitian (Maye Musk) and a South African engineer (Errol Musk), he showed an early aptitude for technology. At age 12, he sold his first video game, Blastar. He emigrated to Canada in 1989 and later attended the University of Pennsylvania, earning degrees in physics and economics. 
His first major successes came in the dot-com era. He co-founded Zip2 (an online city guide sold for nearly $300 million) and then X.com , which evolved into PayPal. The sale of PayPal to eBay in 2002 for $1.5 billion provided the capital that fueled his more ambitious ventures. 
Building Empires: Tesla, SpaceX, and Beyond
Musk is best known for leading the transition to electric vehicles through Tesla. As CEO and product architect, he has pushed the company to innovate in battery technology, autonomous driving (Full Self-Driving), and robotics. Recent updates include advancements in the Optimus humanoid robot lineup, expected to expand capabilities in homes and industry in 2026. 
SpaceX, founded in 2002, has revolutionized space travel with reusable rockets like the Falcon series and the Starship vehicle. The company operates Starlink for global internet access and has secured major NASA contracts. In June 2026, SpaceX’s landmark IPO—the largest in history—raised tens of billions and positioned Musk as the world’s first trillionaire, with the company valued at over a trillion dollars. 
Musk also leads xAI, focused on advancing scientific discovery and understanding the universe through AI (including Grok models). He owns and leads X, aiming to make it a platform for free speech and information.
Other efforts include Neuralink (brain-machine interfaces) and The Boring Company (infrastructure and tunneling).
Impact, Ambitions, and Challenges
Musk’s companies have accelerated electric vehicle adoption, lowered launch costs dramatically, and expanded satellite broadband to remote areas. His vision includes making life multi-planetary to safeguard humanity’s future, with goals for Mars colonization.
However, his path has included setbacks. Critics point to missed timelines on projects, intense work cultures at his companies, and public controversies—ranging from market-moving tweets to political involvement (including a role in the Department of Government Efficiency under a prior administration). 
As of mid-2026, Musk continues posting actively on X about everything from AI efficiency and Tesla updates to broader ideas on technology and society. 
A Complex Legacy
Love him or criticize his methods, Elon Musk’s influence on technology, energy, and space is undeniable. He has inspired millions to dream bigger about humanity’s potential while sparking debates about wealth concentration, regulation, and the pace of innovation.
As SpaceX matures publicly and Tesla pushes deeper into AI and robotics, Musk’s next chapters will likely continue shaping industries for decades. Whether delivering on every promise or not, his relentless drive has already changed the world.

As we start thinking about a land value tax, I asked AI to help with the attribution of costs when a development site is bought, built and sold for houses.

It suggested that with a gross development value (GDV) of £10m, the costs might be:

Build costs (45%) = £4.5m
Infrastructure (8%) = £0.8m
Fees (7%) = £0.7m
Finance (4%) = £0.4m
Sales (3%) = £0.3m
S106/CIL (8%) = £0.8m
Developer profit (17%) = £1.7m
Landowner share (8%) = £0.8m 

After 24% CGT on his share, the landowner has about 6% of the GDV.

Adding up the s.106/CIL, 25% corporation tax on the developer and 24% capital gains tax on the landowner, the State receives about 14% of the total value. That ignores tax on the builders' profits, and SDLT on home buyers.

The State already gets more than twice as much as the person who owned the land. How much more does land need to be taxed?

a chinese lab just open-sourced a model that lands within 1% of claude opus 4.8 on long-horizon coding. then gave it away.

glm-5.2. 753b params, 40b active, mixture of experts, 1m token context. second on code arena. it scores 51 on the artificial analysis intelligence index, ahead of gemini 3.1 pro and deepseek v4.

now the prices. opus runs $5 in / $25 out per million tokens. glm-5.2 runs $1.40 / $4.40. roughly a fifth of the cost, for output a rounding error behind the frontier.

the usual take is "this is about model routing, use the cheap one where you can." sure. but that's the small lesson.

here's the real one. "we use the most advanced ai" is no longer a differentiator, because so does everyone. the frontier is now a commodity available to your competitor, your client, and your client's 19-year-old nephew, at a fifth of last year's price.

for two years the agency pitch leaned on access. we have the good models, we know how to prompt them, that's the value. that pitch is dead. not dying. dead.

when raw intelligence costs about the same as electricity, none of your margin can live on top of the model. it has to live somewhere the model can't reach.

what can't it reach? the offer. the distribution. the trust. knowing which of a business's problems is actually worth solving. the boring delivery work of making it run every day without the owner thinking about it.

that's the whole business now. the model is the cheapest part of your stack, and getting cheaper every quarter.

you can be annoyed that the thing you sold for two years just became free. or you can notice that everyone else selling it is about to find out the hard way, and move first.

the model was never the moat. open source just made that impossible to ignore.

text:
Leonardo da Vinci

Best Quotes

"There are three classes of people: those who see, those who see when they are shown, those who do not see." Leonardo da Vinci

"Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art." Leonardo da Vinci

"Iron rusts from disuse; water loses its purity from stagnation... even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind." Leonardo da Vinci

"Nature is the source of all true knowledge. She has her own logic, her own laws, she has no effect without cause nor invention without necessity." Leonardo da Vinci

Bio

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the ultimate Renaissance man—a polymath who blurred the lines between artist, inventor, engineer, anatomist, and philosopher.

Born in the rolling hills of Tuscany, Italy, as an illegitimate son of a notary, he apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence and went on to redefine human creativity.

If creativity were a sport, da Vinci would be the GOAT, juggling masterpieces like the Mona Lisa while sketching helicopters centuries ahead of their time. Here's a whirlwind tour of his life and legacy:

Early Life and Rise

Birth and Youth: April 15, 1452, in Vinci, near Florence. No formal education, but self-taught in everything from Latin to geometry. By age 20, he was a master painter in the Guild of Saint Luke.

Patronage: Worked for the Medici family in Florence, then Ludovico Sforza in Milan (where he designed war machines and stage sets). Later, he served Cesare Borgia as a military engineer and François I of France, who called him "the greatest of the spirits of all time."

Artistic Masterpieces

Da Vinci's art isn't just pretty—it's a psychological deep dive, with techniques like sfumato (that smoky blending) making his figures feel alive.

Key works:

Mona Lisa (La Gioconda)~1503–1519
Enigmatic smile, stolen gaze, and those eyebrows (or lack thereof). The ultimate portrait.
Louvre Museum, Paris

The Last Supper
1495–1498

Jesus's final meal with the apostles—dramatic perspective and emotion in a Milan refectory wall. (It's flaking, thanks to experimental techniques.)
Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Vitruvian Man~1490
Iconic sketch of ideal human proportions, inscribed with Vitruvius's geometry. Spreads like a Renaissance meme.
Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice

Lady with an Ermine
1489–1490

Portrait of Cecilia Gallerani, Sforza's mistress—elegant, with a fidgety weasel for symbolism.

Czartoryski Museum, Kraków

He left many works unfinished, like The Adoration of the Magi, because perfectionism was his kryptonite.

Inventions and Science

Da Vinci's notebooks (over 7,000 pages, mostly mirrored writing to thwart spies or lefties) are a fever dream of innovation. He dissected cadavers for anatomy studies (illegal but groundbreaking) and dreamed big:

Flying Machines: Ornithopters inspired by birds, plus a parachute design tested successfully in 2000.

text:
A new Harvard study documents a housing market in crisis. But its real argument is more unsettling: the era when an ordinary American could expect to own a home may have been the exception—not the rule.

For half a century, Harvard has been writing versions of the same warning. In 1977, researchers at what was then the Harvard-MIT Joint Center for Urban Studies observed that only the most affluent families in the United States would be able to own their houses if housing trends from the time continued. In 1970, nearly half of all families could afford a median-priced home. By 1975, only 27% could. The study’s authors warned that an average home could cost $78,000 by the 1980s—a number they offered as a sign of alarm. The median price of a new single-family home in 2025 was $417,400.

Nobody listened, and then—briefly, strangely—the warning became wrong. The early 1980s brought punishing interest rates, but the decade that followed delivered falling rates, rising wages, and a housing market that stayed, if not generous, at least navigable for the broad middle class. For a generation, the crisis that Harvard’s researchers had spotted seemed to resolve itself.

But it didn’t.

The Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies’ 2026 State of the Nation’s Housing report is a meticulous account of just how thoroughly that dynamic has returned—and how much worse it may be than it appears. “Across the U.S., persistent affordability challenges and rising economic uncertainty are hurting housing markets,” the authors stated, citing weakening labor markets and plummeting immigration dampening household growth and mobility as sales of existing homes sit at three-decade lows.

It is true that rents have fallen somewhat, but there’s a structural problem: the drivers of demand are weakening. The slowdown in household growth reflects, the Harvard center concludes, “reduced household formation among young adults amid a weakened job market, burdensome student debt and low consumer sentiment.”

The Harvard authors do not say this, but the implication is that what America experienced in the postwar decades—when homeownership surged 20 percentage points in a single generation, when being middle class reliably meant eventually owning a home—was not a natural feature of a capitalist economy. It was the product of a specific, unrepeatable, and heavily subsidized set of historical conditions. And now those conditions are gone.

The window and what created it

The GI Bill sent veterans to the suburbs. Federal mortgage guarantees lowered the barrier to entry for millions of first-time buyers. Highway construction made cheap land available. And strong union density compressed wages upward, so that a factory worker’s income reliably grew faster than a house’s price—until about 1973, just before the Harvard warning about the future trajectory of the national housing market.

“In the past, if you were middle class, it was almost assumed you would become a homeowner,” Ali Wolf, chief economist of the building consultancy Zonda, told Realtor.com in 2024. “Today, the aspiration is still there, but it is a lot more difficult. You have to be wealthy or lucky.”

What changed was not any single policy or market failure, but that the scaffolding holding up the postwar homeownership society came down piece by piece. Union density declined. Real wage growth for non-college workers was largely stagnant for decades until the short-lived “Great Resignation” of 2021—which happened smack dab in the middle of the Pandemic Housing Boom, as home prices surged 54% in a compressed and almost hallucinatory run-up from 2020 to 2022, turning the residual gap between incomes and prices into a chasm.

The 2026 Harvard report documents what that chasm now looks like from ground level. The median existing single-family home in 2025 sold for nearly 5x the median household income—versus a ratio of 3.2x averaged throughout the 1990s. Monthly mortgage payments on that median-priced home, at roughly $2,420 assuming a modest down payment and a 30-year fixed rate, were nearly double what they were at the end of 2020. Just 16% of renter households earned the $120,800 minimum required to afford that home, Harvard calculates. And listings affordable to households earning $75,000 or less, per the National Association of Realtors and Realtor.com , fell from 49% of the national inventory in 2019 to just 23% in March 2026.

The inheritance economy

What makes the current moment distinct from prior affordability crunches—the early 1980s, say, or the aftermath of the 2008 crash—is not just severity but structure. Homeownership is increasingly behaving less like something earned and more like something inherited.

Aggregate homeowner equity reached $34 trillion in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 88% and what Harvard dubbed an “astounding” $16 trillion since 2019. The average homeowner held about $295,000 in home equity. The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco found that children of homeowner parents who extracted equity accumulated roughly one-third more housing wealth by age 30 than children of renters. A May 2026 NBER study using data on more than 3.4 million families found that “housing capital is substantially more persistent across generations than earnings”—and that less than half of that persistence can be explained by what children earn.

The Harvard report supplies the market-level evidence to match. The median first-time buyer is now 40 years old and NAR finds that first-time buyers accounted for just 21% of all purchases — an all-time low. The homeownership rate for households under 35 has fallen to 37%, down from 39% in 2022. The Black-white homeownership gap, at 28.7 percentage points, now exceeds the gap recorded in 1995. So many indicators are near 30-year lows that taken together, they suggest more of a return to the 1990s than the 1970s. The subsequent expansion of homeownership in the early 2000s—which eventually triggered the Great Recession—has been all but unwound.

The labor market that no longer bridges the gap

Postwar workers could often compensate for a lack of inherited capital with rising wages. That mechanism is largely broken.

The United States added 116,000 jobs in 2025—the smallest annual gain in a non-recession year since 2003. The economy has become “low-hire, low-fire”: stable at the top, constrained at the bottom, with diminished churn that limits the income mobility young workers need to accelerate savings. Student loan delinquency rates surged from under 1% in late 2024 to 10% by the end of 2025 after pandemic-era payment relief ended.

Household growth slowed for the third consecutive year, to 1.1 million in 2025 from an annual average of 2.0 million in 2020 and 2021. Many young adults are not forming households at all. The share of Americans who moved in the prior year fell to a record low of 11.2%.

Immigration, historically the most reliable source of renter household growth, has been cut drastically. Net international migration fell from 2.7 million in 2024 to 1.3 million in 2025. The Census Bureau projects a further drop to 321,000 in 2026—roughly a third of the annual average from 2001 to 2019. Harvard is direct about the consequences: the impact of declining immigration on household growth will be “substantial and increasingly evident over time.”

The federal government exits the field

If the postwar housing window was created by policy, its closing is also partly a policy choice. And the 2026 Harvard report is unusually frank about the direction that policy is moving.

Federal rental assistance reaches only about one in four very low-income renter households, leaving 13.8 million income-eligible households unassisted, including nearly 9 million with worst-case housing needs. Public housing budgets have been cut. HUD has proposed eliminating existing disparate-impact language—the rule that considered facially neutral policies unlawful when they produced discriminatory housing outcomes. Fair housing staff have been deeply cut. Major discrimination cases have been dropped.

On homelessness, the administration has moved away from Housing First models toward treatment prerequisites for housing access. Homelessness reached a record 770,000 people on a single night in January 2024, up 33 percent since the start of the pandemic. FEMA attempted to cancel its two largest hazard-mitigation programs in 2025, shifting disaster recovery burdens to states and localities that cannot absorb them.

“Only the federal government has the scale of resources needed to meaningfully reduce the shortage of housing affordable to those with the lowest incomes,” Harvard writes. That government is currently moving in the opposite direction.

A partial window, closing on everyone

There is a necessary complication in the “historical accident” thesis—one that strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

The postwar homeownership surge was not universally accessible. FHA loans explicitly redlined Black neighborhoods. The GI Bill was administered in ways that largely excluded Black veterans from its housing benefits. Restrictive covenants kept communities segregated. The middle-class homeownership society that is now reverting was always a partial society—one that opened its door to many white working-class families while leaving others in the entry hall.

But the reversion is no longer limited to those who were historically excluded. Cost burdens are rising fastest among middle-income households earning between $45,000 and $75,000. A college-educated 30-year-old without parental equity support faces a market that is, in structural terms, the most hostile to first-time buyers in recorded history. The window is closing on nearly everyone except those already inside.

The housing market is evolving, has evolved into a mechanism for compounding wealth upward and foreclosing it downward, over decades, across generations. A labor market too weak to bridge income to asset accumulation is not a headwind to the housing market — it is a structural feature of an economy that has made housing the primary dividing line between the asset-owning and the wage-dependent.

The postwar window is not closing. It has closed. The question Harvard’s 2026 report raises — without quite asking it — is whether America is prepared to acknowledge what replaces it: a housing market sorted not by income, but by inheritance.

text:
A man built a company alone. It took him six months. He sold it for $80 million in cash.

No team. No investors. No office lease. No head of product and no head of engineering and no one arguing about the roadmap.

His name is Maor Shlomo. His company was called Base44. It let anyone describe the software they wanted in plain sentences and get a working app back. Not a template. Not a drag-and-drop builder. A real product from a description.

He launched it in January 2025. By June it had 300,000 users and $3.5 million in annual revenue. Still one person. Still no team.

Wix bought it for $80 million. Six months of work.

And here is the part that does not fit in the old model.

In any previous decade this company would have required twenty engineers and three years and several rounds of venture funding and a sales team and a marketing team and a head of operations and a lot of meetings about the meetings. The tools were too many and too complex and too slow for one person to hold the whole thing alone.

Maor had none of that. He had AI tools that let him build as fast as he could think and judgment to build what people actually needed and the discipline to ship before he was certain it was ready.

It turned out that was enough.

And now the main thing.

The software industry spent fifty years building itself on one assumption: that building software required a company. A team. A structure. A process. The work was simply too large and too technical for any single person to handle from the first line of code to the first paying customer.

And then the tools changed and the assumption broke.

Not in a press release and not in a keynote. In a one-person GitHub repository that sold for $80 million six months after its first commit.

In my opinion this is the year the one-person company stopped being an exception.

Not a side project and not a lifestyle business. A real product with 300,000 users that a single person built and sold for more money than most companies raise in their entire life.

What would you build if a team was no longer what stood between you and shipping it?

A man sold a website with no profits to Yahoo for $5.7 BILLION on April Fool's Day. Yahoo thought it was the deal of the century. They shut it down three years later.

– Mark Cuban grew up in Pittsburgh selling garbage bags door to door at 12 to afford basketball sneakers.

– In 1995 he started a company called Broadcast.com . The idea was simple. Let people listen to out of town sports radio on the internet. That was the whole company.

– In 1998 he took it public. On the first day of trading the stock jumped 250 percent. The company hit $1 BILLION in value. Cubans owned 30 percent of it.

– They had 570,000 users. The company had never made a single dollar of profit.

– Yahoo was in a war with AOL and Microsoft to become the dominant homepage of the internet.

– They were spending BILLIONS buying anything that looked like the future.

– On April 1 1999, April Fool's Day Yahoo bought Broadcast.com for $5.7 BILLION. Cuban's personal share was $1.4 BILLION.

– But Cuban was nervous. The dot-com bubble was clearly out of control. So he paid $20 MILLION in fees to Wall Street banks to lock in a guaranteed price on his Yahoo shares before the market crashed.

– Six months later the bubble burst. Yahoo stock fell from $300 to $5 per share. Had he held on his $1.4 BILLION would have been worth $25 MILLION.

– He walked away with every dollar. Wall Street called it one of the top ten trades of all time.

– Yahoo shut down Broadcast.com in 2002. Three years after paying $5.7 BILLION for it.

– In 2017 Verizon bought all of Yahoo for $4.5 BILLION. Less than what Yahoo paid for Cuban's website alone.

– Cuban used the money to buy the Dallas Mavericks NBA team and became one of the most famous investors on Shark Tank.

A website with no profits sold for $5.7 BILLION on April Fool's Day and shut down three years later.

THIS SOLO DEV MADE $100K FROM A FEATURE OPENAI WAS ALWAYS GOING TO COPY

he built a tiny ChatGPT browser extension called Easy Folders.

the idea was simple: ChatGPT had messy chats, he wanted folders and subfolders like a real file system.

nothing revolutionary.

but it still made over $100,000 in revenue and later sold for five figures.

the playbook:

> built it while working a full-time software engineering job
> had zero browser extension experience
> launched fast instead of waiting for the perfect product
> promoted it on Reddit, Facebook groups, and OpenAI forums
> watched Stripe for the first paying customer
> used customer emails and bug reports as the roadmap

the real win was not the money.

it proved software was not just something he could build for an employer. it was something he could own, ship, sell, and turn into an asset.

then the platform risk hit.

OpenAI shipped Projects.

Easy Folders did not die instantly, but the extension became less essential overnight. Every ChatGPT update could break the product, and now OpenAI had a native feature overlapping with the core use case.

so he sold.

the exit lesson most builders miss:

> sell while growth is still trending up
> serious buyers move fast, so get on calls within days
> buyers care about revenue, traffic, support load, maintenance, growth, and transferability
> clean handover matters: codebase, domain, payment accounts, docs, and how the app actually works

he waited too long and thinks it cost him a few thousand dollars in the final sale price.

the bigger lesson for AI builders:

coding is getting cheaper every month.

the edge is knowing what to build, judging AI output, talking to users, shipping fast, and getting distribution before the platform copies your feature.

small products can still become real assets.

but only if you ship them before the obvious feature becomes native.

THIS IS THE MOST INTERESTING THING YOU'LL READ TODAY!!!

Every time an AI company buys a website ending in “.ai”, a tiny Caribbean island of 15,000 people gets paid. 

It now earns half its entire national budget this way, without building a single piece of AI.

The island is called Anguilla. A British territory in the Caribbean that has always survived on tourism, fishing, and hoping the hurricanes miss it.

Decades ago, long before anyone cared, an internet standards body handed out two-letter codes to countries and territories. The one Anguilla was assigned: “.ai”.

For years it meant nothing. Just a random suffix for a tiny island almost nobody could find on a map.

Then ChatGPT launched. And suddenly every AI company on earth wanted a website that ended in .ai.

OpenAI, Perplexity, Meta, xAI, Google, they all wanted it. Because “.ai” instantly signals what your company does. And to register one, you have to pay a fee. To Anguilla.

The scale of what happened next is staggering.

There are now over a million .ai domains registered. Each one costs around $140 every two years. And roughly 90% of them renew.

So this island of 15,000 people now collects a small tax every single time anyone, anywhere in the world, wants an AI web address.

In 2023 it made about $32 million from this. By 2025 it was pulling in nearly $90 million a year.

That’s close to HALF of the island’s entire government budget. From two letters.

And they’re using it well.

Anguilla has cut its national debt by 37% in under five years. It’s funding free healthcare for every kid under 5 and every senior over 70. It eliminated tax on essential food. It’s building a new international airport. And it’s setting up a sovereign wealth fund to protect the money for future generations.

Meanwhile individual .ai domains are selling for insane prices on the side. The domain bot . ai sold for $1.2 million this year.

Here’s the poetic part.

During the actual gold rush, most miners went broke. The people who got rich were the ones selling picks and shovels.

Anguilla didn’t dig for AI gold. It didn’t train a model or chase funding or compete with anyone.

It just happened to own the two letters everyone else needed.

And it’s quietly getting rich off the entire world’s obsession, one domain at a time.

How a 20-Year-Old Student Spent $20 on Claude, Built an AI Speed Radar in 9 Days, and Sold It for $317,000

Most people use AI to write emails, generate images, or summarize documents.

A 20-year-old student in China reportedly used Claude to build something far more ambitious.

In just 9 days, he created an AI-powered speed radar capable of detecting vehicles and estimating their speed from video. According to the viral story, the project cost him only $20 in Claude credits—and was later sold for $317,000.

If the story is accurate, it perfectly illustrates how AI is changing software development.

He Didn't Invent New Technology

The most interesting part isn't the speed radar itself.

Computer vision already existed.

Object detection models already existed.

Vehicle tracking algorithms were already available.

What he did was connect existing technologies into a working product.

Instead of spending months reading documentation, he used Claude as his engineering partner—asking it to explain concepts, generate code, debug errors, and improve the architecture.

A Working Prototype in Just 9 Days

According to the viral post, within nine days the system could:

Detect vehicles in real time
Track their movement across video frames
Estimate vehicle speed
Display live speed measurements

Just a few years ago, a project like this might have required a small engineering team.

Today, a single developer with the right AI tools can build a functional prototype in a matter of days.

The Real Shift Isn't AI—It's Speed

Many people believe AI is replacing software engineers.

That's not what's happening.

AI is dramatically reducing the time between an idea and a working product.

Instead of spending months researching frameworks, fixing bugs, and writing boilerplate code, developers can iterate continuously with an AI assistant.

That changes the economics of building software.

The New Competitive Advantage

The biggest winners won't necessarily be the people who know the most programming languages.

They'll be the people who can turn ideas into products the fastest.

Knowing how to collaborate with AI—breaking problems into tasks, validating solutions, and iterating quickly—is becoming a competitive advantage in itself.

We're entering an era where execution speed matters more than ever.

every raw source goes into the vault.

Claude reads it, summarizes it, links it, updates the wiki, and turns it into something usable.

he can ask:

“what AI topics are trending that I haven’t covered yet?”

and Claude answers from his own data:

> his YouTube history
> creator clusters
> topic velocity
> X performance
> sponsor deadlines
> old transcripts
> current AI news
> what competitors are covering

the wild part is the memory.

Claude found a case study he covered 3 years ago about ThumbnailTest doing $20K/month, checked what happened after, discovered it sold for six figures, connected it to YouTube launching native thumbnail A/B testing, and pulled out the platform-risk lesson from his own old video.

that is what a second brain is supposed to do.

not store notes.

resurface useful context at the exact moment it matters.

his system has layers:

> Inbox - raw captures waiting to be processed
> Raw - source documents that never get edited
> Wiki - summaries, concepts, entities and links
> War Room - agents collecting YouTube/X/news data 24/7
> Doctrine - Fable-generated strategy backed by receipts
> Armory - future projects the system thinks he should build

then it becomes a loop:

observe -> collect data
orient -> organize the wiki
decide -> generate strategy
act -> execute
measure -> feed results back into the system

the longer it runs, the better it gets.

and because it is all plain Markdown on his computer, no app owns the memory.

Obsidian can disappear. Claude can change. Fable can go away.

the files stay.

the simplest version takes one afternoon:

> install Obsidian
> install Claude Code
> create inbox/raw/wiki folders
> keep the folder structure flat
> add a CLAUDE.md rulebook
> feed it links, transcripts, notes and tasks
> let Claude maintain the graph

most people use notes like a storage unit.

this turns notes into an intelligence system.

bookmark this before your second brain becomes another graveyard of forgotten PDFs

text:
with box our ambition doesn't stop at sandboxes,

we want to build the best cloud for agents, completly top down

soon we’ll want to be building massive, efficient datacenters, all across Europe, for the most powerful agents across the world

this kind of ambition

last year, computers (for humans) sold for $1T worldwide, one fucking trillion per year

agents will need computers too, but at a multiple of that scale

computers in the cloud, always on, of many different kinds and shapes for a range of work never seen before

for most of that work, whether that cloud supports kubernetes, whether it's multi-tenant, where the datacenter lives, what the latency to load a page from its location is, how web primitives will work on it, all of that won't matter at all

because most of the work won't be so much about interacting with us, humans, at least not most of it

clouds of tomorrow won't be optimized for web hosting, or even AI training, they'll be optimized for already super-human agents to do work, simulate, engineer, predict, design, communicate, regulate...

we need this cloud of the future to operate at the largest scale, giving the most freedom and power to agents to be useful, and let's hope for us humans still on this planet, at the best cost/energy/space efficiency, so we don't suck out our entire world in the process, like crushing an ant colony with a bulldozer

and here is our opportunity at @asciidotdev :

on one hand, in Europe today, companies like Hetzner, OVH, Netcup, Scaleway, offer the cheapest, most efficient compute on Earth. this compute is almost ideal for agents in its shape:

hyper cheap VPSs, long lived, stateful, super affordable and efficient

but it's not scalable, and too hard to build agents on top off, with dinosaur era controls and ergonomics

it's because they've started with the datacenter, as operations businesses, from the ground up, and now they're too poor, too slow, and don't have the right talent, to even build the right software for agents on their own cloud, not even talking of massively scaling their offer

on the other hand, us, we've built box ( box.ascii.dev ), an AI sandbox on top of these efficient but barely usable European clouds, stripping all the friction they cause on the software side of things

box is way more focused, simple, and 5 to 25x less expensive than alternatives offered by big cloud

we managed to prove their is growing demand for that, that agents and builders of agents prefer efficiency, simplicity, honesty, over the big cloud mentality of overpricing, bloat, confusion, and total innefficiency compensated by massive evangelization campaigns

box is already put in prod by founders, CTOs, with real products and users, we're scaling with them atm

it builds up trust, for an infra product, trust builds on itself, currently our marketing effort is nearly nothing, just tweeting about the product and its traction, and it gets bigger and bigger every day

if we were to scale this by just 22x this year, which seems quite possible, we'll reach 1m ARR, by compounding more we'll be at 10m ARR in 1.5y, 100m ARR in 2.5y

at this point we'll make 90m in gross margins, and we'd be running 300k sandboxes at all times

this will require us, but also enable us, to start building our own datacenters, certainly in Europe for energy and cost efficiency, as it seems European cloud is consistently the cheaper and more efficient cloud in the Western world, with high standards and good enough freedom to operate (we probably can't do that in China for instance)

of course that's not our next step, the first step is to lock the tech down, scale to a larger usage, 3x to 4x our current usage, going down from the VPS to our own rented bare metal + qemu

then raise capital, hire the most cracked systems engineers, infra engineers, scale further, always going down the abstraction to be more efficient, building up our technical, operational ambition: rent entire racks, then owning some of the space at datacenters, install and managed our own racks, then finally, outscale everything, no one can help scale anymore or be cost efficient enough at scale, so we build our own

if we own this, and if we win, and this is infinitely important to win, we will dictate what comes next on scaling the cloud for agents:

grabbing all the land, covering the Earth with datacenters

or

find another way (space? unlikely to be efficient imo), keep optimizing, grinding the low level, using better sources of energy, inventing better chips

sky is the limit, but we must scale through efficiency, not let lazy people who just want 99.9x margins dictate how compute will scale in the world, otherwise we all lose
